Synopsis: Prohibiting a certain public service company from recovering through rates any costs associated with a supervisor's annual compensation once the compensation exceeds 110% of the maximum annual salary payable to the chair of the Commission for the same calendar year; requiring the Public Service Commission to publish guidance defining "reasonable cost limitations"; requiring each public service company to send a copy of the policy adopted under the Act to the Commission at certain times;  etc.
Title: Investor-Owned Electric, Gas, and Gas and Electric Companies - Cost Recovery - Limitations
Status: In the Senate - First Reading Education, Energy, and the Environment

NarrowSubjects.Name: Salaries and Compensation -see also- Overtime; Reimb. Rates
Utilities -see also- Recycl; Refuse; Sewage; Teleph; Water

bill_summary: This bill prohibits investor-owned electric and gas companies from recovering supervisor compensation costs through rates if the compensation exceeds 110% of the Public Service Commission (PSC) chair's annual salary. It also requires these utilities to adopt board-approved policies to limit rate-recovered expenditures for entertainment, office renovations, travel, and other non-operational activities, following specific guidance published by the PSC.
stakeholders: Investor-owned electric and gas companies, utility supervisors, and utility ratepayers including state and local governments and small businesses.
fiscal_impact_summary: State and local utility expenditures may decrease, or future rate increases may be minimized, due to the new prohibitions and limitations on cost recovery through rates. While the specific fiscal impact cannot be reliably estimated at this time, the bill's regulatory requirements are expected to be absorbed within the existing budgeted resources of the Public Service Commission.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill directly mandates the Public Service Commission (PSC) to publish guidance defining 'reasonable cost limitations' for utility expenditures and to receive and review cost-limitation policies from investor-owned utilities.

As the advocate for residential utility consumers, the Office of the People's Counsel is significantly impacted by changes to utility rate-making laws and will likely monitor compliance with these cost-recovery limitations during rate cases.

The Maryland Energy Administration (MEA) advises the Governor on energy policy and coordinates planning; this bill's changes to utility cost recovery and rate structures directly align with the agency's policy oversight role.

As the primary operational support agency and central procurement authority for the state, the Department of General Services (DGS) manages state utility expenditures, which the fiscal note suggests may decrease as a result of this bill.
The Department of Budget and Management (DBM) oversees state budget execution and fiscal planning; it is impacted by the potential decrease in state utility expenditures mentioned in the fiscal note.

The Office of the Attorney General provides legal counsel to the state and its agencies, including the Public Service Commission, and may be involved in legal interpretations or defenses of the bill's new regulatory limitations.
The Office of Legislative Audits may be responsible for auditing the Public Service Commission's adherence to the bill's requirements during periodic performance or fiscal compliance reviews.

The Office of Administrative Hearings (OAH) provides impartial hearings for contested cases involving state agencies; it may be required to adjudicate disputes regarding the PSC's enforcement of the bill's cost-limitation provisions.

Synopsis: Increasing, from $15,000 to $20,000, the amount allowed as a subtraction modification under the Maryland income tax for retirement income attributable to an individual's employment as a public safety employee; and applying the Act to all taxable years beginning after December 31, 2025.
Title: Subtraction Modification - Public Safety Retirement Income
Status: In the House - Hearing 1/20 at 1:00 p.m.

Emergency Services -see also- Ambul; Emergencies; etc.
Law Enforcement -see also- SRO; Sheriffs; State Police
Rescue Squads -see also- Emergency Medical Serv

bill_summary: This bill increases the maximum Maryland income tax subtraction modification for retirement income received by retired public safety employees—including law enforcement officers, correctional officers, and fire, rescue, or emergency services personnel—from $15,000 to $20,000, provided the individual is at least 55 years old.
stakeholders: Retired public safety employees (including law enforcement, correctional officers, and fire/rescue/emergency personnel) who are at least 55 years of age.
fiscal_impact_summary: State general fund revenues are estimated to decrease by 1,600,000 in FY 2027, while local income tax revenues are projected to decrease by 1,300,000. These revenue losses are expected to increase slightly each year through FY 2031 as the number of eligible retirees and subtraction amounts grow. The Comptroller's Office can implement the changes using existing resources.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: As the state's chief tax collector, the Comptroller is responsible for implementing the income tax subtraction modification, updating tax forms, and managing the resulting reduction in state and local income tax revenues.

The agency administers the retirement and pension systems for state employees, including law enforcement and correctional officers. It is responsible for providing the income data and documentation that retirees use to claim this subtraction modification.
As the principal fiscal agency, DBM must account for the estimated $1.6 million to $1.8 million annual decrease in General Fund revenues in the state budget and long-term fiscal planning.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Department of Public Safety and Correctional Services
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: This agency is the primary employer of correctional officers and many law enforcement officers in Maryland, the groups directly benefiting from the increased retirement income tax subtraction.
The bill's definition of 'correctional officer' specifically includes individuals employed in juvenile facilities, which are managed by DJS.
As the primary state law enforcement agency, the bill directly impacts the retirement benefits and tax liability of its former employees.
The Governor's Office oversees the executive branch and proposes the annual state budget, which will be affected by the recurring reduction in income tax revenue.
DNR employs Natural Resources Police who qualify as law enforcement officers eligible for the public safety retirement subtraction modification.
MDOT oversees the Maryland Transportation Authority (MDTA) Police, whose retirees qualify as law enforcement officers under the bill.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Maryland Institute for Emergency Medical Services Systems
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: MIEMSS regulates and oversees the state's emergency medical services network, including the technicians and paramedics defined as 'emergency services personnel' in the bill.

Synopsis: Exempting spouses and financially dependent children of State or local public safety employees who die as a result of or in the course of performance of duties from paying out-of-state or out-of-county tuition at a public institution of higher education in the State; and altering the method for allocating funds for the Edward T. and Mary A. Conroy Memorial Scholarship Program and the Jean B. Cryor Memorial Scholarship Program.
Title: Higher Education - Student Financial Assistance - Dependents of State or Local Public Safety Employees (Maryland Fallen Heroes Tuition Benefits Act)
Status: Approved by the Governor - Chapter 798

NarrowSubjects.Name: Death -see also- Homicide; Murder; Wrongful Death
Higher Education -see also- Comm Colleges; Med Schools; etc.

bill_summary: The bill exempts spouses and financially dependent children of Maryland public safety employees who died in the line of duty from paying out-of-state or out-of-county tuition at public institutions of higher education. It also restructures the Edward T. and Mary A. Conroy Memorial Scholarship Program and the Jean B. Cryor Memorial Scholarship Program by shifting from an entitlement-based system to a budget-capped system. The Maryland Higher Education Commission is required to develop a formula for allocating scholarship funds, and renewal applicants are given priority over new applicants.
stakeholders: Spouses and financially dependent children of deceased Maryland public safety employees, current and future scholarship recipients under the Conroy and Cryor programs, and Maryland public postsecondary institutions.
fiscal_impact_summary: The bill is expected to cause a significant decrease in State general fund expenditures by eliminating the entitlement aspect of the Conroy and Cryor scholarship programs and capping total awards to the amount provided in the State budget. For context, while FY 2025 scholarship expenditures were approximately 9500000, the FY 2027 budget is set at 7000000, and the statutory minimum mandate is 4000000. Consequently, higher education revenues and expenditures at public colleges and community colleges will decrease as fewer or smaller awards are distributed. The tuition exemption for nonresident dependents of fallen public safety employees is expected to have a minimal fiscal impact due to the small number of eligible individuals.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Governor's Office oversees the executive branch and proposes the state budget, which includes the mandated minimum appropriation for the Edward T. and Mary A. Conroy and Jean B. Cryor Scholarship Fund and influences funding for the tuition exemptions.
The bill explicitly requires the Comptroller to account for the Edward T. Conroy and Jean B. Cryor Scholarship Fund.
The bill explicitly requires the State Treasurer to hold the Edward T. Conroy and Jean B. Cryor Scholarship Fund and receive deposits for the program.

The OAG provides legal counsel to the Maryland Higher Education Commission (MHEC) and state higher education institutions regarding the implementation of new tuition exemptions and regulatory changes.
DBM is responsible for the state budget and fiscal planning; the bill changes scholarship funding from an entitlement to a budget-capped program and mandates specific minimum budget appropriations.

The bill and related scholarship programs provide financial assistance to disabled public safety employees and their dependents, aligning with the department's focus on service delivery to residents with disabilities.
The Jean B. Cryor Memorial Scholarship Program specifically provides financial assistance to the dependents of school employees killed or disabled in the line of duty.
The definition of 'State or local public safety employee' includes law enforcement officers, such as the Natural Resources Police, whose dependents are eligible for the benefits.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Department of Public Safety and Correctional Services
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill's benefits apply to correctional officers and law enforcement officers, who are primarily employed or overseen by DPSCS.
The bill affects law enforcement officers within MDOT's modal administrations (e.g., MDTA Police) whose dependents are eligible for the tuition exemptions and scholarships.
The Edward T. and Mary A. Conroy Memorial Scholarship Program provides significant benefits to veterans and the survivors of military service members.
The bill specifically includes members of the Maryland National Guard in the definition of public safety employees eligible for scholarship and tuition benefits for their survivors.
MHEC is the primary agency responsible for administering the scholarship programs, developing the new allocation formula, and adopting implementing regulations.
As the primary state law enforcement agency, its employees are key subjects of the bill, and their survivors are eligible for the Maryland Fallen Heroes Tuition Benefits.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Governor's Office of Crime Prevention and Policy
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: GOCPP coordinates public safety strategies and tracks law enforcement officer fatalities, which determines eligibility for the benefits established in this bill.

The Board of Public Works oversees significant state fiscal integrity, including the management of funds and contracts related to state higher education property and capital projects mentioned in the fiscal context.
MCSS, an independent unit within MSDE, is relevant as the bill addresses financial assistance for school employees who are victims of acts of violence in the line of duty.
Members of the Maryland National Guard are explicitly defined as public safety employees whose dependents may receive scholarship and tuition benefits under the bill.
As a public institution of higher education, MSU must implement the tuition exemptions and manage the distribution of scholarship funds to eligible students.
OLA conducts audits of state agencies and would be responsible for auditing MHEC's management of the scholarship fund and the new allocation formula.
As a public institution of higher education, SMCM must implement the out-of-state tuition exemptions and administer scholarship awards provided by the bill.
USM institutions are directly impacted by the tuition exemption requirements, and the scholarship award cap is benchmarked against USM resident undergraduate tuition rates.

Synopsis: Requiring that a motor vehicle be at least 25 years old in order to be eligible for registration as a historic motor vehicle; and requiring the Motor Vehicle Administration to reinstate, under certain circumstances, the historic motor vehicle registration of a motor vehicle that had its historic vehicle registration suspended or revoked as a result of the change to the definition of "historic motor vehicle" in Chapter 604 of 2025.
Title: Vehicle Laws – Historic Motor Vehicles – Minimum Age
Status: In the House - Hearing 2/27 at 1:30 p.m.

NarrowSubjects.Name: Age -see also- Age of Maj; Children; Elderly; Inf&Tod.; etc
Historical Matters -see also- Archives; Monumts; Museum; etc
Motor Vehicles -see also- Aband Veh; Ambulances; Buses; etc.

bill_summary: This bill changes the eligibility criteria for a vehicle to be registered as a historic motor vehicle from a model year of 1999 or earlier to a minimum age of at least 25 years. It also requires the Motor Vehicle Administration to reinstate certain historic registrations that were suspended or revoked due to previous law changes and ensures the new criteria apply prospectively.
stakeholders: Owners of motor vehicles at least 25 years old, the Motor Vehicle Administration, and special fund programs including the Maryland Emergency Medical System Operations Fund and the R Adams Cowley Shock Trauma Center.
fiscal_impact_summary: According to the Fiscal Note, State special fund revenues decrease by an estimated $1,800,000 in FY 2027, with the annual decrease growing to $7,900,000 by FY 2031. This impact is caused by more vehicles becoming eligible for historic registration, which carries lower fees and exemptions from the $40 emergency medical services surcharge and emissions inspection fees. Local fiscal impact is expected to be negligible.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The MVA is the primary agency responsible for vehicle registration and the Vehicle Emissions Inspection Program (VEIP). This bill directly modifies eligibility criteria for historic vehicle registrations, changes registration fees, and mandates that the MVA administratively reinstate specific registrations that were previously suspended or revoked.

As the parent department for the MVA, MDOT oversees the Transportation Trust Fund (TTF), which is the primary recipient of registration and VEIP fees. The bill is projected to cause a multi-million dollar annual decrease in TTF revenues and may impact the distribution of transportation grants to local jurisdictions.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Maryland Institute for Emergency Medical Services Systems
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: MIEMSS oversees the state's EMS network, which is significantly funded by the Maryland Emergency Medical System Operations Fund (MEMSOF). The fiscal note indicates that this bill will result in a substantial decrease in revenue for MEMSOF and the Maryland Trauma Physician Services Fund due to the loss of EMS surcharges on vehicles that transition to historic registration.

MDE is responsible for enforcing environmental laws regarding air quality, including the oversight of vehicle emissions. This bill expands the number of vehicles exempt from the Vehicle Emissions Inspection Program (VEIP) by easing the requirements for historic vehicle status.

DBM is responsible for state revenue estimation and fiscal planning. The bill has a notable fiscal impact, with total special fund revenues projected to decrease by nearly $8 million annually by fiscal 2031, affecting multiple state accounts and long-term fiscal planning.

Maryland State Police enforce motor vehicle and criminal laws on state highways. Changes to registration eligibility and the use restrictions associated with historic plates (such as prohibitions on daily commuting) fall under their broad mandate for traffic law enforcement.

Synopsis: Establishing the Maryland New Markets Development Program; requiring the Department of Housing and Community Development to administer the Program; authorizing a credit against the State insurance premium receipts tax and certain State insurance retaliatory taxes, fees, charges, and penalties for certain equity investments in certain community development entities; authorizing the Department to recapture a credit under certain circumstances; limiting the credit amounts that may be issued to $18,750,000 for any taxable year; etc.
Title: Community Development - Maryland New Markets Development Program - Establishment
Status: In the House - Hearing 2/12 at 1:00 p.m. (Economic Matters) and Hearing canceled (Ways and Means)

bill_summary: This bill establishes the Maryland New Markets Development Program within the Department of Housing and Community Development to encourage investment in low-income communities. It provides a nonrefundable tax credit against the state insurance premium receipts tax and insurance retaliatory taxes for businesses that make qualified equity investments in community development entities. The credit is equal to 50% of the purchase price of the investment and is claimed over a seven-year period, starting in the fourth year after the investment is made.
responsible_party: Maryland Department of Housing and Community Development
stakeholders: Qualified community development entities, insurance companies, and businesses located in low-income communities in Maryland.
fiscal_impact_summary: According to the Fiscal Note, the bill is expected to decrease general fund revenues by $2,300,000 annually starting in FY 2030 and FY 2031 as tax credits are claimed. The Department of Housing and Community Development is authorized to issue up to $9,375,000 in credit certificates per biennial application period, with an overall cap of $18,750,000 in any tax year. General fund expenditures will increase by approximately $94,709 in FY 2027 to hire a program manager for administration, with ongoing annual costs. Application fees of $5,000 per application will provide a minimal offset to these costs.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: As the primary implementing agency, the Department of Housing and Community Development (DHCD) is responsible for administering the Maryland New Markets Development Program, processing applications, jointly certifying qualified equity investments, issuing tax credit certificates, and managing compliance and credit recapture.

The bill establishes a tax credit against insurance premium receipts taxes and retaliatory taxes, which are regulated by the Maryland Insurance Administration. The agency is explicitly prohibited from imposing additional taxes on entities for claiming the credit and must honor advisory letters issued by the Department of Housing and Community Development.

The bill has a significant fiscal impact on the state's general fund and requires the creation of a new program manager position within DHCD. As the central agency for budget execution and personnel management, DBM is responsible for the oversight of these fiscal and staffing changes.

As the state's chief financial officer and principal tax collector, the Comptroller monitors state revenue impacts. This bill affects general fund revenues through the issuance of insurance tax credits and the collection of application fees.

The OAG provides legal counsel to DHCD and the Maryland Insurance Administration. It would likely assist in drafting the required regulations for the new program and providing legal support during recapture or enforcement proceedings.

The Maryland Tax Court serves as the highest level of administrative review for tax-related disputes, and could be called upon to adjudicate appeals regarding the final determination of these new insurance-related tax credits.

The bill provides for administrative actions such as the denial of applications and the issuance of recapture orders. Contested decisions by DHCD would likely be adjudicated by the Office of Administrative Hearings to ensure due process for the involved business entities.

The program's focus on stimulating investment in low-income community businesses aligns with the Innovation Team's specific mission to identify and pilot initiatives that reduce child poverty and enhance economic mobility in Maryland.

The Governor oversees the executive branch departments involved in this program, including DHCD and the Maryland Insurance Administration, and the bill impacts the state budget which the Governor is responsible for proposing.

While DHCD is the lead agency, this program is a major economic development initiative aimed at business expansion and job creation, which falls within the broad policy interests of the Department of Commerce.
OLA will be responsible for conducting future fiscal compliance and performance audits of the Maryland New Markets Development Program to ensure it is administered efficiently and according to law.

Synopsis: Requiring the Maryland Higher Education Commission to collect data regarding the parental status of students from each public institution of higher education; requiring public institutions of higher education to collect and report certain demographic data from students; requiring community colleges to adopt a certain plan for pregnant and parenting students; requiring the Commission to submit a report, by September 1, 2027, to certain committees of the General Assembly, that summarizes the data collected.
Title: Public Institutions of Higher Education - Pregnant and Parenting Students - Plan and Reporting
Status: Approved by the Governor - Chapter 735

bill_summary: This bill requires the Maryland Higher Education Commission (MHEC) to collect student-level data regarding the parental status of students from public institutions of higher education, excluding the University of Maryland Global Campus. It mandates that public institutions, including community colleges, adopt and post plans to support pregnant and parenting students by providing referrals to resources like childcare, healthcare providers, and government assistance programs. The bill also expands the definition of 'student data' to allow MHEC to share parental status information with the Maryland Longitudinal Data System.
stakeholders: Pregnant and parenting students, public senior higher education institutions, and Maryland community colleges.
fiscal_impact_summary: State general fund expenditures increase by $51,900 in FY 2027 for MHEC to hire a part-time staff specialist to manage data collection and reporting. Public four-year institutions and community colleges are expected to experience minimal cost increases to collect data and develop required support plans. There is a potential significant increase in general and federal fund expenditures for state assistance programs like Medicaid if institutional referrals lead to increased enrollment in those programs.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The agency is the primary regulatory body tasked by the bill to develop data collection questions, collect student-level parental status data from institutions, adopt implementing regulations, and submit annual summary reports to the General Assembly.

As the state's central coordinating board for postsecondary education, this agency is responsible for the bill's core mandates, including establishing a common format for reporting parental status data and ensuring public institutions comply with the new reporting and planning requirements.

The bill specifically alters the statutory definition of 'student data' to include parental status, authorizing this agency to collect and analyze this new data point from the Higher Education Commission to inform state policy.

The bill requires USM's public senior higher education institutions (with specific exceptions like UMGC) to collect demographic data on parental status and adopt comprehensive support plans for pregnant and parenting students.

As a public institution of higher education, Morgan State University is required to modify its demographic data collection forms and develop and post a plan to support pregnant and parenting students consistent with Title IX.
As an independent public honors college, the agency is mandated by the bill to collect and report parental status data and implement support plans for its pregnant and parenting student population.

The bill requires higher education institutions to provide referrals to health-related government programs administered by this agency, including Medicaid, MCHP, and WIC, which may lead to increased participation and administrative expenditures.

The fiscal note indicates a need for increased general fund expenditures for a new personnel position at the Maryland Higher Education Commission to implement the bill's data collection and reporting requirements.

Institutions must refer students to the Child Care Scholarship Program, which is managed by this department; additionally, the department coordinates with community colleges that are now required to adopt support plans under the bill.

This agency administers the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP), which is explicitly listed as a government assistance program to which institutions must provide referrals for parenting students.
The bill reinforces the rights of students to be free from pregnancy-based discrimination, a protection enforced by the Commission under state anti-discrimination laws.

The bill's focus on supporting parenting students and ensuring they have access to benefits like SNAP and child care directly aligns with this office's mission to reduce child poverty and support underinvested communities.

This agency determines eligibility for Medicaid and MCHP, programs specifically identified in the bill as resources that institutions must include in their required support plans for parenting students.

The bill's data-driven approach to supporting parenting students and enhancing their economic mobility mirrors this team's mission to pilot novel initiatives that reduce poverty and improve outcomes for Maryland families.

Synopsis: Authorizing the State Board of Examiners for Audiologists, Hearing Aid Dispensers, Speech-Language Pathologists, and Music Therapists to issue a limited license to practice music therapy; providing the purpose of the limited license is to permit an individual to practice music therapy while completing certain licensing requirements; and allowing a licensee with a limited license to practice music therapy under the supervision of a fully licensed music therapist.
Title: State Board of Examiners for Audiologists, Hearing Aid Dispensers, Speech-Language Pathologists, and Music Therapists - Authority to Issue Limited Licenses to Practice Music Therapy
Status: Approved by the Governor - Chapter 30
