Death -see also- Homicide; Murder; Wrongful Death

bill_summary: This constitutional amendment proposes to change the selection process for Maryland circuit court judges by eliminating contested elections. Under the bill, judges would be appointed by the Governor with the advice and consent of the Senate, followed by non-contested retention elections where voters decide whether to keep the judge in office. The bill also reduces the term of office for circuit court judges from 15 to 10 years.
responsible_party: Maryland Governor, Maryland State Senate, and the Maryland State Board of Elections
stakeholders: Current and future circuit court judges, judicial candidates, the Governor, the State Senate, and Maryland voters
fiscal_impact_summary: The Fiscal Note indicates that the bill does not affect State or local finances.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill grants the Governor the power to appoint circuit court judges with Senate advice and consent, shifting selection from contested elections to an executive appointment model.
This office is responsible for recruiting and vetting judicial candidates for the Governor, a task that will expand significantly with the inclusion of circuit court judges.
As the administrative lead for the Judicial Branch, the AOC is directly impacted by changes to the tenure, selection process, and retention requirements for judges within the circuit court system.
The agency is responsible for managing the constitutional referendum and the new non-contested retention election format for circuit court judges.
The OAG provides legal counsel to the Governor and the Judiciary regarding constitutional amendments and the implementation of changes to the judicial selection process.
Altering the term of office for circuit court judges from 15 years to 10 years has direct administrative implications for the judicial pension and retirement system managed by this agency.

Synopsis: Requiring 3% of the sales and use tax revenue collected from the sale of cannabis to be distributed to the Maryland Veterans Trust Fund.
Title: Sales and Use Tax - Distribution of Cannabis Sales Tax Revenue - Maryland Veterans Trust Fund
Status: In the House - Hearing 1/29 at 1:00 p.m.
bill_summary: The bill mandates that 3% of cannabis sales and use tax revenue, previously distributed to the State's General Fund, be redirected to the Maryland Veterans Trust Fund. The fund provides assistance to veterans, members of the Maryland National Guard, and their families through grants and loans.
responsible_party: Comptroller and the Maryland Department of Veterans and Military Families
stakeholders: Maryland veterans, members of the Maryland National Guard, their families, and public and private veteran support programs.
fiscal_impact_summary: According to the Fiscal Note, State general fund revenues will decrease by an estimated 4095000 in FY 2027, with nonbudgeted revenues and expenditures for the Maryland Veterans Trust Fund increasing by the same amount. By FY 2031, this redistribution is projected to reach 6222500. The Department of Veterans and Military Families will experience increased administrative workloads, requiring approximately four additional staff members to manage the expanded grant and loan program.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill explicitly requires the Comptroller to quarterly distribute a portion of the cannabis sales and use tax revenue to the Maryland Veterans Trust Fund.

The agency staffs the Maryland Veterans Trust and administers the Maryland Veterans Trust Fund, which will receive increased funding under this bill. The fiscal note indicates a significant increase in administrative workload and the need for additional staff within the department.

The bill redistributes revenue from the General Fund to a nonbudgeted fund, impacting state revenue and the budget execution oversight provided by DBM. It also has implications for state personnel, as the Department of Veterans and Military Families will likely require additional staff to manage the funds.

The Treasurer is responsible for the management and investment of state funds. As the bill increases revenues for the Maryland Veterans Trust Fund, the Treasurer's office would be involved in managing and protecting these funds.

The bill adjusts the distribution of sales and use tax revenue derived from cannabis sales, which is the industry regulated and overseen by the MCA. The MCA's own funding is also derived from the same tax distribution statute modified by the bill.

The Maryland Veterans Trust Fund is specifically established to provide monetary and other assistance to members of the Maryland National Guard and their families, making them direct beneficiaries of the bill's funding.

The Governor's Office oversees the executive branch agencies involved and is responsible for proposing the state budget, which is impacted by the redistribution of tax revenue away from the General Fund.

As the head of the Maryland Military Department and senior advisor on National Guard matters, the Adjutant General is relevant because the bill provides increased support for Maryland National Guard members and their families.

Synopsis: Providing that consumer wire transfers involving electronic funds transfers made ancillary to bank-to-bank transfers via a wire service are subject to certain provisions of the federal Electronic Funds Transfer Act of 1978.
Title: Consumer Protection - Electronic Funds Transfers - Regulations (Elder Fraud Prevention Act of 2026)
Status: In the House - Hearing 2/10 at 1:00 p.m.

NarrowSubjects.Name: Financial Institutions -see also- Banks; Credit Unions; etc.

bill_summary: This bill establishes that consumer wire transfers involving electronic funds transfers (EFTs) made ancillary to bank-to-bank transfers via a wire service are subject to the federal Electronic Funds Transfer Act of 1978. It aims to extend consumer protections, such as liability limits for unauthorized transfers and mandated error resolution procedures, to these specific types of transactions.
responsible_party: The Maryland Department of Labor (Office of Financial Regulation) and the Office of the Attorney General (Consumer Protection Division)
stakeholders: Consumers in Maryland and financial institutions operating in the state, including depository institutions and money transmitters.
fiscal_impact_summary: According to the fiscal note, the bill does not materially affect Maryland State or local government operations or finances.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill directly impacts the regulatory framework for financial institutions operating in Maryland, which are overseen and licensed by the Office of Financial Regulation (OFR) within the Department of Labor. The OFR is responsible for ensuring these institutions comply with state and federal financial regulations.

The bill focuses on consumer protection and fraud prevention. The Office of the Attorney General (OAG) houses the Consumer Protection Division, which is responsible for enforcing state laws against unfair or deceptive trade practices and protecting residents from financial exploitation.

Entitled the 'Elder Fraud Prevention Act of 2026,' the bill's core objective is to protect older adults from financial exploitation. This directly aligns with the Department of Aging's mission to protect the rights and financial security of Maryland's older population.

Synopsis: Requiring a landlord to provide air-conditioning to residential rental units in apartment buildings with four or more individual dwelling units in a certain manner beginning June 1, 2026, for newly constructed residential rental units and beginning October 1, 2026, for residential rental units that undergo renovation that includes the replacement or substantial upgrade of electrical systems or heating systems; and applying the Act prospectively.
Title: Residential Rental Apartments - Air-Conditioning Requirement
Status: In the House - Third Reading Passed (90-30)
bill_summary: This bill requires landlords of apartment buildings with four or more units to provide air conditioning from June 1 through September 30 each year. The requirement applies to newly constructed units starting June 1, 2026, and to existing units that undergo renovations involving the replacement or substantial upgrade of electrical or heating systems starting October 1, 2026. Landlords must maintain a temperature of no more than 80 degrees Fahrenheit in all habitable spaces of the rental units.
responsible_party: Landlords and local government code enforcement agencies
stakeholders: Landlords, tenants in apartment buildings with four or more units, and local housing authorities
fiscal_impact_summary: State operations and finances are not expected to be materially affected. However, local government expenditures may increase significantly, particularly for jurisdictions that own or operate public housing (such as the Housing Authority of Baltimore City) that must comply with the air-conditioning requirements during new construction or major renovations. Small business landlords are also expected to experience a meaningful increase in expenditures for compliance.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: As the central support agency for the Maryland Judicial Branch, the AOC is highly relevant because the bill adds new habitability requirements for residential rentals to the Real Property Article. Disputes over these requirements, including rent escrow and habitability claims, are adjudicated through the state's court system.

The DHCD is the state's primary agency for ensuring access to safe and affordable housing. This bill directly regulates the health and safety standards (air-conditioning) of residential rental units, which falls within the department's mission and programs.

The OAG provides legal counsel to state agencies and enforces state laws regarding consumer protection. Landlord-tenant laws and habitability standards are often interpreted or enforced through the OAG's consumer and civil rights frameworks.

The Department of Aging is dedicated to protecting the rights and quality of life for older adults. Regulation of indoor temperatures is a critical health and safety concern for the elderly population residing in multi-unit apartment buildings.

This department ensures that policies are inclusive and promote safe community living. Many individuals with disabilities are highly sensitive to heat, making state-mandated air-conditioning requirements a significant interest for this agency.

The Commission enforces anti-discrimination laws in housing. Changes to habitability standards under the Real Property Article can intersect with civil rights protections regarding safe and equitable housing conditions.
As the head of the executive branch, the Governor oversees the agencies responsible for housing policy and enforces state laws. The Governor must also sign the legislation into law.

DBM oversees state budget execution and fiscal planning. While the fiscal note indicates no material impact on state finances, DBM monitors all legislation with potential local or small business mandates for broader economic impact.

The fiscal note identifies a 'meaningful' impact on small businesses, specifically landlords. The Department of Commerce is the state's primary agency for supporting businesses and monitoring regulations that affect the economic viability of small business owners.

Synopsis: Establishing enhanced requirements under the Open Meetings Act for county boards of education and the Baltimore City Board of School Commissioners; requiring county boards and the Baltimore City Board of School Commissioners to maintain on their respective websites an archived video recording of each open meeting for which live video streaming was made available for a minimum of 5 years after the meeting; authorizing county boards and the Baltimore City Board of School Commissioners to edit certain content from the recordings; etc.
Title: Open Meetings Act - County Boards of Education - Enhanced Requirements (Local Boards of Education Transparency Act)
Status: In the Senate - Special Order until later today (Senator Feldman) Adopted

NarrowSubjects.Name: Counties -see also- Chartered Counties; Code Counties; etc.
Obscenity -see also- Nudity & Sexual Displays; Pornography

bill_summary: This bill establishes enhanced transparency requirements for county boards of education and the Baltimore City Board of School Commissioners under the Open Meetings Act. It requires these boards to post meeting agendas, minutes, and live video streams of open sessions on their websites, maintain archived recordings for five years, and provide advance notice and materials for upcoming meetings.
responsible_party: County boards of education and the Baltimore City Board of School Commissioners
stakeholders: County boards of education, the Baltimore City Board of School Commissioners, and the public
fiscal_impact_summary: The bill has no impact on State finances. Local boards of education may incur minimal costs to expand digital storage or contract with third-party providers to meet the five-year video retention requirement, but these expenses are expected to be absorbed within existing resources. Local revenues are not affected.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill, known as the Local Boards of Education Transparency Act, imposes new transparency and open meeting requirements on all county boards of education and the Baltimore City Board of School Commissioners. As the state agency responsible for the oversight and leadership of Maryland's public education system, MSDE is highly relevant to the governance and policy changes affecting local school boards.

The Office of the Attorney General provides legal counsel to state agencies on the Open Meetings Act and houses the State Open Meetings Law Compliance Board. The bill specifically requires local boards of education to notify the Compliance Board if they edit archived video recordings, and OAG is responsible for the administrative support and oversight of this regulatory function.

The bill renumbers specific sections of the General Provisions Article that mandate the Department of Information Technology provide technical staff, support, and equipment for livestreaming open meetings for certain state agencies. While the bill does not expand this mandate to include local school boards, it modifies the statutory language governing DoIT's existing responsibilities in this area.

The bill references the Maryland Department of Transportation in the context of its existing requirement to provide video recordings of Vision Zero coordinator meetings. The bill renumbers the specific subsection (3-307(H)) that defines this requirement.

Synopsis: Requiring the Maryland Police Training and Standards Commission to develop a model policy prohibiting the use of a face covering in the performance of duty; requiring a law enforcement agency to adopt a policy consistent with the model policy developed by the Commission; and prohibiting a certain law enforcement officer from wearing a certain face covering while in the performance of duty in the State, except when actively engaged in an undercover operation.
Title: Public Safety - Law Enforcement Officers - Prohibition on Face Coverings
Status: In the House - Hearing 2/24 at 1:00 p.m.

NarrowSubjects.Name: Crimes and Punishments -see also- Penalties and Sentnc; etc.
Law Enforcement -see also- SRO; Sheriffs; State Police
Penalties and Sentences -see also- Death Penalty
Police Conduct -see also- Ethics; Law Enforcement

bill_summary: This bill requires the Maryland Police Training and Standards Commission to develop a model policy prohibiting law enforcement officers from wearing face coverings like balaclavas or ski masks while on duty, with exceptions for undercover operations, medical necessity, religious garments, and tactical safety. Law enforcement agencies must adopt policies consistent with this model. Violations of the prohibition are classified as a misdemeanor and police misconduct, carrying penalties of up to two years' imprisonment and a $2,000 fine, as well as the waiver of civil immunity.
responsible_party: Maryland Police Training and Standards Commission
stakeholders: Maryland law enforcement officers, law enforcement agencies, and the general public
fiscal_impact_summary: The fiscal note indicates that the bill is not anticipated to materially affect state or local operations or finances. While a misdemeanor fine of up to $2,000 is established for violations, no specific revenue or expenditure estimates are provided by the Department of Legislative Services.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Department of Public Safety and Correctional Services
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill mandates that the Maryland Police Training and Standards Commission (MPTSC), which is a unit within this department, develop the model policy prohibiting face coverings and training standards for law enforcement agencies across the state.
As the state's primary law enforcement agency, its sworn members are directly subject to the prohibition on face coverings, and the agency must adopt a policy consistent with the new state model.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Governor's Office of Crime Prevention and Policy
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: This office coordinates state public safety strategies and advises the Governor on criminal justice policies, making it a key stakeholder in the implementation and oversight of law enforcement conduct standards.
The department employs the Maryland Natural Resources Police, who are sworn law enforcement officers subject to the bill's restrictions on face coverings and policy requirements.

The department oversees several law enforcement units, most notably the Maryland Transportation Authority (MDTA) Police, which must comply with the face covering prohibition and adopt the required policy.
This department manages the Maryland Capitol Police, a sworn law enforcement agency that must adopt the model policy and ensure its officers comply with the face covering prohibition.
Many USM member institutions maintain sworn police departments that will be required to adopt the model policy and comply with the bill's restrictions on officer appearance.
The university operates its own sworn police department, which is explicitly subject to the bill's requirements to adopt a policy and prohibit face coverings for its officers.
The OAG provides legal counsel to the MPTSC and other state agencies on the development of the model policy and the legal implications of the new misdemeanor and civil immunity waivers.
The judicial branch utilizes security and law enforcement personnel who may be impacted by these standards, and the agency was identified as a stakeholder in the fiscal analysis.
The Comptroller's office employs sworn agents within its Field Enforcement Division to enforce tax and regulatory laws, making them subject to the bill's provisions.
The department employs security and law enforcement personnel at state-operated health facilities who must comply with the new appearance standards and agency policies.
This agency coordinates standards for school safety personnel, many of whom are sworn law enforcement officers who would be subject to the bill's face covering restrictions.
As a state agency with its own public safety and police functions, the college must ensure its officers comply with the bill's mandates and adopt the required policy.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Maryland Office of the Public Defender
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill creates a new criminal misdemeanor for law enforcement officers, and the OPD would be responsible for representing indigent defendants in these cases.
The agency involves enforcement and compliance personnel who may include sworn law enforcement officers subject to state conduct and appearance standards.
The department regulates various industries and employs investigators; it was consulted as a relevant agency for the bill's fiscal note regarding law enforcement standards.
MSDE houses the Maryland Center for School Safety and oversees school-based policing standards, making the bill relevant to its safety and security policy framework.
As the head of the executive branch, the Governor oversees the agencies and commissions (like MPTSC) responsible for implementing these new standards of police accountability.

Synopsis: Authorizing unaffiliated voters to request to affiliate with a political party at an early voting center before a primary election or at a precinct polling place on a primary election day and vote a provisional ballot for the voter's preferred political party; requiring an election judge to determine if the voter resides in a certain county; applying the Act to all elections beginning with the statewide primary election in 2028; and prohibiting the application of the Act to any special elections held before the 2028 primary.
Title: Election Law - Affiliating With a Party and Voting - Unaffiliated Voters
Status: In the Senate - First Reading Education, Energy, and the Environment

NarrowSubjects.Name: Health -see also- COVID19; EnvHlth; MedCon; etc.
Voting -see also- Absentee and Mail-In Voting

bill_summary: This bill allows voters who are currently unaffiliated with a political party to change their registration to a political party during early voting or on the day of a primary election. Once the change is requested at a polling place or early voting center, the voter is issued a provisional ballot for their newly selected party.
stakeholders: Unaffiliated registered voters in Maryland
fiscal_impact_summary: State and local expenditures are expected to increase by an indeterminate amount beginning in years with primary elections. According to an illustrative estimate in the Fiscal Note, total costs could reach approximately 180000, consisting of 66000 in State general fund expenditures and 114000 in local government expenditures. These costs cover additional paper ballots, provisional ballot election judges, voter education, and administrative revisions.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Maryland State Board of Elections is the primary agency responsible for implementing the bill's provisions, including adopting regulations and procedures for party affiliation changes at early voting centers and polling places, and overseeing the issuance and counting of provisional ballots.

The bill references the Motor Vehicle Administration as a method for notifying changes in party affiliation. Additionally, the MVA's integrated voter registration systems may require updates to accommodate the change in processing party affiliations for unaffiliated voters.

The fiscal note indicates a notable increase in general fund expenditures for the state's share of additional ballots, election judges, and voter education, which falls under DBM's oversight of the state budget.

The Office of the Attorney General serves as the legal counsel to the State Board of Elections and will be responsible for reviewing the new regulations and ensuring the implementation of the bill complies with existing state and federal election laws.

The Governor's Office oversees the executive branch and the State Board of Elections. The office is also responsible for proposing the state budget, which must account for the increased expenditures identified in the fiscal note.
As the parent agency of the Motor Vehicle Administration, MDOT is indirectly impacted by any systems changes or registration coordination requirements mentioned in the bill.

Synopsis: Applying certain campaign finance requirements for a political committee to exploratory committees; establishing requirements and prohibitions for exploratory committees relating to the establishment of the committees, receipt of funds, and permissible disbursements; requiring an authorized candidate campaign committee that results from the exploratory committee to make any equipment purchases from the exploratory committee at the fair market value of the equipment; etc.
Title: Election Law - Campaign Finance - Exploratory Committees
Status: In the House - Hearing 2/04 at 2:00 p.m.

NarrowSubjects.Name: Equipment -see also- Charging; Med. Equip.; MV Equip; etc.
Health -see also- COVID19; EnvHlth; MedCon; etc.
Work, Labor, and Employment -see also- JobTrn; Leave; etc.

bill_summary: This bill establishes and regulates exploratory committees in Maryland for potential candidates to determine their viability for public office. It subjects these committees to the same campaign finance requirements as political committees, with the exception that donations to exploratory committees are not subject to contribution limits. The bill specifies permissible disbursements, such as polling, staff, and office space, and requires that remaining funds be returned to donors or distributed to specific entities like political parties or the Fair Campaign Financing Fund within 120 days of the candidate filing or declining to run.
stakeholders: Potential candidates for public office, political campaign contributors, and the State Board of Elections
fiscal_impact_summary: The State Board of Elections can implement the bill's requirements using existing resources. State special fund revenues for the Fair Campaign Financing Fund may increase annually starting as early as fiscal year 2026 due to the collection of late filing fees or monetary penalties from exploratory committees. Local government finances are not expected to be materially affected.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The State Board of Elections is the primary agency responsible for administering and supervising Maryland's election laws and campaign finance systems. This bill directly amends Title 13 of the Election Law Article, which the Board oversees, and requires them to manage the registration and regulation of exploratory committees.

The Office of the State Prosecutor is responsible for investigating and prosecuting criminal offenses related to the integrity of the electoral process and enforcement of state election laws. This bill expands the scope of campaign finance regulations to include exploratory committees, which fall under the Prosecutor's enforcement jurisdiction.

The Office of the Attorney General provides legal counsel to the State Board of Elections and handles legal interpretations of election law. The fiscal note explicitly mentions that the OAG has previously provided guidance on the legality of exploratory committees under current law.

The State Treasurer's Office is responsible for managing and protecting state funds, including the Fair Campaign Financing Fund. The fiscal note indicates that revenues for this specific fund may increase due to late fees and penalties collected from exploratory committees.

Synopsis: Establishing the Maternal Health Monitoring Pilot Program in the Maryland Department of Health to support pregnant and postpartum Maryland Medical Assistance Program recipients who have higher risks of pregnancy complications because of maternal hypertension or maternal diabetes; requiring the Department to select at least one managed care organization to administer the Program; requiring the managed care organizations to contract with a technology vendor to offer remote patient monitoring services to participants; etc.
Title: Maryland Medical Assistance Program - Maternal Health Monitoring Pilot Program
Status: In the House - Unfavorable Report by Health; Withdrawn

bill_summary: This bill establishes the Maternal Health Monitoring Pilot Program within the Maryland Department of Health to support pregnant and postpartum Medicaid recipients at high risk for complications due to maternal hypertension or diabetes. The pilot program utilizes remote patient monitoring technology to collect health data, which is reviewed by a clinical team including nurses and dietitians to provide health coaching and trigger medical escalations when necessary. The program operates through participating managed care organizations and contracted technology vendors from fiscal 2027 through 2028.
stakeholders: Pregnant and postpartum individuals enrolled in the Maryland Medical Assistance Program with diagnosed maternal hypertension or diabetes; participating Medicaid managed care organizations (MCOs); and health care technology vendors.
fiscal_impact_summary: State Medicaid expenditures are estimated to increase by $300,000 in fiscal 2027 and $300,000 in fiscal 2028 to support the pilot program, with an additional $86,000 in fiscal 2029 for program evaluation and reporting. The bill includes a mandated appropriation of $600,000 for fiscal 2028. Expenditures are expected to be funded 50% by State general funds and 50% by federal funds, with federal fund revenues increasing by $343,000 over the three-year period.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill establishes the Maternal Health Monitoring Pilot Program within the Maryland Department of Health (MDH). As the primary implementing agency, MDH is responsible for selecting managed care organizations, overseeing technology vendors, paying participant fees, ensuring geographic diversity, and submitting a final report on health outcomes and recommendations.

The bill mandates that the Governor include a $600,000 appropriation in the annual budget bill for fiscal year 2028. Additionally, the Department of Health is required to submit a report of its findings and recommendations to the Governor.

DBM is responsible for developing the state's budget and supervising budget execution. Since the bill includes a mandated appropriation for FY 2028 and involves significant fiscal impacts on the Medicaid program, DBM will be responsible for overseeing the allocation and use of these funds.

The OAG provides legal counsel to the Department of Health. They would likely be involved in reviewing the contracts with Managed Care Organizations (MCOs) and advising on the implementation of the pilot program, including potential 1115(a) demonstration waiver applications.

The Board of Public Works oversees significant state expenditures and procurement contracts. The selection and payment of participating Managed Care Organizations (MCOs) to administer the pilot program may require BPW approval depending on the contract structures used.

The MHCC is responsible for planning for health system needs and improving access to care. The pilot program's focus on maternal and neonatal outcomes, and the requirement for data-driven reporting (including claims and electronic health records), aligns with the commission's role in health system monitoring.

The pilot program specifically aims to improve fetal and neonatal outcomes, such as reducing fetal mortality and preterm births. These goals align with the GOC's mission to promote the well-being of Maryland's children.

GOPI utilizes data-driven strategies and performance metrics to oversee state agency activities. The bill requires a comprehensive evaluation and report on specific health metrics (morbidity, mortality, hospital stays) which falls under GOPI's mandate for enhancing government responsiveness and delivering measurable results.

The report required by the bill must include data on hospital readmissions, ICU admissions, and lengths of hospital stays. The HSCRC, which regulates hospital rates and monitors quality and population health outcomes, has a direct interest in these metrics.

Synopsis: Altering the prohibition against taking and breaking open a letter; providing that a person may not knowingly and intentionally open mail addressed to another without permission of the person or an authorized designee; providing certain penalties for violations of the Act; prohibiting the theft of mail under certain circumstances; prohibiting a person from possessing an arrow key under certain circumstances; and providing for concurrent jurisdiction in the District Court and circuit court to try a violation of the Act.
Title: Mail Theft
Status: In the Senate - First Reading Judicial Proceedings

NarrowSubjects.Name: Crimes and Punishments -see also- Penalties and Sentnc; etc.
Penalties and Sentences -see also- Death Penalty

bill_summary: This bill creates specific criminal offenses and graduated penalties for the theft of mail based on the number of items stolen. It also prohibits the unauthorized opening of mail, the theft of mail using an 'arrow key' (a specialized key used by postal and delivery services), and the possession of an arrow key with intent to commit a crime. Additionally, the bill establishes concurrent jurisdiction between the District Court and circuit courts for these offenses.
responsible_party: Maryland Judiciary, Department of Public Safety and Correctional Services, and the Office of the Public Defender
stakeholders: Maryland residents and mail recipients, the U.S. Postal Service, common carrier delivery services, law enforcement, and individuals prosecuted for mail-related offenses.
fiscal_impact_summary: According to the Fiscal Note, the bill is not expected to materially affect State or local finances or operations. While the bill establishes new criminal penalties and fines, the fiscal impact on the Office of the Public Defender and the court system is anticipated to be minimal and absorbable within existing budgeted resources.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill directly alters the criminal jurisdiction of the District Court and circuit courts under the Courts and Judicial Proceedings Article to accommodate new felony mail theft and arrow key offenses, which requires operational coordination from the AOC.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Maryland Office of the Public Defender
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The fiscal note explicitly mentions an increase in workload for the Office of the Public Defender, as the agency will be responsible for representing indigent defendants charged with the newly created misdemeanor and felony offenses.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Department of Public Safety and Correctional Services
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The creation of new felony offenses with sentences of up to five years of imprisonment directly impacts the state's correctional facilities and the Division of Parole and Probation, which are managed by DPSCS.

As the primary state law enforcement agency, the Maryland State Police are responsible for enforcing new criminal statutes and investigating violations related to theft and the possession of burglary-related tools like arrow keys.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Governor's Office of Crime Prevention and Policy
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: GOCPP coordinates state public safety strategies and advises the Governor on criminal justice policy, making the establishment of new criminal classifications for mail theft highly relevant to their mission.
The OAG provides legal counsel to the state on the enforcement of criminal laws and represents the state in civil or criminal appeals resulting from the application of this new legislation.
DJS may be responsible for youth who are charged under these new criminal provisions, necessitating adjustments to juvenile assessment and rehabilitative programming.
The Governor's Office oversees the executive branch agencies responsible for enforcing this law and coordinates the policy initiatives that led to its introduction.

Synopsis: Prohibiting a State entity or a political subdivision of the State from assigning a Confederate name to real property owned by the State or political subdivision; and defining "Confederate name" as any name that commemorates or references any aspect of the states in rebellion, operating as the Confederate States of America, from 1861 to 1865 or any person or entity that serviced voluntarily with or on behalf of the Confederate States of America in any military or civilian capacity.
Title: State and Local Government - Real Property - Confederate Naming Prohibited
Status: In the Senate - Hearing 4/02 at 1:00 p.m.

NarrowSubjects.Name: Counties -see also- Chartered Counties; Code Counties; etc.
Forests and Parks -see also- MdNatlCapPkPlnCm; Plants; etc.

Maryland-National Capital Park and Planning Commission
Public Buildings and Facilities -see also- Stadiums; St Hse

bill_summary: This bill prohibits Maryland State entities and political subdivisions from assigning a Confederate name to any real property owned by the State or local government, including streets, buildings, parks, and subdivisions. The prohibition is prospective, meaning it only applies to property named after the bill's effective date and does not require the renaming of existing property.
responsible_party: State entities in the executive, legislative, and judicial branches, and political subdivisions including counties, municipalities, school districts, and the Maryland-National Capital Park and Planning Commission.
stakeholders: State and local government agencies, Maryland residents, and users of public infrastructure such as schools, parks, and roads.
fiscal_impact_summary: According to the fiscal note, the bill is not anticipated to materially affect State or local government operations or finances. Because the requirements apply only to the naming of new property or future naming decisions and do not mandate the renaming of existing assets, there is no identified fiscal impact.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Department of General Services is the primary operational support agency for the state, responsible for the planning, design, and management of state-owned facilities. As the bill prohibits Confederate naming of State-owned buildings, DGS is the primary implementing agency for new facility naming conventions.

The Department of Transportation oversees the state's highways, bridges, and transit systems. Since the bill specifically includes 'streets' and 'buildings' within the definition of real property, MDOT's modal administrations (like SHA and MTA) are directly restricted in how they name new infrastructure.

The Department of Natural Resources manages over 500,000 acres of public lands, including state parks. The bill's definition of real property includes 'parks,' making DNR a primary agency affected by the prohibition when naming new conservation areas or park facilities.

The bill explicitly applies to all units in the Judicial branch. The Administrative Office of the Courts provides operational support for the Maryland Judicial Branch and would be responsible for ensuring compliance for any new judicial buildings or facilities.

The University System of Maryland manages a vast network of campuses and academic buildings. As a state entity, it must comply with the naming prohibition for all new real property across its 12 institutions.

The State Archives is the central depository for government records and historical research. It is identified as an information source for the bill and would likely be consulted to verify whether a proposed name commemorates a person or entity that served the Confederacy.

The Board of Public Works oversees and approves significant state expenditures, including the acquisition and naming of major state buildings and capital projects. It would serve as a high-level enforcement body for the bill's provisions during the procurement and project approval process.

The Maryland Stadium Authority plans, finances, and builds sports, entertainment, and educational facilities (including public schools). As a state agency involved in the construction of new real property, it is subject to the naming restrictions.

The MDTA manages toll bridges, tunnels, and roads. As an independent state agency that constructs and operates major transportation infrastructure, it must adhere to the prohibition on Confederate names for new facilities.

The bill's definition of 'political subdivision' includes 'school districts.' While naming is often a local board function, MSDE provides oversight and leadership for the state's public education system and facility construction standards.

The Department of Health manages numerous state-owned facilities, including hospitals and local health department buildings, and would be restricted from using Confederate names for any new real property acquisitions.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Department of Public Safety and Correctional Services
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: DPSCS oversees state correctional facilities and pretrial detention centers. Any new facilities or buildings within its jurisdiction would be subject to the bill's naming restrictions.

As a state agency and independent university with its own Board of Regents, Morgan State University would be prohibited from assigning Confederate names to any newly constructed or acquired real property on its campus.
As an independent unit of state government, the college is a 'State entity' under the bill and must comply with the naming restrictions for any new campus buildings or real property.

The Adjutant General oversees the Maryland Military Department, which manages armories and other military facilities. The bill's restrictions apply to any new real property assigned by this department.

The OAG provides legal counsel to all state agencies. It would be responsible for providing legal interpretations of what constitutes a 'Confederate name' or 'voluntary service' under the bill's definitions.

The Department of Planning oversees the Maryland Historical Trust and provides land use policy guidance. It may play a role in advising agencies and local governments on the historical context of names for new subdivisions or landmarks.
As the head of the Executive Branch, the Governor's Office oversees the agencies implementing this policy and ensures that new state real property is named in accordance with the law.

Synopsis: Authorizing the Mayor and City Council of Baltimore City or the governing body of a county or municipal corporation to grant, by law, a credit against the county or municipal corporation property tax on real property if use of the real property has been converted from a retail service station to other certain uses; prohibiting the application of the credit unless the underground storage tanks located on or formerly located on the real property have been permanently closed; and applying the Act to all taxable years after June 30, 2026.
Title: Property Tax Credit - Retail Service Station Conversions
Status: Approved by the Governor - Chapter 643

NarrowSubjects.Name: Counties -see also- Chartered Counties; Code Counties; etc.
Environmental Matters -see also- Conserv; Nat Resrce; Pollut
Laws and Ordinances -see also- Pub Local Laws; Uniform Laws

bill_summary: This bill authorizes local governments in Maryland, including Baltimore City and other counties or municipalities, to establish a property tax credit for properties converted from retail service stations to residential, retail, or mixed-use purposes. The credit is intended to help property owners cover the costs of removing underground storage tanks and remediating environmental contamination. Certain uses, such as discount stores, self-storage facilities, and businesses selling tobacco, electronic smoking devices, or alcoholic beverages, are excluded from the retail definitions for the credit.
responsible_party: Mayor and City Council of Baltimore City, or the governing body of a county or municipal corporation
stakeholders: Property owners of former retail service stations, local governments, and developers or small businesses involved in property conversion and environmental remediation.
fiscal_impact_summary: According to the Fiscal Note, the bill has no impact on State finances. Local property tax revenues may decrease beginning in fiscal 2027 if local governments choose to grant the property tax credit. The exact fiscal impact is indeterminate as it depends on the number of properties converted, their assessed value, local tax rates, and the specific duration and amount of the credits established by local jurisdictions. There are approximately 2,300 properties in the state currently classified as retail service stations.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill explicitly states that the tax credit may not be granted unless underground storage tanks have been permanently closed in accordance with regulations of the Department of the Environment. The agency is also the primary regulator for contamination remediation mentioned in the legislative intent.

As an independent agency providing review for property tax assessment disputes, the PTAAB would be responsible for hearing appeals related to the eligibility or valuation of this specific property tax credit if denied or contested at the local level.

The bill defines excluded 'retail uses' by referencing licenses for cigarettes, tobacco, and alcohol, all of which are industries regulated by the Comptroller. Additionally, the Comptroller oversees motor fuel industry regulations, which include the retail service stations being converted.

The Maryland Tax Court is the highest level of administrative review for tax-related disputes, including those involving property tax credits and assessments. Decisions from the local Property Tax Assessment Appeals Boards regarding this credit could be appealed here.

The bill encourages the conversion of retail service stations into residential or mixed-use properties. This aligns with the agency's mission to ensure access to affordable housing and support community revitalization projects.

The agency promotes sustainable growth and land use planning. The conversion of service stations (often brownfields) into retail or residential uses falls under land use management and regional revitalization strategies coordinated by this department.

The department is responsible for stimulating the economy and attracting businesses. This tax credit serves as an economic development tool to incentivize the reuse of properties and the expansion of retail or residential infrastructure.

The bill references 'Division II of the Alcoholic Beverages and Cannabis Article' to define exclusions for alcoholic beverage license holders. While its primary mission is cannabis regulation, the bill's definitions are tied to the administrative article the MCA operates under.

The Governor oversees the executive branch and signs the bill into law. The bill's focus on environmental remediation and economic mobility aligns with executive policy priorities often managed by the Governor's office.

Synopsis: Requiring the Department of Aging to provide resources, training, grants, and other support to the Maryland Access Point network to create dementia-friendly communities through community-based efforts; and requiring the Maryland Access Point network to provide certain public awareness and educational materials to communities regarding community-based ways to support individuals with dementia.
Title: Department of Aging - Maryland Access Point - Dementia-Friendly Communities
Status: In the House - Hearing 2/05 at 1:45 p.m.

NarrowSubjects.Name: Accessibility - see also- Blind; Deaf; Disabilities; etc

Mental and Behavioral Health -see also- Aut; Cogn; Dev; etc.

bill_summary: This bill requires the Maryland Department of Aging to provide resources, training, grants, and support to the Maryland Access Point (MAP) network to establish dementia-friendly communities. It also mandates that the MAP network provide public awareness and educational materials to help communities support individuals with dementia, reduce stigma, and create safe, inclusive environments.
stakeholders: Individuals living with dementia, their families and care partners, the Maryland Access Point network, local governments, first responders, local businesses, and community groups.
fiscal_impact_summary: According to the Fiscal Note, state general fund expenditures increase by at least $144,700 in fiscal 2027, covering the cost of a dementia-friendly coordinator and the printing and distribution of educational materials. Costs are projected to increase annually to approximately $177,700 by fiscal 2031. Local governments may see an indeterminate increase in revenues and expenditures if the Maryland Department of Aging provides grant funding to local Maryland Access Point offices.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill primarily tasks the Department of Aging with providing resources, training, and grants to the Maryland Access Point network to create dementia-friendly communities. The fiscal note indicates the department will require additional staff and funding to fulfill these mandates.

The bill explicitly requires the Department of Aging to coordinate with the Maryland Department of Health (MDH). Furthermore, MDH is involved in existing dementia public awareness programs and hosts the Virginia I. Jones Alzheimer’s Disease and Related Dementias Council mentioned in the fiscal note.

The bill explicitly requires the Department of Aging to coordinate the Maryland Access Point program with the Department of Disabilities. The program serves individuals with disabilities as well as older adults.
The bill explicitly requires the Department of Aging to coordinate the Maryland Access Point program with the Department of Human Services.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Governor's Office of the Deaf and Hard of Hearing
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill explicitly requires the Department of Aging to coordinate the Maryland Access Point program with the Governor's Office of the Deaf and Hard of Hearing.

The fiscal note identifies a significant increase in general fund expenditures ($144,700 in FY 2027 and more in subsequent years) for staff and materials, which falls under DBM's fiscal and personnel management responsibilities.
The bill requires the Maryland Access Point network to facilitate specialized training for first responders, of which the Maryland State Police is a primary state-level entity.

The bill seeks to make physical environments safe, accessible, and easy to navigate through clear signage and infrastructure, which relates to the operational duties of MDOT agencies like the State Highway Administration.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Executive Commissions, Committees, Task Forces, and Advisory Boards
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The fiscal note highlights the role of the Virginia I. Jones Alzheimer’s Disease and Related Dementias Council, which is an advisory body tasked with updating the State Plan on Alzheimer’s Disease and related issues.

Synopsis: Requiring a county board of education to develop and adopt a policy on the use of personal electronic devices during school hours; requiring the policy to restrict or limit the use of personal electronic devices by students during school hours, except for any purpose documented in the student's education program or Section 504 plan, to monitor or address a student's health issue, or for certain educational purposes; and requiring the policy to be published on the county board's website and in student handbooks.

bill_summary: This bill requires each Maryland county board of education to develop and adopt a policy regarding student use of personal electronic devices during school hours. The policy must prohibit device use for elementary and middle school students and limit device use for high school students, though exceptions are allowed for documented health issues, special education needs (IEP or 504 plans), or specific educational purposes directed by staff.
responsible_party: Maryland State Department of Education and county boards of education
stakeholders: Public school students, teachers, school administrators, and local county boards of education
fiscal_impact_summary: The Maryland State Department of Education and local boards of education can implement the policy development, adoption, and review requirements using existing resources. The bill is not expected to affect state or local revenues.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill directly mandates the Maryland State Department of Education (the 'Department') to review student technology use policies for elementary and middle school students every two years. MSDE is also the primary oversight body for the local boards of education that must develop and adopt these policies.

As an independent unit within the Department of Education, the Center provides a coordinated approach to school safety. Technology use, specifically personal electronic devices like smartphones, is a significant factor in school safety and environment, and the agency is listed as a primary information source in the bill's fiscal note.

The bill includes specific exemptions for students using personal electronic devices as part of an Individualized Education Program (IEP) or Section 504 plan. The Department of Disabilities is the principal agency for coordinating services and inclusive policies for residents with disabilities, including students.

The bill allows an exception for students to use personal electronic devices to monitor or address documented health issues. The Department of Health oversees public health policies and coordinates with local health departments that often support school health services and requirements.

The Office of the Attorney General serves as the primary legal representative for the Department of Education and state agencies. They would be responsible for providing legal counsel regarding the implementation and enforcement of technology use policies and related disciplinary measures like in-school suspensions.

Synopsis: Prohibiting a person from disposing of yard waste collected on the grounds of a State building or State highway in single-use plastic container; requiring a person to collect yard waste on the grounds of a State building or State highway in a container that will not be discarded with the yard waste or in a compostable paper bag; and requiring all yard waste collected on the grounds of a State building or State highway to be disposed of in a certain manner under certain circumstances.

bill_summary: This bill prohibits State employees and contractors from using single-use plastic containers to collect or dispose of yard waste from State buildings and highways. It requires the use of reusable containers or compostable paper bags and mandates disposal at organics or natural wood waste recycling facilities if such a facility is within a 30-mile radius and has capacity. The bill excludes noxious weeds and invasive species.
responsible_party: State agencies managing State buildings and highways, including the Department of General Services, Maryland Department of Transportation, and Department of Natural Resources
stakeholders: State employees and private contractors involved in landscaping and yard waste collection on State property
fiscal_impact_summary: State expenditures may increase slightly due to the higher cost of compostable paper bags compared to plastic ones and potential transport or disposal fees. However, the fiscal impact is not expected to be significant. No impact on State revenues or local government finances is anticipated.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill applies to yard waste collected on the grounds of State buildings and facilities, including the training sites and readiness centers managed by the Maryland Military Department.

The bill applies to 'State buildings,' which include facilities used by the Judicial Branch. The AOC provides operational and financial support to the state's courts and would be responsible for compliance with yard waste disposal rules at court facilities.

The Board of Public Works oversees significant state procurement contracts, including those for landscaping and waste management services that will be affected by the bill's container and disposal requirements.
The authority manages state-owned properties within the Canal Place Heritage Area, which are subject to the bill's requirements for yard waste collection and disposal.
The bill specifically excludes 'noxious weeds' as designated by the Department of Agriculture from its requirements, making the agency responsible for defining the scope of this exemption.
As the principal fiscal agency, DBM is responsible for the budget and personnel impacts across multiple fund types resulting from potential increases in costs for compostable bags and disposal fees.

The bill defines 'State building' to include educational facilities owned or operated by the State, which may include specific facilities under the oversight or management of the Department of Education.

DGS is the primary operational support agency for the construction and maintenance of state-owned facilities. It will be a lead agency in implementing the yard waste collection and disposal standards across its managed portfolio.
The Maryland Department of Health operates various institutional facilities and hospitals with significant grounds that generate yard waste subject to the bill's requirements.
DHS operates local department offices and facilities whose groundskeeping activities must comply with the new disposal and collection standards.
DJS operates secure residential facilities for youth; these grounds are considered State buildings/improved areas subject to the bill's requirements.

The bill specifically includes State parks and recreation centers in the definition of 'State building.' DNR is a primary land manager for the state and will be significantly impacted by the change in yard waste disposal practices.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Department of Public Safety and Correctional Services
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: DPSCS manages extensive correctional facility grounds throughout the state, which generate substantial yard waste that must now be diverted to specific recycling facilities.
The bill's title and definitions explicitly include 'State highways' and 'public mass transportation accommodations' such as terminals or stations, making MDOT a primary implementing agency.
The department manages state veteran cemeteries and the Charlotte Hall Veterans Home, which are State-owned improved areas that generate yard waste.

The bill relies on definitions of 'organics recycling facility' and 'natural wood waste recycling facility' from the Environment Article, and MDE regulates the facilities where yard waste must be diverted.
The Governor's Office oversees executive branch operations and policy implementation related to the management of state facilities and environmental initiatives.
As an independent agency managing an outdoor history museum and archaeological park on state-owned land, it must comply with the bill's yard waste disposal rules.
The corporation manages the Reginald F. Lewis Museum, which is a state-owned structure subject to the bill's yard waste collection requirements.

MES provides technical and operational environmental services to state agencies, including waste management and recycling. It may be called upon to help agencies comply with the bill's disposal requirements.
As a state agency with two campuses, MSD is responsible for managing its grounds in accordance with the bill's yard waste collection and disposal mandates.
The MSA plans and manages major sports and entertainment facilities and state-owned properties, which are subject to the bill's yard waste requirements.
MSP manages barracks and other state-owned buildings across Maryland that are subject to the new yard waste collection standards.
MTA is specifically referenced through the inclusion of public mass transportation accommodations in the definition of a 'State building.'
MDTA manages toll facilities and adjacent lands that fall under the bill's definition of 'State highway,' requiring compliance for its landscaping activities.
Public institutions of higher education are explicitly included in the bill's definition of 'State building,' making Morgan State University directly responsible for compliance.
MVA operates various branch offices and facilities across the state that are considered State buildings subject to the bill.
The OAG will provide legal counsel to state agencies regarding the modification of landscaping and waste disposal contracts to ensure compliance with the bill.
Public institutions of higher education are explicitly included in the bill's definition of 'State building,' making the college directly responsible for compliance.
As the agency responsible for the majority of non-toll State highways, SHA is a primary entity impacted by the bill's highway yard waste collection and disposal rules.
Public institutions of higher education are explicitly included in the definition of 'State building.' USM campuses manage significant grounds and were specifically mentioned in the fiscal note.

Synopsis: Requiring that the salary of certain Sheriffs to be equal to the salary of certain State's Attorneys.

Status: In the House - Hearing 2/04 at 1:00 p.m.

NarrowSubjects.Name: Salaries and Compensation -see also- Overtime; Reimb. Rates

bill_summary: This bill mandates that the annual salaries of Sheriffs in 16 Maryland counties (Allegany, Calvert, Caroline, Carroll, Cecil, Dorchester, Frederick, Garrett, Harford, Kent, St. Mary’s, Somerset, Talbot, Washington, Wicomico, and Worcester) be set equal to the annual salary of the State’s Attorney for the same county.
responsible_party: County governments (County Commissioners and County Councils) of the 16 affected counties
stakeholders: County Sheriffs in Allegany, Calvert, Caroline, Carroll, Cecil, Dorchester, Frederick, Garrett, Harford, Kent, St. Mary’s, Somerset, Talbot, Washington, Wicomico, and Worcester counties.
fiscal_impact_summary: According to the Fiscal Note, the bill does not materially affect State operations or finances. Local government expenditures for most of the affected counties are expected to increase by varying amounts annually beginning in fiscal 2027, as the new salary structures take effect with the next terms of office. Specific dollar estimates for the total impact are unavailable because future salaries for State's Attorneys are often tied to judicial salaries which are subject to future General Assembly actions and local council resolutions.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill amends various sections of the Courts and Judicial Proceedings Article of the Annotated Code of Maryland. As the central support agency for the Maryland Judicial Branch, the Administrative Office of the Courts monitors legislation affecting court officers and the statutory framework of the judicial system.

The bill proposes to repeal and replace language in existing law that ties the salaries of Sheriffs in Calvert, Harford, and St. Mary’s counties to the Department of State Police pay plan (specifically the grade and step of a lieutenant colonel).

The bill alters the salaries of Sheriffs, who are constitutional officers and law enforcement officials often participating in the State Retirement and Pension System. Changes in pensionable salary affect the agency's administration of contributions and future benefit liabilities.

The Office of the Attorney General provides legal counsel to the General Assembly and state agencies. The bill involves constitutional considerations regarding the timing of salary adjustments for public officials, an area where the OAG (via the Counsel to the General Assembly) frequently provides guidance.

bill_summary: The bill establishes the Henrietta Lacks Commission to honor the legacy of Henrietta Lacks and the scientific impact of HeLa cells. The commission is responsible for promoting education about her life, curating a registry of tributes, collaborating with state agencies to include her legacy in tourism campaigns, and promoting economic development in the Turner Station community of Dundalk.
responsible_party: Maryland Department of Social and Economic Mobility
stakeholders: The Turner Station community in Dundalk, the life sciences research community, the Maryland tourism industry, and the descendants and legacy of Henrietta Lacks.
fiscal_impact_summary: According to the Fiscal Note, the bill's requirements can be implemented using existing budgeted resources by the participating State agencies. Commission members receive no compensation but are entitled to reimbursement for travel expenses. The note indicates that while revenues are unaffected, the estimate does not account for the potential costs of specific future actions the commission may take. There is a potential positive local economic impact for Baltimore County.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Governor's Office is responsible for appointing several members to the newly established Henrietta Lacks Commission and receives the commission's annual report on its activities and recommendations.

As the principal fiscal and personnel agency, DBM is responsible for the oversight of state travel regulations under which commission members are reimbursed and would oversee any budget adjustments for the joint staffing requirement.

The Secretary of Commerce is a statutory member of the commission. The commission's mandates include promoting economic development and coordinating tourism campaigns, which are primary functions of this department.
The State Superintendent of Education is a statutory member of the commission. Additionally, the department is one of the agencies required to jointly provide staff for the commission's operations.
The Chair of the State Anatomy Board, which is a unit within the Department of Health, is a statutory member of the commission. The bill also impacts health-related research oversight.
The Maryland State Archives is explicitly required to have a representative on the commission and is one of the agencies responsible for providing joint staff support.
The Office of Appointments will be responsible for the recruitment and vetting of the diverse representatives appointed by the Governor to the Henrietta Lacks Commission.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Executive Commissions, Committees, Task Forces, and Advisory Boards
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: This bill establishes a new state commission to address specific policy issues related to Henrietta Lacks, falling directly into the category of executive bodies managed under this entity.

The commission's membership includes a representative from the Maryland Economic Development Commission, and the fiscal note identifies MEDCO as a key information source and stakeholder in the bill's economic development goals.
The commission is specifically mandated to work with state agencies to include tributes to Henrietta Lacks in state tourism campaigns, a core responsibility of this office.
A representative from the State Ethics Commission is a required member of the new commission, as established by the bill.

bill_summary: This bill prohibits Maryland State agencies from purchasing gasoline-powered leaf blowers starting July 1, 2026, and bans their use by State agencies, contractors, or subcontractors on State property starting January 1, 2031. Executive Branch agencies are required to monitor and enforce their own compliance with these standards.
stakeholders: State agencies, landscaping contractors and subcontractors, and small businesses selling or using landscaping equipment.
fiscal_impact_summary: State expenditures (all funds) will increase starting in FY 2027 due to the higher upfront costs of electric leaf blowers and necessary charging infrastructure. While an overall estimate is unavailable, the Department of Natural Resources anticipates an annual expenditure increase of $76,000 through FY 2031. By FY 2031, State landscaping contract costs may also increase. Local government impact is minimal or none.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: As the primary operational support agency and central procurement authority, DGS is responsible for the purchase of goods (including leaf blowers) and the maintenance of a significant amount of state-owned facilities. The bill's prohibition on purchasing and using gasoline-powered leaf blowers directly impacts their procurement processes and facility management operations.

MDOT manages a vast transportation network including highways, airports, and ports with significant grounds maintenance needs. While the bill excludes certain emergency activities at transportation facilities, general maintenance by MDOT and its contractors will be heavily impacted by the transition to electric equipment.

DNR manages over 500,000 acres of public lands and parks. The fiscal note specifically identifies DNR as an agency that will experience increased expenditures to replace gasoline-powered equipment with battery-operated alternatives.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Department of Public Safety and Correctional Services
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: DPSCS operates numerous correctional facilities with extensive grounds. The fiscal note explicitly mentions that the agency's expenditures may increase significantly due to the migration to electric leaf blowers for facility maintenance.

The bill amends the Environment Article (Subtitle 6, Noise Control), which is administered by MDE. Although individual agencies are responsible for self-monitoring, the statutory changes fall under MDE's regulatory purview.

USM oversees 12 institutions with extensive campus grounds. The fiscal note identifies USM as one of the entities likely to face significant cost increases for equipment replacement and landscaping contracts.

MDH operates various public health facilities, hospitals, and centers with surrounding grounds that require maintenance. The bill will impact their operational costs and contract management for landscaping.
DJS operates secure residential facilities for youth. The maintenance of these facility grounds is subject to the bill's prohibitions on gasoline-powered equipment usage and procurement.

As an independent state agency with its own campus, Morgan State University is responsible for maintaining its grounds and will need to transition its maintenance equipment and contracts to comply with the bill.
As an independent public college, St. Mary's will be required to phase out gasoline-powered leaf blowers for campus maintenance and ensure compliance among its contractors.

MSA manages major sports and entertainment complexes. The transition to electric leaf blowers will impact their maintenance operations and contracts for high-profile facilities like the Camden Yards Sports Complex.

The Maryland Military Department oversees various National Guard facilities and armories across the state. Maintenance of these properties will be subject to the new purchasing and usage restrictions.
The Commission manages a large outdoor museum and archaeological park. The bill will require changes in how they maintain these historic grounds and landscaped areas.

MES provides technical environmental services and manages various sites (such as landfills and water treatment plants). As an agency that frequently acts as a contractor or manager for state land, they must comply with the bill's usage prohibitions.

As the state's principal fiscal agency, DBM will be involved in the long-term fiscal planning and budget execution for agencies needing to fund the replacement of gasoline-powered equipment and potentially higher-cost landscaping contracts.

OAG provides legal counsel to state agencies. They will likely be involved in drafting and reviewing contract language for landscaping services to ensure compliance with the bill's 2031 usage prohibition for contractors.

As the state's chief financial officer, the Comptroller's office processes state expenditures. The transition to potentially more expensive electric equipment and charging infrastructure will affect the state's fiscal records and payments.
MSP operates barracks and headquarters across the state. Maintenance of these law enforcement facilities must comply with the new equipment standards.
MDA manages its own facilities and is involved in soil and resource conservation. The agency will need to ensure its maintenance equipment meets the new non-gasoline requirements.

The Governor's Office oversees the executive branch and proposes the state budget. This bill represents a significant policy shift for executive branch operations and procurement that the Governor's office must coordinate.

bill_summary: This bill authorizes local county boards of education to consider the provision of educator workforce housing as a school purpose, allowing them to utilize land or buildings for this purpose rather than declaring them surplus. It defines educator workforce housing as affordable housing reserved for teachers and school employees who are not top-level administrators. Furthermore, the bill expands eligibility for the Department of Housing and Community Development's Housing Innovation Fund, Housing Innovation Pilot Program, and Neighborhood and Community Assistance Program to include educator workforce housing and adds municipal corporations and county boards of education as eligible recipients of this financial assistance.
responsible_party: Maryland Department of Housing and Community Development (DHCD)
stakeholders: Teachers and local school system employees (excluding strategic administrators), local boards of education, municipal corporations, and the Maryland Department of Housing and Community Development.
fiscal_impact_summary: According to the Fiscal Note, the Department of Housing and Community Development can implement the bill using existing budgeted resources, and state revenues are not affected. Local school boards and municipal corporations become eligible for state financial assistance to develop educator workforce housing. The bill modifies existing programs like the Housing Innovation Fund and the Neighborhood and Community Assistance Program; the latter remains subject to an existing $3,500,000 annual tax credit cap.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: DHCD is the primary implementing agency for the bill, tasked with administering the Housing Innovation Fund, the Housing Innovation Pilot Program, and the Neighborhood and Community Assistance Program, all of which are expanded to include educator workforce housing.

The bill alters the definition of 'school purpose' to include educator workforce housing, which directly impacts local school boards and property management overseen by the Maryland State Department of Education and the State Superintendent.

As the agency responsible for overseeing public school facility needs and capital improvements, the IAC is impacted by changes in how school property is categorized as 'surplus' versus being retained for 'school purposes' like teacher housing.
The Comptroller is responsible for accounting for the Housing Innovation Fund and managing the tax credit certifications and state revenue implications for the expanded programs.
The Treasurer is specifically tasked with holding and investing the Housing Innovation Fund separately, as established by the bill.
The agency provides guidance to local governments on land use and sustainable community designations, which are integral to the housing programs expanded by this bill.
The OAG provides legal counsel to state agencies like DHCD and MSDE regarding the implementation of new definitions for school property and housing program regulations.
DBM oversees the fiscal execution and budgetary appropriations for the Housing Innovation Fund and other DHCD-managed grant programs.
The BPW oversees and approves significant state expenditures and the transfer or lease of state-funded property, which may occur as school boards develop educator housing.
The OLA will likely conduct future performance and compliance audits of the newly expanded programs within DHCD and MSDE.
The Governor's Office coordinates executive policy initiatives and is responsible for signing the bill into law and overseeing the general direction of affordable housing policy.
