bill_summary: This bill updates the Public Access Automated External Defibrillator (AED) Program by defining the role of an AED coordinator, establishing specific registration and maintenance requirements for grocery stores and restaurants, and exempting law enforcement agencies from obtaining certificates for AEDs deployed in patrol vehicles. It also repeals obsolete provisions regarding regional council AED committees to streamline program administration.
responsible_party: State Emergency Medical Services (EMS) Board and the Maryland Institute for Emergency Medical Services Systems (MIEMSS)
stakeholders: Businesses, organizations, associations, law enforcement agencies, grocery stores, and restaurants in Maryland.
fiscal_impact_summary: According to the Fiscal Note, the bill has no state or local fiscal impact as the changes are technical in nature and do not directly affect governmental finances. Small businesses are expected to experience minimal to no economic impact.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Maryland Institute for Emergency Medical Services Systems
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: MIEMSS is the primary state agency responsible for administering the Public Access Automated External Defibrillator Program, overseeing the EMS Board's delegated authority, and providing the forms required for reporting AED usage.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Executive Commissions, Committees, Task Forces, and Advisory Boards
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The State Emergency Medical Services Board (EMS Board), an administrative body, is the primary entity authorized by the bill to adopt regulations, issue certificates, approve training programs, and enforce compliance for the AED Program.

The bill explicitly exempts law enforcement agencies from the requirement to obtain a certificate for AEDs deployed in patrol vehicles, directly impacting the administrative and operational requirements of the State Police.
The bill amends the Health - General Article to require grocery stores and restaurants to comply with the AED Program, impacting businesses regulated and inspected by the Department of Health.
The OAG provides legal counsel to the EMS Board and MIEMSS regarding the drafting of regulations and the interpretation of the bill's civil immunity provisions for registered entities.

The bill amends the Education Article which governs the AED Program; furthermore, local school systems are registered entities that must comply with the new requirements for AED coordinators and maintenance.
Public libraries are mandated by separate law to maintain AEDs and must follow the Program's revised standards for functionality and the designation of an AED coordinator as established in this bill.
As a departmental bill proposed by MIEMSS, the Governor's Office oversees the policy coordination and legislative priorities reflected in these administrative revisions.
DGS manages state-owned facilities, which are defined as 'entities' under the bill and are subject to requirements for AED placement, maintenance, and the co-location of naloxone in public buildings.

Synopsis: Altering the grounds on which the Maryland Insurance Commissioner may deny an applicant for registration as or refuse to renew, suspend, or revoke the registration of a third party administrator; and altering the violations for which the Commissioner may impose civil penalties against a third party administrator.
Title: Insurance – Third Party Administrators – Enforcement
Status: Approved by the Governor - Chapter 141

NarrowSubjects.Name: Insurance -see also- Health Ins; MAIF; Motor Vehicle Ins
Penalties and Sentences -see also- Death Penalty

bill_summary: This bill expands the Maryland Insurance Commissioner's enforcement authority over third party administrators (TPAs). It allows the Commissioner to deny, suspend, or revoke a TPA's registration for violating any part of the State's insurance laws or failing to follow orders and regulations. It also extends the Commissioner's ability to impose civil penalties of up to $10,000 per violation to include any violation of the Insurance Article, rather than just the specific laws governing TPAs.
stakeholders: Third party administrators (TPAs), the Maryland Insurance Administration, and insurance plan participants and beneficiaries.
fiscal_impact_summary: The Maryland Insurance Administration (MIA) can implement the bill's requirements using existing budgeted resources. The imposition of new or expanded civil penalties is not expected to have a material impact on State revenues. There is no material impact on local government finances or small businesses.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Maryland Insurance Administration is the primary agency responsible for regulating third party administrators and requested this bill to expand its enforcement authority and penalty-setting powers under the Insurance Article.

The Office of the Attorney General provides legal counsel to state agencies, including the Maryland Insurance Administration, and represents the state in appeals and enforcement proceedings related to insurance law violations.

The Office of Administrative Hearings provides the impartial hearing process for contested regulatory enforcement cases, including those where the Insurance Commissioner denies or revokes a registration.
The Governor's Office oversees the executive branch and coordinates departmental policy initiatives; this bill is a departmental request from the Maryland Insurance Administration.

Synopsis: Requiring the Secretary of Aging to lead implementation of the Longevity Ready Maryland Plan which is a multisector plan on aging that transforms programs, services, policies, institutions, and systems to address the growing population of older adults in the State; requiring the Department to maintain a publicly accessible resource on the Department's website for monitoring implementation of the Longevity Ready Maryland Plan; and requiring the Department of Aging to staff the Commission on Aging.

bill_summary: The bill codifies the 'Longevity Ready Maryland (LRM) Plan,' which is a multisector strategy designed to transform state programs, services, and policies to better support Maryland's growing population of older adults. It requires the Secretary of Aging to lead the plan's implementation, establishes four-year update cycles for the plan, and reorganizes the Commission on Aging to include a more diverse set of experts and stakeholders.
stakeholders: Older adults in Maryland, family caregivers, Area Agencies on Aging, and professional organizations focused on aging and longevity.
fiscal_impact_summary: According to the Fiscal Note, the bill has no state or local fiscal impact because it primarily codifies existing policies and procedures established under Executive Order 01.01.2024.01. The Department of Legislative Services determined that any economic impact on small businesses would not be a direct result of the bill.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Department of Aging is the primary agency responsible for implementing the Longevity Ready Maryland Plan. The Secretary of Aging is explicitly tasked with leading the multisector plan, coordinating across state agencies, and staffing the Commission on Aging.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Executive Commissions, Committees, Task Forces, and Advisory Boards
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill fundamentally alters the membership, structure, and duties of the Commission on Aging, which is one of the permanent advisory bodies included in this category. It mandates new membership criteria and requires the Commission to advise on the Longevity Ready Maryland Plan.

One of the primary goals of the Longevity Ready Maryland Plan is to optimize health and wellness for older adults. The bill requires cross-sector collaboration with units of state government that manage health and mental health services, which are central to the well-being of older adults.

The bill identifies 'optimizing mobility' as a core goal of the Longevity Ready Maryland Plan and specifically tasks the Secretary of Aging with coordinating programs related to transportation for older adults to support independent living.

The bill aims to 'promote economic opportunity' for older adults. The fiscal note highlights the importance of a multigenerational workforce and upskilling older adults, areas managed by the Department of Labor.

The bill focuses on the 'longevity economy' and promoting economic opportunity. The Department of Commerce is relevant due to the impact of the aging population on the state's GDP, workforce, and business attraction strategies mentioned in the bill's economic impact analysis.

Housing is explicitly listed as a service area that must be evaluated and supported under the Longevity Ready Maryland Plan to assist older adults in leading independent lives in their own homes and communities.

A major goal of the bill is 'preparing State residents to afford longevity.' The Treasurer's Office manages state financial assets and programs like MarylandSaves and Maryland 529 that directly relate to long-term financial security.

This agency provides retirement and emergency savings programs for private-sector workers. Its mission aligns directly with the bill's mandate to prepare residents to afford longevity and ensure economic security in older age.

The Secretary of Aging is a member of the Governor's Executive Council and must report progress on the Longevity Ready Maryland Plan to the Governor annually. The Governor is also responsible for appointing several new members to the Commission on Aging.

The Comptroller's role as the state's chief financial officer is relevant to the bill's goals of preparing residents to afford longevity and assessing the economic impact of the aging population on the state's revenue.

The bill calls for significant policy, systems, and institutional changes at all levels of government. The OAG would be responsible for providing legal counsel to the Department of Aging and other agencies during this multisector transformation.
As the principal fiscal agency, DBM will oversee the budget execution and personnel requirements for the Department of Aging as it implements these new mandates and reporting requirements.
The bill specifically requires that the Commission on Aging include a veteran with a demonstrated interest in the implementation of the Longevity Ready Maryland Plan.

The bill emphasizes supporting older adults in leading independent lives, which often overlaps with disability services. The Longevity Ready Maryland Plan must also coordinate with existing systems that support rehabilitation and wellness for seniors with disabilities.

The bill requires the Department of Aging to maintain a publicly accessible resource on its website for monitoring the implementation of the Longevity Ready Maryland Plan, which may require coordination with DoIT for strategy and security.
The board's mission to develop workforce solutions aligns with the bill's goal of promoting economic opportunity and the fiscal note's emphasis on maintaining older adults in the workforce.

Synopsis: Authorizing the establishment of a medication review committee within the Department of Public Safety and Correctional Services that convenes to determine whether to approve the administration of psychotropic medication to a certain incarcerated individual under certain circumstances; providing that psychotropic medication may not be administered to an incarcerated individual who refuses the medication except under certain circumstances; etc.

bill_summary: This bill establishes a process for the involuntary administration of psychotropic medication to incarcerated individuals within Maryland State correctional mental health facilities. It authorizes the creation of medication review committees to approve such treatments in non-emergency situations when an individual refuses medication and meets specific clinical criteria, such as posing a danger to themselves or others. The bill also outlines the procedural rights of the incarcerated individuals, including the right to a lay advisor, legal representation, and an appeal process through the Office of Administrative Hearings and the circuit court.
responsible_party: Maryland Department of Public Safety and Correctional Services
stakeholders: Incarcerated individuals in State correctional facilities with mental health disorders, mental health professionals (psychiatrists and psychiatric nurse practitioners), and the Office of Administrative Hearings.
fiscal_impact_summary: The Department of Public Safety and Correctional Services (DPSCS) expects to implement the bill using existing budgeted resources. However, the Office of Administrative Hearings (OAH) may experience an indeterminate increase in general fund expenditures beginning in fiscal 2027 to conduct required appeal hearings; as an illustration, the cost of hiring one full-time Administrative Law Judge is estimated at $175,000. Local government finances and the State Judiciary are not expected to be significantly impacted.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Department of Public Safety and Correctional Services
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: As the primary implementing agency, DPSCS is authorized to establish medication review committees, appoint members, manage the lay advisor program, and implement the involuntary medication protocols within its correctional facilities.

The bill explicitly mandates that the Office of Administrative Hearings conduct de novo administrative hearings for incarcerated individuals appealing the decisions of the medication review committees.

The bill requires the Maryland Department of Health (Office of Health Care Quality) to license the mental health care facilities within correctional institutions and mandates that DPSCS submit an annual report to the Department regarding the administration of psychotropic medication.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Maryland Office of the Public Defender
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill establishes significant legal rights and appeal processes for incarcerated individuals, a population primarily served by the Office of the Public Defender in matters related to their confinement and rights.
The OAG provides legal counsel to DPSCS and MDH, and would likely represent the state's interests during administrative hearings at OAH and subsequent judicial reviews in Circuit Court.
The bill establishes a specific judicial review process in the Circuit Court for appeals from OAH decisions, which falls under the operational purview of the Administrative Office of the Courts.

The fiscal note indicates a potential increase in general fund expenditures for the Office of Administrative Hearings to accommodate the new hearing requirements, which DBM would oversee during budget development and execution.

Synopsis: Codifying in State law certain provisions of the Code of Federal Regulations related to mental health parity and clarifying the authority of the Maryland Insurance Administration to enforce certain laws; requiring health insurance carriers to collect and report on data in a certain manner; requiring health insurance carriers to provide certain benefits under certain circumstances; requiring health insurance carriers to explain differences in access to care under certain circumstances; etc.
Title: Health Insurance - Mental Health and Substance Use Disorders - Codification of Federal Requirements
Status: Approved by the Governor - Chapter 11

bill_summary: This bill codifies federal mental health and substance use disorder parity requirements into Maryland law. It requires health insurance carriers to collect and report data to ensure that access to mental health and substance use disorder benefits is comparable to medical and surgical benefits. Carriers must provide meaningful benefits, including core treatments for covered conditions, and the Maryland Insurance Administration is empowered to enforce these parity standards through reviews and administrative orders.
stakeholders: Health insurance carriers and individuals in Maryland with mental health or substance use disorders
fiscal_impact_summary: According to the Fiscal Note, the Maryland Insurance Administration can implement the bill and promulgate regulations using existing budgeted resources. There is no projected impact on the State Employee and Retiree Health and Welfare Benefits Program, and state and local revenues are not affected.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Maryland Insurance Administration is the primary agency responsible for enforcing the bill. As a departmental bill requested by the MIA, the agency will oversee the codification of federal mental health parity requirements, review compliance reports from carriers, and exercise its authority to issue administrative orders or penalties for noncompliance.

The bill regulates health benefit plans sold in the individual and small group markets, which are primarily offered through the Maryland Health Connection, the marketplace administered by the Exchange. The parity requirements directly impact the eligibility and design of the products available on the Exchange.

The Maryland Department of Health oversees behavioral health and substance use disorder services statewide. While the bill regulates private insurance carriers, it directly impacts access to the types of care MDH is tasked with promoting and protecting, and the bill references the Health - General Article regarding penalties for health maintenance organizations.

The Office of the Attorney General serves as the legal representative for the Maryland Insurance Administration. It would be involved in providing counsel on the implementation of these new statutory requirements and representing the state in any legal challenges or enforcement actions resulting from the bill.

The MHCC is responsible for planning for the state's health system needs and improving access to care. Mental health and substance use disorder parity is a critical component of their mission to ensure the availability and quality of health services for Maryland residents.

DBM is the central personnel agency responsible for managing state employee health benefits. Although the fiscal note indicates no current fiscal impact on the state plan, DBM must ensure that the health benefit plans it offers to state employees and retirees remain in compliance with updated state parity laws.

As a departmental bill from an executive branch agency (MIA) approved by the Governor, the Governor's Office is responsible for the overall coordination of these policy initiatives and overseeing the executive branch agencies tasked with enforcement.

Synopsis: Altering provisions relating to criminal background investigations for certain individuals who care for or supervise children; requiring certain facilities to apply to the Criminal Justice Information System Central Repository for a national and State criminal history records check for each employee, employer, individual, or volunteer; and altering provisions relating to the process under which a certain State or local law enforcement agency conducts a certain name-based check on certain individuals.

bill_summary: This bill updates Maryland law to align with federal FBI requirements for criminal background investigations for individuals who care for or supervise children. It expands the list of facilities and individuals required to obtain national and State criminal history records checks, specifically including non-relative individuals providing care due to the sudden unavailability of a child's primary caretaker, and clarifies the dissemination process for background check results to ensure compliance with federal standards.
responsible_party: Department of Public Safety and Correctional Services
stakeholders: Child care centers, family child care homes, child care institutions, schools, foster care homes, recreation centers, child care employees and volunteers, and emergency temporary caregivers.
fiscal_impact_summary: State general fund expenditures are expected to increase minimally, with an illustrative estimate of $39,450 for potential foster care costs if substitute caregivers are unable to serve due to background check requirements. Local government expenditures may increase minimally due to higher workloads for background check processing. State revenues are not materially affected as the bill primarily codifies current practices to maintain access to federal background check data.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Department of Public Safety and Correctional Services
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill was requested by DPSCS and directly affects the Criminal Justice Information System (CJIS) Central Repository, which the department operates. It codifies procedures for processing and disseminating State and national criminal history record information (CHRI).

DHS licenses child care institutions and manages local departments of social services that handle foster care, adoption, and emergency out-of-home placements. The bill alters background check requirements for these programs and caregivers.

MSDE oversees child care centers, family child care homes, and public/private schools. The bill significantly impacts the background check requirements for employees and residents at these facilities.

The bill explicitly includes juvenile detention, correction, and treatment facilities (which DJS operates) in the list of facilities required to obtain criminal history records checks for employees and employers.
The bill applies to home health and residential service agencies licensed by MDH that provide services to minors, requiring their employees to undergo criminal background investigations.
As a primary state law enforcement agency, MSP may be responsible for conducting the national name-based checks authorized by the bill for emergency out-of-home placements.
The bill affects individuals appointed as guardians by a juvenile court, requiring them to obtain criminal history records checks, which involves judicial branch procedures.

The fiscal note indicates a potential increase in general fund expenditures managed by DBM, specifically related to foster care costs if emergency caregivers are disqualified by the new check requirements.
The OAG provides legal counsel to MSDE, DHS, and DPSCS, and would be involved in ensuring the bill's changes successfully bring Maryland into compliance with federal FBI background check standards.
As the agency responsible for school safety technical assistance and training, the expansion of background check requirements for school personnel is relevant to their coordination efforts.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Governor's Office of Crime Prevention and Policy
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: GOCPP coordinates public safety strategies and manages funds for programs related to juvenile delinquency and victim services, which overlap with the bill's child safety and law enforcement objectives.

Synopsis: Altering provisions relating to the reporting and investigation of abuse, neglect, self-neglect, and exploitation of vulnerable adults; and requiring the local department of aging to complete an investigation and make an indicated, not indicated, or undetermined finding within 60 days.

Status: Approved by the Governor - Chapter 652

bill_summary: This bill updates Adult Protective Services laws by redefining terms such as 'abuse', 'neglect', and 'exploitation' to include a 'relationship of trust' requirement and expanding the definition of abuse to encompass psychological harm and sexual abuse. It introduces an online reporting portal, requires investigations to determine a vulnerable adult's 'risk of harm', and mandates specific findings for investigative results (indicated, not indicated, or undetermined) to align Maryland law with federal standards.
responsible_party: Maryland Department of Human Services (DHS) and local departments of social services.
stakeholders: Vulnerable adults, individuals in a relationship of trust with vulnerable adults (such as relatives, friends, and caregivers), health practitioners, police officers, and human service workers.
fiscal_impact_summary: The bill is not anticipated to materially affect State or local government operations or finances. It may help protect federal funding by ensuring Maryland's Adult Protective Services program complies with federal requirements. The Department of Human Services has determined there is minimal or no economic impact on small businesses.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill directly modifies the Adult Protective Services (APS) program, which is administered by the Department of Human Services and its local departments. The Secretary of Human Services is explicitly mentioned in the bill, and the fiscal note identifies DHS as the primary agency involved in these departmental changes.

The bill explicitly states that the Department of Aging may assist in investigations of vulnerable adult abuse or neglect on request. The agency's mission to protect the rights of older adults and individuals with disabilities is directly aligned with the bill's changes to protective services.

The bill identifies police officers as mandatory reporters of vulnerable adult abuse and requires law enforcement agencies to assist in APS investigations. Changes to definitions of abuse, neglect, and exploitation will affect reporting and investigatory protocols for state and local law enforcement.

The bill classifies health practitioners as mandatory reporters. The Department of Health regulates these professionals and provides services to the vulnerable adult population targeted by this legislation.

As the chief legal officer for the state, the OAG provides counsel to DHS and the Department of Aging. The bill modifies the legal definitions and investigative standards within the Family Law Article that the OAG must help interpret and defend.

The fiscal note lists the Judiciary as a source of information. The bill alters statutory definitions used in court proceedings involving vulnerable adults, and its changes to finding categories (indicated, not indicated, etc.) may impact judicial review of APS cases.
The bill defines a 'vulnerable adult' by referencing individuals who lack physical or mental capacity, a population for whom the Department of Disabilities coordinates services and advocacy.

The bill authorizes the use of an online reporting portal for abuse reports. DoIT is responsible for the state's IT infrastructure and strategy, potentially supporting the implementation or security of this digital reporting mechanism.

Synopsis: Establishing the method for calculating the measure of the actual cash value recovery in the settlement of a first-party claim under a residential or commercial property insurance policy issued or renewed on or after October 1, 2026; and requiring an insurer that renews a policy of homeowner's insurance or renter's insurance to notify the insured, in advance of the renewal, of certain differences between the expiring policy and the renewal policy.

Status: In the House - Hearing 2/03 at 1:00 p.m.

bill_summary: This bill establishes a method for calculating actual cash value recovery in first-party property insurance claims, specifically prohibiting insurers from depreciating labor costs during claim settlement. It also requires insurers to provide homeowners and renters with a written notice at least 45 days before a policy renewal that identifies any differences in coverage limits, risks, or deductibles between the expiring and renewal policies.
stakeholders: Homeowners, renters, commercial property insurance policyholders, and insurance companies operating in Maryland.
fiscal_impact_summary: State special fund revenues for the Maryland Insurance Administration will increase minimally in FY 2027 due to rate and form filing fees. General fund revenues from the state's 2% premium tax may be affected if insurers adjust premiums to account for the bill's provisions, though any such impact is expected to be minimal. Enforcement of the bill's requirements can be managed with existing budgeted resources.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Maryland Insurance Administration is the primary agency responsible for regulating insurance in the state and requested this departmental bill. The agency will be responsible for overseeing the new claim settlement standards, processing rate and form filings, and investigating the newly defined unfair claim settlement practices.

The Office of Administrative Hearings adjudicates contested cases for state agencies, including the Maryland Insurance Administration. Enforcement actions against insurers for 'unfair claim settlement practices' defined in this bill would likely be heard by an Administrative Law Judge at this agency.

The Office of the Attorney General serves as legal counsel to the Maryland Insurance Administration and would represent the state in civil litigation or appeals related to the interpretation and enforcement of the new insurance standards.

The Comptroller is the state's principal tax collector. The fiscal note indicates that general fund revenues from insurance premium taxes may be minimally affected if the bill leads insurers to adjust their premiums.

As the principal fiscal agency, DBM is responsible for revenue estimation and long-term fiscal planning. The bill's potential impact on premium tax revenue and the fiscal oversight of the Maryland Insurance Administration falls within its scope.

The bill establishes legal standards for calculating 'actual cash value' in property insurance settlements. While primary enforcement is administrative, these standards may also be applied or litigated in civil cases within the state court system.

The Governor's Office oversees the executive branch, including the Maryland Insurance Administration, and appoints the Insurance Commissioner. The bill is part of the administration's departmental legislative package.

The Office of Legislative Audits conducts periodic fiscal and performance audits of the Maryland Insurance Administration. OLA would evaluate the agency's compliance with and management of the new regulatory requirements during their audit process.

Synopsis: Requiring a certain licensed firearms dealer to notify the Secretary of State Police within 24 hours after the dealer first has knowledge that certain crimes have occurred or certain security features have been compromised; and providing that a person who violates the Act is subject to a civil penalty imposed by the Secretary of up to $250 for a first offense and up to $1000 for a second or subsequent violation.
Title: Public Safety - Licensed Firearms Dealers - Notification Regarding Compromising Events
Status: Approved by the Governor - Chapter 85

NarrowSubjects.Name: Dealers -see also- Motor Vehicle Dealers and Salespeople

bill_summary: This bill requires licensed firearms dealers to notify the Secretary of State Police within 24 hours of any burglary, robbery, or theft of firearms or ammunition, or if required security equipment like cameras or alarms fails. It also modifies civil penalties for security violations, establishing a maximum $250 fine for a first offense and $1,000 for subsequent offenses.
responsible_party: Secretary of State Police (Maryland Department of State Police)
stakeholders: Licensed firearms dealers in Maryland
fiscal_impact_summary: According to the fiscal note, the bill's requirements can be handled using the Department of State Police's existing budgeted resources. Changes to civil penalty provisions are not expected to materially affect state revenues, and there is no fiscal impact on local governments.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Maryland State Police (specifically the Secretary) is the primary agency responsible for enforcing the bill, receiving notifications from dealers, adopting regulations, and imposing civil penalties for noncompliance.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Governor's Office of Crime Prevention and Policy
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: This office advises the Governor on public safety and criminal justice policy. The bill's aim to combat gun violence by ensuring firearms dealer security aligns with their core mission of policy development and interagency collaboration for public safety.

The OAG provides legal counsel to the Maryland State Police. They would likely assist in drafting the required regulations and representing the state in any legal challenges or high-level enforcement actions resulting from the bill.

The OAH adjudicates contested administrative cases for state agencies. If a firearms dealer appeals a civil penalty or license suspension/revocation imposed by the State Police, the hearing would be conducted by an Administrative Law Judge from this office.

The Governor's Office oversees the executive branch and the Maryland State Police. The bill is a departmental bill from the State Police, reflecting the administration's policy priorities regarding public safety and firearms regulation.

This office advises the Governor on public safety and assesses the state's readiness for emergencies. Compromised security features at firearms dealers represent a significant public safety and domestic security risk.

DBM is the principal fiscal agency for the state and oversees the budget execution for the Maryland State Police. While the fiscal note suggests the bill can be handled with existing resources, DBM maintains oversight of the agency's funding.

OLA is responsible for periodic fiscal compliance and performance audits of executive agencies. They may eventually audit the Maryland State Police's management of firearms dealer inspections and penalty collections under this new law.

Synopsis: Transferring the monitoring and security of the home detention programs of the Division of Correction to the Warrant Apprehension Unit of the Intelligence and Investigative Division within the Department of Public Safety and Correctional Services.
Title: Correctional Services - Home Detention - Monitoring and Security
Status: In the House - Unfavorable Report by Judiciary; Withdrawn

NarrowSubjects.Name: Investigations and Inquiries -see also- Crim Bckgrnd Invest
Law Enforcement -see also- SRO; Sheriffs; State Police
Public Safety and Correctional Services, Department of

bill_summary: This bill transfers the responsibility for monitoring and providing security for home detention programs from the Division of Correction to the Warrant Apprehension Unit of the Intelligence and Investigative Division within the Department of Public Safety and Correctional Services. It authorizes unit employees to execute warrants, conduct searches, and make arrests regarding individuals in these programs, provided they meet specific Maryland Police Training and Standards Commission requirements.
responsible_party: Warrant Apprehension Unit of the Intelligence and Investigative Division within the Department of Public Safety and Correctional Services
stakeholders: Incarcerated individuals in home detention programs and employees of the Department of Public Safety and Correctional Services.
fiscal_impact_summary: A formal Fiscal Note with specific revenue or expenditure estimates was not provided in the text. However, the bill involves a transfer of duties between units within the Department of Public Safety and Correctional Services, indicating a reallocation of existing resources and personnel responsibilities rather than a new funding mandate.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Department of Public Safety and Correctional Services
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: This is a departmental bill requested by the Department of Public Safety and Correctional Services (DPSCS). The bill directly impacts the internal operations of the department by transferring the monitoring and security of home detention programs from general correctional employees to the Warrant Apprehension Unit within its Intelligence and Investigative Division.

As the agency responsible for the state budget and personnel management, DBM is relevant because the transfer of duties and the authorization of specific employees to exercise law enforcement powers may involve changes in job classifications, training requirements, and funding allocations for the Intelligence and Investigative Division.

The bill concerns the monitoring of incarcerated individuals and the execution of warrants for offenders on probation, parole, or mandatory supervision, which are matters often originating from or coordinated with the judicial branch.

The OAG serves as the legal counsel for DPSCS and would be responsible for advising the department on the legal implications of transferring warrant execution and arrest powers to a specific unit, as well as ensuring compliance with the Maryland Police Training and Standards Commission requirements.

The bill requires employees of the Warrant Apprehension Unit to meet qualifications and training standards set by the Maryland Police Training and Standards Commission, an entity that works closely with the Maryland State Police and ensures statewide law enforcement standards.

The bill changes the statutory authority and designation of certain employees from 'correctional employees' to members of a specialized investigative unit, which could potentially impact job classifications and collective bargaining unit assignments overseen by PERB.

Synopsis: Requiring an individual to be a participant in the Ignition Interlock System Program as a condition of modification of a suspension or revocation of a license or issuance of a restricted license if the individual violated certain alcohol restrictions.
Title: Vehicle Laws - Ignition Interlock System Program - Required Participation
Status: Approved by the Governor - Chapter 80

BroadSubjects.Name: Vehicle Laws - Rules of the Road

NarrowSubjects.Name: Minors -see also- Age of Majority; Youth

bill_summary: This bill requires individuals of any age to participate in the Ignition Interlock System Program (IISP) as a condition of modifying a license suspension or revocation, or for the issuance of a restricted license, following a violation of a license alcohol restriction. Previously, this mandatory participation for such violations applied primarily to individuals under the age of 21. The bill allows individuals 21 and older to opt into the IISP without appearing before an administrative law judge.
responsible_party: Maryland Department of Transportation Motor Vehicle Administration
stakeholders: Drivers with license alcohol restrictions, the Maryland Department of Transportation, and the Office of Administrative Hearings
fiscal_impact_summary: The bill is not anticipated to materially affect State or local finances or operations. However, it is expected to decrease the number of hearing requests processed by the Office of Administrative Hearings for violations of alcohol-related license restrictions.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: As the parent department of the Motor Vehicle Administration (MVA), MDOT is the primary entity responsible for the bill's implementation. This is a departmental bill requested by MDOT to streamline the Ignition Interlock System Program.
The MVA directly administers the Ignition Interlock System Program (IISP), issues restricted licenses, and manages the suspension and revocation of driver's licenses affected by this legislation.

The bill is expected to decrease the number of hearing requests managed by this office, as it allows certain individuals to opt into the IISP without needing to appear before an administrative law judge.

The bill impacts the conditions under which court-ordered participation in the Ignition Interlock System Program is handled and how judicial findings regarding alcohol restrictions are applied to license modifications.

As the primary agency for traffic law enforcement and highway safety, the State Police are responsible for enforcing the license restrictions and ensuring compliance with ignition interlock requirements during traffic stops.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Governor's Office of Crime Prevention and Policy
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: This agency coordinates public safety and criminal justice strategies, including policies related to impaired driving and recidivism, which are central to the IISP's purpose.

The OAG provides legal counsel to the MVA and MDOT regarding the administration of the IISP and would represent the state in any legal challenges related to license suspensions or program requirements.
The Governor's Office oversees the executive branch agencies implementing the bill and coordinates the policy initiatives that led to this departmental request.
As the principal fiscal agency, DBM oversees the budget execution for MDOT, the MVA, and the Office of Administrative Hearings, all of which see operational changes due to this bill.

Synopsis: Requiring inclusion of certain conditions for lifetime sexual offender supervision; requiring a sexual offender management team to report a certain violation of a condition of lifetime sexual offender supervision to the office of a certain State's Attorney; requiring a certain judge to conduct a certain hearing; requiring a certain sentencing court to adjudicate rather than hear and adjudicate a certain petition; altering the period before a certain petition may be renewed after being denied; etc.
Title: Criminal Procedure - Lifetime Sexual Offender Supervision - Conditions, Violations, and Petitions for Discharge
Status: In the House - Unfavorable Report by Judiciary; Withdrawn

NarrowSubjects.Name: Courts -see also- AppCt; Circuit; District; Orphans'; etc.
Penalties and Sentences -see also- Death Penalty

bill_summary: This bill modifies the regulations for lifetime sexual offender supervision by specifying mandatory conditions, requiring that violations be reported to State's Attorneys, and updating the process for discharge petitions. It mandates that discharge petitions include a risk assessment and polygraph, increases the waiting period for re-petitioning from one year to two years, and ensures victims are notified of such petitions.
responsible_party: Maryland Department of Public Safety and Correctional Services
stakeholders: Sexual offenders subject to lifetime supervision, victims and their representatives, State's Attorneys, the Division of Parole and Probation, and the Maryland Judiciary.
fiscal_impact_summary: The formal Fiscal Note indicates that the bill is not expected to materially affect State or local finances. It primarily clarifies and standardizes operational procedures for the Department of Public Safety and Correctional Services and the court system regarding the management and discharge of individuals under lifetime sexual offender supervision.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Department of Public Safety and Correctional Services
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: DPSCS is the primary agency responsible for the bill's implementation. Its units, the Division of Parole and Probation (DPP) and the Maryland Parole Commission (MPC), are tasked with overseeing lifetime sexual offender supervision, enforcing conditions, and reporting violations. The bill also requires the department to approve sexual offender treatment providers and polygraph examiners.

The bill directly modifies the responsibilities of sentencing and juvenile courts regarding the imposition of special conditions for sexual offender supervision and the adjudication of petitions for discharge. It establishes new requirements for court hearings and notifications to the State's Attorney.

The bill explicitly applies to individuals required to register as sexual offenders through the juvenile court system. It mandates that juvenile courts impose special conditions and adjudicate supervision terms, which impacts the youth and programs managed by DJS.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Executive Commissions, Committees, Task Forces, and Advisory Boards
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Sexual Offender Advisory Board, which falls under this category, is responsible for reviewing Maryland's laws and practices concerning sexual offenders, developing risk assessment criteria, and making recommendations for offender management—all of which are directly impacted by the policy changes in this bill.

The OAG provides legal counsel to the primary implementing agencies (DPSCS and DJS) and represents the state in matters related to criminal procedure. This bill's changes to sentencing and discharge processes for sexual offenders may require legal guidance and representation in future court proceedings.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Governor's Office of Crime Prevention and Policy
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: GOCPP is the state's coordinating body for public safety strategy and manages victim services funding. The bill's focus on enhancing public safety through offender supervision and mandatory victim notification for discharge petitions aligns with GOCPP's mission.

Synopsis: Authorizing the State Superintendent of Schools to declare a prolonged state of emergency for an event that prevents regular, in-person attendance at a public school for at least 14 consecutive school days, subject to certain requirements; and requiring the State Board to adopt certain regulations including establishing minimum criteria for the adoption and implementation of virtual education plans by a county board during a prolonged state of emergency affecting the local school system.
Title: State Superintendent of Schools - Prolonged State of Emergency - Authority to Declare
Status: Approved by the Governor - Chapter 599

NarrowSubjects.Name: General Assembly -see also- AELR Cmte; LegislativePolCmte
Health -see also- COVID19; EnvHlth; MedCon; etc.
Public Schools -see also- Primary Schools; Secondary Sch

bill_summary: This bill authorizes the Maryland State Superintendent of Schools to declare a prolonged state of emergency for individual public schools or local school systems if disasters, public health emergencies, or security threats prevent in-person attendance for at least 14 consecutive days. This declaration enables schools to transition to virtual education under approved plans. The bill shifts the authority to declare these specific education-related emergencies from the Governor to the State Superintendent and establishes protocols for consultation, written notice, and emergency termination by the Superintendent, the State Board of Education, or the General Assembly.
stakeholders: Public school students, parents, teachers, and local school systems in Maryland
fiscal_impact_summary: According to the fiscal note, the bill has no state or local fiscal impact. The State Superintendent can declare and manage prolonged states of emergency using existing resources, and local school systems can meet the bill's requirements for virtual instruction using existing plans and resources without the need for additional funding or staffing.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The State Superintendent of Schools, who leads this department, is granted the primary authority to declare and terminate prolonged states of emergency for public schools, which allows local systems to transition to virtual education.

The bill shifts the authority to declare school-specific emergencies from the Governor to the State Superintendent, though it requires the Superintendent to consult with the Governor before making such a declaration.

The State Superintendent is required to consult with the department in the event of a public health emergency, and the bill explicitly preserves the existing statutory authority of the Secretary of Health during such emergencies.
The department is named as a required consulting partner for the State Superintendent when a prolonged state of emergency is declared due to natural or civil disasters.
The department must be consulted by the State Superintendent before declaring a prolonged state of emergency based on a specific security threat identified by law enforcement.

As the chief legal officer for state agencies, the OAG provides legal counsel to the State Superintendent, the State Board of Education, and the Governor regarding the implementation and legality of emergency declarations.

Specific security threats are a primary trigger for emergency declarations under the bill; the center provides a coordinated approach to school safety and manages safety reporting systems relevant to such threats.
Transitions to virtual education during a declared emergency involve collective bargaining considerations for school employees, a process for which this board has jurisdiction and oversight.
The office advises the Governor on public safety and coordinates disaster response, which are key triggers (security threats and disasters) for the emergency declarations authorized by the bill.

Synopsis: Authorizing the Central Collection Unit and the Child Support Administration to certify certain information about certain restitution, child support, and State debt obligors to a video lottery operator for purposes of enforcing a requirement to intercept certain prize payouts; requiring a video lottery operator to provide certain notice to a debtor that wins a prize to be paid by the operator and withhold all or part of the prize; authorizing certain debtors to appeal the proposed transfer; etc.
Title: Video Lottery Facility Payouts - Intercepts for Restitution Payments, Child Support Payments, and Debts Owed to the State
Status: Approved by the Governor - Chapter 88

NarrowSubjects.Name: Awards, Medals, and Prizes -see also- Gaming&Gambl; Lottery
Debt Collection -see also- Attachments and Garnishments

bill_summary: This bill authorizes the Central Collection Unit and the Child Support Administration to certify information regarding individuals who owe restitution, child support, or State debts to video lottery operators. These operators are then required to intercept and withhold prize payouts from these individuals to satisfy the outstanding debts. The bill also establishes a notification requirement for operators and an appeal process for the affected debtors.
responsible_party: Central Collection Unit (CCU), Child Support Administration (CSA), and the State Lottery and Gaming Control Agency (SLGCA)
stakeholders: Individuals with outstanding state debts, child support arrears, or restitution obligations; video lottery facility operators; and Maryland State agencies including CCU and CSA.
fiscal_impact_summary: According to the Fiscal Note, State revenues across all funds are estimated to increase by at least $3,000,000 annually beginning in fiscal 2027 from prize interceptions. Special fund revenues for the Central Collection Fund are expected to increase by at least $510,000 annually due to the 17% administrative fee charged by the CCU. Local community college revenues may also increase to the extent that gaming prizes are intercepted for debts referred to the CCU on their behalf. State agencies can implement the bill with existing resources.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Maryland State Lottery & Gaming Control Agency
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The agency is the primary regulator of the state's lottery and video lottery facilities (casinos). The bill, which was a departmental request, authorizes the agency's director to jointly adopt regulations and requires the agency to monitor compliance and honor interception requests in a specific priority order.

The department houses the Central Collection Unit (CCU), which is responsible for collecting delinquent state debts and restitution. The bill authorizes CCU to certify these debts to video lottery operators for prize interception, and the Secretary of DBM is authorized to jointly adopt implementing regulations.

The department oversees the Child Support Administration (CSA), which is authorized by the bill to certify child support arrears to video lottery operators for the purpose of intercepting gambling prizes.

The bill establishes an appeal process for individuals whose prizes are intercepted. OAH is the independent agency responsible for conducting these contested case hearings, and the fiscal note indicates it will need to handle an increase in cases and train judges on the bill's provisions.

The department is explicitly authorized in the bill to refer overdue restitution accounts for collection to the Central Collection Unit, which will then use the casino intercept program to recover these funds.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Department of Public Safety and Correctional Services
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The department oversees the Division of Parole and Probation, which is responsible for referring delinquent restitution accounts to the Central Collection Unit for collection via the intercept mechanisms modified by this bill.

The commission coordinates policy for community colleges, which the fiscal note identifies as beneficiaries of the bill. Community colleges refer delinquent accounts to the CCU, and their revenues are expected to increase from improved debt collection at casinos.

Member institutions within the system refer delinquent tuition and fee accounts to the Central Collection Unit. The fiscal note indicates that state institutions will benefit from increased revenues through the interception of video lottery prizes.
As a state agency, the university refers delinquent student accounts to the Central Collection Unit and will likely see an increase in recovered funds through the casino intercept program.
As an independent unit of state government, the college refers delinquent debts to the Central Collection Unit and is a beneficiary of the bill's expanded collection mechanisms.
The fiscal note explicitly identifies MVA fines as typical debts referred to the Central Collection Unit that would be intercepted under this bill.
As the parent agency of the Motor Vehicle Administration (MVA), the department will see increased revenue collection for delinquent fines and fees through the casino intercept program.

The fiscal note mentions that restitution for damage to state property is a typical debt referred to the CCU. As the agency responsible for managing state facilities, DGS is a primary beneficiary of these specific restitution recoveries.

The Comptroller is the state's principal tax collector and a key partner in the existing state debt intercept framework. The bill references the Comptroller's role in income tax refund interceptions in the context of broader state debt collection efforts.

The OAG serves as the chief legal representative for the state agencies involved (SLGCA, DBM, DHS) and would likely provide counsel regarding the regulation and enforcement of the new intercept requirements.
The Governor provides high-level executive oversight of the implementing agencies and signed the legislation into law.

Synopsis: Establishing the Buy Maryland Cybersecurity Tax Credit; stating the purpose of the credit is to promote the cybersecurity industry in the State by helping Maryland businesses and nonprofits purchase cybersecurity technology services from Maryland companies; altering eligibility for the credit; increasing from $200,000 to $1,000,000 the aggregate amount of credits that may be issued for certain cybersecurity purchases; making the credit refundable; etc.
Title: Income Tax – Cybersecurity Technology and Service Tax Credit – Alterations
Status: In the House - Hearing 1/29 at 1:00 p.m.
bill_summary: This bill renames the Cybersecurity Technology and Service Tax Credit to the Buy Maryland Cybersecurity Tax Credit and establishes its purpose as promoting the cybersecurity industry in Maryland. Key changes include expanding eligibility by increasing the revenue cap for qualified sellers to $10,000,000 and removing the employee limit for qualified buyers, making the tax credit fully refundable, and increasing the aggregate credit limit for purchases from a single seller to $1,000,000 per year.
stakeholders: Maryland businesses and nonprofits (buyers), Maryland-based cybersecurity companies (sellers), and small businesses in the cybersecurity technology sector.
fiscal_impact_summary: According to the Fiscal Note, State and local revenues are estimated to decrease by $3,500,000 annually from fiscal 2027 through 2031. This includes an annual general fund revenue decrease of $2,800,000, a $200,000 decrease for the Higher Education Investment Fund, and a $600,000 decrease for the Transportation Trust Fund. Local highway user revenues are expected to decrease by approximately $100,000 per year. These estimates assume the program's existing $4,000,000 annual award cap will be fully utilized as a result of the bill's expanded eligibility and refundability provisions.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: As the primary agency implementing the Buy Maryland Cybersecurity Tax Credit, Commerce is responsible for defining 'qualified buyers' and 'qualified sellers,' approving credit certificate applications, reporting on outcomes, and managing the overall program budget and utilization.

The Comptroller is responsible for processing the tax credits and refunds on income tax returns, and has the authority to make assessments against qualified buyers to recapture tax credits if certification is revoked.

The fiscal note indicates a significant revenue decrease for the Transportation Trust Fund (TTF) and a reduction in expenditures for local highway user revenue grants, both of which fall under the fiscal management of MDOT.

This is a departmental bill proposed by the Department of Commerce, an executive branch agency, and aligns with the Governor's role in overseeing policy initiatives related to economic development and the cybersecurity industry.
The fiscal note identifies the Strategic Energy Investment Fund (SEIF) as a special fund that could potentially lose revenue if certain corporations claim the cybersecurity tax credit.
The bill repeals the authority for the Department of Commerce to establish an expert panel in consultation with TEDCO to assist in determining whether a company is a qualified seller.

The OAG provides legal counsel to the Department of Commerce and the Comptroller in developing the regulations required by the bill and ensuring the enforcement of tax credit revocation and recapture provisions.

The bill's changes are expected to decrease revenues for the Higher Education Investment Fund (HEIF), which supports state policies and funding for postsecondary institutions overseen by the Commission.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Governor's Office of Small, Minority & Women Business Affairs
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill expands the definition of 'qualified seller' to include businesses owned by individuals from groups historically deprived of access to resources, including minority, women, and veteran-owned businesses, which aligns with this office's mission to monitor socioeconomic procurement and business programs.

Synopsis: Authorizing the State Lottery and Gaming Control Commission to establish a certain limit, by regulation, on the amount of money given away as free promotional play by a sports wagering licensee that may be excluded from sports wagering proceeds.
Title: Sports Wagering Proceeds - Promotional Play Exclusion - Limitation
Status: In the House - Hearing 2/05 at 1:00 p.m.

NarrowSubjects.Name: Licenses -see also- AB Lic; Certifications; DrLic; Permits

bill_summary: The bill authorizes the State Lottery and Gaming Control Commission to establish a limit on the amount of free promotional play that sports wagering licensees may exclude from their taxable proceeds after their first full fiscal year of operations.
responsible_party: Maryland State Lottery and Gaming Control Commission
stakeholders: Sports wagering facility licensees, mobile sports wagering licensees, and the Maryland State Lottery and Gaming Control Agency.
fiscal_impact_summary: According to the Fiscal Note, the bill has no state or local fiscal impact because it codifies existing procedures. While the document mentions that related regulatory changes could potentially increase General Fund revenues by $2,000,000 and Blueprint for Maryland’s Future Fund revenues by $6,000,000 annually by lowering promotional play caps, the bill itself is determined to have no direct fiscal effect.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Maryland State Lottery & Gaming Control Agency
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: This bill was requested by the agency and directly grants the State Lottery and Gaming Control Commission the authority to establish limits, via regulation, on promotional play exclusions from sports wagering proceeds. The agency is the primary regulator and implementing body for the bill's provisions.

The Comptroller is the state's principal tax collector. Since sports wagering is subject to state taxes, the definition of 'proceeds'—and the limitations on promotional play exclusions—directly affects the calculation and collection of state revenue from licensees.

The Department of Budget and Management is responsible for revenue estimation and long-term fiscal planning. The fiscal note indicates that limiting promotional play exclusions may increase revenues for the General Fund and the Blueprint for Maryland’s Future Fund, both of which are central to the state budget.

The bill impacts revenue for the Blueprint for Maryland’s Future Fund, which is used to support the state's public education system. As the agency responsible for leading the public education system and managing related state and federal funding, this impact on a dedicated education fund is highly relevant.

The Office of the Attorney General serves as the legal representative and counsel for all state agencies, including the Maryland State Lottery & Gaming Control Agency. They would be involved in the drafting and legal review of the regulations authorized by this bill.

Synopsis: Altering the schedule by which a county and Baltimore City must reimburse the State Department of Assessments and Taxation for the Department's administrative costs.
Title: State Department of Assessments and Taxation – Local Reimbursement for Administration Costs – Alterations
Status: In the House - Unfavorable Report by Ways and Means; Withdrawn

NarrowSubjects.Name: Counties -see also- Chartered Counties; Code Counties; etc.

bill_summary: This bill changes the schedule for when Maryland counties and Baltimore City must reimburse the State Department of Assessments and Taxation (SDAT) for property assessment and information technology costs. It replaces the previous quarterly payment schedule with a new requirement to pay 50% of the costs by October 1, followed by 25% on January 1 and 25% on April 1.
responsible_party: State Department of Assessments and Taxation
stakeholders: Maryland county governments and Baltimore City
fiscal_impact_summary: The bill has no net fiscal impact on State or local government finances. While it alters the timing of reimbursement payments for property tax assessment and information technology services, it does not change the total amount paid by local jurisdictions or received by the State Department of Assessments and Taxation within a fiscal year.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill explicitly requires local jurisdictions to remit administrative reimbursement payments to the Comptroller and authorizes the Comptroller to withhold local income tax distributions from any jurisdiction that fails to make timely payments.

As the principal fiscal agency for the state, the Department of Budget and Management oversees budget execution and the receipt of state revenues, which includes the reimbursements for the State Department of Assessments and Taxation's administrative costs.

The bill specifies the reimbursement of costs for the Office of Information Technology within the assessments department, including funding for projects in the Major Information Technology Development Project Fund, which is overseen by DoIT.

The Governor's Office overseeing the executive branch departments, including the State Department of Assessments and Taxation, and submitted this departmental bill to improve the efficiency of local reimbursement and state accounting processes.
The State Treasurer's Office is the chief financial agency responsible for receiving and depositing state funds, including the administrative reimbursements remitted by local governments.

The board provides administrative review of property tax assessments conducted by the state; this bill alters the funding and reimbursement schedule for the administration that performs the primary valuation work.

Synopsis: Authorizing the Governing Board of the Maryland Longitudinal Data System Center to provide certain student and workforce data to a third-party data center under certain circumstances; requiring each third-party data center to agree to comply with certain requirements relating to the data the center receives; requiring the Center to enter into a written data sharing agreement with certain third-party data centers; requiring the Center to submit a report to certain committees within 30 days of entering into a certain agreement; etc.
Title: Maryland Longitudinal Data System Center - External Data Sharing With Third-Party Data Centers for Multistate Reporting - Authorization
Status: Approved by the Governor - Chapter 100

NarrowSubjects.Name: Work, Labor, and Employment -see also- JobTrn; Leave; etc.

bill_summary: The bill authorizes the Maryland Longitudinal Data System (MLDS) Center to provide individual-level student and workforce data to a third-party data center for the purpose of multistate research and reporting. It establishes strict security and privacy requirements, including mandatory FedRAMP certification for the third-party platform, the use of de-identified data for analysis, and formal data-sharing agreements. The bill also mandates that the MLDS Center Governing Board review these agreements annually and provide reports to the General Assembly, while repealing the Center's previous authorization to share student data with the U.S. Census Bureau.
stakeholders: Maryland students and workforce participants whose data is maintained in the longitudinal system, the MLDS Center, and partner State agencies including the Department of Education and the Department of Labor.
fiscal_impact_summary: The Maryland Longitudinal Data System Center can implement the bill using existing resources, and State revenues are not affected. A grant has already been secured to facilitate the initial multistate data sharing work, ensuring no new fiscal burden on the State. There is no fiscal impact on local governments.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill directly concerns the authority and operations of the MLDS Center, specifically regarding its power to share individual-level student and workforce data with third-party data centers for multistate reporting.
As a primary contributor of student data to the MLDS, MSDE is directly impacted by changes in how that data is shared with external third-party research platforms.
MHEC is a major data contributor to the MLDS. The bill also removes MLDS authority to share data with the Census Bureau for a project (PSEO) that MHEC has now taken over.
MD Labor is the primary source of workforce data for the MLDS. The bill authorizes the sharing of individual-level workforce data with external third-party data centers.
DJS provides juvenile delinquency data to the MLDS and is listed as a source for social determinant data, which may be included in external sharing for research purposes.
DHS provides child welfare data to the MLDS and is listed as a source for social determinant data, which is impacted by new external data sharing protocols.
MDH provides social determinant data to the MLDS that impacts student performance, and this data is subject to the security and sharing provisions of the bill.
The OAG provides legal counsel to the MLDS Center and would be responsible for reviewing the legally required 'written data sharing agreements' with third-party data centers.
DoIT oversees state IT strategy and cybersecurity. The bill mandates specific security standards, such as FedRAMP certification, for any external third-party data centers receiving state data.
As a provider of student and workforce outcome data to the MLDS, the institutions within the USM are impacted by the governance of external data sharing.
As an independent state university that provides data to the MLDS, MSU is affected by the protocols for sharing student data with third-party research platforms.
As a state agency and public honors college that provides data to the MLDS, it is impacted by changes in the longitudinal data sharing framework.

Synopsis: Altering exemptions from the personal property tax for business personal property that has a total original cost below $20,000 by repealing provisions of law that prohibit the State Department of Assessments and Taxation from collecting information or requiring the submission of a personal property tax return from certain businesses that qualify for the exemptions; and applying the Act to all taxable years beginning after June 30, 2026.
Title: Personal Property Tax - Exemptions for Low Assessment - Alteration
Status: In the House - Hearing 1/27 at 2:00 p.m.

NarrowSubjects.Name: Commerce and Business -see also- ElectrComm; ForeignTr; etc.

bill_summary: This bill repeals the prohibition on the State Department of Assessments and Taxation (SDAT) from collecting personal property information or requiring a personal property tax return from businesses that qualify for a tax exemption because their personal property has a total original cost of less than $20,000. By allowing the collection of this information, the bill enables SDAT to verify eligibility for the exemption and conduct audits for tax compliance.
responsible_party: State Department of Assessments and Taxation (SDAT)
stakeholders: Business owners with personal property valued under $20,000, local county and municipal governments, and the State Department of Assessments and Taxation.
fiscal_impact_summary: According to the fiscal note, the bill has no impact on State expenditures or revenues as SDAT can handle the requirements with existing resources. Local government revenues may see a minimal increase to the extent that improved verification and compliance efforts identify businesses that should be paying personal property taxes.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The PTAAB is the administrative body responsible for hearing appeals regarding personal property tax valuations and assessments. This bill, which alters the reporting and exemption verification process for personal property, directly impacts the assessment data that form the basis for cases heard by these local boards.

The Maryland Tax Court adjudicates appeals from the final decisions of the Property Tax Assessment Appeals Boards. As the bill increases SDAT's authority to require returns and verify assessments for small businesses, it may lead to an increase in contested valuations and subsequent appeals to the Tax Court.

The OAG provides legal counsel to state agencies like SDAT and represents the state in tax-related litigation and appeals. This bill's implementation and any subsequent enforcement or disputes regarding the new reporting requirements would involve the OAG.

As the state's chief financial officer and principal tax collector, the Comptroller has a general interest in tax compliance and the administration of personal property tax laws, even though the tax itself is collected locally.

The Department of Commerce is concerned with the regulatory burden and reporting requirements for Maryland businesses. This bill removes an exemption from filing tax returns for many small businesses, which directly affects the business climate the department monitors.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Governor's Office of Small, Minority & Women Business Affairs
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill's impact is specifically targeted at businesses with personal property valued under $20,000, which are primarily small businesses. Changes to their reporting requirements and tax compliance obligations fall within the office's scope of concern for the small business community.

DBM is the principal fiscal agency overseeing state personnel and budget execution. While the personal property tax is local, DBM manages the fiscal planning and resources for the agencies (like SDAT) tasked with implementing the new verification and data collection duties.

bill_summary: The bill prohibits the operation, conduct, or promotion of unauthorized interactive games (online casino-style, lottery, or sports wagering games involving consideration, chance, and reward) in Maryland. It mandates that gaming license applicants and holders report business relationships with entities promoting such games and prohibits the issuance of licenses to persons deriving revenue from illegal gaming markets or high-risk jurisdictions. Violations are classified as misdemeanors subject to fines between $10,000 and $100,000 and license revocation.
responsible_party: Maryland State Lottery and Gaming Control Commission
stakeholders: Gaming license applicants, current licensees, business affiliates of gaming entities, and individuals or entities involved in illegal online gaming markets.
fiscal_impact_summary: State general fund expenditures increase by $110,800 in FY 2027 for the Office of the Attorney General to hire an assistant Attorney General to assist with increased enforcement. Annual costs for this position are projected to rise to $150,500 by FY 2031. Special fund revenues and expenditures for the Problem Gambling Fund may increase minimally from criminal fines of $10,000 to $100,000 per violation. Local government finances are not expected to be materially affected.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Maryland State Lottery & Gaming Control Agency
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: This is a departmental bill requested by the Maryland State Lottery & Gaming Control Agency (SLGCA). The bill grants the agency new regulatory and enforcement authority over illegal interactive games, establishes new licensing disclosure requirements regarding illegal gaming markets, and authorizes the Commission to issue cease and desist notices and revoke licenses.

The fiscal note explicitly identifies a significant fiscal impact for the OAG, requiring $110,800 in FY 2027 to hire an Assistant Attorney General to provide legal guidance and handle increased enforcement and investigations of illegal gaming operations resulting from the bill.

The bill requires that the revocation of a license for accepting revenue from illegal jurisdictions or high-risk jurisdictions must occur after notice and an opportunity for a hearing. The OAH is the independent agency responsible for conducting these administrative hearings for the SLGCA.

The bill creates a new criminal offense in the Criminal Law Article (Section 12-115) regarding the operation or promotion of illegal interactive games. As the state's primary law enforcement agency and a listed information source in the fiscal note, the Maryland State Police are responsible for investigating and enforcing these criminal provisions.

The bill mandates that fines collected from violations of the new interactive gaming prohibitions be distributed to the Problem Gambling Fund. The Maryland Department of Health is typically involved in the administration or provision of services funded by such resources, specifically for behavioral health and addiction treatment.

As the principal fiscal agency, DBM is responsible for the budget execution of the new position within the Office of the Attorney General and oversees the fiscal implications of gaming revenue distributions discussed in the fiscal note.

The Governor's Office oversees the SLGCA as an executive agency and this bill is a departmental request. Additionally, the Governor signs the legislation and coordinates the state's broad public safety and economic policies affected by gaming regulation.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Governor's Office of Crime Prevention and Policy
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: This agency advises the Governor on criminal justice strategies and coordinates public safety efforts. The bill introduces new criminal penalties and law enforcement priorities related to illegal online gaming and international money flows from illegal markets.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Governor's Office of Small, Minority & Women Business Affairs
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: Maryland's gaming licensing framework includes integrated socioeconomic procurement goals (MBE/SBR/VSBE programs). Changes to licensing eligibility and reporting requirements for gaming entities fall under the oversight of this office regarding small and minority business participation.

The Comptroller is the state's principal tax collector and was listed as an information source for the fiscal note. While the bill focuses on licensing and criminal prohibitions, any impact on gaming activities has downstream effects on state revenue collection and financial auditing.
