bill_summary: This bill requires each Maryland county board of education to ensure that every public school regularly restocks dispensers in women's restrooms with menstrual hygiene products to ensure they are available at no charge to students.
stakeholders: Public school students in Maryland and local county boards of education.
fiscal_impact_summary: According to the Fiscal Note, there is no impact on State finances. The impact on local governments is expected to be minimal because the bill clarifies current law that already requires schools to provide these products. Any additional costs associated with ensuring regular restocking are expected to be absorbed by local school systems using existing resources.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Maryland State Department of Education (MSDE) is the primary state agency responsible for overseeing the 24 local school systems. The bill directly amends the Education Article and requires 'the Department' (MSDE) to manage reimbursement requests for dispensers, while providing leadership for the implementation of the new restocking requirements.

As a state-operated public school system providing education for students through age 21, the Maryland School for the Deaf would be expected to comply with public school standards for hygiene and health resources in its restrooms, aligning with the bill's requirements for public schools.

The Office of the Attorney General serves as the primary legal representative for state agencies, including MSDE. It would be responsible for providing legal guidance to the Department and the State Board of Education regarding the enforcement and interpretation of the new restocking mandates.

As the agency responsible for state budget oversight, DBM monitors legislation with fiscal implications. Although the current fiscal note suggests no immediate state fiscal impact for the restocking requirement, DBM tracks potential future funding requests or aid adjustments related to educational mandates.

Synopsis: Expanding eligibility for the Maryland earned income tax credit for  individuals without qualifying children by altering the income thresholds at which the credit phases out; providing that, after the 2025 tax year, the income threshold and phase-out amounts are adjusted annually for inflation; and applying the Act to all taxable years beginning after December 31, 2025.
Title: Earned Income Tax Credit - Individuals Without Qualifying Children - Eligibility
Status: In the House - Hearing 2/12 at 1:00 p.m.
bill_summary: This bill expands eligibility for the Maryland earned income tax credit for individuals without qualifying children by increasing the income threshold at which the credit begins to phase out and providing for annual cost-of-living adjustments starting after tax year 2025.
stakeholders: Low-to-moderate income Maryland residents without qualifying children and Montgomery County
fiscal_impact_summary: State general fund revenues are estimated to decrease by $101,300,000 in FY 2027, with projected annual decreases growing to $117,900,000 by FY 2031. While local revenues are not affected, Montgomery County may experience increased expenditures for its local earned income credit supplement program starting in FY 2027.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Comptroller of Maryland is the primary agency responsible for tax collection and the administration of tax laws. The bill directly requires the Comptroller to implement the expanded Earned Income Tax Credit formulas and calculate annual inflation-based adjustments for the income thresholds.

The Department of Budget and Management is responsible for revenue estimation and fiscal planning. This bill is projected to decrease general fund revenues by more than $100 million annually, which has a significant impact on the state budget and revenue forecasts managed by this department.

The Governor's Office oversees the executive branch and proposes the annual state budget. The significant revenue impact and the policy shift regarding poverty reduction and economic mobility are central to the Governor's executive and budgetary responsibilities.

As the chief financial agency responsible for the management and protection of state funds, the Treasurer's Office is impacted by major changes in state revenue streams and serves on the Board of Public Works, which oversees fiscal integrity.

The Department of Human Services assists Marylanders in economic need. The expansion of the Earned Income Tax Credit aligns with the agency's mission to provide financial support and aid to vulnerable and low-income populations.

The Maryland Tax Court adjudicates disputes regarding income tax and tax credit determinations. Changes to eligibility and phase-out thresholds for the EITC may lead to new cases or appeals within its jurisdiction.

The Innovation Team is tasked with developing strategies for economic mobility. Expanding the EITC for individuals without qualifying children is a key policy mechanism for enhancing economic mobility for low-income workers.

The Office of the Attorney General provides legal counsel to state agencies, including the Comptroller, regarding the interpretation and enforcement of state tax laws and any potential litigation resulting from changes to the tax code.

Synopsis: Authorizing a landlord to impose an increased security deposit if a tenant operates or plans to operate a family child care home on the leased premises; prohibiting a landlord of certain residential rental property from prohibiting or unreasonably limiting the operation of a family child care home on the property; providing that landlords of certain residential rental property are immune from civil liability; authorizing a landlord to require a certain tenant to purchase a liability insurance policy; applying the Act prospectively; etc.
Title: Real Property - Landlord and Tenant - Family Child Care Homes
Status: In the House - Laid Over (Delegate Hartman) Adopted

NarrowSubjects.Name: Insurance -see also- Health Ins; MAIF; Motor Vehicle Ins

bill_summary: This bill prohibits landlords of single-family dwellings from refusing to lease to or unreasonably restricting tenants who operate or plan to operate a registered family child care home. It allows landlords to charge an increased security deposit of up to two months' rent, requires tenants to provide 60 days' notice and liability insurance naming the landlord as an additional insured, and grants landlords immunity from civil liability related to the child care operations.
responsible_party: Maryland State Department of Education and the Maryland Judiciary
stakeholders: Residential landlords, tenants, family child care home operators, and families seeking child care services.
fiscal_impact_summary: According to the fiscal note, the bill is not anticipated to materially affect Maryland State or local government operations or finances. It may have a potential meaningful impact on small businesses by increasing opportunities for family child care home operations. Specific financial impacts include the authorization of higher security deposits for landlords and insurance requirements for tenants.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill defines 'family child care home' by referencing the Education Article and requires tenants to provide the landlord with a registration issued by the Department under Title 9.5, Subtitle 3 to operate on the premises.

The bill requires tenants to provide certificates of insurance naming landlords as additional insureds and allows landlords to mandate liability insurance policies with specific coverage limits ($1,000,000).
The OAG's Consumer Protection Division often handles landlord-tenant disputes and provides guidance on the enforcement of residential lease laws, which this bill substantively amends.

The bill creates new statutory requirements for residential leases and security deposits, and explicitly mentions that tenants may recover up to three times the extra amount charged in a court action for security deposit violations.

The bill's provisions regarding increased security deposits for child care homes are added into a section of the Real Property Article that already references tenant eligibility for utility assistance through DHS.

The bill explicitly states that its provisions do not limit or preempt the local zoning authority of counties or municipalities, a subject area where the Department of Planning provides data analysis and policy guidance.

Synopsis: Prohibiting an individual from smoking, vaping, or consuming cannabis in the passenger area of a motor vehicle in which a minor is an occupant.

bill_summary: This bill prohibits any individual from smoking, vaping, or consuming cannabis in the passenger area of a motor vehicle if a minor is present. Violators are guilty of a misdemeanor and are subject to a maximum fine of $1,000 and/or imprisonment for up to one year.
responsible_party: Maryland Judiciary and the Department of Public Safety and Correctional Services
stakeholders: Motor vehicle drivers and passengers, minors, and Maryland law enforcement agencies
fiscal_impact_summary: The bill's penalty provisions are expected to result in a minimal increase in State and local revenues and expenditures. The Judiciary and law enforcement agencies are expected to implement the bill using existing budgeted resources. Specific aggregate dollar estimates for the total revenue generated from fines are not provided.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: As the primary law enforcement agency for Maryland's highways and state motor vehicle laws, the Maryland State Police would be responsible for enforcing the new prohibition on cannabis use in vehicles with minor occupants.

The MVA maintains driving records and manages the licensing system. Under current laws for similar offenses, the MVA is responsible for assessing points against a violator's license, making them essential for the administrative implementation of the bill's penalties.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Maryland Office of the Public Defender
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill creates a new misdemeanor offense carrying a penalty of up to one year of imprisonment. This directly impacts the OPD, which is mandated to provide legal representation for indigent defendants facing jailable offenses.

The AOC provides support to the state's courts. It would be responsible for managing the administrative and technological processing of new charges, convictions, and fines issued under this updated section of the Transportation Article.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Department of Public Safety and Correctional Services
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: Since the bill establishes a criminal penalty involving potential incarceration for up to one year, the DPSCS would be responsible for individuals sentenced to local or state correctional facilities and those placed on parole or probation.

MDOT is the parent agency for the state's transportation administrations, including the MVA. The bill proposes changes to the Transportation Article, which falls under MDOT's regulatory and operational oversight.

The MCA is the independent agency responsible for regulating the cannabis industry and developing public health regulations. This bill intersects with their mission to ensure the safe and legal consumption of cannabis in Maryland.

As the chief legal representative of the state, the OAG provides counsel to agencies involved in transportation and health and would represent the state in appeals related to this new criminal statute.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Governor's Office of Crime Prevention and Policy
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: GOCPP is the state's primary body for coordinating criminal justice strategies. This bill introduces a new criminal penalty as a matter of public safety policy, which aligns with GOCPP's advisory role.

The Governor's Office for Children focuses on the well-being and health services of Maryland's youth. This bill is intended to protect minors from the environmental health risks of cannabis smoke or vapor in vehicles.

The DHS is responsible for child protection services. Violations of this law involving a minor in a vehicle could lead to child welfare investigations or referrals handled by local departments of human services.

bill_summary: This bill authorizes licensed real estate brokers, associate brokers, and salespersons to act as transaction brokers in residential real estate transactions. In this nonagency relationship, the licensee facilitates the sale or lease of residential property for both parties without representing either party as an agent. The bill defines the limited fiduciary duties of transaction brokers, requires written informed consent from all parties involved, and mandates the State Real Estate Commission to develop a standard consent form for these transactions.
stakeholders: Licensed real estate brokers, associate real estate brokers, and real estate salespersons; residential property buyers, sellers, lessors, and lessees.
fiscal_impact_summary: A formal Fiscal Note is not included in the provided text, and specific dollar estimates are unavailable. The bill requires the State Real Estate Commission to develop and provide a standard consent form to all licensees, which may result in minor administrative expenditures. Additionally, the bill allows for disciplinary actions against licensees who fail to provide required disclosures, which could theoretically result in fine revenue, though no specific amounts are stated.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill regulates licensed real estate brokers, associate brokers, and salespersons, all of whom are overseen by the State Real Estate Commission, a regulatory board within the Department of Labor. The bill specifically tasks the Commission with developing and providing a standard consent form for transaction brokerage.

The Office of the Attorney General provides legal counsel to state boards and commissions, including the State Real Estate Commission. Additionally, its Consumer Protection Division may be involved in overseeing or enforcing consumer rights related to the new nonagency 'transaction broker' relationships established by this bill.

The bill amends the grounds for disciplinary action against real estate licensees. The Office of Administrative Hearings is responsible for conducting the impartial hearings required when the State Real Estate Commission seeks to reprimand, suspend, or revoke a license for violations of these regulations.

bill_summary: This bill requires the Maryland State Department of Education to make a professional development course on educator well-being and flourishing available to all school personnel and administrators by July 1, 2027. The course must cover eight specific dimensions of well-being, including social, physical, and emotional health, and may be provided through synchronous or asynchronous instruction.
stakeholders: Maryland school personnel and administrators
fiscal_impact_summary: State general fund expenditures are not expected to be materially affected as the Maryland State Department of Education can fulfill the bill's requirements using existing resources, such as a course currently provided by Georgetown University. Furthermore, the department is only required to offer the course if it can be done at no cost or at a cost comparable to similar professional development courses. Local school system finances are not affected.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill explicitly mandates the State Department of Education (MSDE) to develop or provide a professional development course on educator well-being and flourishing for all school personnel and administrators.

As an independent unit within MSDE responsible for providing training and fostering supportive learning environments, this agency may be involved in delivering the well-being and flourishing curriculum, particularly regarding the 'feeling safe' component of the environmental well-being dimension.

The Governor's Office oversees the executive branch and MSDE. The Governor must approve the bill, and the office coordinates the policy initiatives and budget proposals that would encompass this educational requirement.

DBM is responsible for supervising budget execution and estimating revenues. While the fiscal note suggests no material impact, the agency monitors the general fund expenditures of MSDE related to program implementation.
The OAG provides legal counsel to MSDE and would likely review any third-party contracts or licenses required to adapt or make available the professional development course specified in the bill.

The MLDS Center links student and workforce data, including educator performance and professional development outcomes. The tracking of completion of this professional development course may eventually integrate into their data collection.

The PERB oversees collective bargaining for public school personnel. Changes to professional development requirements or availability can sometimes intersect with labor-management relations and working conditions for school staff.

bill_summary: This bill requires the Maryland Secretary of Agriculture to submit an annual report identifying additional agricultural equipment that should qualify for an income tax subtraction modification. Additionally, the bill establishes a $1,000 refundable income tax credit for parents who experience a stillbirth, with the credit amount phasing out for individuals with a federal adjusted gross income over $100,000 and for joint filers over $150,000.
responsible_party: Maryland Department of Agriculture and the Comptroller of Maryland
stakeholders: Maryland agricultural producers (farmers) and parents of stillborn children.
fiscal_impact_summary: According to the Fiscal Note, the Maryland Department of Agriculture can implement the bill's reporting requirements with existing budgeted resources and State revenues are not affected. However, the bill text also creates a $1,000 refundable income tax credit for parents of stillborn children for taxable years beginning after December 31, 2026, which would likely result in a future reduction of State income tax revenue not reflected in the provided Fiscal Note's specific figures.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Comptroller is the primary agency responsible for administering the state's tax laws. This bill creates a new refundable income tax credit for parents of stillborn children and modifies an existing subtraction modification for agricultural equipment, both of which require the Comptroller to update tax forms, process claims, and manage the resulting revenue impacts.

The bill mandates that the Secretary of Agriculture report annually to the Governor and General Assembly with recommendations for new equipment to qualify for tax subtractions. Furthermore, the agency is responsible for certifying that taxpayers are in compliance with requirements to receive these tax modifications.

The bill's new $1,000 tax credit is contingent upon the issuance of a 'Certificate of Birth Resulting in Stillbirth' under the Health – General Article. The Department of Health oversees the Vital Statistics Administration, which handles the issuance of such certificates.

As the state's principal fiscal agency, DBM is responsible for revenue estimation and budget supervision. The implementation of a new refundable tax credit and expanded subtraction modifications will affect the state's general fund revenues, requiring DBM's oversight.

The Secretary of Agriculture is required by the bill to submit an annual report specifically to the Governor regarding recommended agricultural equipment for tax modifications. Additionally, the Governor oversees the executive agencies implementing the bill's provisions.

The Maryland Tax Court hears appeals regarding final decisions made by taxing authorities. Disputed claims for the new stillborn child credit or the agricultural equipment subtraction would eventually be adjudicated by this court.

bill_summary: The Maryland Housing Certainty Act mandates that local regulatory authorities and the Maryland-National Capital Park and Planning Commission review housing development applications based on the laws and regulations in effect when a complete application is submitted. The bill grants developers vested rights to authorized use and development for at least five years after approval and prohibits the collection of development impact fees or excise taxes until construction is complete and occupancy permits are issued, with exceptions for certain pre-existing county debt.
responsible_party: Local regulatory authorities and the Maryland-National Capital Park and Planning Commission (M-NCPPC)
stakeholders: Residential housing developers, construction small businesses, local government planning and zoning departments, and the Maryland-National Capital Park and Planning Commission.
fiscal_impact_summary: State finances are not directly affected. Local government expenditures may increase to manage new administrative requirements for tracking application completeness and vesting periods. Local revenues from development impact fees and excise taxes will be delayed until construction completion; while specific loss estimates are unavailable, the aggregate annual revenue from these sources across Maryland counties was approximately 179,217,515 for fiscal 2025. This delay may necessitate increased local borrowing or delayed infrastructure spending.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Governor's Office oversees executive branch policy and proposed this legislation as part of a housing policy agenda. The bill focuses on housing certainty and economic mobility, which are key executive priorities.

The OAG will be responsible for providing legal counsel to state agencies regarding the implementation of the new 'vested rights' statutory framework, which replaces existing common law standards established by the courts.

The bill impacts the business climate for the housing and development industries by providing regulatory certainty and delaying fee collection, which aligns with the agency's mission to stimulate the economy and attract business.

The bill delays the collection of local development impact fees, which are a primary source of funding for local school systems and infrastructure. This delay impacts the timing of revenue for educational facilities.

The bill mandates that permit approvals be governed by laws in effect at the time of application. This potentially affects environmental permits related to housing projects that MDE oversees or coordinates with local jurisdictions.

As the state's primary housing agency, DHCD is directly involved in policy related to residential real estate projects, housing expansion, and the economic vitality of Maryland communities affected by this bill.

MDP is the primary agency for state land use policy and providing guidance to local jurisdictions on planning and zoning. This bill makes significant amendments to the Land Use Article and local permitting procedures, which MDP oversees.
Local development impact fees and excise taxes often fund transportation infrastructure. Delaying these fees affects the funding timeline for roads and transit projects that support new developments.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Governor's Office of Small, Minority & Women Business Affairs
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The regulatory certainty and delayed fee collection provided by the bill may benefit small, minority, and women-owned businesses operating in the residential construction and development sectors.
The bill establishes new statutory 'vested rights' for property use, which will likely lead to increased litigation and requires the judiciary to interpret new legal standards for land use disputes.

The IAC manages funding for school construction projects. The bill's delay of impact fee collection directly impacts the revenue streams that local jurisdictions use to fund the school projects overseen by the IAC.

MEDCO provides financing and real estate development services. Changes in permitting laws and fee collection timing affect the feasibility and financing models of development projects supported by the agency.

The MSA manages the construction of public schools through the Built to Learn Act. The delay in local impact fee collection impacts the overall funding environment for the school facility improvements the MSA executes.

The team is tasked with addressing the Governor's top priorities, including enhancing economic mobility and reducing poverty. Improving housing certainty is a core component of this economic strategy.

The Tax Court adjudicates disputes regarding local taxes, including excise taxes. The bill's new restrictions on the collection of development excise taxes may lead to administrative appeals within this court's jurisdiction.
The bill's impact on land use planning and developer fees affects the economic development and infrastructure funding models of Maryland's 18 rural counties.

This multi-agency initiative is grounded in the land use planning visions that this bill amends. It coordinates sustainable development policy across departments, making it highly relevant to the bill's permitting reforms.

bill_summary: This bill updates the Maryland Public Ethics Law by requiring State officials and candidates for office to disclose interests in virtual currency valued at over $1,000 in their financial disclosure statements. It also expands the scope of the Public Ethics Law to include domestic partners and registered domestic partners in provisions that currently apply to spouses, such as conflict of interest regulations and financial disclosure requirements.
stakeholders: State officials, candidates for State office, registered lobbyists, and the domestic partners or registered domestic partners of these individuals.
fiscal_impact_summary: State expenditures increase by a total of $165,000 in FY 2027 only for the State Ethics Commission to hire contractual information technology services to update electronic training, disclosure, reporting, and audit systems. Of this total, $145,000 is allocated from general funds and $20,000 from the Lobbyist Registration Fund (special funds). The bill has no effect on State revenues or local government finances.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The State Ethics Commission is the primary agency responsible for administering and enforcing the Maryland Public Ethics Law. The bill requires the Commission to update its electronic financial disclosure and lobbying registration systems and training programs, with a projected fiscal impact of $165,000 in FY 2027.

The bill incorporates 'registered domestic partners' into the Public Ethics Law, referencing the Register of Wills as the entity where these partnerships are registered in accordance with the Estates and Trusts Article.

The Governor is a State official subject to ethics disclosures. The bill specifically adds the domestic partner of the Governor to the list of 'restricted individuals' and includes domestic partners in lobbyist reporting requirements related to the Governor's office.

The OSP investigates and prosecutes criminal offenses related to the integrity of state officials and the Public Ethics Law. Changes to financial disclosure requirements, such as reporting virtual currency and domestic partner interests, directly impact their investigative and enforcement jurisdiction.

Judges and judicial appointees are defined as State officials under the Public Ethics Law. The AOC must ensure that judicial branch officials comply with the new disclosure requirements for virtual currency and domestic partners.

The State Treasurer is a constitutional officer subject to these ethics updates. Additionally, the Treasurer manages the Lobbyist Registration Fund, which the fiscal note identifies as the source of $20,000 for the State Ethics Commission's system updates.

The Comptroller is a constitutional officer and State official. The bill includes domestic partners of the Comptroller in lobbyist reporting requirements and expands disclosure obligations for the official.

The Attorney General is a State official. The bill includes domestic partners of the Attorney General in lobbyist reporting requirements and expands disclosure obligations regarding virtual currency and family interests.

The Secretary of State is a State official. The bill includes domestic partners of the Secretary of State in lobbyist reporting requirements and expands conflict of interest and disclosure provisions.
The Lieutenant Governor is a State official. The bill includes domestic partners of the Lieutenant Governor in lobbyist reporting requirements and expands disclosure obligations.

As the central personnel agency, DBM oversees state employee policies. The Public Ethics Law applies to executive branch employees and officials, and the expansion of definitions to include domestic partners affects personnel ethics standards.

OLA conducts fiscal compliance audits of state agencies. They would be responsible for auditing the State Ethics Commission's implementation of the new disclosure schedules and ensuring officials' compliance with the updated laws.

bill_summary: The No Kings Act establishes civil liability for federal law enforcement officers who, while acting under color of law, deprive individuals of rights, privileges, or immunities secured by the U.S. Constitution. The bill allows for the recovery of reasonable attorney's fees and expert witness fees by prevailing plaintiffs, sets a five-year statute of limitations for filing claims, and applies retroactively to causes of action arising on or after March 1, 2025.
stakeholders: Federal law enforcement officers and individuals in Maryland whose constitutional rights are allegedly violated by those officers.
fiscal_impact_summary: A formal Fiscal Note is absent from the provided text, so specific revenue and expenditure estimates are unavailable. The bill establishes a new civil cause of action against federal law enforcement officers, which could increase the caseload and associated administrative costs for the Maryland court system. The bill also explicitly allows courts to award attorney's fees and expert witness fees to prevailing plaintiffs.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill establishes a new civil cause of action within the Maryland judiciary's jurisdiction, directly impacting the caseload and operational procedures of the state court system by adding Subtitle 27 to the Courts and Judicial Proceedings Article.

The OAG is responsible for providing legal counsel to state agencies and would likely handle constitutional challenges, provide interpretive guidance, and analyze the interplay between state and federal law regarding the liability of federal officers.

Maryland State Police frequently collaborate with federal agencies on joint task forces; this legislation alters the legal liability of federal partners in such operations, which could impact interagency cooperation and operational procedures.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Department of Public Safety and Correctional Services
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The department frequently collaborates with federal law enforcement, particularly for fugitive apprehension and task force activities; this bill introduces new state-court litigation risks for those federal partners.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Governor's Office of Crime Prevention and Policy
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: As the coordinating body for public safety and criminal justice policy, GOCPP is impacted by changes to the legal framework governing federal-state law enforcement partnerships and public safety strategies.

The Governor's Office oversees intergovernmental relations with federal entities and manages state executive branch policy, both of which are affected by legislation creating state-court jurisdiction over federal officers.

MDOT's law enforcement components, such as the MDTA Police and those at BWI Marshall Airport, regularly operate alongside federal agencies, making the legal status of federal partners relevant to their collaborative operations.

bill_summary: This bill repeals the criminal prohibitions, associated penalties, and statutory definitions related to drug paraphernalia and controlled paraphernalia in Maryland. Specifically, it eliminates the offenses of using, possessing, delivering, selling, or advertising drug and controlled paraphernalia, which were previously classified as misdemeanors with varying fines and terms of imprisonment.
responsible_party: Maryland Judiciary and the Department of Public Safety and Correctional Services
stakeholders: Individuals who use or possess drug-related paraphernalia, law enforcement agencies, the Maryland court system, and the Office of the Public Defender.
fiscal_impact_summary: According to the Fiscal Note, the bill will result in a minimal decrease in State general fund revenues due to the loss of fines previously imposed in the District Court. State expenditures for the Department of Public Safety and Correctional Services and the Office of the Public Defender are expected to remain stable, as resources will likely be reallocated. Local governments may see a minimal decrease in expenditures due to a reduction in reincarceration, while local revenues are not expected to be materially affected.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: As the state's primary law enforcement agency, the Maryland State Police is responsible for enforcing the criminal laws that this bill proposes to repeal. The removal of drug and controlled paraphernalia prohibitions will directly change their enforcement protocols and training requirements.

The bill will significantly reduce the number of criminal cases related to drug and controlled paraphernalia processed by the Maryland Judicial Branch. The fiscal note explicitly mentions a reduction in caseloads for the courts.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Maryland Office of the Public Defender
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Office of the Public Defender represents indigent individuals charged with the criminal offenses being repealed. The bill will result in a direct reduction in the agency's caseload for these specific charges.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Department of Public Safety and Correctional Services
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: DPSCS manages the incarceration, parole, and probation of individuals involved in the justice system. The repeal of these offenses will lead to a reduction in the number of individuals entering the state's correctional and supervision systems.

DJS is responsible for youth involved in the juvenile justice system. Since youth are subject to the criminal laws being repealed, this bill will decrease the number of juveniles entering supervision or residential facilities for paraphernalia-related offenses.

The bill modifies Title 5 of the Criminal Law Article, which defines the Department of Health as the primary oversight agency. The decriminalization of paraphernalia, which includes hypodermic needles and syringes, is a major public health policy shift relevant to the department's mission.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Governor's Office of Crime Prevention and Policy
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: This office advises the Governor on criminal justice strategy and coordinates public safety policies. The total repeal of paraphernalia-related criminal penalties is a major shift in state criminal justice policy that falls within their strategic planning and coordination scope.

As the chief legal officer for the state, the Office of the Attorney General provides counsel to state agencies and the General Assembly on the interpretation of the Maryland Criminal Law Article and will oversee the legal implications of these repeals for state agencies.

The Governor's Office oversees the executive branch and coordinates state policy. This bill represents a significant change in the state's approach to drug-related criminal law, aligning with broader executive policy initiatives.

bill_summary: This bill establishes the Commission on the House of Reformation and Instruction for Colored Children to investigate the historical operations, resident deaths, and unmarked graves at the former reformatory institution. The commission is tasked with identifying the deceased through archaeological and DNA analysis, notifying descendants, and recommending systemic reforms, reparations, and a permanent memorial.
stakeholders: Descendants of children buried at the site, former residents of the institution, African American communities in Maryland, and state agencies such as the Department of Juvenile Services and the Maryland Historical Trust.
fiscal_impact_summary: State general fund expenditures increase by $1,050,000 in FY 2027, reflecting funding included in the FY 2027 budget. Additional indeterminate expenditure increases may occur in FY 2028 and FY 2029 to support the commission's work. The Office of the Attorney General is expected to staff the commission using existing resources. Local government finances are not expected to be materially affected.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Attorney General chairs the commission, and the office is responsible for providing staff, administering funding, making public member appointments, procuring services, and exercising subpoena power for the investigation.

The Secretary of Juvenile Services is a member of the commission. The department operates the successor facility (Cheltenham Youth Detention Center) and its records and facilities are primary subjects of the commission's investigation.

The Director of the Maryland Historical Trust, which resides within this department, is a member of the commission. The commission must also consult with the Trust on archaeological methods and safety regarding the disinterment of human remains.
The State Archivist is a member of the commission, and the agency's records are a primary source for the historical research and identification of children buried at the site.
The commission is required to consult with the department regarding safety methods for disinterment and is granted access to the department's medical and administrative records for the investigation.
The Chief Archaeologist of the State Highway Administration is specifically named as a member of the commission, providing technical expertise for the archaeological surveys.

The State Superintendent of Schools is a member of the commission. Additionally, the commission is tasked with recommending educational initiatives to incorporate the history of the institution into the state's curriculum.
The Secretary of Human Services is a member of the commission, reflecting the department's role in oversight of children's welfare and historical state care.
The Secretary of General Services is a member of the commission, likely due to the agency's role in managing state-owned facilities and grounds where the cemetery is located.
The Secretary of Veterans and Military Families is a member of the commission and is involved in developing the cemetery conservation plan.

As the parent agency of the State Highway Administration, the department's Chief Archaeologist is a member of the commission, and the agency is mentioned in the fiscal note regarding the investigation.
The commission is required to submit both initial and final reports of its findings and recommendations to the Governor.
As the principal fiscal agency, DBM oversees the state budget which provides the funding for the commission's operations and contracted research.
The bill bypasses certain confidentiality statutes related to court records, granting the commission access to sealed juvenile records held by the Judiciary.
A representative from the University of Maryland Francis King Carey School of Law is a member of the commission, and USM institutions are prioritized for procurement of research services.
As a prominent Historically Black College and University (HBCU) in Maryland, the university is a preferred institution for the procurement of goods and services required by the commission.

bill_summary: This bill requires the Commissioner of Labor and Industry to post a user-friendly, searchable database of active elevator inspection certificates on the Maryland Department of Labor's website. responsible_party: Commissioner of Labor and Industry, Maryland Department of Labor
stakeholders: Elevator owners and lessees, the general public, and the Maryland Department of Labor
fiscal_impact_summary: The Maryland Department of Labor can likely implement the bill with existing resources. However, if current online resources (such as an Excel spreadsheet) do not meet the user-friendly database requirement, general fund expenditures may increase by a one-time cost of $75,000 to add a module to the existing internal database. There is no impact on state revenues or local government finances.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill explicitly requires the Commissioner of Labor and Industry, an official within the Maryland Department of Labor, to create and maintain the searchable elevator inspection certificate database on the department's website. The department is the primary agency responsible for enforcing the public safety laws related to elevator inspections.

As the agency responsible for the state's information technology strategy and digital services, the Department of Information Technology may provide technical oversight, support, or implementation services for the creation of the user-friendly searchable database module required on the state's website.

The fiscal note indicates a potential one-time general fund expenditure of $75,000 to implement the database module if existing resources are insufficient. DBM oversees state budget execution and fiscal planning related to these expenditures.

bill_summary: This bill revises, restates, and recodifies the laws governing the Janet L. Hoffman Loan Assistance Repayment Program (LARP). While primarily a technical and stylistic revision, the bill modifies eligibility requirements for certain professionals: it limits lawyer eligibility to graduates of Maryland law schools, removes certain degree requirements for specified licensed clinical counselors, and narrows teacher eligibility to those who qualify for the Nancy Grasmick Public School Professional Award.
responsible_party: Maryland Higher Education Commission's Office of Student Financial Assistance
stakeholders: Graduates of Maryland colleges and law schools, public school teachers, nurses, mental health professionals, licensed clinical counselors, and veterinary practitioners and technicians.
fiscal_impact_summary: State general fund expenditures for the Janet L. Hoffman Loan Assistance Repayment Program are budgeted at 4,100,000 for fiscal 2027. Although the bill modifies eligibility criteria for certain professional categories, it is not expected to alter total program spending, as applicants may be placed on a waiting list if funds are exhausted. The Maryland Higher Education Commission may incur a minimal, one-time increase in general fund expenditures in fiscal 2027 for computer programming updates. There is no local fiscal impact.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Maryland Higher Education Commission (MHEC) is the primary agency responsible for administering the Janet L. Hoffman Loan Assistance Repayment Program (LARP) through its Office of Student Financial Assistance. The bill recodifies the program's laws and alters eligibility criteria for various professional categories.
The bill mandates that the Maryland Department of Health (MDH) determines the 'high-need geographic areas' where clinical counselors must practice to qualify for the loan repayment program.

The bill outlines eligibility for education-related professionals, including public school teachers, nurses, and mental health professionals. It references teaching licenses issued by the Department and alternative preparation programs approved by the State Superintendent.
As the state's principal fiscal agency, DBM is impacted because the fiscal note indicates a likely increase in general fund expenditures for MHEC to update programming for eligibility changes.
The bill includes specific loan repayment provisions for veterinary practitioners and technicians; MDA is the primary state agency overseeing the agricultural and animal health community.
Graduates of Maryland's public universities are primary beneficiaries of the LARP. The bill specifically revises eligibility requirements for graduates of colleges and universities in the State.

As a state-funded institution, Morgan State's graduates are eligible participants in the loan assistance program, and the university has a vested interest in financial support for its alumni in high-need fields.
Graduates of St. Mary's College of Maryland who enter public service fields covered by the bill are eligible for the Janet L. Hoffman LARP.
The OAG provides legal counsel to MHEC and other state agencies, and would be responsible for ensuring that the code revisions and resulting regulations are legally sound.

The MLDS links student and workforce data; changes to loan repayment eligibility for graduates in specific workforce sectors relate to the system's role in analyzing student performance and workforce outcomes.

bill_summary: The Maryland Family Utility Tax Relief Act authorizes local governments, including Baltimore City, counties, and municipalities, to establish a property tax credit for homeowners who spend 25% or more of their net household income on utility services such as electricity, gas, water, and internet.
responsible_party: Mayor and City Council of Baltimore City or the governing body of a county or municipal corporation
stakeholders: Homeowners paying significant portions of their income on utilities and local Maryland government taxing authorities.
fiscal_impact_summary: The bill permits local jurisdictions to grant property tax credits, which would lead to an indeterminate reduction in local property tax revenues if adopted. Because the implementation of the credit is optional for local governments and no formal Fiscal Note was provided in the text, specific dollar estimates are unavailable.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill creates a new local property tax credit. The Property Tax Assessment Appeals Board is the independent agency responsible for hearing appeals regarding property tax assessments, exemptions, and various property tax credits.

The Maryland Tax Court is the highest level of administrative review for tax-related disputes in the state, including factual determinations and adjudications involving property tax credits and assessments.

The bill establishes a tax credit based on the percentage of income spent on utility services (electricity, gas, water, and internet). The Office of the People's Counsel is the primary advocate for the interests of residential utility consumers regarding the affordability and reliability of these services.

The bill defines eligibility based on 'household net income,' which refers to earnings after legally required withholdings. Verification of an applicant's income for this tax credit would likely require data or verification from the Comptroller, who serves as the state's chief tax collector and manager of income tax records.
The bill's tax credit is triggered by expenses for utility services, including electricity, gas, and water, all of which are industries regulated by the Public Service Commission.

The Department of Human Services administers energy assistance and aid to residents in economic need. The population targeted by this bill (households spending over 25% of income on utilities) overlaps significantly with the demographic served by the department's Office of Home Energy Programs.

The process applies to the departments of Agriculture, Environment, Health, Human Services, and Labor, and departments are authorized to charge a fee of up to $100 for this service, which may be waived based on income level.

Expenditures are estimated at $22,500 in FY 2028 and $23,500 in FY 2029 before the bill's termination. Revenue impact is indeterminate but expected to be minimal, as the $100 maximum fee may be offset by administrative costs and required fee waivers for individuals with incomes at or below 300% of the federal poverty level.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Governor's Office oversees the executive departments mandated to implement the predetermination review process and will receive reports on the implementation and costs of the program by October 2028.

The Office of the Attorney General provides legal counsel to the impacted departments regarding the interpretation and implementation of the new predetermination review process, particularly its binding nature.

The Department of Agriculture is one of the five primary departments required to establish a predetermination review process and report on its implementation. The fiscal note identifies specific IT programming costs for this agency.

The Department of Budget and Management is responsible for the state's personnel and budget execution; it will oversee the funding for new contractual positions and IT upgrades necessitated by the bill at the departments of Labor and Agriculture.
The Department of the Environment is explicitly named as a department required to implement the criminal history predetermination review process and submit progress reports to the General Assembly.

The Maryland Department of Health is a primary implementing agency for the predetermination process, managing a high volume of professional licensing boards that will be impacted by the new requirements.
The Department of Human Services is explicitly mandated by the bill to implement the predetermination review process for its occupational licenses and certificates.

The Department of Information Technology may be involved in supporting the computer programming and online application updates required by agencies like the Department of Agriculture to implement the review process.

The Department of Labor is a primary implementing agency and, according to the fiscal note, will require additional contractual staff to manage the administrative workload of the predetermination process due to its extensive licensing responsibilities.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Department of Public Safety and Correctional Services
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill explicitly removes this department from the definition of entities prohibited from denying licenses solely based on criminal history under this section. Additionally, it manages the criminal history records that the other departments will review.
The Maryland State Police may be involved in providing or validating criminal history records used by the five departments during the predetermination review process.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Governor's Office of Crime Prevention and Policy
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The office advises on criminal justice strategies and the rehabilitation of justice-involved individuals, which aligns with the bill's policy of removing barriers to employment for ex-offenders.
The board coordinates workforce solutions and paths to prosperity; removing licensing barriers for individuals with criminal records is a key component of state workforce participation strategy.

The bill specifies that the District Court of Maryland (part of the Judicial Branch supported by the AOC) is responsible for determining whether an individual's income qualifies them for a fee waiver for the predetermination review.

The Commission enforces anti-discrimination laws in state contracts and employment; the bill's provisions regarding the use of criminal history in licensing decisions overlap with the Commission's oversight of fair practices.
As a regulatory unit within the Maryland Department of Health, the Commission is subject to the bill's requirements for units within the primary departments to implement predetermination reviews.
The OAH adjudicates contested cases from state agencies; denials of licenses or certifications following a predetermination review could result in appeals that are heard by Administrative Law Judges.
This agency is a division of the Maryland Department of Health that issues CDS permits, making it a licensing unit that must comply with the bill's predetermination review mandates.

Synopsis: Repealing the restriction on the number of wine festival licenses that the Board of License Commissioners for Prince George's County may issue annually; and repealing a prohibition on issuing a wine festival license for use in the 24th legislative district.
Title: Prince George's County - Alcoholic Beverages - Wine Festival Licenses PG 316-26
Status: Approved by the Governor - Chapter 824
bill_summary: This bill renames the Prince George’s County Wine Festival license to the wine festival license and authorizes the Prince George’s County Board of License Commissioners to issue multiple wine festival licenses annually, repealing the previous limit of one license per year. It also removes the prohibition against issuing a wine festival license in the 24th legislative district.
responsible_party: Board of License Commissioners for Prince George’s County
stakeholders: Retail alcoholic beverages license holders, Class 3 winery license holders, Class 4 limited winery license holders, and residents of the 24th legislative district in Prince George's County.
fiscal_impact_summary: There is no State fiscal impact. Locally, the bill does not materially affect Prince George’s County operations or finances. Prince George's County anticipates a negligible revenue increase of approximately $225 annually, calculated from the issuance of up to three additional wine festival licenses at a fee of $75 each.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Comptroller is explicitly tasked with regulating the alcohol industry in Maryland. This bill modifies licensing provisions for wine festivals in Prince George's County, which falls under the broader scope of alcohol regulation.

The bill mandates that the Board of License Commissioners ensure the primary focus of wine festivals is the promotion of Maryland wine. This aligns with the Department of Agriculture's mission to promote the economic viability of agribusiness and the marketing of local agricultural products.

The Department of Commerce oversees tourism and economic development. Wine festivals serve as economic activities and attractions that contribute to the state's competitive position and the growth of the beverage industry.

Wine festivals are recreational and cultural attractions that stimulate the tourism economy. The bill's expansion of the number of festivals in Prince George's County provides additional opportunities for tourism promotion and destination marketing.

Synopsis: Altering the amounts of certain capital grants calculated based on highway user revenues that are required to be appropriated to Baltimore City, counties, and municipalities in certain fiscal years; etc.
Title: Transportation - Highway User Revenues Capital Grants - Calculation
Status: In the House - Hearing 2/10 at 1:00 p.m. (Appropriations)

NarrowSubjects.Name: Counties -see also- Chartered Counties; Code Counties; etc.
Motor Vehicles -see also- Aband Veh; Ambulances; Buses; etc.
Transportation -see also- Aircraft; Airports; Boats; etc

bill_summary: This bill makes permanent the higher distribution levels of highway user revenues to Baltimore City, counties, and municipalities that were previously scheduled to decrease in fiscal year 2028. By altering the statutory formula, it ensures that local governments continue to receive capital transportation grants at the fiscal year 2026 and 2027 rates indefinitely.
stakeholders: Baltimore City, Maryland counties, and municipalities
fiscal_impact_summary: According to the fiscal note, while overall Transportation Trust Fund expenditures are not affected, the bill requires the Maryland Department of Transportation to redirect capital funding from its own programs to local governments. Between fiscal 2028 and 2031, an estimated $401.1 million in total will be redirected, with annual local revenue increases of $96.3 million in FY 2028, $98.8 million in FY 2029, $101.6 million in FY 2030, and $104.4 million in FY 2031.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Board of Public Works, which includes the Governor, Comptroller, and Treasurer, oversees significant state expenditures and fiscal integrity. This bill involves a substantial redirection of funds within the Transportation Trust Fund and Gasoline and Motor Vehicle Revenue Account, affecting state capital programs and fiscal planning.

The Comptroller is responsible for collecting the revenues that populate the Gasoline and Motor Vehicle Revenue Account, including motor fuel taxes and vehicle titling taxes. The bill alters the distribution formula for these specific state revenues.

DBM is the principal agency for state budget development and long-term fiscal planning. The bill requires a significant, permanent shift in state funding priorities by redirecting over $400 million in capital grants to local governments over a four-year period.

MDOT is the primary agency impacted as it manages the Transportation Trust Fund and the Gasoline and Motor Vehicle Revenue Account. The bill directly alters the statutory formula MDOT uses to distribute highway user revenues to local governments and will require MDOT to redirect funds from state-level projects to local capital grants.

The Governor's Office oversees the executive branch and MDOT, and is responsible for proposing the annual state budget. This bill dictates a permanent change in how a major portion of state transportation revenue is allocated.

The Treasurer's Office is the chief financial agency responsible for managing state funds, including the Transportation Trust Fund. It also manages state debt and serves on the Board of Public Works, which monitors the fiscal impact of such revenue shifts.

Synopsis: Repealing an exemption from the sales and use tax for certain sales of certain personal property for use at certain qualified data centers under certain circumstances; and repealing the authorization for a governing body of a county or municipal corporation to reduce or eliminate the assessment of certain personal property used in certain qualified data centers.
Title: Sales and Use Tax and Property Tax - Exemptions for Data Centers - Repeal
Status: In the House - Hearing 2/12 at 1:00 p.m.

NarrowSubjects.Name: Counties -see also- Chartered Counties; Code Counties; etc.

bill_summary: This bill repeals the sales and use tax exemption for personal property used in qualified data centers and removes the authority of local governments to reduce or eliminate property tax assessments for such data center equipment.
responsible_party: Maryland Comptroller and the State Department of Assessments and Taxation
stakeholders: Data center owners and operators, local governments, and the State of Maryland.
fiscal_impact_summary: State general fund and Blueprint for Maryland’s Future Fund revenues are expected to increase starting in fiscal 2027. While the increase could be significant, specific dollar estimates are unavailable because the Comptroller and the Department of Commerce do not have data on the value of exemptions currently utilized. Local property tax revenues may also increase to the extent that local governments previously exempted data center personal property.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Comptroller's Office is the state's principal tax collector for sales and use taxes. The bill repeals Section 11-239 of the Tax - General Article, which currently requires the Comptroller to issue certificates of eligibility for data center exemptions and allows for the recapture of unpaid taxes—duties that would be abolished by this act.

The bill explicitly defines the Department of Commerce as the agency responsible for certifying the eligibility of data centers for tax exemptions. Repealing these sections removes the department's statutory authority to process applications, certify applicants, and manage the list of eligible entities for the Comptroller.

As the principal fiscal agency, DBM is responsible for estimating revenues and supervising budget execution. The bill is projected to have a significant positive impact on General Fund revenues and the Blueprint for Maryland's Future Fund, both of which are managed and forecasted by DBM.

The Governor's Office oversees the executive branch and proposes the annual state budget. This bill represents a significant shift in state fiscal policy and economic incentives, directly affecting the Governor's revenue projections and economic development strategy.

The bill repeals the authority of local governments to reduce or eliminate property tax assessments for data centers. This change is likely to result in increased assessments and tax liabilities for these facilities, potentially leading to an increase in valuation disputes and appeals adjudicated by the PTAAB.

The Maryland Tax Court is the highest administrative body for tax disputes, hearing appeals from the Comptroller and Property Tax Assessment Appeals Boards. It would be responsible for adjudicating legal disputes arising from the repeal of these sales and property tax exemptions.

The fiscal note indicates that the repeal of these exemptions will increase revenue for the Blueprint for Maryland's Future Fund. This fund provides critical financial support for the state's public education system and initiatives overseen by MSDE.

MEDCO is tasked with attracting and retaining industry in Maryland. The repeal of significant tax incentives for data centers impacts the economic landscape and financial tools available for promoting business growth in the technology sector.

The OLA conducts fiscal and compliance audits of state agencies. The repeal of these specific tax provisions changes the compliance and regulatory framework that OLA must monitor during its periodic audits of the Comptroller and the Department of Commerce.

Synopsis: Requiring the Governor, in each of fiscal years 2028 through 2030, to appropriate to the Maryland Child Care Credential Program $5,687,000.
Title: Maryland Child Care Credential Program - Extension of Funding
Status: Approved by the Governor - Chapter 623

NarrowSubjects.Name: Job Training -see also- Continuing Ed; Vocational Rehab

bill_summary: This bill mandates specific annual funding of $5,687,000 for the Maryland Child Care Credential Program for fiscal years 2028 through 2030, supporting achievement bonuses, training reimbursements, and training vouchers for child care providers.
responsible_party: Maryland State Department of Education (MSDE), Office of Child Care (OCC)
stakeholders: Child care staff and administrators, and small business child care providers.
fiscal_impact_summary: State general fund expenditures increase by $5,687,000 annually from fiscal 2028 through 2030 due to the reestablishment of mandated funding for the Maryland Child Care Credential Program. While the program has recently been funded through the Blueprint for Maryland's Future Fund, that fund is projected to be exhausted by fiscal 2028, requiring general fund support. There is no fiscal impact on local governments.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Maryland State Department of Education (MSDE) is the primary agency responsible for the oversight and leadership of the state's public education and child care systems. Its Office of Child Care (OCC) directly administers the Maryland Child Care Credential Program, awarding achievement bonuses, training reimbursements, and vouchers to child care providers.

The Department of Budget and Management (DBM) is responsible for developing the state's budget and supervising budget execution. This bill reestablishes a mandated general fund appropriation of approximately $5.7 million per year from FY 2028 through FY 2030, which DBM must integrate into the state's long-term fiscal planning.

The Governor's Office is responsible for proposing the annual state budget and overseeing the executive branch. This bill specifically mandates that the Governor appropriate specific funding levels for the Maryland Child Care Credential Program in the annual budget bill for several fiscal years.

The Governor's Office for Children (GOC) coordinates statewide efforts to promote the well-being of children and families and reduce child poverty. Improving the credentials and retention of the child care workforce through this funding mandate directly aligns with GOC's mission to enhance support networks for families and children.

The Governor's Workforce Development Board (GWDB) is the governor's chief policy-making body for the state's workforce system. This bill's focus on professional development and credential attainment within the child care sector is a specific workforce development strategy that aligns with GWDB's goal of creating pathways to prosperity for Maryland workers.

The Maryland State Innovation Team is tasked with piloting initiatives to address the Governor's top priorities, specifically reducing child poverty. Because child care access and quality (supported by a credentialed workforce) are critical components of poverty reduction and economic mobility, this program is relevant to their data-driven policy focus.

Synopsis: Altering the method for calculating the maintenance of effort amount county governing bodies are required to appropriate to the school operating budget by requiring an annual inflation adjustment.
Title: Primary and Secondary Education - Maintenance of Effort - Inflation Adjustment (Maintenance of Effort Modernization Act)
Status: In the House - Hearing 2/24 at 1:00 p.m.

NarrowSubjects.Name: Counties -see also- Chartered Counties; Code Counties; etc.
Education -see also- ContEd; DrvEd; HigherEd; etc.
Primary Schools -see also- Private Schools; Public Schools
Secondary Schools -see also- Private Schools; Public Sch

bill_summary: The Maintenance of Effort Modernization Act modifies the calculation for the minimum funding level that Maryland counties must provide to local school systems. It requires the per-pupil local appropriation for public schools to be increased annually by an inflation adjustment, which is defined as the lesser of the increase in the implicit price deflator for State and local government expenditures, the Consumer Price Index for the Washington Metropolitan Area, or 5%.
responsible_party: Maryland county governing bodies, including county councils, boards of county commissioners, and the Mayor and City Council of Baltimore.
stakeholders: Maryland county governments, local boards of education, and public school students.
fiscal_impact_summary: The bill mandates a local spending increase by requiring that the annual per-pupil maintenance of effort (MOE) appropriation be adjusted for inflation (capped at 5%). This results in a mandated increase in local expenditures for elementary and secondary education. Specific dollar estimates from a formal Fiscal Note were not provided in the bill text, but the mandate explicitly requires higher local funding levels based on inflationary indices.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Maryland State Department of Education (MSDE) is the primary agency responsible for overseeing public education funding and ensuring that the 24 local school systems comply with state mandates, including the Maintenance of Effort (MOE) requirements altered by this bill.
The Governor's Office oversees the executive branch and proposes the annual state budget; changes to school funding formulas significantly impact state education policy and fiscal priorities.
As the principal fiscal agency, DBM is responsible for long-term fiscal planning and estimating revenues; changes to local education funding mandates affect the overall fiscal landscape of the state.
The OAG provides legal counsel to state agencies and the General Assembly regarding the interpretation and enforcement of state laws, including changes to the Education Article.

The OLA conducts fiscal compliance audits of state agencies and local school systems, ensuring that funding is appropriated and managed according to statutory requirements like the Maintenance of Effort.

The bill explicitly references the 'amount of the expenditure authorized for debt service and capital outlay' as an exception in the school funding calculation, which falls under the purview of the IAC.
The agency's mission to reduce child poverty and improve access to education is directly impacted by changes in the adequacy and calculation of local education funding.

Synopsis: Repealing the prohibition against intentionally inflicting bodily harm, permanent disability, or death on an animal owned or used by a law enforcement unit; prohibiting a person from harassing, interfering with, injuring, or killing or causing serious physical injury to an emergency response animal; and establishing that a person who violates the Act is guilty of a misdemeanor and subject to imprisonment for up to 2 years, or a fine of up to $10,000, or both upon conviction.
Title: Criminal Law - Emergency Response Animal - Prohibited Actions Against
Status: Approved by the Governor - Chapter 402

bill_summary: This bill redefines and expands legal protections for animals used by law enforcement and search and rescue teams. It replaces the existing felony charge for harming a law enforcement animal with several misdemeanor charges for intentionally harassing, interfering with, injuring, or killing an 'emergency response animal,' which specifically includes dogs and horses. The bill also establishes specific penalties for these actions, including enhanced penalties if the acts occur during the commission of another crime, while providing legal defenses for necessity or protection against excessive force.
responsible_party: Maryland Judiciary, Department of Public Safety and Correctional Services, and State and local law enforcement units
stakeholders: Law enforcement officers, search and rescue personnel, handlers of emergency response dogs and horses, and the general public.
fiscal_impact_summary: According to the Fiscal Note, the bill is not expected to materially affect State or local government finances. The reclassification of certain crimes from felonies to misdemeanors may shift some cases from circuit courts to the District Court, but the volume of such cases is historically low. No specific dollar estimates for revenue or expenditure changes were provided.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: As the primary statewide law enforcement agency, the Maryland State Police utilizes K9 units and other animals in its operations. The bill directly protects these 'emergency response animals' and regulates the legal defenses available to individuals who may interfere with or harm them.

The bill's definition of 'emergency response animal' specifically includes search and rescue dogs and horses directed by a State agency to locate or rescue individuals, a function often coordinated or supported by MDEM.

The Maryland Natural Resources Police, a unit within DNR, utilizes K9s for law enforcement and search and rescue efforts in state parks and waterways, both of which are covered by the bill's expanded protections.
The bill repeals a felony and replaces it with several specific misdemeanors, which impacts court jurisdiction, caseloads, and the processing of criminal charges within the Maryland Judicial Branch.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Maryland Office of the Public Defender
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The creation of new misdemeanor offenses and the modification of existing penalties for actions against emergency response animals will directly impact the caseload and defense strategies of public defenders representing indigent clients.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Department of Public Safety and Correctional Services
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: DPSCS utilizes K9 units for security within correctional facilities. Furthermore, the bill's changes to criminal penalties for animal cruelty and the potential for incarceration in state or local facilities affect the department's oversight of justice-involved individuals.
MDOT oversees the Maryland Transportation Authority (MDTA) Police and the Transit Police, both of which utilize K9 units for security and law enforcement at toll facilities and transit hubs.
The OAG provides legal counsel to state law enforcement agencies and represents the state in criminal appeals, including those involving the newly established misdemeanor offenses.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Governor's Office of Crime Prevention and Policy
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: GOCPP serves as the primary coordinating body for public safety and criminal justice strategies, and this bill modifies criminal law regarding the protection of law enforcement and emergency response assets.
The MDA oversees programs related to animal health and is the lead agency for general agricultural leadership, though its primary focus is not criminal law enforcement.
The Governor must sign the bill into law and oversees the executive branch departments (like MSP and MDEM) that employ these emergency response animals.

Synopsis: Establishing certain consumer protection requirements for registered cemeterians, registered cemetery operators, and certain permit holders and licensees that sell or offer for sale pet cremation services for pet remains; establishing the duties of certain persons responsible for returning pet cremains to certain animal owners after cremation; and providing certain penalties for a first violation of the Act, increasing with the second violation, and for a third violation a fine of up to $15,000, and imprisonment of up to 3 years or both.

bill_summary: This bill, titled the Pet Cremation and Burial Services Consumer Protection Act, establishes regulatory requirements for providers of pet cremation and burial services. It mandates that providers distribute clear written descriptions of cremation types (private, partitioned, or communal) and provide certificates of authenticity to pet owners upon returning remains. Additionally, it requires providers to maintain detailed records for five years and designates violations as unfair or deceptive trade practices under the Maryland Consumer Protection Act, subject to specific civil and criminal penalties.
responsible_party: Maryland State Board of Morticians and Funeral Directors
stakeholders: Pet owners, veterinarians, pet shops, funeral directors, and operators of pet cemeteries and crematories.
fiscal_impact_summary: The fiscal impact on the State and local governments is expected to be minimal and absorbable within existing budgeted resources. While the bill establishes new criminal fines (up to $15,000 for a third offense) and civil penalties (up to $5,000), total State revenues are not expected to be materially affected. Small businesses providing pet cremation services may experience a meaningful impact due to new disclosure, recordkeeping, and procedural requirements.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill establishes new misdemeanor criminal penalties and allows the Attorney General to file civil actions in court for violations, which directly impacts the workload and administrative operations of the state court system.
The bill specifically requires registered cemeterians, cemetery operators, and licensees to distribute written descriptions of their pet cremation services to the Department of Agriculture.

As the state's principal fiscal agency, DBM oversees the budgets of the Department of Health and Department of Labor, both of which will require existing or additional resources to enforce the bill's new regulatory requirements.

The bill establishes new consumer protection and disclosure requirements for pet cremation under the Health Occupations Article, which is overseen by the State Board of Morticians and Funeral Directors, an entity within the Department of Health.
The bill establishes requirements for registered cemeterians and cemetery operators, who are currently regulated by the Office of Cemetery Oversight within the Department of Labor.

The Governor's Office oversees the executive branch agencies responsible for implementing the bill (MDH, Labor, and Agriculture) and is responsible for the final approval and enactment of the legislation.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Maryland Office of the Public Defender
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill creates new misdemeanor offenses punishable by fines and imprisonment; the Office of the Public Defender is responsible for representing indigent individuals charged with these crimes.

OAH is responsible for adjudicating contested cases and disciplinary actions that may arise if the State Board of Morticians or the Office of Cemetery Oversight takes enforcement action against a licensee or registrant for violating the bill's provisions.

The bill categorizes violations as unfair or deceptive trade practices under the Maryland Consumer Protection Act and explicitly authorizes the Attorney General to pursue civil enforcement, including seeking injunctions and civil penalties.

Synopsis: Requiring an election of members of the Calvert County, Cecil County, Garrett County, Montgomery County, Queen Anne's County, and St. Mary's County boards of education who represent a specific district to be decided by a plurality of the votes cast within that district.
Title: County Boards of Education - Elections - District Voting (Fair Representation Act)
