bill_summary: This bill requires that elections for certain county boards of education (Calvert, Cecil, Garrett, Montgomery, Queen Anne's, and St. Mary's) for members representing specific districts be decided by a plurality of the votes cast within those individual districts, rather than by a countywide vote.
responsible_party: The Maryland State Board of Elections and the local boards of elections in Calvert, Cecil, Garrett, Montgomery, Queen Anne's, and St. Mary's counties
stakeholders: Voters and candidates for the county boards of education in Calvert, Cecil, Garrett, Montgomery, Queen Anne's, and St. Mary's counties
fiscal_impact_summary: Specific dollar estimates are unavailable as a formal Fiscal Note was not provided. The bill text does not explicitly state financial implications such as fee changes, tax credits, or new spending mandates, though implementation would require administrative adjustments to ballot programming by local boards of elections.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: As the agency responsible for supervising and administering elections in Maryland, the State Board of Elections must oversee the transition from at-large to district-only voting for the specified county boards of education, including ballot preparation and voting system configuration.

The Maryland State Department of Education (MSDE) oversees the 24 local school systems, several of which will have the governance structure and election methods for their boards of education fundamentally changed by this legislation.

The Office of the Attorney General serves as the chief legal counsel for the State Board of Elections and the Department of Education, and it would be responsible for providing legal guidance on the constitutionality and implementation of the Fair Representation Act.
The Governor's Office oversees the executive departments responsible for implementation and handles the final approval and enactment of legislation affecting local government structure.
The judicial branch may be required to adjudicate potential legal challenges regarding district boundaries or election results under the new plurality voting system within specific districts.

Synopsis: Prohibiting a person from distributing personal identifying information or images of a student enrolled in an institution of secondary education or an institution of postsecondary education with intent or knowledge that the information will be used to harm the student or with reckless disregard for the risk the information will be used to harm the student; and providing that a person who violates the Act is guilty of a misdemeanor and is subject to imprisonment of up to 1 year or a fine of up to $5,000 or both.
Title: Criminal Law – Distribution of Students’ Personal Information – Prohibition
Status: In the House - Hearing 2/19 at 1:00 p.m.

Higher Education -see also- Comm Colleges; Med Schools; etc.

Secondary Schools -see also- Private Schools; Public Sch

bill_summary: This bill prohibits the intentional distribution of a student's personal identifying information or image without express permission when done with the intent or reckless disregard that the information will be used to harm the student. The prohibition applies to students in both secondary and postsecondary institutions, and violators are subject to misdemeanor penalties including up to one year of imprisonment and/or a fine of up to $5,000.
responsible_party: Maryland Judiciary, Maryland State Department of Education, and University System of Maryland
stakeholders: Students in grades 6 through 12, postsecondary students, parents or guardians of minor students, and educational institutions.
fiscal_impact_summary: The bill is expected to have a minimal fiscal impact on the state and local governments. General fund revenues may increase minimally from criminal fines of up to $5,000 per violation. State and local expenditures may increase minimally to account for incarceration costs. The Judiciary, Office of the Public Defender, and institutions of higher education are expected to implement the bill's requirements using existing budgeted resources.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Governor's Office oversees the executive branch and coordinates policy initiatives, including new criminal laws and safety protections for students.
The OAG serves as the chief legal officer for the state and would provide counsel to state agencies and educational institutions on the implementation and interpretation of this new criminal statute.
DBM is responsible for fiscal planning and oversight. The bill is noted to have a potential increase in general fund expenditures related to incarceration and personnel requests.
The Department (MSDE) oversees the secondary education institutions (grades 6-12) specifically regulated by the bill's provisions regarding student personal information.
Because the bill applies to students in secondary education (middle and high school), DJS would be responsible for the supervision and rehabilitation of any minors who violate the prohibition.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Department of Public Safety and Correctional Services
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: DPSCS is responsible for managing the incarceration and community supervision of individuals convicted of the new misdemeanor established by the bill.
MHEC is the regulatory and coordinating board for higher education; it oversees the postsecondary institutions that must adhere to the bill's restrictions.
As the primary state law enforcement agency, the Maryland State Police would be responsible for investigating criminal violations of the new law.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Governor's Office of Crime Prevention and Policy
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: This office advises the Governor on criminal justice strategies and manages funds for victim services and public safety, aligning with the bill's focus on preventing student harm.
The AOC provides central support for the Judiciary, which will manage the processing of new criminal cases and the collection of fines resulting from the bill.
MCSS coordinates school safety efforts and would likely develop training and resources for schools to comply with these new privacy protections.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Maryland Office of the Public Defender
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The OPD will provide legal representation to indigent defendants charged with the new misdemeanor, and they specifically identified a potential workload impact.
As a public postsecondary institution, Morgan State is directly subject to the bill's requirements regarding the distribution of its students' personal information.
As a public honors college, Saint Mary's is directly subject to the bill's requirements regarding the distribution of its students' personal information.
The USM governs multiple postsecondary institutions affected by the bill; member institutions raised administrative and liability concerns noted in the fiscal analysis.

Synopsis: Requiring the Motor Vehicle Administration to issue a single registration plate to all classes of vehicles; providing for the method of attachment of the registration plate to the rear of certain vehicles; and requiring the publisher of the Annotated Code of Maryland to make certain corrections.
Title: Motor Vehicle Laws - Registration Plates - Single Registration Plate
Status: In the House - Hearing 2/19 at 1:00 p.m.

bill_summary: The bill requires the Maryland Motor Vehicle Administration to issue only one registration plate for all classes of vehicles, rather than two for most vehicles. It specifies that the single plate should be attached to the rear of the vehicle, except for tractors, which must display the plate on the front.
stakeholders: Maryland vehicle owners, the Motor Vehicle Administration, the Maryland Transportation Authority, and law enforcement agencies.
fiscal_impact_summary: State Transportation Trust Fund expenditures are estimated to decrease by approximately 1,900,000 in FY 2027 and 2,500,000 annually thereafter due to reduced costs for license plate production. These savings are required to be retained in the Transportation Trust Fund. However, the Maryland Transportation Authority estimates a potential loss of up to 35,000,000 in nonbudgeted toll revenues due to reduced vehicle identification capabilities. General fund revenues from traffic fines are expected to decrease by about 200,000 annually. No material local fiscal impact is anticipated.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill directly requires the Motor Vehicle Administration to change its registration plate issuance policies, transitioning from two plates to one for most vehicle classes, which has direct operational and budgetary impacts.

As the parent agency of the Motor Vehicle Administration and the Maryland Transportation Authority, MDOT oversees the Transportation Trust Fund, which will retain the expenditure savings and absorb the revenue losses resulting from the bill.

The MDTA faces a significant loss in nonbudgeted revenue (estimated at $35 million annually) because toll collection systems rely on front-facing cameras to identify vehicles without E-ZPass when rear plates are obscured.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Department of Public Safety and Correctional Services
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The department's Maryland Correctional Enterprises (MCE) operates the tag plant that manufactures license plates; the reduction in plate production will impact training activities for incarcerated individuals and the unit's raw material costs.

The Maryland State Police identified concerns that shifting to a single registration plate standard makes vehicle identification more difficult for law enforcement officers during investigations and patrol.
The judicial branch will see a reduction in cases and associated fine revenue following the elimination of the misdemeanor penalty for failing to display two registration plates.
As the state's chief financial officer, the Comptroller is relevant to the monitoring of the resulting decrease in General Fund revenues from traffic fines.
The department is responsible for state budget oversight and the fiscal impacts on the General Fund and Transportation Trust Fund described in the fiscal note.
As the executive branch lead, the Governor's Office oversees the implementation of transportation policy and the administrative agencies (MDOT and MVA) primary to this bill.

Synopsis: Adding candidates for State Senator and member of the House of Delegates to the candidates authorized to receive public contributions from the Fair Campaign Financing Fund; establishing qualifications that a candidate for State Senator or member of the House of Delegates must meet to qualify as an eligible candidate to receive public contributions from the Fund; etc.

bill_summary: This bill expands the Maryland Public Financing Act to include candidates for the State Senate and House of Delegates, allowing them to receive public matching contributions from the Fair Campaign Financing Fund. It establishes specific eligibility criteria, including minimum numbers of small-dollar private contributions and aggregate fundraising totals, and sets matching ratios and maximum limits on public contributions for these legislative candidates.
stakeholders: Candidates for the Maryland State Senate and House of Delegates, Maryland residents making small-dollar campaign contributions, and the State Board of Elections.
fiscal_impact_summary: According to the fiscal note, State general fund expenditures increase by up to 32,900,000 in FY 2030 to fulfill a mandated appropriation to the Fair Campaign Financing Fund for the 2030 elections. The State Board of Elections will incur administrative costs of 10,320 in FY 2029 for computer programming and approximately 500,000 annually in FY 2030 and FY 2031 for contractual auditors. Additionally, the Office of the State Prosecutor requires 139,032 in general fund expenditures annually beginning in FY 2030 to hire an investigator for campaign finance violation cases.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: As the primary implementing agency, the State Board of Elections is responsible for certifying eligible candidates, authorizing distributions from the Fair Campaign Financing Fund, and managing the campaign finance reporting system.

The Comptroller is responsible for administering the Fair Campaign Financing Fund, processing tax checkoff revenues, and making distributions to candidates upon authorization by the State Board of Elections.

The Governor is mandated to include specific appropriations in the annual budget bill if the Fair Campaign Financing Fund is insufficient and is also an official subject to the bill's fundraising restrictions during legislative sessions.

The Office of the State Prosecutor investigates and prosecutes campaign finance violations; the fiscal note explicitly states the agency will require an additional investigator to handle the increased workload from General Assembly candidates.

As the principal budget agency, DBM is responsible for the development and execution of the state budget, including the mandated appropriations required by the bill to support the Fair Campaign Financing Fund.

The Treasurer's Office is responsible for investing the money in the Fair Campaign Financing Fund and the Treasurer is specifically named as an official subject to the bill's fundraising restrictions during session.
The Attorney General serves as the legal representative for state agencies like the State Board of Elections and is also named as an official subject to the bill's fundraising restrictions.
The Lieutenant Governor is specifically listed as an official subject to the bill's restrictions on fundraising activities during the regular session of the General Assembly.

The Office of Legislative Audits is responsible for conducting fiscal compliance audits of state agencies and programs, which would include the oversight of the expanded public financing program and its associated fund.

Synopsis: Authorizing the County Commissioners of Queen Anne's County to use revenue from development impact fees to finance the capital costs related to the replacement of public school facilities.

bill_summary: This bill expands the authorized uses of revenue from development impact fees in Queen Anne's County to include the financing of capital costs associated with replacing public school facilities.
responsible_party: County Commissioners of Queen Anne's County
stakeholders: Residents, students, and the public school system of Queen Anne's County
fiscal_impact_summary: According to the fiscal note, there is no state or local fiscal impact. The bill does not alter the amount of development impact fees collected or imposed by Queen Anne's County but instead expands the eligible uses for existing fee revenue to include school construction-related capital costs.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Interagency Commission on School Construction (IAC) is responsible for overseeing the planning and funding of public school construction and capital improvement projects. This bill directly concerns the local funding mechanisms for school facility replacement, and the fiscal note lists the IAC as an information source.

The fiscal note specifies that counties imposing development impact fees must annually report information regarding the collection and use of these fees to the Maryland Department of Planning (MDP). This bill expands the authorized uses of these fees in Queen Anne's County, which will be reflected in reports submitted to the MDP.

The Maryland State Department of Education (MSDE) provides leadership and oversight to public school systems. Since this bill provides a new local funding avenue for the replacement of public school facilities, it is relevant to the agency's mission regarding educational infrastructure.

The Rural Maryland Council (RMC) addresses challenges facing Maryland's rural counties, including Queen Anne's. The bill affects local infrastructure and economic development tools (impact fees) specifically within a rural jurisdiction.

This multi-agency initiative coordinates sustainable development and land-use planning. Development impact fees are a key planning tool used to mitigate the impacts of new construction, making the bill relevant to the initiative's oversight of infrastructure development.
The Governor's Office is responsible for signing or vetoing legislation passed by the General Assembly. This bill requires executive action to become law.
The Office of the Attorney General provides legal counsel to state agencies and the General Assembly, typically reviewing bills for legal sufficiency and constitutional compliance.

The Secretary of State is the custodian of official state records, including laws and executive orders. Once the bill is signed by the Governor, the Secretary of State will manage the recording of the new law.

Synopsis: Authorizing an individual to apply to be approved as a foster parent by the local department of social services for the county where the individual resides or a county adjacent to the county where the individual resides; prohibiting a local department from denying an application to be a foster parent due to the applicant's county of residence if the individual resides in the same county as, or an adjacent county to, the county where the local department is located; etc.
Title: Foster Care – Adjacent County Applicants and Reporting Requirements
Status: In the House - Hearing 2/19 at 1:00 p.m.

NarrowSubjects.Name: Counties -see also- Chartered Counties; Code Counties; etc.

bill_summary: This bill allows individuals to apply to be approved as foster parents by the local department of social services in their county of residence or any adjacent county. It prohibits local departments from denying applications based on residency if the applicant lives in an adjacent county and requires each local department to submit quarterly reports to the Department of Human Services regarding the number of children waiting for placement and the number of vacant foster care placements available.
stakeholders: Prospective foster parents, children in the foster care system, and local departments of social services.
fiscal_impact_summary: State general fund expenditures are expected to increase by $40,000 in FY 2027 for one-time programming costs to implement reporting requirements. The Department of Human Services (DHS) further estimates an annual cost of approximately $5,300,000 for 48 additional staff members to manage workloads across adjacent jurisdictions, although the Department of Legislative Services notes these workload increases are dependent on actual applicant volume and could not independently verify the staffing requirement. The bill is not anticipated to materially affect local government finances.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: As the primary agency responsible for child welfare and the oversight of local departments of social services, DHS is the lead agency for implementing the new foster parent application residency rules and managing the required quarterly reporting on placements.

The fiscal note estimates a potential significant increase in general fund expenditures ($5.3 million) and the addition of 48 staff positions, which falls under DBM's responsibility for budget development and personnel management.
The fiscal note identifies potential impacts on school transportation for foster children who may be placed in homes in adjacent counties, which affects local school systems overseen by MSDE.

The bill's focus on improving foster care placement and supporting children waiting for homes aligns with the GOC's mission to promote the well-being of Maryland's children and coordinate support networks.
The OAG provides legal counsel to state agencies like DHS and would be responsible for advising on the implementation of the new residency requirements and related regulatory updates.
Foster care placements are often the result of juvenile court commitments; changes in application and placement procedures may impact court-related case management and coordination.
The Governor's Office oversees the executive branch and proposes the annual state budget, which would need to reflect the significant fiscal impact and staffing increases identified for this bill.

Synopsis: Altering the definition of "nonprofit housing corporation" for purposes of eligibility for an exemption from real property taxes and special assessments of the State or a political subdivision; exempting certain real property owned by certain subsidiary entities of a certain nonprofit housing corporation from taxes and special assessments of the State or a political subdivision; etc.

bill_summary: This bill redefines nonprofit housing corporation to include 501(c)(3) organizations focused on affordable housing and expands state and local property tax and special assessment exemptions to their subsidiary entities. It also defines affordable housing criteria based on federal tax credits or specific income and rent restrictions, while excluding certain properties in Baltimore City and projects that received prior local financial assistance.
responsible_party: State Department of Assessments and Taxation
stakeholders: Nonprofit housing corporations, subsidiary entities of nonprofit housing corporations, low-income households seeking affordable housing, and local governments.
fiscal_impact_summary: State and local property tax revenues will decrease by an indeterminate amount beginning in fiscal 2027. The specific financial impact depends on the number of nonprofit housing corporations and subsidiaries that qualify for the tax exemption under the bill's expanded definitions. State and local expenditures are not directly affected.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: This bill directly amends the Housing and Community Development Article of the Maryland Code, specifically altering the definition and tax-exempt status of nonprofit housing corporations and their subsidiaries, which fall under the department's primary mission of fostering affordable housing.
As the state's chief financial officer and tax collector, the Comptroller is directly impacted by changes to tax-exempt statuses and definitions that result in a decrease in State tax revenues.
The Treasurer manages state funds, including the Annuity Bond Fund which relies on property tax revenues for debt service. A decrease in property tax revenue affects state financial management.
DBM is responsible for revenue estimation and long-term fiscal planning. The bill's indeterminate impact on state property tax revenues requires the department to adjust fiscal projections.

The OAG would provide legal counsel to the Department of Housing and Community Development and other state entities regarding the interpretation and implementation of the revised definition of 'nonprofit housing corporation'.
The Governor oversees the executive branch and housing policy; this bill represents a notable shift in affordable housing policy and tax exemptions, which are key executive priorities.

This board hears appeals regarding property tax assessments and exemptions. Altering the eligibility for nonprofit housing corporations and their subsidiaries directly impacts the scope and criteria of their administrative reviews.
The Tax Court adjudicates appeals from taxing authorities. Changes to property tax exemptions for housing corporations may lead to factual and legal disputes that would be heard by this court.

The bill includes provisions that exempt real property of nonprofit housing corporations from certain judicial processes, such as levy and sale by virtue of an execution, which impacts court operations regarding judgment enforcement.

The Department of Planning promotes sustainable growth and land use; the expansion of affordable housing through tax incentives is a relevant component of state land use and community development policy.

The Innovation Team's mandate includes identifying strategies to reduce child poverty and enhance economic mobility, both of which are central goals of the affordable housing expansion addressed in this bill.

Synopsis: Authorizing the Attorney General to investigate, commence, and prosecute or defend any suit or action that holds certain entities accountable for tortious or otherwise unlawful conduct that has contributed to climate change; authorizing the Attorney General to hire outside counsel to assist with an action under the Act if the Attorney General makes a certain determination; establishing the Climate Crimes Accountability Fund as a special, nonlapsing fund; etc.

bill_summary: The Climate Crimes Accountability Act authorizes the Maryland Attorney General to investigate and prosecute large fossil fuel entities with a market capitalization over $1 billion for conduct contributing to climate change, such as fraud or deception. The bill establishes the Climate Crimes Accountability Fund to receive settlement and judgment revenues, which will be used to fund programs that prevent, mitigate, or repair climate-related harms and to cover legal expenses associated with these actions.
responsible_party: Maryland Office of the Attorney General and Maryland Department of Emergency Management
stakeholders: Publicly traded fossil fuel companies with a market capitalization over $1 billion, Maryland residents, and State and local agencies involved in climate change mitigation.
fiscal_impact_summary: State special fund revenues and expenditures are expected to increase by an indeterminate but potentially significant amount, likely starting in FY 2028, depending on the success of litigation. The Office of the Attorney General estimates administrative staffing costs of $560,800 in FY 2027. The Maryland Department of Emergency Management estimates administrative costs of $196,400 to manage the fund, though these may be delayed until revenues are realized. General fund revenues may increase from interest earnings in FY 2028. Local governments may see increased revenue from grant distributions.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill explicitly authorizes the Attorney General to investigate, commence, and prosecute civil or criminal suits against large fossil fuel companies for conduct contributing to climate change. The OAG is also authorized to hire outside counsel and would receive funding for litigation expenses from the new Climate Crimes Accountability Fund.

According to the fiscal note, MDEM is the administrator of the newly created Climate Crimes Accountability Fund (CCAF). The agency would be responsible for managing the fund and distributing money for programs that prevent, mitigate, or repair harms caused by climate change, such as storm damage and flooding.

The bill adds new provisions directly to the Environment Article and addresses environmental harms like air pollution. MDE is the primary agency for climate policy in Maryland and would likely be a major recipient of fund distributions for climate mitigation and restoration programs.

The fiscal note indicates significant personnel and expenditure impacts for the OAG and MDEM. As the principal personnel and budget agency, DBM would oversee the creation of new positions and the execution of the special fund within the state budget.
The State Treasurer is required to hold the new Climate Crimes Accountability Fund separately and invest its money in the same manner as other state funds.
The Comptroller is responsible for accounting for the new special fund and managing the interest earnings that, under certain conditions, will be credited to the fund or the General Fund.

The Climate Crimes Accountability Fund specifically targets harms related to public health, including vectorborne and waterborne pathogens and extreme heat waves, which fall under the Maryland Department of Health's mandate.

The bill references definitions for saltwater intrusion from the Natural Resources Article and targets fund usage for ecosystem changes, wildfires, and saltwater intrusion, which are core DNR responsibilities.
The bill authorizes new types of litigation and specific procedures (like assigning comparative responsibility) that the state judiciary must apply in climate-related tort actions.

As the head of the executive branch, the Governor oversees the agencies implementing this bill (OAG, MDEM, MDE) and proposes the budget that will include the newly created Climate Crimes Accountability Fund.
The fund may be used to address drought and ecosystem changes, which directly impact the economic viability of farming and the agricultural community overseen by MDA.
The fund can be used to repair infrastructure harms caused by climate change, such as flooding and storm damage to state highways and transit systems managed by MDOT.

Synopsis: Authorizing the Department of Housing and Community Development to adopt certain regulations related to affirmatively furthering fair housing; providing that certain discriminatory housing practices may be committed without intent; prohibiting a person from acting in a certain manner that has a discriminatory effect; and providing that certain conduct necessary to achieve certain nondiscriminatory interests does not constitute a certain violation.

bill_summary: This bill authorizes the Maryland Department of Housing and Community Development to adopt regulations requiring political subdivisions and housing authorities to affirmatively further fair housing. It also prohibits housing practices that have a 'discriminatory effect' (disparate impact) regardless of intent, defining such effects as those that create or perpetuate segregated housing patterns, while establishing a defense for actions necessary to achieve legitimate, non-discriminatory interests where no less discriminatory alternative exists.
responsible_party: Maryland Department of Housing and Community Development, Maryland Commission on Civil Rights, and the Office of the Attorney General
stakeholders: Maryland residents (specifically those in protected classes), local governments, housing authorities, landlords, and property owners.
fiscal_impact_summary: According to the fiscal note, the bill is not anticipated to materially affect State or local government operations or finances. It aligns Maryland law with the federal Fair Housing Act and judicial precedents regarding disparate impact theory in housing discrimination cases. Small business impacts are expected to be minimal as the bill codifies existing legal frameworks.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: As the primary agency responsible for enforcing Maryland's anti-discrimination laws in housing, MCCR is directly impacted by the bill's expansion of prohibited acts to include those with a 'discriminatory effect' regardless of intent.

The bill specifically authorizes this department to adopt regulations related to affirmatively furthering fair housing and mandates that it require political subdivisions and housing authorities to submit fair housing assessments.

The bill explicitly references the Attorney General's authority to investigate, prosecute, and remediate conduct that constitutes a civil rights violation, which includes the discriminatory housing acts defined in the bill.

This agency is responsible for conducting administrative hearings for housing discrimination claims brought through the Commission on Civil Rights, and the bill clarifies the legal standards for such cases.

The bill requires local jurisdictions to include fair housing assessments in the housing element of their comprehensive plans, a process that falls under the Department of Planning's technical assistance and land use oversight.
The bill provides for civil actions in State courts for alleged discriminatory housing practices, potentially impacting the judicial branch's caseload and legal interpretations of disparate impact.
Since disability is a primary protected class in fair housing law, this department is impacted as it advocates for the rights and community living accessibility of individuals with disabilities.
Military status is a protected class under the housing discrimination laws modified by this bill, making it relevant to the department's advocacy and support for military families.

bill_summary: This bill establishes the Prince George's County Teen Pregnancy Support Program to assist pregnant and parenting students in public high schools by providing child care vouchers, parenting education, and other resources. To fund the program, the bill requires the Prince George's County Circuit Court to collect a $100 fee for certain child support-related court filings, which is remitted to the Prince George's County Board of Education.
responsible_party: Prince George's County Board of Education
stakeholders: Pregnant and parenting students in Prince George's County public high schools; individuals filing for child support decrees, modifications, or enforcement in Prince George's County; Maryland Child Support Administration.
fiscal_impact_summary: State general fund expenditures increase by approximately $200,000 annually starting in FY 2027 for the Child Support Administration to pay filing fees, plus a one-time expenditure of $8,630 in FY 2027 for Judiciary programming. Local revenues and expenditures in Prince George's County increase by up to $1,100,000 annually from the new $100 court filing fee dedicated to the Teen Pregnancy Support Program.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill requires the Prince George’s County Circuit Court to collect a new $100 fee in child support cases. The Administrative Office of the Courts (AOC) provides operational and technological support to the state's courts and will need to implement programming changes to facilitate the collection and remittance of this fee.

The bill's new court fee will impact the Child Support Administration (CSA), which is a division of DHS. According to the fiscal note, the CSA will be required to pay these fees in cases it files, resulting in an estimated $200,000 increase in general fund expenditures annually.

The bill establishes the Teen Pregnancy Support Program within the Prince George’s County public school system and adds a new section to the Education Article. As the oversight and leadership agency for Maryland's 24 local school systems, MSDE is responsible for setting educational policies and standards that govern such programs.

DBM is the principal fiscal agency for the State. The bill is expected to increase State General Fund expenditures by approximately $208,600 in FY 2027 and $200,000 annually thereafter, requiring DBM's oversight regarding budget execution and fiscal planning.

The bill includes parenting education as a component of the new program. MDH jointly develops school health standards and guidelines with MSDE, which include Family Life and Human Sexuality standards related to the bill's objectives.

The Governor's Office for Children focuses on reducing child poverty and improving access to health services and economic opportunities. This program, which provides child care vouchers and support for teen parents, aligns with the office's mission to promote the well-being of Maryland's children and families.

bill_summary: This bill requires each Maryland county board of education to implement a student attendance policy that allows for excused or discretionary absences for students participating in civic engagement activities. These activities include testifying at legislative hearings, meeting with members of a legislative body, advocating for policy issues, and participating in the Maryland General Assembly Page Program. The policy must allow for at least 15 hours or two school days for these activities, and such absences cannot be factored into a student's chronic absenteeism calculation.
stakeholders: Public school students in Maryland and local school systems
fiscal_impact_summary: The bill has no financial impact on State or local government. According to the Fiscal Note, local school systems can modify their attendance policies and track civic engagement absences using existing resources.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: As the primary oversight agency for Maryland's public education system, MSDE is responsible for state attendance policies and is specifically granted authority under the bill to deem certain activities as civic engagement for the purpose of excused absences.

This agency links and analyzes student performance and absenteeism data. The bill explicitly states that excused absences for civic engagement may not be included in calculations of chronic absenteeism, which directly impacts the agency's data reporting and analytical functions regarding student outcomes.

The Governor's Office for Children leads efforts to promote child well-being and access to educational opportunities. This bill supports youth development by facilitating student participation in the policy-making process, which aligns with the office's mission to improve opportunities for Maryland's children.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Executive Commissions, Committees, Task Forces, and Advisory Boards
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill's definition of a 'legislative body' includes entities appointed by the Governor or local executives that are subject to the Open Meetings Act. Many executive commissions and task forces fall under this definition, serving as the venues where students would engage in the activities mentioned in the bill.

bill_summary: This bill authorizes the Maryland State Archives to establish and update fees for the care, preservation, and reproduction of various records—including land records, plats, and vital records—through the formal regulatory process rather than through independent establishment.
stakeholders: The general public, researchers, the State Roads Commission, the State Highway Administration, and the Maryland court system.
fiscal_impact_summary: The bill is expected to have no direct state or local fiscal impact. According to the Fiscal Note, the changes are procedural, shifting the method of setting fees to the regulatory process without directly altering existing revenue or expenditures. Local government operations and finances are not anticipated to be materially affected.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: As the primary subject of the bill, the State Archives is granted the specific authority to establish fees for its services through the regulatory process rather than by independent administrative decision.

The bill specifically identifies the State Highway Administration (a modal administration of MDOT) as an entity to which the State Archives may charge fees for the cost of electronically posting and maintaining images of plats.

The bill explicitly mentions the courts as entities that may be charged fees for the posting of plats. It also maintains provisions regarding fee exemptions for land records requested by clerks of the court with judicial approval.

The bill concerns fees for copying and searching 'vital records,' which are defined by their filing requirements with the Department of Health. MDH was also a stakeholder consulted in the fiscal analysis.

As the chief legal officer for state agencies, the OAG would be responsible for providing legal counsel to the State Archives and reviewing the proposed regulations mandated by this bill for legal sufficiency.

bill_summary: This bill prohibits the manufacturing, sale, purchase, or transfer of machine gun convertible pistols and pistol converters in Maryland, with the prohibition taking effect on January 1, 2027. It defines machine gun convertible pistols as semiautomatic pistols that can be readily converted into machine guns using common household tools and authorizes the Department of State Police to adopt regulations and publish a list of prohibited firearms. The bill includes specific exceptions for law enforcement, inherited firearms, and transfers between immediate family members.
stakeholders: Licensed firearms dealers, manufacturers, individual firearm owners, law enforcement agencies, and the Maryland Handgun Roster Board.
fiscal_impact_summary: State general fund expenditures increase by $220,200 in FY 2027 for the Department of State Police to hire one trooper and one administrative officer to evaluate the handgun roster and manage the list of prohibited firearms. Ongoing annual costs are projected to reach $262,900 by FY 2031. There is a potential minimal increase in State revenues and expenditures due to the application of existing misdemeanor penalties (up to 3 years imprisonment and/or a $5,000 fine). Local fiscal impact is expected to be minimal, and small businesses in the firearms industry may experience a meaningful impact.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: As the primary law enforcement agency for the state and the entity overseeing the Handgun Roster Board, MSP is responsible for implementing the bill. The bill specifically authorizes MSP to adopt regulations and publish the list of prohibited machine gun convertible pistols. The fiscal note identifies a need for $220,216 in FY 2027 for MSP to hire a trooper and an administrative officer to evaluate thousands of firearms and manage the new regulations.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Department of Public Safety and Correctional Services
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: DPSCS is responsible for the supervision and rehabilitation of justice-involved individuals. Since the bill creates new misdemeanor offenses and increases penalties for firearm crimes involving rapid fire activators (up to 3 years imprisonment), this agency will be responsible for the resulting incarceration and parole/probation oversight.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Maryland Office of the Public Defender
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The OPD is responsible for providing legal representation to indigent defendants. The creation of new criminal offenses related to machine gun convertible pistols will increase the caseload for OPD attorneys who must defend individuals charged under these new statutes.
The AOC provides operational support to the state's courts. The bill's expansion of firearm crimes will lead to additional criminal cases being filed and adjudicated in the Maryland court system.

The OAG serves as the primary legal representative for the state and provides counsel to state agencies like the Maryland State Police. They would be involved in providing legal guidance on the development of regulations and representing the state in any legal challenges or appeals related to the new law.

As the principal fiscal and personnel agency, DBM will be involved in the allocation of the $220,216 identified in the fiscal note for new personnel at the Maryland State Police and will oversee the personnel management of these new roles.

The Governor's Office oversees the executive branch and coordinates policy initiatives. The Governor must sign the bill into law and oversees the agencies (MSP and DPSCS) responsible for enforcement and corrections.

The Adjutant General oversees the Maryland National Guard. The bill specifically exempts members of the National Guard from the firearm prohibitions while acting within the scope of official business.

DNR includes the Natural Resources Police. These officers are law enforcement personnel of the State who are specifically exempted from the bill's prohibitions while acting within the scope of their official business.

MDOT oversees various transportation-related law enforcement entities (such as Maryland Transportation Authority Police) and the bill explicitly mentions exemptions for railroad police officers, making it relevant to the state's broader transportation security and police framework.

bill_summary: House Bill 578 updates Maryland's endangered and threatened species laws by defining 'foreseeable future' and 'harm,' authorizing the designation of 'essential habitats,' and requiring decennial and quinquennial reviews of conservation regulations. It also prohibits the taking of migratory birds protected under federal law as of January 1, 2025, while mandating state-level authorizations for taking black vultures if federal protections are repealed or removed.
stakeholders: Maryland Department of Natural Resources, state and local government agencies, small businesses involved in land development, and the general public.
fiscal_impact_summary: State and local expenditures may increase starting in fiscal 2027 to implement and enforce new habitat and migratory bird protections. The Department of Natural Resources expects additional resources will be required for permit reviews and enforcement, but the specific financial impact is currently indeterminate.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: DNR is the primary agency responsible for implementing the bill, including managing the Irreplaceable Natural Areas Program, designating essential habitats, adopting management protocols, and promulgating regulations for endangered species and the taking of black vultures.

As noted in the fiscal note, the bill's strengthened protections for fish, wildlife, and migratory birds could impact the capital programs and infrastructure projects of MDOT's various administrations, such as SHA and MTA.

The bill explicitly requires the Secretary of DNR to consult with the Secretary of Agriculture regarding conservation programs. Additionally, the provisions regarding black vultures significantly impact the agricultural community.
DGS manages the planning, design, and construction of state-owned facilities; its capital projects may be impacted by the bill's new definitions for 'harm' and 'essential habitat' designations.
The OAG will be responsible for providing legal counsel to DNR regarding the new regulatory definitions of 'harm' and 'foreseeable future' and representing the agency in potential litigation.
MDP provides land use policy guidance and works with DNR on conservation initiatives. Essential habitat designations under the bill will intersect with the state's land use planning goals.
The BPW must approve the acquisition of land or interests in land for the conservation of threatened or endangered species, which is a program requirement under the bill.
The OAH would adjudicate contested cases resulting from DNR's enforcement of new regulations or the denial/granting of permits related to the taking of species or habitat modification.
As a state agency with significant capital construction programs across multiple institutions, USM was identified in the fiscal note as a potentially impacted entity.
The IAC oversees public school construction; projects could be affected by more stringent habitat and species protections established in the bill.
The MSA's construction activities, including professional sports venues and public schools, may be subject to the bill's new habitat and wildlife regulations.
This multi-agency initiative coordinates sustainable development and environmental protection, aligning directly with the bill's focus on biodiversity and habitat management.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Governor's Council on the Chesapeake Bay
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Council advises on the restoration of the Bay watershed; the bill's habitat protections for endangered fish and wildlife are integral to these restoration efforts.
As a state agency with its own capital construction projects, MSU may be impacted by habitat and wildlife protections affecting urban campus development.
As an independent state unit with a waterfront campus, SMCM's construction or maintenance activities could be affected by new fish and habitat regulations.
DBM oversees DNR's budget and personnel, which the fiscal note indicates may need to increase to support the new regulatory and enforcement duties required by the bill.

Synopsis: Exempting the first $50,000 of the assessment of a dwelling in Baltimore County from the State property tax if the homeowner is at least 65 years old and qualifies for the homestead property tax credit; altering the calculation of the homestead property tax credit for a homeowner in Baltimore County who is at least 65 years old; requiring the governing body of Baltimore County to grant a credit against the county property tax imposed on certain real property if the homeowner is at least 65 and as certain qualifications; etc.

bill_summary: House Bill 579 establishes property tax relief for Baltimore County homeowners aged 65 and older who qualify for the homestead property tax credit. The bill exempts the first $50,000 of a dwelling's assessment from State property taxes, requires the Baltimore County government to grant a local property tax credit for the first $50,000 of assessment, and sets the homestead credit percentage at 100%, effectively capping annual taxable assessment increases at 0% for these eligible seniors.
responsible_party: Maryland State Department of Assessments and Taxation and the Baltimore County government
stakeholders: Homeowners in Baltimore County who are at least 65 years old and qualify for the homestead property tax credit.
fiscal_impact_summary: According to the fiscal note, State Annuity Bond Fund revenues will decrease by approximately $5,000,000 annually beginning in FY 2027, potentially requiring a State property tax rate increase or a General Fund appropriation to cover debt service. Baltimore County property tax revenues are estimated to decrease by approximately $43,700,000 in FY 2027 and FY 2028, with future revenue losses potentially increasing as assessments rise.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Board of Public Works sets the annual State property tax rate required to pay debt service on State general obligation bonds. As the bill creates a partial exemption and alters credit percentages that reduce Annuity Bond Fund revenues by $5 million annually, the Board will be responsible for adjusting the tax rate or overseeing the allocation of other funds to maintain debt service coverage.

As the principal fiscal and personnel agency, DBM oversees budget development and revenue estimation. The fiscal note indicates that the $5 million reduction in Annuity Bond Fund revenues may require a General Fund appropriation to cover debt service on State bonds, a process that falls under DBM's direct responsibility for budget execution and planning.

This independent agency provides administrative review for property tax assessment disputes, including tax exemptions and credits. By establishing a new partial exemption and a mandatory property tax credit for seniors in Baltimore County, the bill creates new criteria for eligibility that will likely result in appeals to the local boards overseen by this agency.

The Treasurer is a member of the Board of Public Works and is responsible for managing state funds and the debt service on State bonds. Since State property tax revenues are dedicated to the Annuity Bond Fund for bond repayment, the Treasurer is directly impacted by the bill's projected revenue decrease.

The Comptroller serves as the state's chief financial officer and is a member of the Board of Public Works. The agency oversees state revenue collection and fiscal integrity, both of which are impacted by the $5 million decrease in State property tax revenue and the mandatory adjustments to local tax credits.

The Tax Court is the highest level of administrative review for tax disputes, including real property assessments and credits. It will have jurisdiction over any appeals resulting from the newly established senior property tax exemptions and homestead credit alterations in Baltimore County.

The Governor's Office proposes the annual state budget and coordinates executive branch policy. The Governor also sits on the Board of Public Works, which must decide how to address the revenue shortfall caused by the bill's tax exemptions and credits for Baltimore County seniors.

The bill's primary objective is to provide property tax relief to residents who are at least 65 years old. This directly impacts the economic quality of life for the population served and advocated for by the Maryland Department of Aging.

The Office of the Attorney General provides legal counsel to state agencies and boards, including the Board of Public Works and taxing authorities. The office will be responsible for providing legal guidance on the implementation of the bill's age-specific property tax mandates.

The bill explicitly lists the Register of Wills as one of the specific offices for which Montgomery County may adopt ranked-choice or approval voting methods. The bill authorizes new voting methods for the election of Judges of the Circuit Court. The Administrative Office of the Courts provides central operational, legal, and financial support for the Maryland Judicial Branch and its judges.

The fiscal note identifies a notable impact on the State's general fund expenditures (estimated at $245,000 in FY 2028). As the principal fiscal agency, DBM is responsible for budget development and supervision of budget execution.

The OAG serves as the chief legal officer for the state and provide counsel to the State Board of Elections. The introduction of novel voting methods likely requires legal review and guidance to ensure compliance with constitutional and state laws.

The Governor's Office oversees the executive branch, including the State Board of Elections, and the Governor is responsible for signing or vetoing the legislation and proposing the budget that would include the state's share of implementation costs.

The Secretary of State is the principal custodian of the state's official records, including the laws and executive orders related to the administration of elections and the formal commissions for state officials.

bill_summary: This bill requires the Baltimore County Board of Elections to verify a voter's signature on an absentee ballot envelope against their registration record before the ballot can be counted. stakeholders: Absentee voters in Baltimore County, the Baltimore County Board of Elections, and military personnel and their families serving overseas.
fiscal_impact_summary: The bill is expected to increase administrative and operational costs for the Baltimore County Board of Elections to implement signature verification and witness signature tracking. agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill directly mandates the State Board of Elections to establish guidelines and adopt regulations for the verification of signatures on absentee ballots specifically for Baltimore County.

The implementation of signature verification processes for absentee ballots involves significant administrative and personnel costs, which fall under the fiscal and budget execution oversight of this department.
The bill includes specific witness signature exemptions for active-duty uniformed service members and their families serving overseas, a population this department is tasked with supporting.

Signature verification against registration records requires the use of the statewide voter registration system, potentially necessitating IT updates or technical coordination overseen by this agency.

As an emergency measure, the bill requires the Governor's immediate signature to take effect and involves the oversight of executive agencies responsible for election law implementation.

bill_summary: This bill proposes a constitutional amendment to be known as the Clean Maryland Democracy Amendment. It guarantees equal voting rights for all eligible voters and mandates the creation of a Maryland Voting Rights Act by July 1, 2028, to protect against discrimination and ensure access for disabled and language-minority voters. Additionally, it prohibits political spending by foreign governments, nationals, or foreign-influenced corporations, requires disclosure of the ultimate sources of significant political funding by July 1, 2027, and establishes the Maryland Fair Elections Program to provide public campaign financing for candidates for the General Assembly starting with the 2030 elections.
responsible_party: Maryland General Assembly, State Board of Elections, and Office of the State Prosecutor
stakeholders: Eligible Maryland voters, candidates for the General Assembly, foreign-influenced corporations, and small businesses providing campaign services.
fiscal_impact_summary: If approved by voters in 2026, State general fund expenditures are expected to increase by $127,791 in FY 2028 for the Office of the State Prosecutor to hire an investigator for enforcement. While the exact cost of the Maryland Fair Elections Program cannot be reliably estimated, public campaign matching funds are expected to cost in the millions of dollars. There are also anticipated administrative costs for the Office of the Attorney General to enforce the Maryland Voting Rights Act. Local government finances may also be impacted by the new voting rights requirements.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The State Board of Elections is the primary agency responsible for administering election laws, certifying voting systems, and regulating campaign finance. This bill creates a new public campaign financing program (Maryland Fair Elections Program) and new disclosure requirements for political spending, which the SBE would likely oversee.

The fiscal note specifically identifies a need for additional staffing (one investigator) within the OSP to enforce the prohibition on foreign influence in elections and investigate potential violations by foreign-influenced corporations.

The OAG serves as the primary legal representative for state agencies and enforcer of state laws. The fiscal note indicates the OAG would likely require an additional Assistant Attorney General to handle enforcement of the new Maryland Voting Rights Act.

The proposed constitutional amendment specifically mandates that the Maryland Voting Rights Act includes provisions for access to voting for disabled individuals, which aligns with this department's mission to improve service delivery and integration for residents with disabilities.

As the principal fiscal agency, DBM is responsible for the state budget and personnel. The bill requires the creation of a 'stable and sustainable source of revenue' for a new fund and involves significant long-term fiscal planning and potential increases in state personnel expenditures.

The Governor's Office oversees policy initiatives and the executive branch. This constitutional amendment proposes fundamental changes to state democracy, the elective franchise, and budget priorities related to campaign financing.

The bill requires the Maryland Voting Rights Act to include a private right of action, which would lead to litigation in the state's judicial system that the AOC supports operationally and financially.

The Treasurer is the custodian of state funds. The establishment of the Maryland Fair Elections Fund would fall under the Treasurer's responsibility for managing, investing, and distributing state funds.

As the chief financial officer and tax collector, the Comptroller would be involved in identifying and managing the 'stable and sustainable source of revenue' required to fund the Fair Elections Program.

The bill requires disclosure of the 'true, ultimate sources of significant funds used for political spending.' Implementing such a transparent and complex reporting system would likely require DoIT's strategy, infrastructure, and cybersecurity oversight.

The bill prohibits denying, diluting, or abridging the right to vote based on race, color, language minority status, or disability. The Commission enforces anti-discrimination laws and may have a role in education or investigating related complaints.

The Secretary of State is the custodian of official records, including executive orders and laws, and is responsible for processing constitutional amendments and returns to the Governor following elections.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Maryland Department of Transportation (MDOT) is the parent agency for the Motor Vehicle Administration and oversees the Transportation Trust Fund (TTF). This bill significantly reduces TTF revenue by an estimated $29 million starting in FY 2027.

The Motor Vehicle Administration (MVA) is the primary agency responsible for vehicle titling and the collection of the vehicle excise tax. The bill creates a new exemption category for rental vehicles that the MVA must implement and manage.

As the state's chief financial officer and tax collector, the Comptroller is responsible for managing state revenues and accounts, including the Gasoline and Motor Vehicle Revenue Account mentioned in the bill's distribution sections.

The Department of Budget and Management (DBM) handles revenue estimation and long-term fiscal planning. The significant decrease in excise tax revenue impacts the overall state budget and the fiscal health of the Transportation Trust Fund.

The Governor proposes the annual state budget and oversees executive branch policy. This bill reverses tax changes previously established in the Budget Reconciliation and Financing Act (BRFA) of 2025, impacting the Governor's fiscal strategy.
The State Treasurer's Office acts as the custodian of state funds, including the receipt and management of revenues flowing into the Transportation Trust Fund.
The Office of the Attorney General provides legal counsel to the MVA and MDOT regarding the application of the Transportation Article and new tax exemptions.

The IAC oversees funding and execution of public school capital projects. Changes to vendor registration policies for the Prince George's County Board of Education may affect the pool of eligible vendors for construction projects managed or funded through the IAC.

In addition to agricultural land preservation, the proceeds may now be used for programs, services, or initiatives intended to enhance the commercial viability or environmental sustainability of agriculture in Howard County.
responsible_party: Howard County Director of Finance and the Howard County Council
stakeholders: Agricultural land owners, farmers, and the agricultural business community in Howard County
fiscal_impact_summary: The bill has no direct impact on State or local finances, as it does not change the local transfer tax rate or the percentage of revenue allocated to the fund. It only renames the fund and broadens the permitted uses of the existing revenue stream. According to the fiscal note, Howard County's fiscal 2026 budget allocates approximately $7,800,000 in transfer tax revenue to this fund.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill focuses on agricultural land preservation and enhancing the commercial viability and environmental sustainability of farming, which are core components of the Maryland Department of Agriculture's mission.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Maryland Agricultural & Resource-Based Industry Development Corp.
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill's expansion of the Howard County fund's scope to include 'innovation' and 'commercial viability' directly mirrors MARBIDCO's mission to support the profitability and sustainability of Maryland's agricultural industries through targeted financial services and partnerships.

The Department of Planning is responsible for land use planning and environmental preservation. Alterations to local agricultural land preservation funds are relevant to the state's broader strategies for sustainable growth and land resource management.
The bill aligns with this multi-agency initiative's goals of preserving farmland, protecting the environment, and promoting sustainable development through coordinated land-use planning.

The bill mentions using proceeds for the 'environmental sustainability' of agriculture, which intersects with the Department of the Environment's role in implementing state environmental laws and protecting natural resources.

The Governor's Office oversees the executive branch and coordinates policy initiatives; the Governor signed this bill into law, making it relevant to the executive's legislative agenda for local and state-level agricultural support.

The Rural Maryland Council advocates for rural interests and agriculture. Since Howard County contains rural agricultural areas, the council has a general interest in policies affecting local agricultural funding and innovation.

bill_summary: This bill prohibits individuals in Wicomico County from standing in roadways, shoulders, median dividers, or intersections that the county or a municipality has determined to be 'inherently dangerous' in consultation with the Maryland State Highway Administration. It mandates the installation of appropriate warning signs before a police officer can issue a citation for a violation of the act.
responsible_party: Wicomico County, municipal corporations within Wicomico County, and the Maryland State Highway Administration
stakeholders: Pedestrians, motorists, and law enforcement officers in Wicomico County
fiscal_impact_summary: The bill does not materially affect State or local operations or finances. The State Highway Administration can manage the bill's requirements using existing resources, and Wicomico County's finances are not expected to be significantly impacted.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill explicitly requires Wicomico County to consult with the State Highway Administration to determine if a State roadway is 'inherently dangerous' and mandates that any signs installed on State highways must have SHA's approval.

As the parent agency of the State Highway Administration (SHA), the Department of Transportation oversees the broader transportation policy and infrastructure standards impacted by this bill in Wicomico County.

As the primary law enforcement agency for state highways, the Maryland State Police will be responsible for enforcing the new standing prohibition and issuing citations in accordance with the bill's conditions.

The bill creates a new violation within the Transportation Article; the Administrative Office of the Courts will oversee the judicial processing and adjudication of any citations issued for these violations.
The bill addresses a specific public safety and community management issue in Wicomico County, which is one of the 18 rural counties supported and advocated for by the Rural Maryland Council.

The Office of the Attorney General provides legal counsel to the State Highway Administration and the Maryland State Police, and may be required to interpret the new statutory language or signage requirements.

As an agency within the Department of Transportation that manages driving records and traffic safety, the MVA may be minimally impacted by the creation of new roadway violations, even if primarily pedestrian-focused.

bill_summary: This bill establishes the Task Force to Study Forced Infant Separation From Incarcerated Individuals. The task force is charged with researching the prevalence of pregnant and postpartum individuals in Maryland's prisons, evaluating the impact of infant separation, studying best practices from other jurisdictions, and recommending legislation to facilitate bonding between incarcerated parents and their children.
responsible_party: Governor’s Office of Crime Prevention and Policy
stakeholders: Incarcerated pregnant and postpartum individuals, their infants and families, the Maryland Department of Public Safety and Correctional Services, the Maryland Department of Health, and legal and social work professionals.
fiscal_impact_summary: The bill's fiscal impact involves costs for the Governor's Office of Crime Prevention and Policy to staff the task force and provide travel reimbursement for its members. While the bill explicitly allows for travel expense reimbursement as provided in the State budget, specific dollar estimates are unavailable as a formal fiscal note was not provided in the text.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill stipulates that members of the Task Force are entitled to reimbursement for expenses under the Standard State Travel Regulations, which are administered by the Department of Budget and Management.

The Secretary of Health is a designated member of the Task Force, which is tasked with studying the health-related impacts of forced infant separation and the needs of postpartum incarcerated individuals.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Department of Public Safety and Correctional Services
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Secretary of Public Safety and Correctional Services is a member of the Task Force. The Task Force is specifically required to study the number of pregnant and postpartum individuals in State prisons and the capacity of the Division of Correction to create specialized housing space for them.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Executive Commissions, Committees, Task Forces, and Advisory Boards
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill establishes a new Task Force to Study Forced Infant Separation From Incarcerated Individuals, which falls under this category of state entities.
The Governor is responsible for appointing ten of the fifteen members of the Task Force, representing various professional backgrounds and lived experiences.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Governor's Office of Crime Prevention and Policy
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Governor's Office of Crime Prevention and Policy is mandated to provide staffing for the Task Force, and its Executive Director is responsible for designating the chair.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Maryland Office of the Public Defender
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Public Defender is a designated member of the Task Force, which aligns with the agency's mission to protect parental rights and provide defense in juvenile and family matters.
The Office of Appointments will assist the Governor in recruiting and vetting the ten diverse members to be appointed to the Task Force.

bill_summary: This bill prohibits unauthorized access to or interference with critical infrastructure and public safety answering points (PSAPs). It defines critical infrastructure as systems and assets vital to the State, such as those related to public security, health, and utilities, and establishes new felony offenses and penalties for actions intended to interrupt or impair these services.
responsible_party: Maryland Department of Public Safety and Correctional Services and the Maryland Judiciary
stakeholders: Operators of critical infrastructure including public utilities, transportation, and health care facilities; public safety answering point (9-1-1 center) personnel; and law enforcement agencies.
fiscal_impact_summary: The formal fiscal note indicates that the bill is not expected to materially affect State or local finances or operations. While the bill establishes new felony penalties and potential fines of up to $50,000, specific dollar estimates for total revenue or expenditure changes are unavailable as the overall fiscal impact is projected to be minimal.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The department oversees the Maryland 9-1-1 Board and coordinates preparedness for emergencies. The bill specifically addresses interference with public safety answering points (PSAPs), which are central to the state's 9-1-1 system.

The department is responsible for the state's cybersecurity and IT infrastructure. The bill targets unauthorized access to computer networks and virtual assets, which falls directly under the agency's security and strategy mandate.
As the primary law enforcement agency for the state, the Maryland State Police are responsible for investigating criminal violations of the state's computer laws and ensuring public peace.

This office coordinates homeland security efforts and assesses readiness for emergencies. Protecting critical infrastructure from intentional interference is a core component of its disaster prevention strategy.
The bill's definition of 'critical infrastructure' explicitly includes public transportation systems. The department operates major transit networks that could be impacted by such interference.
The commission regulates public utilities such as electricity and natural gas. These services are specifically named in the bill as critical infrastructure components subject to protection.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Maryland Institute for Emergency Medical Services Systems
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The agency regulates the state's emergency medical services network and communications infrastructure, which relies on the functionality of public safety answering points.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Department of Public Safety and Correctional Services
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The department manages correctional facilities and public safety security. Additionally, the bill creates new felony penalties that directly affect the correctional population managed by the agency.
The agency provides operational and legal support to the judicial branch, which will process the criminal cases and felony prosecutions resulting from violations of this bill.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Maryland Office of the Public Defender
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The office provides legal representation to indigent defendants. The creation of new felony offenses for infrastructure interference will impact the agency's caseload.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Governor's Office of Crime Prevention and Policy
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The office advises the Governor on criminal justice strategies and manages public safety funds. The bill's focus on new criminal offenses for infrastructure interference aligns with its policy mandate.
The OAG is the chief legal representative for the state and provides counsel to agencies involved in infrastructure protection and law enforcement.
The department oversees public water and wastewater systems, which are included in the bill's definition of critical infrastructure related to public utilities.
The agency coordinates energy planning and policy. Electricity and natural gas services are specifically identified as critical infrastructure in the context of this legislation.
The bill defines critical infrastructure to include assets vital to public health and specifically mentions health care facilities, which are regulated by the department.
As the primary manager of state-owned facilities and physical infrastructure, the department is responsible for the security and maintenance of the types of assets the bill seeks to protect.
The office oversees the executive branch and coordinates policy initiatives. The Governor signed the bill and oversees the departments tasked with protecting critical infrastructure.
The bill's framework and the expanded infrastructure definitions include public schools. The agency provides coordination for school safety across the state.
The office advocates for utility consumers. Since the bill concerns the reliability and integrity of public utility infrastructure (electric/gas), it is relevant to consumer interests.

Synopsis: Altering the distribution of sales and use tax revenues to require the Comptroller to pay to the City of Baltimore one-third of the revenues from sales and use taxes collected and remitted from sales that occur within the City of Baltimore.
Title: Sales and Use Tax - Distribution - City of Baltimore
Status: In the House - Hearing 2/12 at 1:00 p.m.
bill_summary: This bill requires the Comptroller of Maryland to distribute one-third of the sales and use tax revenue collected from retail sales within Baltimore City directly to Baltimore City. This revenue is currently distributed to the State General Fund and the Blueprint for Maryland's Future Fund.
stakeholders: Baltimore City government and residents, the Maryland Department of Budget and Management, and the Blueprint for Maryland's Future Fund.
fiscal_impact_summary: State general fund revenues are projected to decrease by approximately $185.5 million and Blueprint for Maryland’s Future Fund (BMFF) revenues by $25.5 million in fiscal 2027. Baltimore City revenues are expected to increase by an equivalent total of $211.1 million in fiscal 2027, rising to $234.0 million by fiscal 2031. To offset the loss of revenue to the BMFF, State general fund expenditures are projected to increase by $51.7 million in fiscal 2028 and between $26.8 million and $28.3 million annually through fiscal 2031.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Comptroller is the primary agency responsible for collecting and distributing sales and use tax revenues. This bill explicitly mandates that the Comptroller pay a specific portion of those revenues to the City of Baltimore.

The bill creates a significant reduction in General Fund revenues (estimated at over $185 million initially) and impacts the Blueprint for Maryland's Future Fund, necessitating major adjustments to state fiscal planning, revenue estimation, and budget execution.

The bill reduces the percentage of sales and use tax revenues flowing into the Blueprint for Maryland's Future Fund, which MSDE uses to support educational initiatives. The fiscal note indicates that future general fund expenditures will be required to offset this shortfall.

The Governor is responsible for proposing the annual state budget and overseeing the executive branch. This bill introduces a substantial long-term fiscal impact on the state's General Fund that must be accounted for in the Governor's budget proposals.

As the agency responsible for the management, protection, and distribution of state funds, the Treasurer is impacted by large-scale changes to the state's revenue distribution and the resulting shifts in general fund balances.

The OAG provides legal counsel to the Comptroller and the General Assembly regarding the interpretation and implementation of tax and distribution statutes, including ensuring the legality of the new distribution mechanism.

Synopsis: Altering eligibility for a credit against the State income tax for physician preceptors by repealing a requirement that a student in a physician preceptorship program be enrolled in a medical school or medical training program in the State and reducing the required number of hours for a preceptor rotation for community-based clinical training; limiting to $100,000 the excess amount of tax credit certificates the Department may carry forward; and applying the Act to taxable years beginning after December 31, 2025.
