bill_summary: This bill modifies the State income tax credit for licensed physicians who serve as uncompensated preceptors in areas with healthcare workforce shortages. It expands eligibility to include physicians supervising students from out-of-state medical schools, reduces the required hours per rotation from 100 to 90, and caps the amount of unused tax credit certificates that can be carried forward to $100,000.
stakeholders: Licensed physicians serving as preceptors, medical students from accredited in-state and out-of-state medical schools, and Maryland residents in health care workforce shortage areas.
fiscal_impact_summary: State general fund revenues may decrease beginning in fiscal 2027 to the extent that the bill's changes increase utilization of the tax credit. The Department of Health is authorized to issue up to $100,000 in tax credit certificates annually, and the bill establishes a $100,000 limit on the aggregate amount of unissued credits that may be carried forward from prior years. Historical utilization of the credit averaged approximately $30,000 per year from 2020 through 2024. There is no local fiscal impact.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Maryland Department of Health is the primary agency responsible for administering the tax credit program, which includes identifying healthcare workforce shortage areas, processing applications, issuing tax credit certificates, and adopting regulations.

As the state's principal tax collector, the Comptroller is responsible for processing the income tax credits claimed by physicians and receiving mandatory annual reports from the Department of Health regarding the certificates issued.

The bill explicitly requires the Maryland Department of Health to consult with the Governor's Workforce Development Board to identify healthcare workforce shortage areas and to adopt regulations for the tax credit program.

The Department of Budget and Management is responsible for revenue estimation and fiscal planning; the bill has a direct impact on general fund revenues due to the alterations in tax credit eligibility and caps.

The Department of Labor is involved in workforce development and adult learning; although the Governor's Workforce Development Board is the primary consultative body named, the Department of Labor was included in the fiscal analysis of the bill's impact on the state's labor force.

The Governor's Office oversees the executive branch agencies (MDH and GWDB) responsible for implementing the program and is involved in the broader policy initiative of addressing healthcare workforce shortages.

Synopsis: Conforming the Maryland Uniform Simultaneous Death Act to the Uniform Simultaneous Death Act; providing that a surviving individual who does not survive the death of another individual for at least 120 hours is deemed to have predeceased the other individual for purposes relating to the inheritance of property; establishing evidentiary procedures for determining an individual's death or survival in certain circumstances; providing for liability under the Act in connection with the distribution of disputed assets; etc.
Title: Estates - Maryland Uniform Simultaneous Death Act
Status: Approved by the Governor - Chapter 509

NarrowSubjects.Name: Courts -see also- AppCt; Circuit; District; Orphans'; etc.
Death -see also- Homicide; Murder; Wrongful Death
Vital Records -see also- Death; Divorce; Marriage

bill_summary: This bill updates the Maryland Uniform Simultaneous Death Act to align with the 1993 version of the uniform act. It establishes a requirement that an individual must be proven by clear and convincing evidence to have survived another person or a specific event by at least 120 hours to be legally recognized as a survivor for property inheritance and distribution. The bill also sets evidentiary standards for determining death, creates a presumption of death after a five-year absence, and provides liability protections for third-party payors who distribute assets in good faith reliance on governing instruments.
responsible_party: Maryland Judiciary (Administrative Office of the Courts), Orphans' Courts, and the Register of Wills
stakeholders: Heirs, beneficiaries of estates and insurance policies, co-owners of property with rights of survivorship (joint tenants), and third-party payors such as trustees and insurance companies.
fiscal_impact_summary: According to the fiscal note, the bill does not materially affect State or local government finances.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Register of Wills is primarily responsible for the administrative probate of estates, including the timely administration of decedents' estates and the collection of inheritance taxes. This bill fundamentally changes the legal standard for determining survivorship (the 120-hour rule) for property distribution, which is a core function of the probate process managed by this agency.

The bill establishes evidentiary procedures for determining death or survival and deals with the distribution of disputed assets within the court system. The AOC provides operational and legal support to the Maryland Judicial Branch, which will adjudicate disputes arising from these new statutory requirements.

The bill explicitly includes insurers as 'payors' and identifies insurance policies as 'governing instruments.' It provides specific rules for how insurance proceeds should be distributed when survival cannot be established, which falls under the regulatory purview of the MIA.

The bill defines 'governing instruments' to include retirement or similar benefit plans and defines 'payors' to include government agencies. The SRA manages death benefits for state employees and teachers, and this bill's 120-hour survival requirement would govern the distribution of these benefits in simultaneous death scenarios.

As the chief legal officer for the state, the OAG provides legal counsel to state agencies and the General Assembly on the implementation and interpretation of new laws, including the Uniform Simultaneous Death Act.

The bill mentions escheatment to the State under certain conditions. The Comptroller's office manages unclaimed property and state revenues, which may be impacted if property lacks eligible heirs under the new 120-hour survival rule.

The bill defines 'payor' to include government agencies and 'governing instrument' to include retirement and benefit plans. As the central agency for state employee benefits, DBM has a secondary interest in how survival rules affect benefit payouts.

The bill references specific sections of the Health - General Article regarding the determination of death and the issuance of death certificates, which are managed by the Maryland Department of Health.

bill_summary: This bill modifies the Community Choice Aggregation Pilot Program in Montgomery County by delaying the program's start date to April 1, 2026, extending its duration from seven to nine years, and pushing back the deadlines for the Public Service Commission to report on the program's status and effectiveness.
stakeholders: Residential and small commercial electric customers in Montgomery County.
fiscal_impact_summary: The Maryland Public Service Commission and the Office of People’s Counsel can implement the bill's changes using existing budgeted resources. There is no significant impact on state revenues or local finances during the five-year period covered by the fiscal note. While the underlying pilot program is projected to reduce annual household electricity costs by approximately $84 to $211, these changes are considered external to state and local government budgets.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Public Service Commission is the primary agency responsible for administering the Community Choice Aggregation Pilot Program, conducting the required studies, and submitting the specified reports to the Governor and General Assembly.

The Office of the People's Counsel is explicitly mentioned in the fiscal note as having the capacity to implement the bill's changes and is responsible for representing the interests of residential utility consumers in such pilot programs.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Executive Commissions, Committees, Task Forces, and Advisory Boards
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill specifically requires the Public Service Commission to seek the advice and recommendation of the Community Choice Energy Workgroup, which is a state advisory body, regarding the pilot program study.
The bill alters the statutory deadlines for reports that must be submitted to the Governor regarding the effectiveness and findings of the Community Choice Aggregation Pilot Program.

As the state agency responsible for coordinating energy policy and planning, the MEA monitors pilot programs like community choice aggregation that impact the state's energy market and sustainability goals.

The Office of the Attorney General provides legal counsel to the Public Service Commission and the General Assembly regarding the implementation and statutory interpretation of utility-related pilot programs.

bill_summary: This bill authorizes the Maryland Board of Physicians to issue a non-renewable limited license to practice medicine to internationally trained physicians who meet specific education, training, and examination requirements. It establishes two pathways for these physicians to transition to full licensure and modifies the conditions under which physicians licensed in other jurisdictions may practice in Maryland hospitals without a local license. Additionally, it requires Maryland medical schools to collaborate on the development of a state standard of care assessment.
stakeholders: Internationally trained physicians, out-of-state physicians, Maryland Board of Physicians, Maryland healthcare facilities (hospitals and clinics), and Maryland medical schools.
fiscal_impact_summary: The Fiscal Note indicates that Maryland Board of Physicians special fund expenditures will increase by $1,103,246 in fiscal year 2028, rising to approximately $1,287,600 by fiscal year 2031, to cover additional staff (licensure analysts) and contractual services (translation, background checks, and software updates). Special fund revenues are expected to increase by an indeterminate amount from new application fees beginning in fiscal year 2028. There is no projected impact on local government finances.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Maryland Board of Physicians (MBP), which is a regulatory body within the Department of Health, is the primary agency responsible for implementing the new limited license for internationally trained physicians. The bill also identifies local health departments as potential community sponsors and mentions the MDH Office of Population Health Improvement in the fiscal note.

The bill explicitly tasks the University of Maryland School of Medicine, a constituent institution of the University System of Maryland, with collaborating to develop the new State standard of care assessment and establishing an entity to serve as the examiner.

The OAG serves as the primary legal counsel for state boards and commissions, including the Board of Physicians. They will likely be involved in drafting the necessary regulations, advising on disciplinary record reviews, and handling legal matters related to the new licensure pathway.

The fiscal note indicates a significant impact on state expenditures, including the addition of two new licensure analyst positions and over $1 million in ongoing costs, which falls under DBM's responsibility for budget development and personnel management.

The fiscal note identifies $125,000 in one-time software update expenses to incorporate the new limited license into the state's existing licensing and practitioner profile systems, which DoIT oversees as the central IT agency.

The Governor's Office oversees the executive branch and coordinating policy initiatives. The Board of Physicians is required to report on its implementation progress to the General Assembly, a process the Governor's Office typically monitors for administrative compliance.

The bill specifies that the Board must consider medical disciplinary history from any branch of the uniformed services or the U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs when determining eligibility for licensure or practice exemptions.

The bill identifies 'rural health clinics' as eligible community sponsors for internationally trained physicians. RMC advocates for rural healthcare access and may be involved in regional cooperation efforts related to this workforce initiative.

bill_summary: This bill requires hospitals, in order to qualify for a license on or after October 1, 2026, to qualify as a nonprofit organization under federal law and be registered as a nonprofit with the State. Hospitals must maintain nonprofit status as a condition of licensure, and ownership of a licensed hospital may only be transferred to a nonprofit organization on or after the specified date.
responsible_party: Maryland Department of Health (Office of Health Care Quality) and the Secretary of State
stakeholders: Maryland hospitals, hospital owners, potential hospital purchasers, and the Maryland Department of Health.
fiscal_impact_summary: The bill does not materially affect Maryland State or local governmental operations or finances. According to the Fiscal Note, there is no small business impact and no impact on local government units.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Maryland Department of Health is the primary agency responsible for the licensure and oversight of hospitals through its Office of Health Care Quality; this bill establishes nonprofit status as a mandatory condition for such licensure.
The Secretary of State registers and oversees charitable and nonprofit organizations in Maryland; the bill explicitly requires hospitals to be registered with the State as nonprofit organizations.
HSCRC regulates hospital revenues and compiles community benefit reports for nonprofit hospitals; this bill ensures all licensed hospitals in Maryland will fall under this nonprofit reporting regime.

MHCC oversees the Certificate of Need process required for hospital operations and ownership changes; the bill's restriction of ownership transfers to nonprofit entities directly impacts these regulatory functions.
The OAG provides legal counsel to the Department of Health and its commissions regarding the implementation and enforcement of hospital licensure and regulatory requirements.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: MHHEFA provides tax-exempt financing specifically for nonprofit health institutions; by requiring all hospitals to be nonprofits, the bill defines the total potential client base for the agency's financing programs.

The Governor's Office oversees the executive branch and coordinates policy initiatives; the bill represents a significant shift in the state's policy regarding the ownership and regulation of healthcare facilities.
As the state's principal fiscal agency, DBM monitors the budget execution and personnel requirements of the agencies tasked with implementing the new licensure and registration standards.
OAH adjudicates contested administrative cases and would serve as the venue for appeals if a hospital's license is denied or revoked due to non-compliance with the nonprofit requirements.

As the parent agency of the State Highway Administration and Motor Vehicle Administration, MDOT oversees the state's transportation network and coordinate safety policies and technical implementation related to automated traffic enforcement.
The Comptroller is relevant because the bill requires local jurisdictions to remit any citation revenue that exceeds 10% of their total annual revenue to the Comptroller's office.

The Maryland Tax Court serves as the final administrative body for tax disputes, including property-related tax assessments and exemptions. Contested decisions from local appeals boards regarding the eligibility for this transfer tax exemption would ultimately be adjudicated by this agency.

The Department of Housing and Community Development is tasked with supporting homeownership and community revitalization. This bill, which provides a significant tax exemption for first-time home buyers, directly aligns with the agency's mission to make housing more accessible and affordable for Maryland residents.

As the state's chief financial officer and principal tax collector, the Comptroller oversees the enforcement of tax laws and the administration of exemptions, even those collected at the local level through judicial land records.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The board is responsible for hearing appeals regarding property tax assessments and credits at the local level. This bill mandates a specific homestead credit percentage for Baltimore County, which directly impacts the board's adjudicatory responsibilities in that jurisdiction.

The Tax Court serves as the highest level of administrative review for tax disputes, including real property assessments and credits. It would adjudicate any appeals arising from the implementation of this specific homestead credit change in Baltimore County.
The OAG provides legal counsel to the General Assembly and state agencies regarding the validity and implementation of tax laws and mandates on local government entities.

The Governor's Office coordinates policy initiatives and manages intergovernmental relations. A state-mandated fiscal change for a major jurisdiction like Baltimore County falls under its oversight of executive policy and economic impact.
As the principal fiscal agency for the state, DBM monitors long-term fiscal planning and the economic health of the state's jurisdictions, even when there is no direct impact on the state budget.
As the state's chief financial officer, the Comptroller monitors revenue trends and fiscal policies across the state, including local tax changes that may impact the broader economic environment.

The homestead property tax credit is a key mechanism for maintaining housing affordability and stability. Changes to this credit in a large county directly relate to the department's mission to support secure housing for residents.

Property tax assessment caps are a vital protection for older adults on fixed incomes. The department advocates for policies that ensure housing stability and a high quality of life for Maryland's senior population.
The team's mission includes enhancing economic mobility. Tax relief through homestead credits in Baltimore County can impact the economic stability and mobility of families in the region.

Property tax structures and credits can influence land-use patterns and residential development, which are central to the department's role in promoting sustainable growth and providing policy guidance to local governments.

bill_summary: The Arbitration Reform for State Employees Act of 2026 alters the collective bargaining process for certain State employees by requiring the selection of a neutral arbitrator and establishing a binding arbitration process in the event of a negotiation impasse. It further mandates that the Governor include appropriations in the annual budget bill necessary to implement all terms and conditions of employment set forth in ratified memoranda of understanding. This mandate is contingent on the passage of a constitutional amendment to be presented to Maryland voters in 2026.
responsible_party: The Governor of Maryland and the Department of Budget and Management
stakeholders: State employees, exclusive employee representatives (unions), State institutions of higher education, and the Maryland Environmental Service.
fiscal_impact_summary: State expenditures (all funds) are estimated to increase by at least 150000 annually beginning in fiscal 2028 to cover costs for neutral arbitration services and additional labor relations personnel. More significant fiscal impacts related to State personnel salaries and benefits may occur starting in fiscal 2029, depending on the outcomes of binding arbitration. The bill's implementation is contingent upon the ratification of a constitutional amendment by voters at the November 2026 general election.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Governor is a primary party in collective bargaining for State employees and is constitutionally responsible for submitting the annual budget. This bill mandates that the Governor include specific appropriations for Memoranda of Understanding (MOUs) in the budget and participate in a new arbitration process.

DBM is the principal fiscal and personnel agency responsible for developing the state budget and managing state employee resources. The fiscal note indicates DBM would require additional personnel to manage the new arbitration requirements and labor relations workload.

PERB is the central agency responsible for administering and standardizing collective bargaining for the public sector. This bill directly alters the statutory collective bargaining framework (Title 3 of the State Personnel and Pensions Article) that PERB oversees.

The bill includes a constitutional amendment that must be submitted to the voters at the November 2026 general election. The Board of Elections is responsible for supervising and administering this referendum process.

MES is explicitly named as a party whose MOUs must be funded in the state budget bill. The fiscal note suggests the bill could potentially alter MES's nonbudgeted status, subjecting it to the state budget process for the first time.

USM is specifically mentioned as an entity whose MOUs must be funded in the budget. The bill also specifies that the Chancellor or their designee serves as the representative in collective bargaining negotiations.
Morgan State University is explicitly identified in the bill as a party to the collective bargaining process and its MOUs are included in the mandatory budget appropriation requirement.
St. Mary's College is explicitly named as a party to the collective bargaining process and is subject to the new budget mandate for funding MOUs.

As the chief legal officer for the State, the OAG provides counsel to the Governor and state agencies regarding the implementation of the new arbitration process and the proposed constitutional amendment.
The bill authorizes neutral arbitrators to direct the production of revenue and expenditure estimates from the Bureau of Revenue Estimates, which is housed within the Comptroller's Office.

The Treasurer is part of the consensus revenue monitoring group whose data may be subpoenaed by arbitrators. Additionally, the mandate for MOU funding affects the state's overall fiscal management handled by the Treasurer.

MDOT is the parent agency for several administrations (MAA, MDTA) whose employees are covered by the collective bargaining changes, including specific provisions for the BWI Fire and Rescue Department.
The bill contains specific sections regarding impasse and arbitration for the uniformed fire employees of the BWI Airport Fire and Rescue Department, which is operated by the MAA.
MDTA employees and police officers (below a certain rank) participate in the collective bargaining system affected by this bill, as noted in the bill's supplemental policy information.

The bill expands collective bargaining to include fringe benefits. The Retirement Agency administers the pension and benefit systems that may be fiscally impacted by the outcomes of new MOUs or arbitration awards.

The Board of Public Works oversees significant state contracts and expenditures. While the budget mandate is legislative, the resulting MOUs often involve contracts and personnel actions that fall under BPW's broad fiscal oversight.

The bill does not materially affect State operations or finances, and Prince George’s County expenditures are not impacted.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Comptroller is the state's principal regulator for the alcohol and tobacco industries, both of which are directly regulated by the bill's provisions on licensing fees and advertising restrictions.

As the chief legal officer for the state, the OAG provides legal counsel to state boards and would represent the state in any constitutional or legal challenges regarding the bill's advertising restrictions and beneficial ownership requirements.

The bill explicitly increases the annual license fee for the University College Center for Adult Education of the University of Maryland and impacts other college athletic event venue licenses within the system.
The bill's restrictions on the advertisement of tobacco and vaping products align with the department's public health mission to protect residents and regulate products harmful to public health.

The bill increases fees for Class B-AE (Arts and Entertainment) licenses, which are used by venues that the Department of Commerce supports as part of its mission to promote the arts and tourism in Maryland.

Synopsis: Requiring the Director of Education and Workforce Skills Training for Correctional Institutions to consult with the State Correctional Ombudsman about the operation of education and workforce skills training programs in adult correctional institutions; establishing the Certified Peer Recovery Specialist Training Program for Incarcerated Individuals in the Maryland Department of Labor; and authorizing the Governor in fiscal year 2028 and each fiscal year thereafter to provide sufficient funding for the program in the annual budget bill.
Title: Correctional Education and Workforce Skills Training Programs - State Correctional Ombudsman and Certified Peer Recovery Specialist Training Program for Incarcerated Individuals
Status: In the House - Hearing 2/19 at 1:00 p.m.

bill_summary: This bill establishes the Certified Peer Recovery Specialist Training Program for Incarcerated Individuals within the Maryland Department of Labor. It requires the Director of Education and Workforce Skills Training for Correctional Institutions to consult with the State Correctional Ombudsman and mandates the creation of staff positions to support the training program. The program aims to train incarcerated individuals as peer recovery specialists to support others with mental health or substance use disorders and prepare them for post-release employment.
stakeholders: Incarcerated individuals in Maryland adult correctional institutions and the Maryland Department of Labor.
fiscal_impact_summary: General fund expenditures are estimated to increase by $332,200 in fiscal 2028. This includes approximately $204,924 for two new program administrator positions at the Maryland Department of Labor and $127,314 for program enhancements, such as increased daily wages for incarcerated trainees and expanded professional development resources. Annual expenditures are projected to remain between $327,100 and $345,200 through fiscal 2031.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill establishes the Certified Peer Recovery Specialist Training Program for Incarcerated Individuals within the Department of Labor and requires the department to create at least two staff positions to manage and support the program.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Department of Public Safety and Correctional Services
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill requires the department to use appropriated funds to enhance the daily wages of incarcerated individuals participating in the program and provides for professional development resources. The program operates within correctional facilities managed by the department.

The bill requires the Department of Labor to consult with the Maryland Department of Health regarding the administration of the peer recovery training program, which focuses on behavioral health and community recovery services.

The bill anticipates significant fiscal impact starting in FY 2028, including the creation of new personnel positions and budget appropriations that DBM must oversee and manage as the state's principal fiscal agency.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Executive Commissions, Committees, Task Forces, and Advisory Boards
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill mandates the Director of Education and Workforce Skills Training for Correctional Institutions to consult with the State Correctional Ombudsman and advises the Correctional Education Council regarding program operations.

The Governor is responsible for including appropriations for the program in the annual budget bill starting in FY 2028, and the bill requires consultation with the Maryland Office of Overdose Response, which operates within the executive branch.
The bill references the Education Article regarding teacher qualification standards for workforce skills training programs in correctional institutions.
As the chief legal representative for state agencies, the OAG would provide legal counsel to the multiple departments involved in implementing and coordinating this new inter-agency training program.

Synopsis: Authorizing a person to use living shorelines as a certain erosion control measure; applying the Act only to a shoreline stabilization project for which any portion of the project is in an area that is not designated as appropriate for structural stabilization measures by Department mapping; requiring that certain regulations adopted by the Department of the Environment require the Department to take certain action during the evaluation of a certain waiver request; requiring the Department to develop a certain scoring system; etc.
Title: Department of the Environment - Waivers for Living Shorelines and Nonstructural Shoreline Stabilization Measures - Regulations and Scoring System
Status: Approved by the Governor - Chapter 321

NarrowSubjects.Name: Environmental Matters -see also- Conserv; Nat Resrce; Pollut
Intergovernmental Cooperation -see also- AdmAgn; Cmts; etc.
Natural Resources -see also- Coal; For&Pks; Rivers; etc.
Plants -see also- Invasive Species; Trees; Weeds

bill_summary: This bill defines 'living shorelines' and establishes them, along with nonstructural shoreline stabilization measures, as the required method for protecting property against erosion unless a waiver is granted by the Maryland Department of the Environment (MDE). It mandates that MDE develop a scoring system to evaluate waiver requests, requires site visits within 45 days of a request, involves local soil conservation districts in the evaluation process, and requires stakeholder engagement and reporting on the waiver process.
stakeholders: Waterfront property owners, marine contractors, local soil conservation districts, small businesses, and State and local government agencies.
fiscal_impact_summary: MDE can implement the bill with existing budgeted resources. State and local expenditures for agencies undertaking shoreline stabilization projects may increase beginning in fiscal 2027 due to potential project delays or requirements. MDE special fund revenues from application fees—which range from $290 for small projects to over $9,720 per acre for large projects—may increase if the bill leads to more structural stabilization projects, as nonstructural projects are currently exempt from such fees. Specific aggregate fiscal estimates are unavailable.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill is the primary implementing agency for the Department of the Environment (MDE). MDE is responsible for adopting regulations, developing a scoring system for waiver requests, conducting site visits, notifying local soil conservation districts, and reporting on stakeholder engagement regarding living shorelines and erosion control.

The bill requires MDE to consult with the Department of Natural Resources (DNR) to adopt regulations. Furthermore, the bill amends the Natural Resources Article and relates to shoreline stabilization within the context of DNR's conservation and public lands management mission.

The bill requires MDE to notify local Soil Conservation Districts (SCDs) of waiver requests and allow them to provide recommendations. These districts are often associated with or coordinated by the Maryland Department of Agriculture (MDA), which conducts soil conservation activities.

As an agency responsible for state highways, bridges, and the Port of Baltimore, MDOT manages significant infrastructure on shorelines. The fiscal note indicates that state agencies undertaking shoreline stabilization projects (like MDOT) may see increased expenditures.

The Maryland Environmental Service (MES) provides technical and operational services related to water, dredging, and environmental infrastructure for state and local governments. They are likely to be involved in the design or implementation of living shoreline projects for public entities.

The fiscal note identifies the Board of Public Works as a source of information. The Board is responsible for issuing licenses for activities in State wetlands, which is directly impacted by the bill's changes to shoreline stabilization requirements.

The Office of the Attorney General provides legal counsel to the Executive branch, including MDE and DNR, and will likely assist in the drafting and legal review of the new regulations and waiver processes mandated by the bill.

The agency summary specifically notes that the college has a waterfront campus. As a state agency and waterfront landowner, it may be directly impacted by changes in shoreline stabilization requirements for any future erosion control projects.

The bill was a priority of the executive branch (signed by the Governor) and requires MDE to report to the General Assembly. The Governor's Office oversees policy initiatives and intergovernmental relations related to environmental restoration.

As the principal fiscal agency, DBM oversees the budget execution and personnel of implementing agencies like MDE. The fiscal note identifies potential expenditure increases for multiple state fund types, which DBM would manage.

Synopsis: Requiring each county board of education to collect data on energy usage and report the data collected to the Interagency Commission on School Construction; requiring the Commission to adopt regulations specifying the data to be collected and the means and frequency of reporting; and requiring the Commission to analyze the data collected and provide recommendations for improving school building energy efficiency and usage.

Status: In the House - Hearing 3/19 at 1:00 p.m.

bill_summary: This bill requires Maryland's county boards of education to collect data on energy usage in school buildings and report it to the Interagency Commission on School Construction (IAC). The IAC is responsible for setting regulations for this data collection and reporting, analyzing the gathered information, and providing recommendations to improve the energy efficiency of school buildings.
stakeholders: Local boards of education, public school systems, and the Interagency Commission on School Construction.
fiscal_impact_summary: The Interagency Commission on School Construction can implement the bill's requirements using existing resources. Similarly, local school systems are expected to be able to collect and report the required energy usage data using existing resources, as they already maintain energy policies and have access to utility data. There is no projected impact on state or local revenues.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill explicitly mandates the Interagency Commission on School Construction to adopt regulations for school energy data collection, receive reports from local boards, analyze the data, and provide recommendations for energy efficiency improvements.

The fiscal note identifies MEA as a key partner that coordinates with the Interagency Commission on School Construction to develop energy reporting templates and manages programs like the Decarbonizing Public Schools Program to support local school systems with energy data analytics.

As the agency responsible for the oversight and leadership of the state's 24 local school systems, MSDE is relevant because the bill imposes new data collection and reporting requirements on those local boards of education.

This multi-agency initiative focuses on sustainable development and reducing the state's carbon footprint; the bill's focus on school building energy efficiency aligns with these planning visions and statewide goals.

Synopsis: Applying certain provisions of law governing the confidentiality of medical records to crisis pregnancy clinics.
Title: Health Facilities - Confidentiality of Medical Records - Crisis Pregnancy Clinics
Status: In the House - Hearing 2/18 at 1:30 p.m.

NarrowSubjects.Name: Health -see also- COVID19; EnvHlth; MedCon; etc.
Health Care Facilities -see also- Clinics; Hospices; etc
Records -see also- Land Records; Vital Records

bill_summary: This bill expands the definition of a 'health care provider' under Maryland's Confidentiality of Medical Records Act to include crisis pregnancy clinics, including mobile facilities that provide pregnancy-related care. This ensures that these clinics, even if not covered under the federal Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act (HIPAA), are legally required to maintain the confidentiality of patient medical records and obtain consent for disclosure.
stakeholders: Crisis pregnancy clinics, mobile facilities providing pregnancy-related health care, and patients of these facilities.
fiscal_impact_summary: The Fiscal Note indicates that the bill has no state or local fiscal impact as the changes are technical in nature. The impact on small businesses is estimated to be minimal.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill amends Section 4-301 of the Health - General Article, which falls under the Department's regulatory oversight. By expanding the definition of 'health care provider' to include crisis pregnancy clinics, the Department is responsible for the policy implications and administrative oversight of medical record confidentiality standards for these newly included facilities.

As the chief legal officer for the state, the OAG provides legal counsel to the Department of Health and the General Assembly. The OAG would be involved in interpreting the application of these confidentiality laws and potentially enforcing them or representing the state in legal challenges related to the new definitions.

The Governor's Office oversees the executive branch and coordinates policy initiatives. Since reproductive health and medical privacy are significant policy areas, this bill aligns with the administrative oversight and policy coordination functions of the office.

As an independent regulatory agency within the Department of Health, the Commission is tasked with increasing accountability and improving access to health care. The bill's focus on clinical accountability regarding patient records relates to the Commission's broader mission.

Synopsis: Altering the jurisdiction of the Health Services Cost Review Commission; and requiring the Commission, in carrying out certain responsibilities relating to evaluating facility resources to meet certain financial requirements and reviewing costs and rates of hospital services, to take into account all costs incurred or expenditures made by a health facility in connection with the operation of the facility.
Title: Health Services Cost Review Commission – Health Facilities – Jurisdiction and Rate Setting
Status: In the House - First Reading Health

bill_summary: This emergency bill expands the jurisdiction of the Maryland Health Services Cost Review Commission (HSCRC) to include costs incurred by health facilities when employing or contracting with physicians and other professional providers for which there is no offsetting revenue. It requires the Commission to account for all such expenditures when evaluating a facility's financial status and performing rate-setting duties.
stakeholders: Maryland health facilities (hospitals), physicians, professional health care providers, Medicaid recipients, and health care purchasers.
fiscal_impact_summary: HSCRC special fund expenditures increase by $350,000 in FY 2026, $250,000 in FY 2027, and $50,000 annually thereafter for contractual services. Special fund revenues may increase beginning in FY 2027 if HSCRC increases hospital user fees. Medicaid expenditures (split 50% general funds and 50% federal funds) could increase by an estimated $45,600,000 annually starting in FY 2027 if hospital rates are adjusted to cover physician losses, which are valued at approximately $1,140,000,000 statewide.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: As the primary agency identified in the bill, the HSCRC's jurisdiction is directly expanded to include certain physician and professional provider costs. The bill mandates that the Commission incorporate these costs into its hospital rate-setting and global budget evaluation processes.

The HSCRC is an independent commission within the Department of Health. Additionally, the fiscal note indicates that the bill will likely lead to a significant increase in Medicaid expenditures (potentially $45.6 million annually), which are administered by the Department.

DBM is responsible for the state's fiscal planning and budget execution. The bill's potential multi-million dollar impact on General Fund expenditures via Medicaid requirements would directly affect the state budget development and revenue estimations overseen by DBM.

The OAG provides legal counsel to state agencies, including the HSCRC and the Department of Health. The expansion of statutory jurisdiction and the implementation of new rate-setting mandates would require legal guidance and potential representation in regulatory challenges.

The Governor's Office oversees executive branch agencies and the annual state budget proposal. The bill's impact on the state's all-payer model contract (AHEAD) and the significant fiscal implications for the state budget fall under the Governor's policy and budgetary coordination responsibilities.

Synopsis: Authorizing the use of noise abatement monitoring systems in the City of Frederick to enforce certain motor vehicle noise requirements.
Title: City of Frederick - Noise Abatement Monitoring Systems - Authorization
Status: In the Senate - Hearing 4/09 at 2:30 p.m.

NarrowSubjects.Name: Investigations and Inquiries -see also- Crim Bckgrnd Invest
Law Enforcement -see also- SRO; Sheriffs; State Police
Penalties and Sentences -see also- Death Penalty
Records -see also- Land Records; Vital Records

bill_summary: This bill authorizes the City of Frederick to implement noise abatement monitoring systems to detect and enforce motor vehicle noise limits. The systems utilize sensors and cameras to identify vehicles exceeding noise limits by at least 5 decibels. Violators are subject to a warning for a first offense and a civil penalty of up to $75 for subsequent offenses, with revenues used for program costs and public safety.
responsible_party: City of Frederick law enforcement agency
stakeholders: Motor vehicle owners and operators in the City of Frederick
fiscal_impact_summary: State general fund revenues from contested cases in District Court may increase minimally through fiscal 2029. Local revenues and expenditures for the City of Frederick will increase to implementation and operation of the systems; fine revenues of up to $75 per violation are restricted to program costs and public safety purposes. The Judiciary identifies a $1,400,000 cost for a general IT upgrade to manage automated enforcement systems, though this is not exclusively attributable to this bill.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill requires the District Court to prescribe uniform citation forms and sets procedures for adjudicating noise abatement violations. The fiscal note also indicates a significant potential expenditure for the Judiciary to upgrade IT systems to handle the expansion of automated enforcement systems.

The MVA is responsible for enforcing the payment of civil penalties by refusing to register or reregister vehicles with outstanding noise monitoring violations. The bill also requires local jurisdictions to coordinate with the Administration to rescind administrative penalties in specific error cases.

The bill mandates that noise abatement monitoring systems must be accompanied by signage that complies with the manual and specifications for a uniform system of traffic control devices adopted by the State Highway Administration.

The bill requires the City of Frederick to submit a detailed report on the implementation, effectiveness, and fiscal performance of the noise abatement monitoring systems to the Governor by December 1, 2027.

As the parent agency for the MVA and SHA, MDOT oversees the various administrations and modal policies impacted by the expansion of automated vehicle enforcement and signage standards on state-regulated roadways.

The OAG may be called upon to provide legal counsel to the Governor or involved state agencies regarding the implementation and legality of the expanded local enforcement authorities granted by the bill.

DBM monitors state revenues and expenditures; the fiscal note identifies a minimal increase in general fund revenues and potential fiscal impacts related to judicial IT infrastructure necessitated by the expansion of automated enforcement.
The Comptroller is the state's chief financial officer and manages the general fund, which will receive revenues from contested noise abatement citations that proceed through the District Court.

Synopsis: Prohibiting an occupant from using the occupant's self-service storage facility beyond the term of a rental agreement after delivery of a notice of nonrenewal; requiring an operator to give an occupant at least 30 days after delivery of a notice of nonrenewal to remove the occupant's personal property from the self-service storage facility; requiring an operator to give an occupant notice of intent to dispose of the occupant's personal property at least 10 days before the operator disposes of that personal property; etc.
Title: Commercial Law - Self-Service Storage Facilities - Alterations
Status: Approved by the Governor - Chapter 216

NarrowSubjects.Name: Commerce and Business -see also- ElectrComm; ForeignTr; etc.

bill_summary: This bill updates the Maryland Self-Service Storage Act to allow for electronic rental agreements and establish specific procedures for the nonrenewal of leases. It requires operators to provide occupants with at least 30 days' notice to remove personal property and requires a separate 10-day notice of intent to dispose of any property remaining after the nonrenewal period has elapsed.
responsible_party: Maryland Office of the Attorney General (Consumer Protection Division)
stakeholders: Occupants and operators of self-service storage facilities
fiscal_impact_summary: According to the Fiscal Note, the bill does not materially affect State or local government finances or operations. The impact on small business operators is expected to be minimal.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: As the head of the executive branch, the Governor's Office is responsible for overseeing the execution of state laws and signing legislation into law. The office also coordinates policy initiatives related to commercial regulations and consumer rights.

The Office of the Attorney General (OAG), specifically through its Consumer Protection Division, is responsible for enforcing state laws that protect consumers in commercial transactions. This bill amends the Commercial Law Article regarding the rights of occupants in self-service storage facilities, and the OAG was consulted for the fiscal note regarding its impact.

bill_summary: This bill enters Maryland into the Interstate Podiatric Medical Licensure Compact, providing a streamlined process for podiatrists to obtain expedited licenses to practice in other member states. It establishes the Interstate Podiatric Medical Licensure Compact Commission to oversee the compact, manage a coordinated information system for licensing and disciplinary data, and handle enforcement and dispute resolution between member states.
responsible_party: Maryland State Board of Podiatric Medical Examiners
stakeholders: Podiatrists, patients, and the Maryland State Board of Podiatric Medical Examiners.
fiscal_impact_summary: State special fund revenues and expenditures for the State Board of Podiatric Medical Examiners (BPME) are expected to increase by an indeterminate amount. Revenue will be generated from expedited licensure fees, while expenditures will include an annual assessment to the Interstate Commission and administrative costs for processing applications and maintaining a coordinated information system. No local government fiscal impact is expected.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Maryland Department of Health (MDH) is the primary agency impacted as it oversees the State Board of Podiatric Medical Examiners, which will be responsible for issuing expedited licenses and performing criminal background checks. The bill also specifically requires MDH to notify the Department of Legislative Services when the compact's entry conditions are met.
This bill enters Maryland into a new interstate compact, the Interstate Podiatric Medical Licensure Compact, and establishes Maryland's membership in the associated Interstate Commission.

The OAG serves as the chief legal officer for MDH and its boards. Furthermore, the bill explicitly states that the Interstate Commission shall defend its representatives in civil actions subject to the approval of the Attorney General of the member state.

The Governor's Office oversees the executive branch and the board involved in the compact. The Governor appoints the members of the State Board of Podiatric Medical Examiners (who may serve as commissioners) and receives annual reports from the Interstate Commission.

As the principal fiscal and personnel agency, DBM is relevant because the bill has fiscal implications for a state board (BPME), involving indeterminate increases in special fund revenues and expenditures for licensure and commission assessments.

The Office of Appointments assists the Governor in vetting and recommending candidates for state boards. This bill utilizes members of the State Board of Podiatric Medical Examiners to serve as Maryland's voting representatives (Commissioners) on the Interstate Commission.

Synopsis: Requiring the Governor annually to proclaim April as Maryland Climate Education Month; and requiring the proclamation to urge participation in climate activities and initiatives and the taking of certain actions.
Title: Commemorative Months - Maryland Climate Education Month
Status: In the House - Hearing 3/17 at 1:00 p.m.

NarrowSubjects.Name: Environmental Matters -see also- Conserv; Nat Resrce; Pollut

bill_summary: This bill requires the Governor to annually proclaim April as Maryland Climate Education Month to encourage public participation in climate change educational activities and initiatives, and to promote actions toward the state's climate commitments.
stakeholders: Maryland residents, primary and secondary schools, institutions of higher education, research organizations, and environmental advocacy groups.
fiscal_impact_summary: There is no state or local fiscal impact. According to the fiscal note, commemorating Maryland Climate Education Month does not affect State finances.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill explicitly requires the Governor to annually proclaim April as Maryland Climate Education Month and specifies the contents of the proclamation.
As the primary agency for environmental protection and climate policy, MDE is responsible for the state's climate commitments and initiatives mentioned in the bill.
The bill focuses on climate education and names primary and secondary schools in the preamble as critical partners in the state's effort to raise awareness.
The Secretary of State is the official custodian of the Governor's proclamations and executive orders, making them responsible for the administrative processing of this annual requirement.
MEA is responsible for renewable energy and energy efficiency programs that directly contribute to the State's climate commitments referenced in the bill.
The bill's preamble cites the protection of the state's natural resources and the Chesapeake Bay, which are primary management responsibilities of DNR.
The bill identifies institutions of higher education as forefront partners in climate change research and education efforts related to the commemorative month.
This multi-agency initiative coordinates efforts regarding climate and sustainable development, aligning with the bill's goal of fostering a culture of sustainability.

Synopsis: Altering the qualifications for counsel to local boards of elections to require that counsel be a registered voter of the State instead of the applicable county.
Title: Local Boards of Elections - Board Counsel - Qualifications
Status: Approved by the Governor - Chapter 256

NarrowSubjects.Name: Health -see also- COVID19; EnvHlth; MedCon; etc.

bill_summary: This emergency bill changes the qualifications for legal counsel to local boards of elections. Instead of requiring the counsel to be a registered voter of the specific county for which they serve, the bill allows any individual who is a registered voter of the State of Maryland and admitted to practice law in the State to be appointed or retained.
stakeholders: Local boards of elections and attorneys admitted to practice law in Maryland
fiscal_impact_summary: According to the Fiscal Note, the bill has no State fiscal impact and does not materially affect local government finances.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Maryland State Board of Elections (SBE) is the primary state agency responsible for supervising the activities of local boards of elections. This bill directly alters the statutory qualifications for the legal counsel that these local boards are authorized to appoint or retain.

The OAG serves as the chief legal officer for the State of Maryland and provides counsel to state agencies, including the State Board of Elections. Changes to the professional and residency qualifications of legal representatives within the state's election apparatus are of legal interest to the OAG.

The Governor's Office oversees the executive branch and the administrative support for the Governor, who must sign this emergency bill into law. Additionally, the Governor appoints the members of the local boards of elections who will be hiring the counsel affected by this bill.

Synopsis: Extending by one year the time period during which a holder of a certain dispensary license may continue to deliver medical cannabis; increasing from 10 to 20 the number of individuals a micro dispensary is permitted to employ; altering certain provisions relating to training requirements for certain cannabis agents; and requiring the Maryland Cannabis Administration to give priority to applications for  programs that were previously approved as responsible vendor training programs when reviewing training programs for approval.
Title: Cannabis - Licensees - Dispensary Licenses, Micro Dispensary Employees, and Cannabis Agent Training Programs
Status: Approved by the Governor - Chapter 375

NarrowSubjects.Name: Health -see also- COVID19; EnvHlth; MedCon; etc.
Job Training -see also- Continuing Ed; Vocational Rehab
Licenses -see also- AB Lic; Certifications; DrLic; Permits
Work, Labor, and Employment -see also- JobTrn; Leave; etc.

bill_summary: The bill increases the number of employees a micro dispensary licensee may employ from 10 to 20 and extends the authorization for certain medical cannabis dispensaries to continue delivery services until July 1, 2027. It also renames the 'responsible vendor training program' to the 'cannabis agent training program,' modifies its curriculum requirements, and changes the required training frequency for cannabis agents from annually to every two years.
stakeholders: Micro dispensary licensees, medical cannabis dispensary licensees, registered cannabis agents, and providers of cannabis agent training programs.
fiscal_impact_summary: The Maryland Cannabis Administration can implement the bill with existing resources. The bill does not materially affect State revenues and has no impact on local government finances. It is determined to have a meaningful positive economic impact on small businesses by allowing micro dispensaries to hire more staff and making training requirements more relevant and less frequent.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Maryland Cannabis Administration is the primary regulator and the entity that requested the bill. It is responsible for implementing the new training program requirements, adopting regulations for the curriculum, and managing the increased employee limits and delivery extensions for licensees.

The Office of the Attorney General provides legal counsel to the Maryland Cannabis Administration and will be responsible for reviewing the new regulations and statutory changes for legal sufficiency.

The bill adds public health and safety standards to the training curriculum for cannabis agents. The Department of Health oversees the Cannabis Public Health Fund and coordinates with public health advisory bodies on cannabis-related health impacts.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Executive Commissions, Committees, Task Forces, and Advisory Boards
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Advisory Board on Medical and Adult-Use Cannabis and the Cannabis Public Health Advisory Council are tasked with studying and making recommendations on the cannabis industry, including the safety and compliance issues addressed by the bill's training and micro-dispensary provisions.
The Governor oversees the executive branch and the Maryland Cannabis Administration. The Governor is also responsible for signing the bill into law.
As the state's principal fiscal agency, the Department of Budget and Management supervises budget execution and estimates revenue implications for the Maryland Cannabis Administration.

The Department of Commerce manages the Cannabis Business Assistance Fund. The bill's changes to employee caps and delivery authorizations support the economic growth and operational viability of small cannabis businesses.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Governor's Office of Small, Minority & Women Business Affairs
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: This office advocates for small and minority-owned businesses. The bill specifically benefits social equity micro-dispensary licensees by increasing their authorized employee count and extending delivery permissions.

Synopsis: Altering the definition of "military-connected student" under the Purple Star Schools Program to conform with certain terms defined under State law; and establishing the Purple Star Colleges Program to recognize certain colleges that provide strong services and support for military-connected students.

bill_summary: This bill establishes the Purple Star Colleges Program to recognize institutions of higher education and private career schools that provide support and services for military-connected students. It also modifies the definition of 'military-connected student' for the existing Purple Star Schools Program to align with state law, specifically including dependents of service members killed in the line of duty.
stakeholders: Military-connected students (service members, veterans, spouses, and dependents), public and private institutions of higher education, and private career schools.
fiscal_impact_summary: State general fund expenditures for the Maryland Higher Education Commission increase by $43,800 in FY 2027 and $46,400 in FY 2028 to hire a contractual half-time program manager to establish program criteria and regulations. Participation by public four-year institutions, community colleges, and private career schools is voluntary; while seeking the designation may increase their operational expenditures, these costs are expected to be absorbable. The Maryland State Department of Education can update regulations for the existing Purple Star Schools Program using existing resources.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Maryland Higher Education Commission is the primary agency responsible for administering the new Purple Star Colleges Program, including establishing criteria for designation, reviewing applications, and adopting regulations.
The bill amends the definition of 'military-connected student' for the existing Purple Star Schools Program, which is overseen and managed by the Maryland State Department of Education.

The program directly serves and recognizes institutions that support veterans, service members, and their dependents, which aligns with this agency's mission to assist Maryland's military-connected families in securing services.
As the state's primary public higher education system, its constituent institutions are eligible to apply for and benefit from the Purple Star College designation established by this bill.
As an independent public university, Morgan State University is eligible to seek designation under the Purple Star Colleges Program to support its military-connected students.
As Maryland's public honors college, it is eligible to participate in the program and seek recognition for its services to military-connected students.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Executive Commissions, Committees, Task Forces, and Advisory Boards
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill requires the Maryland Higher Education Commission to consult with the Maryland College Collaboration for Student Veterans Commission—a body that falls under this category—to develop program criteria and regulations.

The fiscal note indicates a need for general fund expenditures to hire contractual personnel at the Maryland Higher Education Commission to manage the new program, which requires DBM's fiscal oversight.

The Governor's Office coordinates policy initiatives and oversees the executive branch; this bill creates a new executive program and requires regulatory adoption that aligns with state policy priorities regarding veterans.

Synopsis: Requiring certain hospitals licensed in the State to comply with certain staffing standards to establish and maintain a clinical staffing committee and to implement a clinical staffing plan; requiring each staffing committee to develop a staffing plan; requiring the chief nursing executive of each hospital to produce a draft clinical staffing plan and submit it to the clinical staffing committee of the hospital; requiring, beginning in 2028, by July 1 each year, each hospital to implement a clinical staffing plan; etc.

bill_summary: The Safe Staffing Act of 2026 requires licensed hospitals in Maryland (excluding state-run facilities) to establish clinical staffing committees and implement annual clinical staffing plans. These plans must be developed by the hospital's chief nurse executive and finalized by a committee consisting of both managers and employees, taking into account patient acuity, staff skill mix, and federal staffing standards.
responsible_party: Licensed hospitals and the Maryland Department of Health
stakeholders: Hospital clinical staff (including nurses, certified nursing assistants, and technicians), hospital administrators, and hospital patients.
fiscal_impact_summary: The fiscal note indicates that the bill does not directly affect state or local governmental operations or finances. While the bill requires hospitals to establish committees and implement staffing plans, it is expected to have no direct state expenditure or revenue impact.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill adds a new part to the Health - General Article, which falls under the regulatory purview of the Maryland Department of Health. As the agency responsible for licensing hospitals and health care facilities in the State, MDH (specifically the Office of Health Care Quality) oversees compliance with health care standards and the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services (CMS) Conditions of Participation referenced in the bill.

The HSCRC is an independent agency within MDH that regulates hospital rates and revenues. Mandatory clinical staffing plans and committees will directly impact hospital labor costs and operational expenses, which are critical factors in the Commission's 'all-payer' rate-setting system and cost-containment efforts.

The MHCC is responsible for health system planning and improving the quality of care. Staffing levels are a key metric in assessing hospital performance and quality, making this legislation relevant to their mission of increasing accountability and informing public health policy.

The bill focuses on workforce management within hospitals, including the creation of committees comprised of employees (nurses, aides, technicians). This intersects with the Department of Labor's role in protecting workers and overseeing workplace safety and labor-related standards.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Maryland Institute for Emergency Medical Services Systems
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: MIEMSS oversees the state's emergency medical services and trauma systems. Clinical staffing levels in hospitals significantly impact hospital capacity and the ability to accept emergency patients, which directly affects ambulance 'wall time' and overall EMS system efficiency.

The OAG provides legal counsel to the Department of Health and other executive agencies. They would be responsible for advising on the implementation of these new statutory requirements and representing the State in any enforcement actions or legal challenges related to the new staffing regulations.

The Governor's Office oversees the executive branch and coordinates health policy initiatives. The bill requires the Governor's final approval and aligns with broad executive branch goals regarding public health safety and healthcare workforce standards.

Synopsis: Requiring research facilities that are located in the State and required to submit an Animal and Plant Health Inspection Service Form 7023 to pay contributions for the Human-Relevant Research Fund to the Department of Agriculture, rather than the Maryland Department of Health; and establishing that a research facility that fails to pay the contribution required by the Act may be subject to a civil penalty of not more than $1,000 per day.

Status: Approved by the Governor - Chapter 385

bill_summary: This bill transfers the responsibility for collecting annual contributions for the Human-Relevant Research Fund from the Maryland Department of Health to the Maryland Department of Agriculture. Research facilities in the state that are required to submit a federal Animal and Plant Health Inspection Service (APHIS) Form 7023 must pay these contributions based on the number of animals used in research. The collected funds are distributed to the Maryland Technology Development Corporation (TEDCO) to provide grants and loans for research into human-relevant alternatives to animal testing.
stakeholders: Research facilities using animals for testing in Maryland, including public and private higher education institutions, the Maryland Department of Agriculture, and the Maryland Technology Development Corporation (TEDCO).
fiscal_impact_summary: According to the Fiscal Note, State general fund expenditures for the Maryland Department of Agriculture increase by $42,900 in FY 2027 (growing to $54,200 by FY 2031) to hire a half-time administrative officer for collection and compliance tracking. Special fund revenues for the Human-Relevant Research Fund (HRRF) administered by TEDCO will continue and may increase if collection efforts under the Department of Agriculture are more successful than previous efforts. While total potential annual revenue was previously estimated at $915,000, only $185,000 has been collected to date.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill transfers the responsibility for collecting annual contributions for the Human-Relevant Research Fund from the Department of Health to the Department of Agriculture. The agency will require additional staff to manage collection and tracking compliance.

TEDCO administers the Human-Relevant Research Fund (HRRF). The bill changes the entity that collects and distributes the funds into the HRRF, which may impact the efficiency and volume of revenue received for the fund's grants and loans.
The bill repeals the Department of Health's authority and responsibility to collect contributions from research facilities for the Human-Relevant Research Fund.

Several public senior institutions of higher education within the University System of Maryland are research facilities subject to the animal research contribution requirements and may also be eligible for grants from the HRRF.
As a public research university, Morgan State may be among the institutions required to pay the research facility contribution or may apply for research funding through the HRRF.
The fiscal note indicates a need for a new half-time position at the Department of Agriculture to implement the bill, which falls under DBM's oversight of personnel and state expenditures.
The bill maintains civil penalties for research facilities that fail to pay the required contribution, which may result in litigation or administrative actions within the judicial system.
The OAG provides legal counsel to the agencies involved (MDA, MDH, and TEDCO) regarding the transfer of statutory duties and the enforcement of civil penalties.
As the state's chief financial officer, the Comptroller is involved in the oversight of state revenue collection and the distribution of funds into special accounts like the HRRF.
The Treasurer's Office manages state funds and special fund accounts. The HRRF is a special, nonlapsing fund that receives the contributions collected under this bill.
As an independent public honors college, it may be subject to the contribution requirements if it operates a research facility submitting APHIS Form 7023, or it may apply for HRRF grants.

Synopsis: Establishing a certain rebuttable presumption that a statement made by a minor during a custodial interrogation is involuntary and is inadmissible in a juvenile or criminal proceeding against the minor if the law enforcement officer intentionally used information known by the officer to be false in order to elicit the statement.
Title: Custodial Interrogation of Minors - Admissibility of Statements (Exonerated 5 Act)
Status: In the House - Hearing 2/19 at 1:00 p.m.

NarrowSubjects.Name: Law Enforcement -see also- SRO; Sheriffs; State Police
Minors -see also- Age of Majority; Youth

bill_summary: This bill creates a rebuttable presumption that statements made by a minor during a custodial interrogation are involuntary and inadmissible in court if law enforcement officers intentionally used false information to elicit the statement. To overcome this presumption, the State must provide clear and convincing evidence that the statement was voluntary and not made in response to the false information.
responsible_party: Maryland Judiciary and Law Enforcement Agencies
stakeholders: Minors in custodial interrogation, law enforcement officers, and the Maryland court system.
fiscal_impact_summary: According to the Fiscal Note, there is no fiscal impact on state or local government because the bill is procedural in nature and does not directly affect finances or operations.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: As the state's primary law enforcement agency, the Maryland State Police are directly responsible for conducting custodial interrogations and would be governed by the bill's new evidentiary standards regarding the use of false information with minors.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Maryland Office of the Public Defender
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Office of the Public Defender represents indigent minors in juvenile and criminal proceedings. The bill provides a new legal basis for their attorneys to challenge the admissibility of client statements made during interrogations.

The Department of Juvenile Services manages youth in the juvenile justice system. Since the bill directly impacts the legal proceedings and admissibility of evidence for these youth, it affects the agency's rehabilitative and legal coordination efforts.

The bill establishes new procedural and evidentiary rules for juvenile and criminal courts, requiring the Judicial Branch to adjust how judges evaluate the admissibility of statements and the application of rebuttable presumptions.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Governor's Office of Crime Prevention and Policy
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: This office coordinates state public safety strategy and advises the Governor on criminal justice policy. The bill represents a significant shift in interrogation policy and the protection of minors' rights within the justice system.

The Center oversees school safety personnel, including School Resource Officers who may be involved in the custodial interrogation of minors. The agency may need to update training and certification standards based on this legislation.

The Attorney General represents the state in criminal appeals and provides legal counsel to state agencies. This bill changes the legal standard for voluntariness, which would be a central issue in many appeals involving minor defendants.

The office is focused on child well-being and the ENOUGH Initiative. Protecting minors from coercive interrogation tactics aligns with its mission to support historically underinvested and vulnerable youth populations.

Several modal administrations within MDOT, including the Maryland Transportation Authority and the Maryland Transit Administration, maintain their own police forces that conduct custodial interrogations.
The Natural Resources Police are state-authorized law enforcement officers who may conduct custodial interrogations of minors during the enforcement of conservation and criminal laws.
Member institutions within the University System maintain campus police departments that are subject to state laws regarding the interrogation of minors who may be on campus or involved in incidents.
The Commission enforces anti-discrimination and civil rights laws. The protection of minors' due process rights during police interrogations is a significant civil rights issue.

DHS acts as the primary social service provider for vulnerable children. The agency often coordinates with law enforcement when children in their care or under their supervision are involved in legal matters.
As an independent state agency with its own police force, Morgan State must ensure its officers comply with the bill's requirements during interrogations involving minors.
As a state agency with security and law enforcement functions, the college must ensure its operations align with new legal standards for the interrogation of minors.

Synopsis: Establishing the Commission on Historic, Cultural, and Civic Contributions in Education to study and make recommendations to the State Board of Education and the Maryland Higher Education Commission about certain lessons currently taught in public schools; requiring the Commission to study school calendars and make recommendations to the State Board and the General Assembly; and requiring the State Board to identify existing courses and materials to be updated into professional development courses under certain circumstances.
