bill_summary: This bill restructures the oversight of the Maryland Transit Administration (MTA) by replacing the Baltimore Regional Transit Commission with two new bodies: the Board of Directors for Baltimore Core Transit Service and the Commuter Services Advisory Board. It mandates specific staffing levels for these boards, including Deputy Administrators and analysts, and transfers authority to determine qualifications and compensation for certain MTA management positions to the Maryland Transportation Commission. Additionally, the bill requires a technical study to be conducted on the potential creation of a statewide rail authority.
responsible_party: Maryland Transit Administration and Maryland Department of Transportation
stakeholders: Transit riders in the Baltimore metropolitan area, MARC and commuter bus passengers, MTA employees, labor unions, and residents of Baltimore City, Baltimore County, and Anne Arundel County.
fiscal_impact_summary: According to the Fiscal Note, known Transportation Trust Fund (TTF) expenditures increase by a net of 319,456 in FY 2027, with subsequent annual net increases ranging from 210,500 to 310,100 through FY 2031. These estimates reflect the cost of five new staff positions and a 100,000 one-time study fee, offset by approximately 500,000 in annual savings from the repeal of the Baltimore Regional Transit Commission. Additional indeterminate expenditures, potentially totaling several hundred thousand dollars annually, may result from management salary adjustments determined by the Maryland Transportation Commission.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Governor has significant appointment power under the bill, including appointing five members and the chair of the Board of Directors for Baltimore Core Transit Service, as well as the chair and members of the Commuter Services Advisory Board.

The Secretary of Budget and Management is required to review proposed salary adjustments for specific MTA management positions to determine if they pose an adverse impact on special fund expenditures. DBM also manages state personnel resources and benefits.

MDOT is the parent agency of the MTA. The bill reforms MDOT's transit operations, requires the Secretary to serve on the new boards, and mandates that MDOT contract for a technical study on a potential rail authority.

This bill is the primary reform act for the MTA, establishing two new oversight boards, requiring new staffing (Deputy Administrators and analysts), and changing how management personnel are appointed and compensated.
As the chief legal officer for state agencies, the OAG will provide legal counsel regarding the implementation of the new boards, their bylaws, and the modified personnel rules for MTA management.

The bill specifies that management personnel appointed under the new Maryland Transportation Commission guidelines are state employees entitled to participate in the State Retirement and Pension System.
The Office of Appointments will be responsible for recruiting and vetting the various individuals the Governor must appoint to the two new boards established by the bill.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Executive Commissions, Committees, Task Forces, and Advisory Boards
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill establishes two new oversight and advisory bodies: the Board of Directors for Baltimore Core Transit Service and the Commuter Services Advisory Board.
The bill requires the new boards to establish conflict of interest standards consistent with the Maryland Public Ethics Law, which is administered and enforced by this commission.

OLA is responsible for conducting fiscal compliance audits of executive branch agencies and will likely review the MTA's compliance with the new personnel and board staffing requirements mandated by this bill.

The bill requires that both the Board of Directors for Baltimore Core Transit Service and the Commuter Services Advisory Board include a member who represents riders with accessibility challenges, which aligns with this department's mission.
The bill involves employees who are members of labor unions and references collective bargaining agreements, fall under the jurisdiction of the PERB for labor-management relations.

Synopsis: Applying certain rate schedule requirements for large load customers to certain data centers; and modifying, from September 1, 2026, to January 1, 2027, the date by which certain electric companies must submit to the Public Service Commission for approval certain rate schedules for large load customers.
Title: Large Load Customers - Data Centers and Rate Schedule Requirements
Status: In the House - Hearing 3/03 at 1:00 p.m.

NarrowSubjects.Name: Commerce and Business -see also- ElectrComm; ForeignTr; etc.
Utilities -see also- Recycl; Refuse; Sewage; Teleph; Water

bill_summary: This bill expands the definition of "large load customers" under Maryland's electricity regulations to include all data centers, regardless of their specific power demand or capacity. It requires electric companies to submit specific rate schedules for these customers to the Public Service Commission (PSC) to ensure that data centers cover the costs of any electric transmission or distribution infrastructure required to serve them. The legislation is intended to prevent residential ratepayers from bearing the financial risks or subsidizing the infrastructure costs associated with high-energy-demand data center facilities. Additionally, the bill adjusts the deadlines for electric companies to submit these rate schedules and for the PSC to adopt necessary regulations.
stakeholders: Data center developers and operators, investor-owned electric companies, electric cooperatives, municipal electric utilities, and residential electricity ratepayers in Maryland.
fiscal_impact_summary: Specific dollar estimates are unavailable as a formal Fiscal Note was not provided with the text. However, the bill specifies that large load customers, including data centers, are responsible for covering the costs associated with electric system buildouts required to interconnect and serve them. This mechanism is designed to protect residential retail electric customers from financial risks and ensures that cost allocations do not result in unreasonable subsidies by other customer classes.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Public Service Commission is the primary regulatory body responsible for implementing the bill, including approving specific rate schedules for large load customers and adopting mandatory regulations to carry out the act.

The bill explicitly states its intent is to protect residential retail electric customers from the financial risks associated with large load customers, which directly aligns with the mission of the Office of the People's Counsel to advocate for residential utility consumers.

The Maryland Energy Administration advises on state energy policy and manages the Strategic Energy Investment Fund; changes to rate structures for massive energy users like data centers impact statewide energy planning and efficiency goals.

The Office of the Attorney General provides legal counsel to the Public Service Commission and other state agencies, and would be involved in the legal review and defense of the new rate schedules and regulations.

As the state's primary economic development agency, the Department of Commerce is significantly impacted by changes to utility rate schedules for data centers, which are a key target for business attraction and job creation.
MEDCO provides financing and real estate development services to businesses and frequently supports the development of large-scale infrastructure projects like data centers.

The Department of Information Technology oversees the state's IT strategy and infrastructure; changes to the regulatory and cost landscape for data centers may impact the state's long-term digital and data management goals.

The bill addresses the buildout of electric transmission and distribution systems required to serve large load customers, which often requires environmental permits and review overseen by the Department of the Environment.

The Department of Planning coordinates land use and infrastructure development; the proliferation of data centers and the associated utility buildout are significant factors in state land use planning.
The Governor's Office oversees the executive branch and coordinates high-level policy initiatives, including those related to energy regulation, economic development, and consumer protection.

Synopsis: Altering the membership of the Montgomery County Board of Elections to consist of seven regular members and to no longer include substitute members; altering the number of members on the county board required to be members of the majority party and the principal minority party; and altering the votes required for the county board to appoint an election director.
Title: Montgomery County Board of Elections - Membership MC 6-26

bill_summary: This bill changes the structure of the Montgomery County Board of Elections by increasing the number of regular members from five to seven and eliminating the two substitute member positions. Under the new structure, four members must be from the majority party and three from the principal minority party. The bill also increases the minimum number of affirmative votes required to appoint an election director from three to four and updates the procedures for filling vacancies.
stakeholders: Montgomery County registered voters, members of the Montgomery County Board of Elections, and political parties in Montgomery County.
fiscal_impact_summary: According to the Fiscal Note, the bill has no impact on State finances and does not directly affect Montgomery County finances.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill explicitly tasks the Governor with appointing the members of the Montgomery County Board of Elections from lists provided by political central committees. It also maintains the Governor's authority to remove members for cause.

As the state agency responsible for supervising and administering elections, the State Board of Elections has direct oversight of local boards. This bill alters the structure and appointment process of one of its constituent local boards.

This office assists the Governor in recruiting and vetting candidates for state boards and commissions. It will be responsible for managing the expanded number of regular member appointments for the Montgomery County Board of Elections mandated by this bill.

bill_summary: This bill authorizes the Montgomery County Board of Education to satisfy state school operation requirements by meeting a minimum number of school hours instead of both days and hours under certain emergency conditions, such as severe weather or natural disasters. To use this flexibility, schools must remain open for at least 175 days, and the board must provide hourly employees with opportunities to make up any lost wages and report school operation data to the State Board of Education and the General Assembly.
stakeholders: Students, teachers, and hourly employees of Montgomery County Public Schools
fiscal_impact_summary: There is no impact on state finances. Locally, Montgomery County Public Schools may realize cost savings of approximately $1,900,000 for each instructional day avoided, primarily due to reduced expenditures on hourly staff salaries, substitute teachers, and bus fuel. The bill's requirement to provide hourly employees with make-up wage opportunities is not expected to significantly increase expenditures as these employees currently receive pay during emergency closures.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Maryland State Department of Education (MSDE) is the primary state-level agency responsible for overseeing public education and ensuring local school systems follow state laws. The bill requires Montgomery County to report to the State Board of Education (which MSDE supports) regarding school operations and modifies statutory attendance requirements found in the Education Article.

The bill includes a specific labor provision requiring the local school board to provide hourly employees with an opportunity to make up lost wages through other duties if schools are open for fewer than 180 days. As the state agency that oversees labor relations for public school systems, PERB is relevant to these types of employment and wage-related mandates.

The bill's provisions allowing for modified school schedules are specifically triggered by emergencies such as natural disasters, civil disasters, or severe weather conditions. While MDEM does not manage school calendars, they are the primary agency responsible for coordinating the state's response to the hazards that activate the bill's provisions.

The OAG provides legal counsel to the State Board of Education and the Department of Education. They would likely be involved in interpreting the legal shifts in the Education Article and ensuring the bill's emergency provisions are implemented correctly by state actors.

As the chief executive, the Governor oversees the executive branch, including MSDE. Furthermore, the bill is an emergency measure that takes effect immediately upon enactment, requiring gubernatorial signature.

DBM is the principal fiscal agency for the state. Although the fiscal note indicates no direct impact on state expenditures, DBM monitors the fiscal health and operations of state-funded entities like MSDE.

bill_summary: This bill establishes the Maryland Office of the Inspector General (OIG) and the State Transparency Commission to provide oversight of executive branch units. The OIG is tasked with investigating waste, fraud, and corruption, implementing AI-powered technology for real-time monitoring of state transactions, and conducting efficiency reviews of state agencies. It also extends whistleblower protections to state employees who report misconduct to the office.
responsible_party: Maryland Office of the Inspector General
stakeholders: Executive branch agencies and state employees
fiscal_impact_summary: The bill results in an indeterminate increase in state expenditures to fund the Maryland Office of the Inspector General's operations, including salaries for the Inspector General and staff, the establishment of office space, and the procurement of AI monitoring technology. While the Governor is authorized to transfer funds and positions from existing units to the new office, specific dollar estimates are unavailable as a formal Fiscal Note was not provided in the source text.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Governor is a member of the State Transparency Commission created by the bill, which appoints and oversees the Inspector General. Additionally, the Governor is authorized to transfer positions and funds to the new Office.

The bill establishes an Inspector General with auditing and investigative powers over executive agencies, creating significant overlap with OLA's fiscal compliance and performance audit functions. The bill specifically requires the IG to avoid duplicative audits.

DBM is responsible for the state budget and personnel management. The bill involves funding for the new Office, the transfer of state positions, and expanded whistleblower protections for state employees.

There is substantial overlap between GOPI's mission of efficiency and performance metrics and the OIG's new mandate to establish Key Performance Indicators (KPIs) and conduct efficiency reconstruction reviews for agencies.

The OAG is involved in whistleblower disclosures and provides legal counsel to state agencies. The Inspector General is required to refer discovered criminal activity to appropriate law enforcement or prosecutorial agencies like the OAG.

The OSP investigates and prosecutes misconduct in office and corruption. The Inspector General's investigations into waste, fraud, and abuse in state units would likely result in referrals to the OSP for legal action.

The BPW oversees major state expenditures and contracts. The Inspector General is tasked with monitoring units for procurement anomalies and waste, which directly intersects with BPW's oversight role.
DGS is the central procurement authority and manages state facilities. The OIG is mandated to flag procurement anomalies and has the authority to establish and equip office space.

The bill requires the Inspector General to implement AI-powered technology to flag waste and fraud in real-time within state units, which would require significant coordination with or impact on DoIT's infrastructure and strategy.
The Inspector General's mandate to investigate misconduct and corruption within the executive branch overlaps with the State Ethics Commission's responsibility to enforce public ethics laws.
The MSP is the primary state law enforcement agency and would likely receive referrals from the Inspector General regarding criminal activity discovered during audits or investigations.
DJS is specifically named in the bill's amendments to the whistleblower protection laws, ensuring its employees are protected when reporting to the Inspector General.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Department of Public Safety and Correctional Services
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: DPSCS is specifically named in the bill's amendments to the whistleblower protection laws, ensuring its employees are protected when reporting to the Inspector General.

As the chief financial officer and a member of the Board of Public Works, the Comptroller's agency is subject to OIG oversight, KPIs, and potential efficiency reviews regarding revenue collection and auditing.
The Treasurer manages state funds and serves on the Board of Public Works. The OIG's mission to identify waste and fraud in state spending directly impacts the Treasurer's management of state assets.

PERB oversees collective bargaining and labor relations for state employees. The bill's provisions regarding personnel transfers to the OIG and whistleblower protections fall under PERB's general area of labor law enforcement.
As a major executive department, MDH will be subject to the OIG's new KPI requirements, annual efficiency goals, and AI-powered real-time monitoring of transactions and procurement.
As a principal executive department with significant contracting and procurement activities, MDOT will be a primary subject of OIG oversight, audits, and performance metrics.

The bill requires the Inspector General to obtain approval for subpoenas from a judge of the Circuit Court, involving the judicial branch and its administrative support infrastructure in the OIG's investigative process.

bill_summary: This bill authorizes Montgomery County to use crosswalk monitoring systems in school zones to record and cite drivers who fail to stop for pedestrians in crosswalks. The systems may be used on local or State highways within school zones if authorized by local law and the State Highway Administration, respectively. Drivers caught by these systems are subject to a civil penalty of up to $40, which does not result in points on their license or impact insurance rates. The bill also requires Montgomery County to report on the program's effectiveness and costs by December 1, 2027.
responsible_party: Montgomery County Department of Transportation and local law enforcement agencies
stakeholders: Drivers and pedestrians in school zones within Montgomery County, and the Montgomery County local government.
fiscal_impact_summary: Montgomery County expenditures and revenues will increase starting in FY 2027 if it chooses to implement the program; revenues from the $40 civil penalties will be used to cover system costs, with any remaining balance dedicated to public safety. State general fund revenues from contested cases in District Court may increase minimally. The Judiciary noted a potential $1,400,000 cost for a general system-wide IT upgrade for automated enforcement, though this is not exclusively attributed to this specific bill.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill mandates that the District Court handle all contested citations and requires the Chief Judge of the District Court to adopt procedures and prescribe a uniform citation form for the crosswalk monitoring system. It also defines the admissibility of recorded images as evidence in court proceedings.

The SHA is specifically authorized to approve the use of crosswalk monitoring systems on State highways within school zones and is responsible for placing signage on State highways providing notice that the systems are in use.
The MVA is responsible for enforcing the civil penalties by refusing or suspending the registration of a motor vehicle if a citation is not paid or contested.

As the parent agency for SHA and MVA, MDOT oversees the modal administrations responsible for authorizing the systems on state roads and managing the vehicle registration penalties associated with the program.
The bill requires the political subdivision to remit civil penalty funds to the Comptroller if the remaining balance after costs exceeds 10% of the county's total revenues for the fiscal year.

The Montgomery County Department of Transportation is required to submit a formal report to the Governor by December 1, 2027, regarding the effectiveness, costs, and reliability of the crosswalk monitoring systems.

The OAG serves as the legal counsel to the state agencies involved (MDOT, SHA, MVA, and the Judiciary) and may be involved in advising on the implementation and legal defenses established by the bill.

bill_summary: This bill requires health care facilities, including hospitals and ambulatory surgical facilities, to adopt and implement policies by January 1, 2028, that necessitate the use of smoke evacuation systems during surgical procedures likely to generate surgical smoke.

stakeholders: Health care facilities, surgical staff (surgeons, nurses, anesthesiologists, and surgical technologists), and patients.
fiscal_impact_summary: The Maryland Office of Health Care Quality (OHCQ) can monitor compliance within its existing budgeted resources. The bill has no impact on State revenues or local government finances. While health care facilities will incur costs to implement smoke evacuation systems, the fiscal note indicates no small business effect.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill requires health care facilities, such as hospitals and ambulatory surgical facilities, to implement surgical smoke policies. The Maryland Department of Health, specifically the Office of Health Care Quality (OHCQ), is responsible for regulating these facilities and ensuring compliance with state health and safety standards.

The bill addresses surgical smoke, which is a workplace health and safety hazard. The Department of Labor oversees workplace safety and labor laws (including the Maryland Occupational Safety and Health program), making them relevant to the enforcement of standards that protect surgical staff.

As the operator of major academic medical centers and affiliated hospitals that perform surgical procedures, the University System of Maryland must ensure its facilities adopt and implement the required smoke evacuation policies.
The OAG provides legal counsel to the Department of Health and would assist in drafting regulations or defending enforcement actions related to the new surgical smoke evacuation requirements.

The OAH would be responsible for adjudicating any contested cases or appeals if a health care facility's license is challenged by the Department of Health for non-compliance with the bill's requirements.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Department of Public Safety and Correctional Services
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The department operates correctional facilities that may include medical units or infirmaries where surgical procedures are performed. These facilities would need to comply with the bill's mandate to use smoke evacuation systems.

responsible_party: Maryland State Department of Assessments and Taxation
stakeholders: Commercial real property owners, county governments, and municipal corporations
fiscal_impact_summary: Specific dollar estimates are unavailable as a formal Fiscal Note was not provided in the text. However, the bill allows local governments to challenge commercial property assessments under specific sales conditions, which could lead to increased property tax revenues for the state and local jurisdictions. The State Department of Assessments and Taxation would likely incur additional administrative costs to process these new petitions.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: This board is the primary administrative body that hears appeals from property tax assessments. This bill would likely increase its case volume by authorizing local governments to challenge commercial assessments.
As the highest level of administrative review for tax disputes, this court would adjudicate further appeals stemming from the new local-government petitions authorized by the bill.

The OAG serves as the primary legal representative for the State and its agencies; it would provide legal counsel to the assessment department and represent the state in any resulting appeals or litigation.
DBM oversees the state's fiscal planning and budget execution. Changes in commercial property assessments affect local wealth metrics, which are central to state aid and funding formulas.

The state's educational funding formulas for local school systems rely on property wealth calculations. Altering how commercial properties are assessed could impact the distribution of state education funds.
Commercial property tax levels are a key factor in Maryland's business climate. This department monitors policies that affect economic development and the financial burden on commercial enterprises.
As the state's chief financial officer, the Comptroller monitors state revenues and fiscal policy, both of which are influenced by changes in the property tax assessment process.

The Governor's Office oversees the executive branch departments involved in property assessment and is responsible for proposing the state budget, which is impacted by assessment-based revenue and wealth metrics.

bill_summary: This bill establishes a data broker registry in Maryland, requiring businesses that knowingly collect and sell or license personal consumer data to register annually with the Office of the Attorney General beginning in 2028. Data brokers must pay a tiered registration fee based on revenue, disclose their data collection and sharing practices, and provide contact information for consumer inquiries. The bill also requires the creation of a publicly searchable database of registered brokers and mandates a report on compliance and consumer protection recommendations by 2029.
responsible_party: Maryland Office of the Attorney General
stakeholders: Data brokers operating in Maryland and Maryland residents
fiscal_impact_summary: The bill requires the Office of the Attorney General to establish a tiered registration fee structure in an amount sufficient to cover the administrative costs of the program. Failure to register may result in civil fines of up to $10,000 per violation. While these provisions create revenue and expenditure frameworks, specific dollar estimates from a formal Fiscal Note are unavailable.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill explicitly mandates the Office of the Attorney General to establish and maintain the Data Broker Registry, create a searchable database, set registration fees, adopt regulations, and enforce penalties for non-compliance.

As the agency responsible for the state's IT infrastructure and digital services, DoIT would likely provide technical support and oversight for the publicly accessible, searchable database required by the bill.
DBM oversees the state budget and personnel; it will be involved in the fiscal implementation of the new registry, managing the revenue from tiered fees and the associated administrative costs.
The Comptroller's Office is responsible for collecting state revenues. This agency would likely manage the collection and processing of the tiered registration fees established under this bill.
The OAH would be responsible for adjudicating contested cases if a data broker appeals a civil fine or violation notice issued by the Office of the Attorney General.
The judicial branch would be responsible for processing any civil enforcement actions or legal appeals resulting from the Attorney General's enforcement of the data broker regulations.
The Department of Labor regulates various businesses and industries. This bill introduces a new regulatory framework for data brokers, a commercial sector that impacts Maryland consumers.
The Governor's Office oversees the executive branch and coordinates major policy initiatives like the establishment of a new statewide consumer protection registry.
The Department of Commerce monitors business regulations and fees for their impact on the state's economy and business climate, which would include the new requirements for data brokers.

bill_summary: Beginning in the 2027-2028 school year, this bill requires the Montgomery County Board of Education to close public schools for student attendance on specific holidays: the first day of Diwali, Eid Al-Adha, Eid Al-Fitr, Lunar New Year, and Rosh Hashanah, as well as Yom Kippur and Juneteenth.
stakeholders: Students, faculty, and staff of Montgomery County Public Schools
fiscal_impact_summary: The bill has no state fiscal impact. These expenses include hourly wages, benefits, substitute teachers, and bus fuel. agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: As the primary agency responsible for the oversight and leadership of Maryland's public education system, MSDE is responsible for ensuring that local school systems like Montgomery County comply with state laws regarding mandatory school days and hours as established in Section 7-103 of the Education Article.

The OAG provides legal counsel to the State Department of Education and the General Assembly, and would be responsible for advising on the legal implementation and interpretation of county-specific school holiday mandates within the broader context of state education law.

GOCI manages various ethnic, cultural, and faith-based commissions. This bill mandates public school holidays for several specific religious and cultural observances (including Diwali, Eid al-Adha, Eid al-Fitr, Lunar New Year, and Rosh Hashanah), which directly aligns with GOCI's mission of community engagement and cultural advocacy.

The Governor's Office oversees executive branch policy initiatives and the Department of Education. As this bill mandates a policy change for a major local jurisdiction's school calendar, it falls under the Governor's broader administrative and policy-setting coordination duties.

Synopsis: Prohibiting certain insurers and dental plan organizations from prohibiting an assignment of benefits to a provider who is a dentist by an insured or refusing to directly reimburse a nonpreferred provider who is a dentist; requiring a nonpreferred provider who is a dentist and who seeks an assignment of benefits from an insured or enrollee to provide certain information to the insured or enrollee before performing a health care service and submit a disclosure form to document the assignment of benefits; etc.

bill_summary: This bill requires health insurers and dental plan organizations to allow patients to assign their insurance benefits to a dentist, ensuring that the dentist is reimbursed directly by the insurance provider regardless of whether they are a preferred provider. Dentists who seek an assignment of benefits must provide patients with specific disclosures, including cost estimates and a notice of their nonpreferred status, before performing services.
stakeholders: Dentists, dental plan organizations, health insurance carriers, and dental patients
fiscal_impact_summary: According to the Fiscal Note, the bill results in a minimal increase in special fund revenues for the Maryland Insurance Administration starting in FY 2027 due to $125 rate and form filing fees. Any additional workload for the agency can be managed within existing resources. There is no local fiscal impact, though small business dental practices may see a meaningful impact by gaining the ability to receive direct reimbursement through assignment of benefits.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Maryland Insurance Administration is the primary implementing agency. The Insurance Commissioner is explicitly charged with developing the required disclosure forms for dentists and overseeing compliance by insurers and dental plan organizations. The agency will also collect form filing fees associated with the bill.

The bill regulates the conduct of dentists, who are licensed and regulated under Title 4 of the Health Occupations Article. The Department of Health oversees the boards that govern these medical professionals and their clinical practices.

The Office of the Attorney General serves as the legal counsel for the Maryland Insurance Administration and the Department of Health. They would be responsible for reviewing the legality of the new disclosure forms and defending any regulatory challenges to the new reimbursement rules.

As the administrator of Maryland's health insurance marketplace, the Exchange must ensure that dental plan organizations (DPOs) offering coverage through the marketplace comply with these new assignment of benefits and reimbursement requirements.

The Commission is responsible for health system planning and promoting transparency in health care costs. The bill's requirements for dentists to provide cost estimates and balance billing disclosures to patients align with the Commission's mission to improve informed decision-making.

The Office of Administrative Hearings may be required to adjudicate contested cases involving insurers or dental plan organizations that fail to comply with the reimbursement and assignment of benefits mandates established by the bill.

bill_summary: This bill requires the Maryland Department of Health to ensure the establishment and operation of at least 24 licensed adolescent psychiatric inpatient beds in Prince George's County by December 31, 2028. The bill also establishes a competitive grant program for capital costs such as construction and renovation and requires annual reports on adolescent psychiatric bed capacity and emergency department boarding through 2030.
stakeholders: Adolescents (ages 12-16) in Prince George's County, the Maryland Department of Health, the Prince George's County Local Behavioral Health Authority, hospitals, psychiatric facilities, and the Maryland Medical Assistance Program.
fiscal_impact_summary: The bill mandates the establishment of 24 inpatient beds and a competitive capital grant program, which will result in significant State expenditures for construction, renovation, safety upgrades, and workforce start-up costs. Specific dollar estimates from a Fiscal Note were not included in the provided text.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Maryland Department of Health (MDH) is the primary agency tasked with implementing the bill, including ensuring the establishment of 24 beds in Prince George's County, issuing RFPs, administering the grant program, and reporting data annually.
The HSCRC regulates hospital rates and revenues; the bill specifically requires recommendations for rate changes needed to maintain adolescent psychiatric inpatient bed capacity.

The MHCC is responsible for planning health system needs and regulating hospital capacity; it would likely oversee the Certificate of Need process for the new beds and provide the required regulatory recommendations.
DBM oversees the state budget and would be involved in managing the funding for the mandated competitive grant program and potential personnel needs for MDH's implementation of the bill.
The Board of Public Works must approve significant state procurement contracts, RFPs, and grant disbursements proposed by the Department of Health under this bill.

The GOC coordinates services to improve the well-being of children and families; increasing adolescent psychiatric bed capacity aligns with its mission to strengthen support networks for vulnerable youth.

The Governor's Office oversees the executive branch, including MDH, and will receive the annual reports mandated by the bill regarding psychiatric bed capacity and emergency department boarding metrics.
The OAG provides legal counsel to state agencies and would be responsible for reviewing the legal sufficiency of the RFPs, contracts, and grant program regulations developed by MDH.

Youth in the juvenile justice system frequently require inpatient psychiatric services; increasing bed capacity in Prince George's County would directly impact the placement options and service availability for DJS-involved youth.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Maryland Institute for Emergency Medical Services Systems
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: MIEMSS coordinates the state's emergency medical network; the bill's focus on emergency department boarding and psychiatric overstays involves the pre-hospital and hospital transfer systems managed by the agency.

DHS serves vulnerable children, including those in foster care who may require inpatient psychiatric care; the availability of beds in Prince George's County affects DHS's ability to provide necessary treatment for children in its care.
As a member of the Board of Public Works, the Comptroller must review and approve the fiscal integrity of the contracts and grant awards required to establish the new psychiatric beds.
As a member of the Board of Public Works, the Treasurer is involved in approving the procurement and financing aspects of the capital projects and grants authorized by the bill.

The bill requires that access to these beds be provided regardless of payer source; the MIA regulates private insurers and ensures compliance with laws related to medical necessity and behavioral health coverage.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Maryland Health & Higher Educational Facilities Authority
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: MHHEFA assists non-profit hospitals and health organizations with financing capital projects; they may be a resource for institutions seeking to supplement the bill's grant funds for construction or renovation.

bill_summary: This bill streamlines the credentialing process for health care providers joining insurance carrier panels by shortening notification deadlines, requiring the use of a centralized online credentialing system, and prohibiting carriers from charging application fees. It also requires carriers to maintain accurate provider directories, expands protections for essential community providers, and establishes civil penalties for carriers that fail to meet procedural timelines.
stakeholders: Health care providers, health insurance carriers, health care facilities, and health insurance enrollees.
fiscal_impact_summary: According to the Fiscal Note, any impact on the Maryland Insurance Administration can be handled with existing budgeted resources, and State revenues are not affected. The bill repeals the authorization for carriers to charge provider application fees and establishes civil penalties of 500 dollars per day for carriers that fail to meet specified notification deadlines, with penalties paid directly to the provider. There is no impact on local government finances.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: As the primary regulator of the state's insurance market, the Maryland Insurance Administration is the lead agency responsible for implementing the bill. The Insurance Commissioner is tasked with adopting regulations for the online credentialing system, designating uniform credentialing forms, collecting vendor reports, and enforcing carrier compliance with notice and directory update requirements.

The bill's definition of 'carrier' includes Managed Care Organizations (MCOs), which are overseen by the Department of Health as part of the Medicaid program. Additionally, the bill provides specific credentialing protections and panel participation requirements for behavioral health providers, local health departments, and Federally Qualified Health Centers, all of which fall under the department's scope.

The Office of the Attorney General serves as the primary legal counsel for the Maryland Insurance Administration. The OAG would be involved in the drafting of new regulations required by the bill and would provide legal support for the enforcement of civil penalties against insurance carriers that fail to meet notice requirements.

The Maryland Health Benefit Exchange administers the state's insurance marketplace (Maryland Health Connection) and relies on the accuracy of provider directories. The bill's mandates for carriers to use the online credentialing system as the primary source for updates and to increase update frequency directly impact the quality of data provided to consumers on the Exchange.

The Maryland Health Care Commission is responsible for planning for health system needs and improving access to care. The bill's focus on streamlining provider credentialing and ensuring the accuracy of provider networks aligns with the Commission's mission to increase accountability and transparency in the healthcare system.

The bill explicitly includes school-based health centers in the list of providers that carriers are prohibited from limiting on their provider panels, which is relevant to the department's role in overseeing health services provided within the public school system.

The Office of Administrative Hearings may be required to adjudicate disputes if insurance carriers contest civil penalties or regulatory enforcement actions taken by the Maryland Insurance Administration under the provisions of this bill.

stakeholders: Graduate-level clinical interns in counseling, social work, and psychology; licensed clinical professional supervisors; health insurance carriers; outpatient health care facilities; and insured patients.
fiscal_impact_summary: State special fund revenues for the Maryland Insurance Administration will increase minimally in fiscal 2027 due to $125 rate and form filing fees. agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: As the primary regulator of health insurance in the state, the MIA is responsible for enforcing the reimbursement mandate and reviewing the resulting rate and form filings from insurers. The fiscal note explicitly mentions a minimal increase in MIA special fund revenues from these filings.

The bill directly involves the scope of practice and clinical supervision requirements for counselors, social workers, and psychologists, all of whom are licensed by boards under the Department of Health. The department was also a key information source for the fiscal note.
The bill's mandates apply to individual and group health insurance policies, which include plans offered and administered through the state's health insurance marketplace.

The OAG provides legal counsel to the Maryland Insurance Administration and the Department of Health, and will likely be involved in interpreting and defending the legal application of the new reimbursement requirements.

The commission oversees the standards and approval of the graduate programs in counseling, social work, and psychology that the clinical interns must be enrolled in to qualify for reimbursement under this bill.

The University System of Maryland includes several institutions that offer the graduate-level programs and clinical internship opportunities targeted by this legislation, directly impacting their students' clinical training and placement ecosystem.

As a state agency and public university with graduate programs in these fields, Morgan State's clinical interns and their associated outpatient training partners are affected by the new reimbursement structure.
As a public higher education institution, any of its students participating in relevant clinical graduate programs would be affected by the insurance reimbursement changes for their services.

bill_summary: This bill authorizes the Calvert County government to grant a property tax credit for real property that was previously used exclusively as a tobacco barn. fiscal_impact_summary: The bill has no impact on state finances. Calvert County property tax revenues will decrease starting in fiscal 2027 if the local governing body chooses to grant the credit. agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: As the head of the executive branch, the Governor is responsible for signing the bill into law and oversees the agencies involved in state tax policy and agricultural support.

The bill focuses on properties formerly used for tobacco farming and land qualifying for agricultural use assessments, which falls under the department's mission to promote the economic viability of Maryland's agricultural industry.
The agency is involved in sustainable growth and land-use planning; property tax credits for agricultural land are a mechanism used to influence rural land preservation and development patterns.
The Tax Court is the final administrative body for adjudicating tax disputes, including appeals regarding property tax assessments and credits that have passed through the local appeals board.

The Council advocates for the interests of Maryland's rural counties, including Calvert County, and supports agricultural preservation and economic development within those regions.

stakeholders: Maryland property owners and taxpayers
fiscal_impact_summary: According to the fiscal note, the bill has no impact on State finances. Local county expenditures are not expected to be significantly affected by the requirement to include a website address or QR code on tax bills, and there is no direct impact on county revenues.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Property Tax Assessment Appeals Board (PTAAB) is directly responsible for hearing disputes over various property tax credits. Increased visibility of these credits could lead to an increase in the number of cases adjudicated by the Court if credits are denied or disputed.

The Department of Aging advocates for older adults, many of whom are eligible for specific property tax relief programs such as the Homeowners' Tax Credit. Improved notice through digital means like QR codes directly assists this agency's constituency in accessing financial support that improves their quality of life and housing security.

The Department of Disabilities works to ensure accessible housing and community living for individuals with disabilities. Several property tax credits are specifically designed for people with disabilities or disabled veterans, and this bill facilitates easier access to those benefits.

Many Maryland counties offer property tax credits specifically for veterans and their families. This agency is responsible for assisting veterans in securing state benefits, and improved notice of these credits on property tax bills aligns with their mission of advocacy and resource access.

The Innovation Team is tasked with piloting novel initiatives to enhance economic mobility and improve services for Maryland families. Using digital technology like QR codes to facilitate access to property tax credits is an example of the service-delivery improvements the team is designed to support.

The Governor's Office of Performance Improvement (GOPI) focuses on enhancing the responsiveness and efficiency of government operations. The bill's requirement to utilize data-driven and accessible communication methods (QR codes and centralized webpages) to deliver government services (tax credits) fits within GOPI's mandate.

As the state's principal tax official, the Comptroller has a general interest in the administration of tax laws and the distribution of information regarding tax credits, even though property taxes are primarily administered at the local level.

The Governor's Office oversees the executive branch and coordinates policy initiatives. The bill aligns with the Governor's broader priorities regarding economic relief and modernized service delivery.

This office focuses on enhancing economic mobility and reducing poverty. Property tax credits serve as a significant financial relief tool for low-income families, contributing to the office's core mission.

Documentation must include specific details like the type of activity, description of the injury, and whether medical treatment was recommended, and must be recorded within 24 hours. Local school systems are required to submit an aggregated annual report of these injuries to the Maryland State Department of Education beginning July 1, 2027.
stakeholders: Public high school student-athletes, coaches, athletic trainers, school nurses, and local school systems.
fiscal_impact_summary: The bill has no impact on State revenues or expenditures as the Maryland State Department of Education can implement requirements using existing resources. Local school systems may incur minimal additional costs for training and technology; for example, St. Mary's County Public Schools estimates an annual cost of $7,500 for injury tracking technology.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: As the primary agency overseeing Maryland's public education system, the Department is responsible for receiving annual reports from local school systems, maintaining compliance, and collaborating with others to adopt regulations and standardized reporting forms for sports injury logs.

The bill explicitly requires the Maryland Department of Health to collaborate with the State Department of Education to develop regulations and standardized reporting forms for high school athletic injury recordkeeping.

As a state agency providing public education through age 21, the Maryland School for the Deaf functions as a public school that must comply with the bill's requirements to maintain standardized injury logs for its athletic activities and retain them for safety reviews.

The bill's recordkeeping requirements are intended for 'safety review purposes,' aligning with this agency's role in developing resources and providing a comprehensive approach to school safety for public and private schools.

The Governor's Office oversees the executive branch departments (MSDE and MDH) responsible for implementing the bill and maintains ultimate authority over state law enforcement and policy coordination.

The OAG will be responsible for providing legal counsel to the implementing agencies during the regulatory process and ensuring that standardized reporting forms comply with the federal and state privacy laws (such as FERPA) mentioned in the bill.

Synopsis: Exempting certain owner-occupied residential real property from execution on a judgment in a certain amount and subject to certain adjustments; and applying the Act prospectively.
Title: Courts - Exemptions From Execution on Judgments - Residential Real Property
Status: In the Senate - First Reading Judicial Proceedings

NarrowSubjects.Name: Elderly Persons (65+) -see also- Elder Abuse and Neglect

bill_summary: This bill increases the exemption amount for owner-occupied residential real property from execution on a judgment, including property held in a revocable trust. It establishes an exemption limit of $150,000 for most individuals and $300,000 for individuals aged 60 or older who are veterans or have a disability. Additionally, the bill provides for periodic inflation adjustments to these exemption amounts beginning in 2027.
stakeholders: Maryland homeowners, debtors, creditors, veterans, and individuals with disabilities.
fiscal_impact_summary: According to the Fiscal Note, the bill does not directly affect State or local finances or operations. While it modifies the amounts and types of property exempt from execution in civil and bankruptcy proceedings, it does not mandate State expenditures or impact State revenue.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill amends the Courts and Judicial Proceedings Article to change legal exemptions for judgments on residential real property. As the central support agency for the Maryland Judicial Branch, the AOC is responsible for implementing policies and operational changes within the state's courts.

The bill establishes specific, higher homestead exemption limits ($300,000) for individuals who are at least 60 years old. This directly impacts the department's mission to protect the rights and quality of life for older adults in Maryland.

The bill includes specific provisions for veterans who are at least 60 years old, granting them a higher exemption amount in bankruptcy proceedings. The agency is responsible for advocating for and assisting veterans in securing benefits.

The bill provides higher exemption amounts for individuals with certified disabilities who are at least 60 years old. This relates to the department's role in coordinating services and improving policy outcomes for residents with disabilities.

The bill's primary focus is protecting owner-occupied residential real property from execution on judgments. This aligns with the agency's mission to ensure residents have access to safe, secure housing and to promote community economic vitality.

The bill increases protections for debtors facing economic need or bankruptcy by exempting more equity in their primary residence. This affects the vulnerable populations and individuals in economic need that the department serves.

The OAG serves as the chief legal officer for the state and provides counsel to the General Assembly and state agencies. The bill involves significant changes to civil procedure and property law, which may require legal interpretation or guidance from the OAG.

Synopsis: Imposing a limit of four on the number of terms a person may serve in the General Assembly; providing that a certain term limit does not apply to terms that began before the 2030 gubernatorial election; and specifying how service for a partial term shall be considered for purposes of the term limits.
Title: General Assembly - Term Limits
Status: In the House - Hearing 3/16 at 12:00 p.m.

NarrowSubjects.Name: General Assembly -see also- AELR Cmte; LegislativePolCmte

bill_summary: This bill proposes a constitutional amendment to limit members of the Maryland General Assembly to serving no more than four terms. Terms beginning before the 2030 gubernatorial election are not counted toward this limit, and individuals serving at least two years of a four-year term are considered to have served a full term.
stakeholders: Current and future members of the Maryland General Assembly and registered voters in Maryland
fiscal_impact_summary: The fiscal note indicates no discernible effect on State pension liabilities, contribution rates, or revenues. While the amendment could theoretically reduce pension expenditures because members would be limited to 16 years of service—which is less than the 22.25 years required to reach the maximum benefit cap—any such impact is considered minimal and would not occur within the next five fiscal years, as the limit applies only to terms starting in 2030 or later.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: As mandated by Section 3 of the bill, the proposed constitutional amendment must be submitted to the qualified voters of Maryland during the November 2026 general election. The State Board of Elections is the primary agency responsible for administering this referendum, managing the ballot language, and overseeing the vote collection and certification process.

The fiscal note specifically analyzes the impact on the Legislative Pension Plan (LPP), which is administered by the Maryland State Retirement Agency. The proposed 16-year term limit (four terms) is shorter than the 22 years and three months currently required to earn full retirement benefits, which would impact the accrual of benefits and long-term liabilities for the system.

According to Section 3 of the bill and Article XIV of the Maryland Constitution, all election returns regarding constitutional amendments must be submitted to the Governor. The Governor is then responsible for issuing a proclamation regarding the results and overseeing the final adoption process of the amendment.

The OAG acts as the chief legal representative for the state and the General Assembly. The office is responsible for reviewing the legal sufficiency of constitutional amendments and would likely be involved in drafting or reviewing the specific ballot language presented to voters.

The Secretary of State is the principal custodian of the state's official records, including laws and constitutional changes. If the amendment is adopted by voters, the Secretary of State will be responsible for maintaining the updated constitutional record.

Synopsis: Specifying that certain documentation may establish lawful authority to sell certain telecommunications equipment as junk or scrap metal; requiring certain junk dealers, scrap metal processors, and antique dealers to register and provide a description including certain information of purchased telecommunications equipment with a certain law enforcement official; prohibiting certain individuals from destroying telecommunications infrastructure in a certain manner; and providing certain penalties for violations of the Act.
Title: Telecommunications Infrastructure - Protections
Status: Approved by the Governor - Chapter 546

NarrowSubjects.Name: Commerce and Business -see also- ElectrComm; ForeignTr; etc.
Crimes and Punishments -see also- Penalties and Sentnc; etc.
Equipment -see also- Charging; Med. Equip.; MV Equip; etc.
Law Enforcement -see also- SRO; Sheriffs; State Police
Penalties and Sentences -see also- Death Penalty

bill_summary: This bill prohibits the reckless or malicious defacement, damage, or destruction of telecommunications infrastructure and establishes these actions as a misdemeanor. It also expands the definition of junk or scrap metal to include telecommunications equipment and requires junk dealers and scrap metal processors to verify a seller's legal authority to sell such items through specific documentation, such as a bill of sale or a letter of authorization.
responsible_party: Junk dealers, scrap metal processors, and State and local law enforcement agencies
stakeholders: Telecommunications companies, junk dealers, scrap metal processors, law enforcement agencies, and individuals selling scrap metal
fiscal_impact_summary: The bill is not expected to materially affect State or local government operations or finances. It establishes a misdemeanor penalty for damaging infrastructure, which includes a fine of up to $500 and/or imprisonment for up to six months. Small business impact is expected to be minimal.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Governor's Office oversees the executive branch and has final approval authority over the bill. The legislation aligns with executive priorities regarding public safety and the protection of critical state infrastructure.

The OAG provides legal counsel to the state agencies implementing the bill, such as the Department of Labor and Maryland State Police, and represents the state in criminal appeals resulting from the new misdemeanor offense.
As the agency responsible for the state's telecommunications strategy and infrastructure, DoIT is a key stakeholder in the protection of broadband and fiber optic networks defined in the bill.

The Department of Labor is the primary regulator of junk dealers and scrap metal processors. The bill adds significant new identification, documentation, and record-keeping requirements for these businesses under the Business Regulation Article.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Department of Public Safety and Correctional Services
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: DPSCS oversees the state's correctional facilities and community supervision. The bill creates a new misdemeanor offense with potential imprisonment of up to six months, which falls under their oversight of justice-involved individuals.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Maryland Office of the Public Defender
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Office of the Public Defender will be responsible for representing indigent defendants charged with the new misdemeanor for defacing or destroying telecommunications infrastructure.

The Judicial Branch, supported by the AOC, will process and adjudicate the new criminal cases and potential civil disputes arising from the expanded regulations on junk dealers and infrastructure protection.

The Maryland State Police is the primary law enforcement agency responsible for enforcing the state's criminal laws, investigating the destruction of infrastructure, and receiving transaction records from junk and scrap metal dealers.
The PSC regulates many of the telecommunications and utility companies whose infrastructure (such as telephone poles and small cell facilities) is specifically protected by the bill's new provisions.

Synopsis: Establishing a temporary to-go event permit in Worcester County; authorizing the Board of License Commissioners for Worcester County to issue a temporary to-go event permit to a holder of a Class B liquor license or a Class D license under certain circumstances; establishing a Class C per diem municipal to-go beer, wine, and liquor license in the county; authorizing the Board to issue a Class C per diem municipal to-go beer, wine, and liquor license to certain municipalities in the county; etc.
Title: Worcester County - Alcoholic Beverages - Temporary To-Go Event Permit and Class C Per Diem Municipal To-Go Beer, Wine, and Liquor License
Status: Approved by the Governor - Chapter 834

NarrowSubjects.Name: Age -see also- Age of Maj; Children; Elderly; Inf&Tod.; etc
Fees -see also- Attys' Fees; Devt Fees & Taxes

bill_summary: This bill establishes a temporary to-go event permit and a Class C per diem municipal to-go beer, wine, and liquor license in Worcester County. The license allows the towns of Berlin, Pocomoke City, and Snow Hill to designate special event areas for up to seven days, while the permit authorizes local Class B and Class D license holders to sell alcoholic beverages in approved to-go cups for consumption within those designated areas.
responsible_party: Worcester County Board of License Commissioners
stakeholders: Municipal governments of Berlin, Pocomoke City, and Snow Hill; Class B and Class D alcoholic beverage license holders in Worcester County; and residents and visitors of these municipalities.
fiscal_impact_summary: According to the Fiscal Note, Worcester County revenues will increase starting in fiscal 2027 based on the issuance of new licenses and permits. The fee for the Class C per diem municipal to-go license is $45 per day, and the fee for the temporary to-go event permit is $20 per day. Total revenue increases cannot be reliably estimated as they depend on the number of applications. There is no impact on State finances, and local monitoring can be handled with existing resources.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Governor's Office is responsible for signing legislation into law and overseeing the executive branch's enforcement of state laws. This bill requires the Governor's signature to take effect and impacts the regulatory duties of the executive branch regarding alcoholic beverages.

As the state's principal regulator of the alcohol industry, the Comptroller is responsible for overseeing the enforcement of tax laws and industry regulations. This bill establishes new license and permit types within the Alcoholic Beverages and Cannabis Article, which falls under the Comptroller's general regulatory and oversight scope.

The OAG serves as the chief legal officer for the state and provides counsel to state boards and commissions, including the Worcester County Board of License Commissioners, on the interpretation and enforcement of the Alcoholic Beverages and Cannabis Article.

The bill creates 'special event areas' and to-go beverage permits in municipal centers of Worcester County, such as Berlin and Snow Hill. These measures are designed to enhance recreational attractions and promote tourism within the county's historic and commercial districts.

The Maryland State Police provide support to local law enforcement and ensure public peace across the state. This bill mandates the adoption of regulations regarding public safety and event security for special event areas where alcohol consumption is authorized, which may require coordination or support from the State Police during regional events.

Synopsis: Requiring membership in the Correctional Officers' Retirement System for certain local detention center officers of Allegany County in the event Allegany County becomes a participating governmental unit in the Correctional Officers' Retirement System; and providing that certain local detention center officers who join the Correctional Officers' Retirement System and receive certain service credit shall no longer be members of the Employees' Pension System.
Title: Correctional Officers' Retirement System - Allegany County
Status: Approved by the Governor - Chapter 179
bill_summary: This bill mandates that Allegany County detention center officers become members of the Correctional Officers’ Retirement System (CORS) if the county elects to participate in the system. It provides for the transfer of service credits from the Employees’ Pension System (EPS) to CORS and exempts transferring officers from paying the difference in member contribution rates for their prior service.
stakeholders: Allegany County detention center officers and the Allegany County government
fiscal_impact_summary: The bill has no impact on State finances. For Allegany County, an actuarial analysis indicates that pension liabilities would increase by approximately $2.4 million. Net employer contributions are estimated to increase by approximately $165,000 annually beginning in fiscal 2028, reflecting the higher employer contribution rate for CORS compared to EPS, partially offset by a new entrant liability credit.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The SRA is the primary agency responsible for the administration and management of the State Retirement and Pension System (SRPS), which includes both the Employees' Pension System and the Correctional Officers' Retirement System. This bill directly mandates the SRA to manage the transfer of membership and creditable service for Allegany County detention center officers into the state-administered CORS.

The OAG serves as the chief legal representative for the state and provides counsel to the State Retirement Agency. They would be responsible for the legal interpretation and implementation of the bill's specific provisions regarding the transfer of service credits and the exemption from standard pension transfer laws (Title 37).

As the principal fiscal and personnel agency for Maryland, DBM oversees the state's employee resources and benefits. While the fiscal impact of this bill is localized to Allegany County, the department maintains a general interest in the policy changes affecting the state-run pension systems and personnel classifications within CORS and EPS.

Synopsis: Designating the Freedom Flag, designed and created by Richard Nicholas Melito of Richmond, Virginia, to memorialize the victims of the events of September 11, 2001, as the State symbol of remembrance for the attacks of September 11.
Title: State Designations - Symbol of Remembrance for September 11 - Freedom Flag
Status: In the House - Hearing 3/17 at 1:00 p.m.

BroadSubjects.Name: State Government - Agencies, Offices, and Officials

bill_summary: This bill designates the Freedom Flag, which was designed and created by Richard Nicholas Melito of Richmond, Virginia, as the official Maryland State symbol of remembrance for the terrorist attacks of September 11, 2001.
stakeholders: Maryland citizens and victims and families affected by the September 11 terrorist attacks
fiscal_impact_summary: Specific dollar estimates are unavailable as a formal Fiscal Note was not included in the provided text; however, the designation of a State symbol typically does not have a significant fiscal impact on state or local government revenues or expenditures.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Secretary of State is the principal custodian of the state's official records and handles the processing of laws and commissions, including the documentation of official state symbols.

The Maryland State Archives maintains the Maryland Manual On-Line and is responsible for the preservation of state historical records. The agency will need to update state symbol records and history to include the Freedom Flag.
As the head of the executive branch, the Governor's Office oversees policy initiatives and the administration of state laws, including the formal adoption and use of new state designations.

The State House Trust oversees the management and use of the public areas of the State House and surrounding grounds, and would be involved if the new symbol of remembrance is displayed at the historic site.

The Department of General Services manages state-owned facilities and procurement. It would handle the logistical aspects if the state decides to procure or physically display the newly designated flag at state office buildings.

Synopsis: Altering the definition of "solar permitting software" for purposes of provisions regarding permitting and inspections of residential solar energy systems; altering from August 1, 2025, to August 1, 2027, the date by which certain counties and municipalities must implement certain solar permitting software; requiring, on or before August 1, 2027, certain counties and municipalities to authorize remote inspections of certain residential solar energy systems; etc.
Title: Residential Solar Energy Systems - Local Inspections and Permitting
Status: In the House - Hearing 3/03 at 1:00 p.m.

NarrowSubjects.Name: Codes -see also- Annotated Code of Md; Building Codes
Counties -see also- Chartered Counties; Code Counties; etc.

Fees -see also- Attys' Fees; Devt Fees & Taxes
Health -see also- COVID19; EnvHlth; MedCon; etc.

bill_summary: This bill mandates that all Maryland counties and municipalities implement automated solar permitting software and authorize remote inspections for residential solar energy systems by August 1, 2027. It caps total solar permitting fees at $200 and remote inspection fees at $100, while prohibiting manual reviews of applications processed via the software. The bill also authorizes the Attorney General to seek judicial enforcement for noncompliance.
responsible_party: Maryland Energy Administration, the Maryland Office of the Attorney General, and Maryland local governments
stakeholders: Residential solar energy system installers, homeowners, and local government permitting and inspection departments
fiscal_impact_summary: Local government revenues are expected to decrease due to the imposition of a $200 cap on residential solar permitting fees and a $100 cap on remote inspections. Implementation of the required automated software may result in additional expenditures for counties and municipalities, though the Maryland Energy Administration may provide financial support if funds are available. A formal Fiscal Note was not provided with the text, so specific aggregate dollar estimates are unavailable.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill explicitly defines 'Administration' as the Maryland Energy Administration (MEA). MEA is responsible for determining if solar permitting software is maintained and has the authority to delay or suspend implementation requirements if state or federal funding is insufficient to support local jurisdictions.
The bill grants the Attorney General explicit authority to seek judicial enforcement against any county or municipality that fails to comply with the new solar permitting and inspection requirements.

The bill requires solar permitting software to automate plan reviews according to the Maryland Building Performance Standards and electrical codes, which are traditionally overseen and regulated by the Department of Labor.

The bill impacts local government permitting and land-use processes. The Department of Planning provides guidance to local governments on sustainable growth and land use, making the regulation of residential solar infrastructure relevant to their coordination with municipalities.

The implementation of the bill's requirements by local governments is contingent upon the availability of state or federal funds provided through the Maryland Energy Administration. DBM would oversee the allocation and execution of such state funds.

Synopsis: Increasing from 1 year to 3 years the statute of limitations for a civil suit to enforce certain local consumer protection codes for which equitable relief, a fine, or a penalty is provided.
Title: Statute of Limitations - Civil Suits to Enforce Local Consumer Protection Codes
Status: In the Senate - Third Reading Passed with Amendments (37-0)

NarrowSubjects.Name: Penalties and Sentences -see also- Death Penalty

bill_summary: This bill increases the statute of limitations from one year to three years for civil suits filed to enforce the Baltimore City Consumer Protection Code. The three-year window begins when Baltimore City authorities discovered or reasonably should have known of the violation.
stakeholders: Consumers and businesses in Baltimore City, and the Baltimore City government.
fiscal_impact_summary: The bill does not materially affect State finances. Local revenues for Baltimore City may increase from fines and penalties collected in civil enforcement cases that can now proceed under the extended three-year statute of limitations. Any increase in local expenditures for enforcement is expected to be offset by the additional revenue generated.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill extends the statute of limitations for civil suits filed under the Baltimore City Consumer Protection Code from one year to three years. The Administrative Office of the Courts is responsible for providing operational and legal support to the state's court system, where these civil actions are adjudicated.

The Office of the Attorney General enforces state consumer protection laws and provides legal counsel to state and local entities. Although the bill specifically targets the Baltimore City code, the agency monitors and advises on consumer protection enforcement and was consulted for the bill's fiscal note.
The Governor's Office oversees the executive branch and coordinates statewide policy initiatives. The Governor is also responsible for signing the bill into law once passed by the General Assembly.

Synopsis: Establishing the Maryland Commission on Women's Health Advancement to study the feasibility of establishing a State women's hospital in Southern Maryland and a statewide clinical network to advance women's health; requiring the Commission by January 1, 2027, to submit to the Governor and the General Assembly an initial action plan, including a timeline, milestones, and specific research objectives; etc.
