bill_summary: This bill expands the eligibility for the homestead property tax credit in Washington County to include an additional residence owned by a homeowner. Under current law, the credit is restricted to a homeowner's principal residence only.
responsible_party: Maryland State Department of Assessments and Taxation
stakeholders: Homeowners in Washington County who own more than one residential property.
fiscal_impact_summary: State Annuity Bond Fund revenues are estimated to decrease by approximately $39,500 annually beginning in fiscal 2027. Washington County property tax revenues are estimated to decrease by approximately $613,200 annually starting in fiscal 2027. These estimates are based on the assumption that 10% of residential properties not currently receiving the credit would qualify as an additional residence; the fiscal note indicates that if 25% of such properties qualified, the local revenue loss would exceed $1.5 million annually.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Property Tax Assessment Appeals Board is the independent agency responsible for hearing second-level administrative appeals regarding property tax assessments and credits. This bill directly expands the scope of property eligible for the Homestead Property Tax Credit in Washington County, which will likely lead to an increase in appeals regarding eligibility and valuation of 'additional residences.'

As the highest level of administrative review for tax disputes in Maryland, the Maryland Tax Court adjudicates cases involving real property assessments and tax credits. The creation of a new category of eligible properties for the homestead credit in Washington County will fall under its jurisdiction for final administrative appeals.

The State Treasurer's Office manages the state's funds, including the Annuity Bond Fund. The fiscal note indicates a direct decrease in revenues for the Annuity Bond Fund because of the expanded tax credit, impacting the state's long-term financial management and debt service funds.

As the state's chief financial officer and tax collector, the Comptroller oversees state revenues. The bill impacts state property tax revenues which are part of the broader fiscal oversight and reporting responsibilities of the Comptroller's office.

The bill contains specific provisions and definitions regarding 'agricultural ownership entities' and homesites on land receiving agricultural use assessments. The MDA is relevant as it oversees the economic viability of the agricultural community impacted by these tax changes.

DBM is responsible for estimating state revenues and long-term fiscal planning. The projected reduction in property tax revenue from the expansion of this credit must be accounted for in the state's fiscal forecasting and budget development.

The Rural Maryland Council advocates for the interests of Maryland's rural counties, including Washington County. This bill provides a specific financial benefit and tax relief for property owners in a rural jurisdiction within the Council's purview.

The OAG provides legal counsel to the General Assembly and the State Department of Assessments and Taxation (the implementing agency). They will be responsible for interpreting the new statutory language and defending the state's implementation of the expanded credit.

The Board of Public Works oversees state fiscal integrity and bond issuances. Since the bill reduces revenue to the Annuity Bond Fund (used to pay debt service on state bonds), the Board has a vested interest in the fiscal impact on the state's credit and capital project funding.

The Governor's Office oversees the executive branch agencies responsible for implementing the tax credit (primarily the State Department of Assessments and Taxation) and is responsible for the state's annual budget, which will be affected by the revenue decrease.

The Department of Planning promotes sustainable growth and manages land use policy. Property tax credits are a significant factor in residential development and land use patterns, which are core interests of the department's planning initiatives.

DHCD works to ensure residents have access to affordable housing. While this is a tax credit for existing properties, it relates to the broader goal of housing affordability and homeownership stability.

Synopsis: Allowing a credit against the State income tax for 25% of an investment made in qualified Maryland companies up to $1,000,000; providing that investments in companies engaging in certain emergent technology may qualify for the tax credit subject to certain requirements; providing that a qualified investor shall make an investment in a qualified Maryland company within a certain amount of time after the Department issues an initial tax credit certificate; etc.
Title: Income Tax – Angel Investor Tax Credit for Investments in Emergent Technology

bill_summary: This bill establishes the Angel Investor Tax Credit to incentivize investments in early-stage Maryland companies specializing in emergent technologies, specifically artificial intelligence, quantum computing, and cybersecurity. It creates the Angel Investor Tax Credit Reserve Fund and allows qualified investors to claim a state income tax credit equal to 25% of their investment, up to $1,000,000 per investment.
stakeholders: Individual and entity investors, early-stage technology companies in Maryland specializing in AI, quantum computing, or cybersecurity, and the Maryland Department of Commerce.
fiscal_impact_summary: The bill mandates that the Governor include an appropriation of at least $25,000,000 to the Angel Investor Tax Credit Reserve Fund in the annual budget bill. As tax credits are certified, the Comptroller transfers funds from the Reserve Fund to the General Fund to offset revenue losses. Administrative costs for the Department of Commerce are also paid from the Reserve Fund. Specific dollar estimates from a formal Fiscal Note are unavailable, but the bill text explicitly establishes this $25,000,000 annual spending mandate.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Department of Commerce is the primary agency responsible for administering the Angel Investor Tax Credit program, including reviewing and approving applications from both investors and companies, issuing tax credit certificates, and conducting outreach to stakeholders.

The Comptroller is responsible for processing the tax credits, receiving notifications of certificates, managing the transfer of funds from the Reserve Fund to the General Fund, and jointly adopting regulations with the Department of Commerce.
The Treasurer is mandated to manage, invest, and reinvest the money within the newly established Angel Investor Tax Credit Reserve Fund, ensuring that interest earnings accrue back to the Fund.
DBM is responsible for state budget development and revenue estimation. This bill requires a mandatory annual budget appropriation of at least $25 million for the tax credit reserve fund.
The bill requires the Governor to include a specific minimum appropriation in the annual budget bill and oversees the executive department (Commerce) tasked with the program's implementation.
The OAG provides legal counsel to the Department of Commerce and the Comptroller, particularly in the drafting and adoption of regulations required to implement and monitor the tax credit program.

As a major network of institutions of higher education, the University System of Maryland is a designated target for outreach by the Department of Commerce regarding the investment opportunities in emergent technologies.
Morgan State University is an institution of higher education explicitly identified as a target for outreach to connect emergent technology research and development with angel investors.
Saint Mary's College is an institution of higher education identified as a target for Department of Commerce outreach efforts related to the new tax credit program.
The Tax Court may be involved in adjudicating appeals from investors or companies regarding the revocation of tax credit certifications or disputes over recaptured credits.

Synopsis: Requiring provider agencies to pay at least $17 per hour to personal care aides and to provide a certain notice regarding the wage to personal care aides; and requiring provider agencies to provide personal care aides with a certain minimum amount of earned sick and safe leave.
Title: Maryland Medical Assistance Program - Provider Agencies - Wages and Leave for Personal Care Aides
Status: In the House - Hearing 3/03 at 1:00 p.m.

NarrowSubjects.Name: Salaries and Compensation -see also- Overtime; Reimb. Rates
Work, Labor, and Employment -see also- JobTrn; Leave; etc.

bill_summary: This bill requires provider agencies that receive reimbursement from the Maryland Medical Assistance Program (Medicaid) to pay personal care aides a minimum wage of $17 per hour and provide at least 24 hours of paid earned sick and safe leave annually. It also mandates that the Maryland Department of Health monitor compliance and report on the feasibility of increasing the minimum wage to $20 per hour and ensuring that 80% of Medicaid payments are directed toward aide compensation.
stakeholders: Personal care aides, provider agencies reimbursed by the Maryland Medical Assistance Program (excluding those under the Developmental Disabilities Administration), and the Maryland Department of Health.
fiscal_impact_summary: The bill mandates a $17 per hour minimum wage and paid sick leave for personal care aides, which will likely result in increased expenditures for the Maryland Medical Assistance Program. However, specific total dollar estimates are unavailable as a formal Fiscal Note was not included in the provided text.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill directly impacts the Maryland Department of Health (MDH) as it mandates new wage and leave requirements for provider agencies reimbursed by the Maryland Medical Assistance Program (Medicaid), which MDH administers. MDH is responsible for monitoring compliance, taking enforcement actions such as program suspension or termination, and submitting a report to the General Assembly regarding Medicaid payment allocations and future wage increases.

The bill establishes specific wage floors and sick and safe leave requirements for personal care aides, which are matters typically regulated by the Department of Labor. Furthermore, the bill explicitly amends the Labor and Employment Article to resolve potential conflicts between these new requirements and existing state sick and safe leave laws.

The requirement for provider agencies to pay a minimum wage of $17 per hour for Medicaid-reimbursable services will likely necessitate an increase in Medicaid provider reimbursement rates. As the principal fiscal agency, DBM will be responsible for managing the significant budgetary impact and fiscal planning required to fund these state-mandated wage increases.

The personal care services impacted by this bill (such as Community First Choice and Community Options) are essential for Maryland's older adults. The Department of Aging oversees long-term care advocacy and support for this population, and changes to the workforce and reimbursement structure for these services directly affect their mission and the quality of care for their constituents.

The bill affects the delivery of home- and community-based services that are vital to individuals with disabilities. As the agency responsible for coordinating services and policies for Marylanders with disabilities, the Department has a significant interest in the stability and compensation of the personal care aide workforce.

The Office of the Attorney General provides legal counsel to the Department of Health and the Department of Labor. They would be involved in interpreting the new statutory requirements and defending any enforcement actions taken by the state against non-compliant provider agencies.

The bill authorizes the Department of Health to take enforcement actions against provider agencies, including suspension or termination from the Medicaid program. Such actions are typically contested cases that would be adjudicated by Administrative Law Judges within the Office of Administrative Hearings.

Synopsis: Requiring the State Highway Administration to expand the scope of the Maryland Route 410 (East-West Highway) Pedestrian Safety Action Plan project to include the public rights-of-way along East-West Highway from the intersection of Maryland Route 500 (Queens Chapel Road) east to U.S. Route 1 (Baltimore Avenue).
Title: State Highway Administration - Maryland Route 410 (East-West Highway) Pedestrian Safety Action Plan - Expansion
Status: In the House - Hearing 2/26 at 1:00 p.m.
bill_summary: This bill requires the Maryland State Highway Administration to expand the scope of the Maryland Route 410 (East–West Highway) Pedestrian Safety Action Plan project. The expansion extends the project area to include the segment from MD 500 (Queens Chapel Road) to U.S. Route 1 (Baltimore Avenue) to address safety concerns and improve multimodal infrastructure.
stakeholders: Pedestrians, bicyclists, transit users, and motorists in Prince George's County, specifically those using the MD 410 corridor between MD 500 and U.S. Route 1.
fiscal_impact_summary: The bill will likely increase State Highway Administration expenditures to cover the costs of planning, design, and construction for the additional segment of the MD 410 corridor. However, a formal Fiscal Note with specific dollar estimates was not included in the provided text.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill explicitly mandates that the State Highway Administration expand the scope of the Maryland Route 410 Pedestrian Safety Action Plan to include a specific segment of the highway.

As the parent agency of the State Highway Administration, the Maryland Department of Transportation oversees the state's transportation network and initiated the original safety project mentioned in the bill.
The bill's preamble emphasizes the need for modern and accessible infrastructure to ensure equitable access for people with disabilities, a core focus area for this department.
Expanding the scope of a state highway project has fiscal implications for the state budget and project execution, which this department supervises.
The office oversees the executive branch and coordinates policy initiatives like the Vision Zero principles and pedestrian safety policies cited in the bill.
The agency provides the crash data and traffic safety enforcement that support the documented safety needs addressed by the Pedestrian Safety Action Plan.
The OAG provides legal counsel to the State Highway Administration and Department of Transportation regarding statutory mandates and the management of public rights-of-way.
The bill notes that the highway corridor connects educational institutions, making the safety improvements relevant to the center's mission of fostering safe environments for students.
The bill's focus on context-driven corridor improvements and connectivity between residential and commercial centers aligns with the department's role in sustainable growth and land use planning.

Synopsis: Prohibiting individuals who experienced a pregnancy loss from being subject to investigation, civil liability, or criminal prosecution except under certain circumstances; establishing a private right of action for a violation of a certain prohibition against investigations of pregnancy loss; providing that an incidence of pregnancy loss does not constitute probable cause to issue a certain search warrant, except under certain circumstances; etc.
Title: Public Health - Pregnancy Loss - Prohibited Actions (Pregnancy Outcome Protection Act)
Status: In the House - Hearing 3/05 at 1:00 p.m. (Judiciary)

bill_summary: The Pregnancy Outcome Protection Act prohibits the investigation, civil liability, or criminal prosecution of individuals for experiencing a pregnancy loss, including miscarriages, stillbirths, and self-managed abortions. It also protects healthcare providers from liability for supporting patients in these circumstances and restricts the disclosure of medical records related to pregnancy loss. Additionally, the bill establishes that pregnancy loss does not constitute probable cause for a search warrant and allows for a private right of action and criminal penalties against those who violate these protections.
stakeholders: Individuals who experience pregnancy loss, healthcare providers, doulas, and law enforcement agencies
fiscal_impact_summary: A formal Fiscal Note is not available. The bill establishes criminal fines for violations, including up to 5000 dollars for standard offenses and up to 100000 dollars for offenses involving deception, which could result in an indeterminate increase in state revenue. There may also be indeterminate costs for the state and local governments associated with law enforcement training and potential civil litigation.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Maryland Institute for Emergency Medical Services Systems
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill defines 'Provider' to include individuals authorized under the Health Occupations Article. MIEMSS regulates the emergency medical services network and personnel who provide health care and support during pregnancy-related emergencies, meaning its regulated providers are subject to the bill's prohibitions on reporting and investigation.

As a primary law enforcement agency, Maryland State Police is considered an 'investigating entity' under the bill. The legislation explicitly restricts law enforcement's ability to investigate pregnancy loss, obtain search warrants related to it, and subjects them to civil liability and criminal penalties for violations.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Maryland Office of the Public Defender
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill creates new misdemeanor offenses for individuals or entities that knowingly violate its provisions and maintains restrictions on criminal prosecutions. The Office of the Public Defender would be responsible for representing indigent defendants in these criminal or juvenile proceedings.

The OAG serves as the chief legal representative for the state and provides counsel to state agencies and the Governor. It would be responsible for advising investigating entities (such as DHS and DJS) on compliance with this act and representing the state in civil or criminal appeals related to pregnancy loss investigations.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Governor's Office of Crime Prevention and Policy
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: GOCPP is the primary coordinating body for public safety and criminal justice strategies. This bill significantly alters criminal justice policy and law enforcement protocols regarding pregnancy outcomes, affecting the office's policy development and public safety coordination.

The bill establishes a new private right of action for individuals subject to prohibited investigations and creates new misdemeanor penalties. This impacts the judicial system by introducing new civil and criminal case types and affecting search warrant procedures.

The bill adds new sections to the Health - General Article and regulates 'Providers,' which include health care professionals and various facilities (hospitals, clinics, crisis centers) regulated by MDH. MDH is responsible for setting health policy and overseeing the conduct of health care institutions and practitioners impacted by these new reporting and liability prohibitions.

The bill explicitly names the Social Services Administration and Child Protective Services within DHS as 'investigating entities.' It places specific legal prohibitions on their ability to investigate individuals for pregnancy loss, impacting their operational procedures in cases of potential neglect or abuse.

DJS is explicitly named as an 'investigating entity' in the bill. The legislation prohibits the department from subjecting individuals to investigation for pregnancy loss unless specific conditions are met, directly affecting its intake and investigative protocols for youth.

DBM is responsible for the state budget and personnel. As several state agencies (MDH, DHS, DJS, MSP) face operational changes and potential civil liability under this bill, DBM would be involved in overseeing the fiscal impact and resource allocation necessary for implementation.

The Governor's Office oversees the executive branch and coordinates major policy initiatives. This bill introduces a significant new policy framework (Pregnancy Outcome Protection Act) affecting multiple executive departments and law enforcement protocols.

Synopsis: Requiring the seller in a certain retail contract to provide notice of certain changes in mandatory fees and payments and other required disclosures; and altering certain fees a council of unit owners or a homeowners association or its agent may charge for providing certain disclosures.
Title: Condominiums and Homeowners Associations - Resale Contracts - Notice Requirements (Keeping Affordable Housing Affordable Act)
Status: In the Senate - Second Reading Passed

NarrowSubjects.Name: Fees -see also- Attys' Fees; Devt Fees & Taxes
Real Estate -see also- Agents and Brokers

bill_summary: The bill alters the disclosure and notice requirements for the resale of condominium units and lots in homeowners associations. It requires sellers to notify purchasers of changes in mandatory fees exceeding 10% or other material changes that occur after the initial disclosure. The bill reduces the maximum fee that a council of unit owners or a homeowners association can charge for disclosure certificates from $250 to $100, shortens the response time for providing these certificates to 10 days, and repeals the requirement for the Department of Housing and Community Development to adjust these fees for inflation.
responsible_party: Maryland Department of Housing and Community Development
stakeholders: Buyers and sellers of residential property in condominiums and homeowners associations, condominium councils of unit owners, homeowners associations, and property management companies.
fiscal_impact_summary: According to the fiscal note, the bill is not expected to materially affect State or local operations or finances. It establishes a $100 cap on fees for resale disclosure certificates (reduced from $250) and removes the Department of Housing and Community Development's responsibility to adjust these fees biennially for inflation.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill explicitly repeals the requirement for the Department of Housing and Community Development (DHCD) to biennially adjust the maximum fees for condominium and homeowners association resale certificates and to maintain a list of these fees on its website.

The Office of the Attorney General's Consumer Protection Division is involved in the oversight of real estate disclosure requirements and was a primary information source for the fiscal analysis of this bill.

The Maryland Department of Labor oversees the Real Estate Commission and professional licensing related to real property transactions; it was also consulted for the fiscal note regarding the impact on real estate practices.
The bill alters contract enforceability requirements for the resale of condominiums and homeowners association lots, which impacts the judicial process and litigation related to real estate disputes.

Synopsis: Requiring drug manufacturers and certain patient advocacy organizations to register with the Maryland Department of Health before conducting a disease awareness campaign in the State; and requiring that materials produced and distributed as part of a disease awareness campaign disclose the drug or device that the drug manufacturer is marketing for the medical condition that is the focus of the disease awareness campaign.
Title: Public Health - Drug Manufacturer-Funded Disease Awareness Campaigns - Registration and Required Disclosure

bill_summary: This bill requires drug manufacturers and patient advocacy organizations that receive funding from such manufacturers to register with the Maryland Department of Health before conducting disease awareness campaigns. It mandates disclosure of any related drugs or devices being developed or marketed and requires campaign materials to include a disclosure statement if a specific product is being marketed.
stakeholders: Drug manufacturers, patient advocacy organizations, and the general public.
fiscal_impact_summary: The state fiscal impact is indeterminate because sufficient information was not available for the fiscal note at the time of publication. There is no local fiscal impact, and the impact on small businesses is expected to be minimal.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill explicitly designates the Maryland Department of Health as the primary agency responsible for registering drug manufacturers and patient advocacy organizations, receiving required disclosures about medical conditions and products, and adopting regulations to implement the new disease awareness campaign oversight.

The Office of the Attorney General serves as legal counsel to the Department of Health for regulation development. Additionally, the office's Consumer Protection Division may be involved in enforcing the disclosure requirements for public-facing campaign materials.
As the principal fiscal and personnel agency, DBM will be involved in evaluating and managing the budgetary and staffing needs for the Department of Health to administer a new registration program.

The Office of Administrative Hearings would be responsible for adjudicating any contested cases or appeals resulting from the Department of Health's enforcement of registration requirements or penalties associated with non-compliance.

Synopsis: Prohibiting sellers of certain pharmaceutical drugs and devices from giving or offering to give to health care professionals gifts in a calendar year that have a total combined retail value of more than $50.
Title: Pharmaceutical Drugs and Devices - Gifts to Health Care Professionals - Prohibition
Status: In the House - Hearing 3/12 at 1:00 p.m.

NarrowSubjects.Name: Crimes and Punishments -see also- Penalties and Sentnc; etc.
Drugs -see also- Cannabis; ControlDangSubst; Pharm; etc.
Penalties and Sentences -see also- Death Penalty

bill_summary: This bill prohibits sellers of pharmaceutical drugs and devices from offering or giving gifts to healthcare professionals that exceed a total retail value of $50 within a single calendar year. The definition of gifts includes payments, food, entertainment, and travel, but excludes peer-reviewed medical literature. Individuals who violate this prohibition are guilty of a misdemeanor and may face fines up to $5,000 or imprisonment for up to six months.
stakeholders: Pharmaceutical drug and device sellers, licensed or certified healthcare professionals authorized to prescribe or recommend medical products, and health occupation regulatory boards.
fiscal_impact_summary: The Maryland Department of Health and various health occupations boards can manage the bill's requirements using existing budgeted resources. While the bill establishes a misdemeanor penalty with fines up to $5,000, these provisions are not expected to significantly impact state revenue. There is no projected impact on local government finances, and the impact on small businesses is expected to be minimal.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill amends the Health - General Article and relates to the regulation of pharmaceutical drugs and devices, as well as health care professionals licensed under the Health Occupations Article, both of which fall under the primary regulatory authority of the Maryland Department of Health.

As a division of MDH that regulates practitioners, researchers, and medical establishments regarding controlled substances, this agency is directly involved in the oversight of the professionals and types of products targeted by the gift prohibition.

The OAG serves as the chief legal officer for state agencies, including the Department of Health and its health occupation boards, and would be responsible for providing legal counsel on the enforcement and interpretation of this new prohibition.
The bill creates a new misdemeanor offense for violating the gift prohibition, which will be adjudicated within the state's court system overseen by the Administrative Office of the Courts.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Maryland Office of the Public Defender
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: As the agency responsible for providing legal representation to indigent defendants, the OPD would represent individuals charged with the new misdemeanor established by this bill.
The Maryland State Police is responsible for enforcing criminal laws across the state and could be involved in investigating violations of the new criminal provision regarding prohibited gifts.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Department of Public Safety and Correctional Services
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill establishes a penalty of up to six months of imprisonment for violations, which may impact the state's correctional or pretrial detention facilities managed by DPSCS.
The Governor's Office oversees the executive branch and coordinates policy initiatives, including health policy and the implementation of new laws within the Executive Department.

Synopsis: Authorizing a pharmacist to order certain vaccinations for individuals who are at least 3 years old without having to also administer the vaccination.
Title: Health Occupations - Pharmacists - Vaccination Orders
Status: Approved by the Governor - Chapter 270

bill_summary: This bill authorizes a pharmacist to order vaccinations for individuals who are at least three years old without requiring the pharmacist to also administer the vaccine. The authorization covers influenza, COVID-19, and public health emergency vaccines, as well as other FDA-approved or CDC-recommended vaccines for older age groups. Pharmacists must meet specific training, certification, and reporting requirements, including informing the caregivers of child patients about the importance of well-child visits and referring them to pediatric primary care providers.
responsible_party: Maryland Department of Health and the State Board of Pharmacy
stakeholders: Pharmacists, adult caregivers, child patients (age 3 and older), and adult patients.
fiscal_impact_summary: According to the Fiscal Note, the bill has no State or local fiscal impact, as the changes are technical in nature and do not directly affect governmental finances. Small business impact is considered minimal.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Department of Health is the primary agency responsible for the regulations mentioned in the bill. It oversees the State Board of Pharmacy, which regulates the pharmacists granted new authority by this bill, and manages the ImmuNet Program, where all vaccination orders must be reported. Additionally, the department must consult with the boards of Physicians and Nursing to establish criteria for vaccination protocols.

The OAG provides legal counsel to the Department of Health and the various health occupation boards involved in the bill. They would be responsible for reviewing the new regulations and protocols developed to allow pharmacists to order vaccinations without administering them.

The Governor's Office is responsible for the final approval and signing of the bill into law. As the head of the executive branch, the Governor also oversees the Department of Health and its boards in the implementation of the new policy.

The bill mandates that pharmacists report 'all vaccinations administered OR ORDERED' to the ImmuNet Program. As the agency responsible for the state's information technology strategy and data governance, DoIT manages the underlying infrastructure and security for such statewide health databases.

Synopsis: Requiring certain nonprofit hospitals to provide a certain value of community benefits each year; requiring the Health Services Cost Review Commission to report on the compliance of nonprofit hospitals with the community benefits requirement to the Attorney General and the Comptroller; authorizing the Comptroller to revoke the tax-exempt status of a nonprofit hospital under certain circumstances; and altering the requirements of a community benefit report.
Title: Nonprofit Hospitals - Community Benefits
Status: In the House - Hearing 3/04 at 1:00 p.m.

NarrowSubjects.Name: Health -see also- COVID19; EnvHlth; MedCon; etc.
Penalties and Sentences -see also- Death Penalty
Public Benefits -see also- Housing; MedAsst;  SupplNutrAsstP

bill_summary: This bill requires Maryland nonprofit hospitals (excluding those in counties with fewer than 50,000 residents) to provide community benefits equal to either 100% of their tax-exempt benefits or at least 5% of their net patient revenue if charity care is at least 4% of net patient revenue. It mandates annual reporting to the Health Services Cost Review Commission (HSCRC), which must report noncompliance to the Attorney General and the Comptroller. The Comptroller is authorized to revoke a hospital's tax-exempt status for failure to comply. The bill also establishes daily civil monetary penalties for hospitals that fail to submit their annual community benefit reports on time.
responsible_party: Health Services Cost Review Commission (HSCRC), Maryland Comptroller, and the Maryland Attorney General
stakeholders: Maryland nonprofit hospitals, hospital patients, the Health Services Cost Review Commission, and Maryland taxpayers
fiscal_impact_summary: Specific dollar estimates from a formal Fiscal Note are unavailable. However, the bill text identifies potential financial impacts including an indeterminate increase in state revenue through civil monetary penalties ($600 to $11,000 per day depending on hospital size) and the potential revocation of tax-exempt status for noncompliant hospitals. Nonprofit hospitals may also face increased expenditures to meet the mandated community benefit spending thresholds.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The HSCRC is the primary implementing agency for this bill. It is responsible for establishing a workgroup, adopting regulations, collecting community benefit reports from hospitals, evaluating compliance, reporting non-compliance to the Comptroller and Attorney General, and levying civil monetary penalties.

The bill explicitly requires the Comptroller to receive reports from the HSCRC, verify hospital non-compliance with community benefit standards, and revoke or reinstate the tax-exempt status of nonprofit hospitals based on those findings.

The bill requires the HSCRC to submit reports identifying non-compliant hospitals to the Attorney General. Additionally, the OAG provides legal counsel to state agencies like the HSCRC and Comptroller in enforcing regulations and defending against potential litigation.

The HSCRC is an independent regulatory agency located within the Maryland Department of Health. The bill's requirements directly impact hospital regulation and the administration of the Maryland Medical Assistance Program (Medicaid), which is cited in the bill's definition of indigent care.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Executive Commissions, Committees, Task Forces, and Advisory Boards
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill mandates the establishment of the Community Benefit Reporting Workgroup, a body of stakeholders tasked with providing knowledge and recommendations regarding hospital spending and reporting standards.

As the highest level of administrative review for tax-related disputes, the Maryland Tax Court would likely adjudicate appeals from hospitals following the Comptroller's decision to revoke their tax-exempt status.
The OAH would likely handle contested cases and appeals regarding civil monetary penalties imposed by the HSCRC for failure to file required community benefit reports.

bill_summary: This bill requires the Department of Housing and Community Development (DHCD) to conduct a study and make recommendations regarding residential-in-commercial-zone (RICZ) laws, which require local jurisdictions to allow multifamily residential or mixed-use developments in certain commercially zoned areas. The study must compare Maryland's potential laws with those in other states and assess impacts on infrastructure, housing production, and local economic goals.
responsible_party: Department of Housing and Community Development (DHCD)
stakeholders: Local jurisdictions, multifamily and mixed-use developers, and residents of urban, suburban, and rural communities.
fiscal_impact_summary: According to the Fiscal Note, State general fund expenditures increase by $75,000 in fiscal 2027 for DHCD to hire contractual services to assist in completing the study within the required timeframe. There is no direct impact on local government finances, and there is no fiscal impact in fiscal 2026.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill explicitly tasks the Department of Housing and Community Development with conducting the study of 'residential-in-commercial-zone' laws, making recommendations, and reporting the findings to the Governor and General Assembly.

As the state's lead agency for land use planning and sustainable growth, the Department of Planning is a primary stakeholder in zoning legislation and is listed as a key information source for this study.
The study must assess the impact of RICZ laws on local economic development goals, which is central to the mission of the Department of Commerce.
The study is required to assess impacts on local infrastructure and provide recommendations on off-street parking requirements, which fall within the technical and policy scope of MDOT.
The Governor's Office coordinates state policy and is the primary recipient of the study's findings and recommendations.
The bill has a notable fiscal impact of $75,000 in general fund expenditures for contractual services, which falls under DBM's oversight of the state budget.
This multi-agency initiative's focus on community revitalization and sustainable land use aligns with the bill's 'Bring Back Main Street' theme and the assessment of mixed-use development.
The OAG would likely provide legal counsel and review regarding the comparison of RICZ laws enacted in other states as required by the study.
The bill requires the study to provide recommendations on special considerations for rural areas, which is the primary focus of this council.

Synopsis: Clarifying the Consumer Price Index used to determine the cost-of-living adjustments for retirees of the State Retirement and Pension System in certain years.
Title: State Retirement and Pension System – Cost–of–Living Adjustments – Clarification
Status: Approved by the Governor - Chapter 56

NarrowSubjects.Name: Health -see also- COVID19; EnvHlth; MedCon; etc.

bill_summary: This emergency bill establishes a methodology for determining the Consumer Price Index (CPI) value for October 2025, which was not published by the federal government due to a shutdown. For the purposes of calculating retiree cost-of-living adjustments (COLAs) effective July 1, 2026, and July 1, 2027, the bill mandates that the October 2025 CPI value be the average of the September 2025 and November 2025 CPI values.
responsible_party: Board of Trustees for the State Retirement and Pension System
stakeholders: Retirees of the Maryland State Retirement and Pension System and participating local government units.
fiscal_impact_summary: The fiscal note indicates the bill likely has no discernible effect on State or local pension liabilities or contribution rates. Although the bill's methodology results in a slightly higher calculated COLA rate (0.067 percentage points) than one interpretation of current law, the impact is mitigated by statutory COLA caps and the fact that any change in liabilities is amortized over 10 to 15 years. No effect on revenues is expected.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Maryland State Retirement Agency is the primary agency responsible for managing the State Retirement and Pension System (SRPS) and calculating the cost-of-living adjustments (COLAs) for retirees. This bill directly dictates the methodology they must use to address a missing CPI data point for their calculations.

As the principal fiscal and personnel agency, DBM is responsible for the state's long-term fiscal planning and the state budget, which includes funding for pension contribution rates. Any change in COLA calculations affects pension liabilities and the overall state budget.

The Comptroller is the state's chief financial officer responsible for paying state bills and employees, including distributing pension benefits to retirees that will be adjusted based on the bill's methodology.

The State Treasurer manages state funds and serves on the Board of Public Works, which oversees fiscal integrity. The SRPS is a significant component of the state's financial management and long-term liabilities.

The Board of Public Works oversees and approves significant state expenditures and protects the state's fiscal integrity. Pension liabilities are a major factor in the state's long-term financial health.

The Office of Legislative Audits conducts fiscal compliance audits of executive branch agencies, including the State Retirement Agency, and will be responsible for ensuring the COLA calculations comply with this new statutory methodology.
Maryland's public school teachers are members of the Teachers' Retirement and Pension Systems, one of the primary groups whose retirement benefits are adjusted by the COLAs addressed in this bill.
Members of the Maryland State Police are part of the State Police Retirement System, which receives COLAs that will be calculated using the method established by this bill.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Department of Public Safety and Correctional Services
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The department's correctional officers are members of the Correctional Officers' Retirement System, which is subject to the COLA calculations impacted by this legislation.
The Maryland Judicial Branch personnel and judges are members of the retirement systems whose future cost-of-living adjustments are clarified by this bill.
MDOT employees are participants in the state retirement systems affected by these COLA calculation adjustments.

The Governor's Office oversees the executive branch and proposes the annual state budget, which must account for any changes in pension liabilities and state contribution rates resulting from benefit adjustments.

stakeholders: Local governments (Participating Governmental Units), county governments, and eligible local employees including law enforcement officers, firefighters, and correctional officers.

bill_summary: This bill alters the membership of the Baltimore County Board of Education. Starting with the 2030 general election, the board's composition will change from seven elected and four appointed members to nine elected members and two appointed members. Each of the nine elected members will represent one of the county's nine councilmanic districts, and the Governor will appoint two members at large.
stakeholders: Voters and residents of Baltimore County, the Baltimore County Board of Education, and the Governor of Maryland.
fiscal_impact_summary: According to the Fiscal Note, there is no state fiscal impact, and the bill is not expected to have a material fiscal impact on Baltimore County Public Schools.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill increases the number of elected members from seven to nine based on new councilmanic districts, requiring the State Board of Elections to adjust district mapping, candidate certification, and ballot administration for Baltimore County for the 2030 election cycle.

The Office of Appointments assists the Governor in recruiting and vetting candidates for state boards; it will manage the process for the two at-large members appointed by the Governor to the Baltimore County Board of Education.
The Governor is the appointing authority for the at-large members of the Baltimore County Board of Education and oversees the implementation of changes to executive branch-related appointments.
As the oversight body for Maryland's public education system, the Department of Education has a regulatory interest in the governance and membership structure of local boards of education.

The Office of the Attorney General provides legal counsel to the Governor and state agencies regarding the legal framework and implementation of statutory changes to public boards.

bill_summary: This bill increases the minimum population required to incorporate a new municipality from 300 to 600 residents. It requires an organizing committee to provide comprehensive reports to the county government regarding the fiscal effects, expected services, and potential adverse economic impacts of incorporation. If a referendum request is signed by at least 40% of the registered voters in the area proposed for incorporation, the county commissioners or council must approve the request and schedule a vote for the next general election.
responsible_party: County Commissioners, County Councils, Municipal Organizing Committees, and the Office of the Attorney General
stakeholders: Residents and registered voters in unincorporated areas, county governments, and organizing committees seeking municipal incorporation.
fiscal_impact_summary: Specific dollar estimates are unavailable because a formal Fiscal Note was not provided with the text. However, the bill creates administrative impacts for counties, which must verify petitions, host reports on their websites, and potentially conduct mandatory referendums. The bill also requires organizing committees to conduct fiscal analyses comparing projected expenditures to local income tax revenues.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill explicitly mandates the Office of the Attorney General to create a standard petition form for use by organizing communities seeking municipal incorporation and to provide this form to county boards of elections.

The bill involves county boards of elections in the distribution of incorporation petition forms and requires that mandatory referendums for municipal incorporation be held during the next general election, which is overseen by the State Board of Elections.

As the agency responsible for providing technical assistance and policy guidance to local governments regarding land use and sustainable growth, the Department of Planning is relevant to the processes of forming new municipal boundaries and governance structures.

The bill requires organizing committees to report on projected local income tax revenue as part of the incorporation process; the Comptroller is responsible for the collection and distribution of these tax revenues to local jurisdictions.

The Maryland State Archives is the central depository for government records, including municipal charters; successful incorporations under this bill would result in new legislative records for the Archives to preserve and make accessible.

Synopsis: Establishing a Task Force to Modernize County and Municipal Revenue Structures to study and evaluate the revenue structure of the county and municipal governments within the State; and requiring the Task Force to submit a report of its findings and recommendations to the Governor and certain committees of the General Assembly by December 1, 2026.

bill_summary: This bill establishes the Task Force to Modernize County and Municipal Revenue Structures to evaluate the current revenue-raising capabilities of Maryland's local governments, explore untapped revenue sources, and analyze the impact of potential new revenue streams on the cost of living.
stakeholders: County and municipal governments, Maryland taxpayers, and the Department of Legislative Services
fiscal_impact_summary: The bill is expected to have a minimal state fiscal impact. The Department of Legislative Services (DLS) is responsible for staffing the task force and can likely do so using existing budgeted resources. While significant administrative or research demands could lead to additional general fund expenditures for contractual staff, such costs are not currently estimated. Reimbursements for task force members are assumed to be minimal and absorbable within existing resources. There is no local fiscal impact.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Comptroller or their designee is a named member of the Task Force. As the state's chief financial officer and principal tax collector, the agency is central to any study of revenue structures and tax laws.
The Secretary of Budget and Management or their designee is a named member of the Task Force. DBM is the principal fiscal agency responsible for state budget and revenue estimation.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Executive Commissions, Committees, Task Forces, and Advisory Boards
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill creates a new Task Force to Modernize County and Municipal Revenue Structures, which falls under this collective entity of advisory bodies.
The Task Force is required to submit a report of its findings and recommendations to the Governor, and it involves the participation of executive branch department heads.

Local revenue structures frequently involve development impact fees, excise taxes, and land-use assessments, which are integral to the Department of Planning's mission to promote sustainable growth and infrastructure development.

Property tax is the largest locally generated revenue source for counties and municipalities. The Task Force's evaluation of these revenue structures directly relates to the board's role in reviewing property tax assessment disputes.
Changes to local revenue structures can impact the state's economic competitiveness and business environment, which the Department of Commerce is tasked with monitoring.
The OAG provides legal counsel to the state agencies and officials serving on the Task Force and would advise on the legal authority of local governments to implement new revenue sources.
As the highest level of administrative review for tax-related disputes, the Tax Court is impacted by policy recommendations that could change the structure or implementation of local taxes.
The Council advocates for the interests of Maryland's 18 rural counties, which face unique challenges in their revenue structures and tax bases that the Task Force will evaluate.

The Task Force is specifically required to analyze the impact of revenue sources on the overall affordability of goods and services and the cost of living, which aligns with the Innovation Team's focus on economic mobility.
The Task Force's goal is to modernize and evaluate the efficiency of government revenue structures, aligning with GOPI's mandate to enhance the efficiency and accountability of government operations.

bill_summary: This bill prohibits the Office of the Chief Medical Examiner from using the hydrostatic lung test, also known as a lung float test, during perinatal autopsies for a period of two years. Additionally, it requires the Maryland Department of Health to conduct a study and report to the General Assembly by December 1, 2027, regarding the efficacy and necessity of the test as an autopsy tool.
responsible_party: Maryland Department of Health and the Office of the Chief Medical Examiner
stakeholders: Parents and legal representatives of deceased infants, medical examiners, and authorized pathologists.
fiscal_impact_summary: According to the Fiscal Note, Maryland Department of Health general fund expenditures will increase by $35,700 in FY 2027 and $18,000 in FY 2028. These costs are for hiring a part-time contractual health policy analyst to complete the mandated report on the lung float test's efficacy. The bill has no impact on state revenues or local government finances.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill primarily affects the Office of the Chief Medical Examiner, which is a unit within the Department of Health. Furthermore, the Secretary of Health is responsible for reviewing autopsy findings and referring appeals to the Office of Administrative Hearings. The Department is also mandated to lead a study and submit a report on the efficacy of the lung float test, resulting in a direct fiscal impact of $53,700 over two fiscal years.

The bill requires the Maryland Department of Health to consult with the Office of the Attorney General on the mandated report. Additionally, the Attorney General's Office would be responsible for representing the Chief Medical Examiner and other state pathologists in any civil actions authorized by the bill for violations of the lung float test ban.

The bill updates provisions in the Health - General Article that require the Secretary of Health to refer appeals concerning medical examiner findings and conclusions on cause and manner of death to the Office of Administrative Hearings.

The bill authorizes parents, guardians, or legal representatives to bring civil actions for violations of the lung float test ban and allows for the appeal of administrative decisions to circuit courts of competent jurisdiction, impacting court caseloads and judicial administration.

The bill modifies the Public Safety Article to require law enforcement agencies to reopen or reinvestigate death investigations if a medical examiner's findings are amended to undetermined or homicide, directly impacting the operations of the State's primary law enforcement agency.

As the principal fiscal and personnel agency, the Department of Budget and Management will oversee the allocation of general funds and the creation of the part-time contractual health policy analyst position required by the Maryland Department of Health to fulfill the bill's reporting mandate.

bill_summary: This bill modifies the definition of adjusted actual income used in the Maryland child support guidelines. responsible_party: Maryland Judiciary and the Department of Human Services
stakeholders: Parents with child support obligations and their children living in the household.
fiscal_impact_summary: According to the fiscal note, this bill does not materially affect State or local government operations or finances.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Administrative Office of the Courts provides operational and legal support to the judicial branch, where judges and magistrates apply the state's child support guidelines to establish and modify awards.

The Department of Human Services is the primary agency responsible for child support services in Maryland, and its local departments must utilize these guidelines for administrative calculations and enforcement actions.
This office leads efforts to reduce child poverty and improve family well-being, goals that are directly influenced by the economic support levels established through child support guidelines.

The Innovation Team is charged with piloting initiatives to reduce child poverty and enhance economic mobility, making the technical adjustment of child support calculations relevant to their policy focus.

The Office of the Attorney General provides legal counsel to the Department of Human Services and its Child Support Enforcement Administration regarding the interpretation and enforcement of family law.
The Governor's Office coordinates executive policy initiatives and oversees the agencies responsible for the administration of family law and child support services.

The Administrative Office of the Courts provides operational and technological support for the judicial branch. This bill directly modifies access and confidentiality rules for juvenile court records managed by the court system.

The OAG provides legal counsel to state agencies regarding the implementation of state laws. This bill involves complex privacy, confidentiality, and liability issues related to juvenile records that would require legal interpretation and guidance.

responsible_party: Maryland Department of Public Safety and Correctional Services
stakeholders: Healthcare facility staff and patients, religious congregations, law enforcement, and the Maryland judicial system.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The judicial branch, supported by the Administrative Office of the Courts, is responsible for adjudicating the new felony charges created by this bill and overseeing the sentencing phase for violations occurring in medical facilities or places of worship.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Department of Public Safety and Correctional Services
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill creates a new felony offense with a potential 10-year prison sentence that may be served consecutively, directly impacting the correctional population and facility management overseen by this department.

As the head of the executive branch, the Governor's Office oversees the coordination of public safety policy and the state agencies responsible for enforcing the provisions of the Sacred Places Safety Act.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Governor's Office of Crime Prevention and Policy
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: This office is the state's primary coordinating body for criminal justice strategies and public safety policy, making it a key stakeholder in the implementation of new penalties for crimes of violence in sensitive locations.

bill_summary: This bill grants the Public Service Commission (PSC) greater administrative autonomy by establishing it as an essential government function and requiring it to create an independent personnel management system separate from the State Personnel Management System. It exempts the PSC from most State procurement laws and all State and local taxation, expands the duties of the Executive Secretary, and requires annual independent audits of the commission's financial accounts.
stakeholders: Employees of the Public Service Commission, regulated public utility companies, and the Maryland Department of Budget and Management.
fiscal_impact_summary: According to the Fiscal Note, State special fund expenditures increase by a net of $100,600 in FY 2027. This figure accounts for the addition of three human resources positions at the PSC ($325,892 as introduced in the FY 2027 budget) to manage the new independent personnel system, offset by $192,810 in savings from the commission no longer utilizing the Department of Budget and Management's (DBM) shared services. Consequently, DBM reimbursable revenues and expenditures decrease by $192,810 annually starting in FY 2027. The bill also exempts the PSC from State and local taxation and provides procurement flexibility, which may impact operational efficiency.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: As the primary subject of the bill, the Commission is granted significant administrative flexibility, including the establishment of an independent personnel management system and exemption from most state procurement laws.

The bill removes Commission employees from the State Personnel Management System (SPMS) overseen by DBM and transitions the Commission's budget process to informational status only, resulting in a loss of reimbursable revenue and oversight.

The bill exempts the Commission from most state procurement laws; however, exempt agencies typically must still have their procurement policies and procedures approved by the BPW to ensure fiscal integrity.
The bill removes DGS oversight of the Commission's procurements, which currently applies once certain thresholds are met, and exempts the Commission from central procurement authority.
The bill explicitly states that the Commission is subject to audit and examination of its accounts and transactions by the OLA at any time.

The bill mandates that the Commission collaborate with the Office of Security Management and submit cybersecurity reports to the State Chief Information Security Officer, both of which are within DoIT.

The bill exempts the Commission from state and local taxation, which falls under the Comptroller's jurisdiction as the state's principal tax collector, and the Comptroller also serves on the Board of Public Works.

The Commission is required to establish its own personnel management system, which may affect collective bargaining and grievance procedures for its employees, who remain under PERB's general jurisdiction for state workers.
The bill defines the Commission's authority as an essential government function and clarifies its status as an independent unit within the Executive Department.

The OAG provides legal counsel to all state agencies and would likely advise the Commission and DBM on the legal transition to an independent personnel and procurement system.

The bill references statutory requirements for record destruction and the role of the Executive Secretary in keeping Commission records, which falls under the Archives' oversight of government records of permanent value.

stakeholders: Heirs and legatees of deceased homeowners, particularly those who are low-income, elderly, or disabled; legal services organizations; and Maryland county governments.
fiscal_impact_summary: Beginning in FY 2028, the bill mandates an annual state general fund expenditure of $250,000 and a collective local government payment of $500,000 to the Legacy Protection Fund, resulting in $750,000 in annual special fund revenues and expenditures. Expanding eligibility for the homeowners' and homestead property tax credits is expected to cause an indeterminate, though likely limited, decrease in state and local property tax revenues starting in FY 2027.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Governor's Office oversees the executive branch, including the department implementing the program (SDAT). The Governor is responsible for proposing the annual budget, which must now include a $250,000 mandated appropriation for the Legacy Protection Fund.

The Comptroller is responsible for accounting for the Legacy Protection Fund and managing the accrual of interest on State money, which is specifically altered by this bill for fiscal years 2024 through 2028.

The Treasurer is responsible for holding, investing, and allocating net interest for the newly created Legacy Protection Fund, and manages the state's debt service which is impacted by the reduction in property tax revenues for the Annuity Bond Fund.
The OAG provides legal counsel to state agencies, including the State Tax Sale Ombudsman and SDAT, regarding the implementation of the new Legacy Protection Program and the processing of grants.

The bill directs the Ombudsman to establish grant eligibility criteria that prioritizes elderly heirs, which aligns with the Department of Aging's mission to protect the rights and quality of life for older adults.
DBM is the principal fiscal agency responsible for budget development. This bill creates a mandated appropriation and has a notable fiscal impact on general fund expenditures and revenue accounting.
The bill directs the Ombudsman to establish grant eligibility criteria that prioritizes disabled heirs, aligning with the department's role in improving services for residents with disabilities.

The bill's purpose is to prevent tax sales and allow heirs to remain in their homes, directly supporting the department's mission of ensuring access to secure housing and providing homeless solutions.
The Legacy Protection Program assists residents in economic need to prevent the loss of their homes, which is a core focus of the social services provided by DHS.
The bill establishes a new grant program for legal services organizations and individual heirs. The GGO assists state agencies in managing such funding and ensuring compliance.

The bill requires the creation of guides for probating estates, a process handled by the judicial branch. The AOC provides operational and legal support to the state's courts during these proceedings.
The Board of Public Works oversees significant state expenditures and contracts; the bill requires the Ombudsman to contract with a vendor for an installment payment program.
The bill addresses the Governor's priorities of reducing child poverty and enhancing economic mobility by protecting intergenerational wealth and family housing.
The Tax Court is the highest level of administrative review for disputes regarding property tax assessments and credits, which are substantively altered by this bill for heirs.

PTAAB hears appeals regarding property tax assessments and credits. The bill's expansion of homeowners' and homestead tax credit eligibility to heirs will directly impact the cases heard by these local boards.
The bill explicitly requires the State Tax Sale Ombudsman to collaborate with the Registers of Wills to develop step-by-step guides for heirs to navigate probate and become record title holders.
The bill addresses property tax challenges that impact rural homeowners and heirs, aligning with the Council's mission to foster economic development and improve quality of life in rural counties.

bill_summary: This bill authorizes the Comptroller of Maryland to settle a State claim against a business entity that has permanently ceased operations regardless of how long the claim has been in arrears, effectively removing the two-year waiting period required for other types of settlements.
stakeholders: Business entities that have permanently ceased operations with outstanding State debt, the Comptroller's Office, and local jurisdictions receiving shared tax revenues.
fiscal_impact_summary: State tax revenues (general and special funds) are projected to increase by approximately $250,000 annually beginning in fiscal 2027. General fund expenditures for the Comptroller's Office will increase by $74,100 in fiscal 2027 for staff to process additional settlements, rising to $98,500 by fiscal 2031. Local income tax and highway user revenues may also see an indeterminate increase.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill grants the Comptroller direct authority to settle state claims in arrears for businesses that have permanently ceased operations. The fiscal note explicitly identifies a fiscal impact on the Comptroller's Office, including a potential increase in revenue and the need for a new revenue administrator position to handle the increased volume of settlement claims.

As the principal fiscal and personnel agency, DBM is affected by the bill's impact on state general fund revenues and the budgetary requirement for an additional personnel position within the executive branch to implement the bill's provisions.

The fiscal note indicates that settlements of corporate income tax claims will affect the Transportation Trust Fund (TTF) and expenditures for local highway user revenue grants, which are managed under the multi-modal transportation network overseen by MDOT.

The bill requires settlement sums to be paid into the State Treasury. As the chief financial agency responsible for receiving and depositing state funds, the Treasurer's Office is directly involved in the fiscal workflow established by this legislation.

The bill stipulates that the Comptroller must be satisfied that a claim cannot be collected through 'legal process' before settling. The OAG, as the chief legal officer, provides counsel to state agencies regarding the feasibility of legal collection and represents the state in related matters.

The Governor oversees the executive branch agencies authorized to settle these claims and is responsible for the overall fiscal planning and executive branch operations impacted by the bill's revenue and expenditure changes.

bill_summary: This bill authorizes pharmacists to order tests for and treat certain minor medical conditions, including influenza, strep throat, and COVID-19, under protocols established by the Maryland Board of Pharmacy. It also repeals the Nonoccupational Postexposure Prophylaxis (nPEP) Standing Order Program, instead authorizing the Maryland Department of Health to create statewide protocols for HIV prevention and treatment medications.
responsible_party: Maryland Department of Health and the State Board of Pharmacy
stakeholders: Pharmacists, pharmacy technicians, pharmacy students, and patients seeking treatment for minor conditions or HIV prevention services.
fiscal_impact_summary: State expenditures increase by $155,000 in FY 2027, comprising $42,100 in general funds for protocol development and $112,800 in special funds for Board of Pharmacy oversight and staffing. Special fund expenditures continue annually, reaching $146,700 by FY 2031, which may be offset by increased licensing fees. There is no local fiscal impact.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Maryland Department of Health is the primary implementing agency. The bill authorizes the Department to establish statewide protocols for HIV prevention and treatment, and the State Board of Pharmacy (an agency within MDH) to establish protocols for minor conditions. The fiscal note also identifies a direct increase in MDH expenditures for personnel to implement these protocols.

The OAG provides legal counsel to the Department of Health and the Board of Pharmacy. It will be responsible for reviewing the legality of the new statewide protocols and assisting in the drafting of regulations required by the bill.

The bill impacts health insurance coverage for drugs and services provided by pharmacists. The MIA regulates the insurance market and must ensure that carriers comply with state laws regarding coverage and the prohibition of prior authorization for certain treatments like HIV postexposure prophylaxis.

DBM is the state's principal fiscal and personnel agency. The bill has a notable fiscal impact requiring the addition of both general fund and special fund positions (contractual and part-time staff) at MDH and the Board of Pharmacy.

The MHCC is responsible for health system planning and improving access to care. This legislation directly impacts healthcare access by significantly expanding the clinical scope of practice for pharmacists across the state.

The Governor's Office oversees the executive branch and coordinates major policy initiatives. This bill represents a significant shift in public health policy and requires the Governor to propose the associated funding increases in the state budget.

bill_summary: This bill requires the Maryland Health Care Commission and the Maryland Medical Assistance Program to jointly study the impact of providing Medicaid reimbursement for room and board services at hospice houses. The study must analyze potential cost savings associated with hospice care, projected fiscal impacts, and clinical outcomes such as hospital readmission rates and emergency department utilization, with a final report due by December 1, 2026.
stakeholders: Maryland Medical Assistance Program enrollees, hospice house providers, and the Maryland Department of Health
fiscal_impact_summary: State Medicaid expenditures increase by up to $52,000 in FY 2027 only for contractual services required to complete the study. These costs are expected to be split equally between state general funds ($26,000) and federal funds ($26,000), with federal fund revenues increasing accordingly. The Maryland Health Care Commission can participate using existing resources. There is no local fiscal impact.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill directly impacts the Department of Health as it requires the Maryland Medical Assistance Program (Medicaid), which is administered by the department, to conduct a joint study and submit a formal report to the General Assembly regarding hospice reimbursement.

The Maryland Health Care Commission is explicitly named in the bill as one of the two primary agencies responsible for conducting the study and analyzing the impact of hospice room and board reimbursement.

The study focuses on hospice care utilization and end-of-life services, which are critical components of the long-term care advocacy and services provided to the older adult population overseen by this department.

The bill requires an analysis of avoided inpatient hospital stays and emergency department utilization costs, which directly relates to the commission's role in regulating hospital rates and containing healthcare cost growth.

The bill has a direct fiscal impact of approximately $52,000 for contractual services to prepare the study, requiring DBM's oversight of budget execution and long-term fiscal planning for the Medicaid program.

The OAG provides legal counsel to the Department of Health and the Maryland Health Care Commission, and may be involved in reviewing the regulatory changes or statutory impacts explored in the hospice reimbursement study.
As the head of the executive branch, the Governor's Office oversees the Department of Health and is responsible for proposing the state budget, which must accommodate the fiscal impact of this study.

The department is concerned with services provided in integrated settings for Marylanders with disabilities; end-of-life care policy changes for Medicaid enrollees are relevant to their advocacy and coordination mission.

bill_summary: This bill requires the Maryland Department of State Police to conduct a study and make recommendations regarding the employment, commissioning process, training, jurisdiction, and regulatory oversight of special police officers (SPOs). The department must consult with law enforcement associations, government agencies, and security training academies, and submit its findings and recommendations to the Governor and General Assembly by December 1, 2026.
stakeholders: Special police officers, local and county governments, private employers of special police officers, law enforcement associations, and security training academies.
fiscal_impact_summary: According to the fiscal note, the Department of State Police can implement the study and reporting requirements using existing budgeted resources. There is no anticipated effect on state revenues or local government finances.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill explicitly mandates the Department of State Police to conduct a comprehensive study on special police officers, document licensing requirements, and submit a final report of findings and recommendations.
The bill specifically requires the Department of State Police to consult with a representative of the Office of the Secretary of State as part of the mandated study on special police officers.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Department of Public Safety and Correctional Services
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The study involves training requirements for special police officers. Under current law, the Maryland Police Training and Standards Commission (MPTSC), which resides within DPSCS, is consulted regarding the approval of training courses for these officers.

The Department of State Police is required to submit the final report of findings and recommendations to the Governor. Additionally, under current law, the Governor is the official who appoints and deputizes individuals as special police officers.
The OAG serves as the primary legal representative for the Maryland State Police and may provide legal counsel regarding the regulatory oversight and jurisdiction analysis required by the study.

Public school systems are authorized under current law to apply for the appointment of special police officers to protect students and property. Changes to SPO requirements or jurisdiction could impact school staffing and safety protocols.
As an independent unit within MSDE focused on school safety, this agency is impacted by policies regarding special police officers who are often utilized for security in educational settings.
Colleges and universities are among the entities authorized to employ special police officers. The study's recommendations on training and jurisdiction may affect campus security operations.
As a public institution of higher education, it is authorized to employ special police officers for property protection and may be impacted by the results of the study.
As a public liberal arts college, it is among the entities that may utilize special police officers and thus has an interest in the study's findings regarding employment and operations.

As the principal fiscal and personnel agency, DBM monitors legislation with fiscal impacts. While the fiscal note indicates requirements can be handled with existing resources, DBM oversees the state's personnel and budget execution for the conducting agency.
