bill_summary: House Bill 1153 prohibits health insurance carriers and managed care organizations from downcoding medical claims—unilaterally changing service codes to lower-paying ones—without a clinical documentation review. The bill requires carriers to provide written notice and justification to health care providers before downcoding, allows providers to appeal these decisions, and mandates that final downcoding determinations be made by board-certified or eligible physicians. Additionally, it establishes a fine of up to $10,000 per violation and requires carriers to report downcoding data to the Maryland Insurance Commissioner.
responsible_party: Maryland Insurance Commissioner and the Maryland Department of Health
stakeholders: Health care providers (including physicians, hospitals, and freestanding medical facilities), health insurance carriers, nonprofit health service plans, health maintenance organizations (HMOs), managed care organizations (MCOs), and participants in the Maryland Medical Assistance Program.
fiscal_impact_summary: Specific dollar estimates from a formal Fiscal Note are unavailable. The bill establishes a fine of up to $10,000 for each violation. Financial implications likely include increased administrative costs for the Maryland Insurance Administration and the Maryland Department of Health, as well as potential increases in reimbursement expenditures for the Maryland Medical Assistance Program and state-regulated health plans due to restricted downcoding practices.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: As the primary regulator of health insurance in Maryland, the Insurance Administration is responsible for enforcing the new prohibitions on downcoding, collecting quarterly reports from carriers on downcoding activities, and administering the fines of up to $10,000 per violation.

The bill explicitly amends the Health - General Article to apply the new downcoding protections to Managed Care Organizations (MCOs) within the Maryland Medical Assistance Program (Medicaid), making the department responsible for oversight of these standards within the state's Medicaid system.

The bill classifies final decisions to downcode a claim leading to nonpayment as 'coverage decisions' under Title 15, Subtitle 10D of the Insurance Article, which are subject to the administrative appeal process often adjudicated by this office.

As the agency that manages the State Employee Health and Welfare Benefits Program, DBM is impacted by changes in claim reimbursement procedures and coding standards used by the carriers that provide benefits to state employees.

The bill regulates the reimbursement practices of health maintenance organizations and insurers, many of which offer plans through the Maryland Health Connection marketplace administered by the Exchange.

The commission regulates hospital rates and financial stability; because the bill specifically includes hospitals in the definition of 'health care providers' protected from downcoding, it impacts hospital reimbursement and revenue integrity.

The OAG provides legal counsel to the Maryland Insurance Administration and the Department of Health and would be involved in defending regulatory actions or interpreting the new legal definitions created by the bill.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Maryland Institute for Emergency Medical Services Systems
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill contains specific provisions prohibiting downcoding for emergency services based on final diagnosis rather than presenting symptoms, which relates to the EMS and emergency care standards overseen by MIEMSS.

The commission's role in improving access to health care and increasing accountability in the health system is relevant to regulations that impact provider reimbursement and the financial viability of health services.

Synopsis: Altering a certain definition of restrictive housing; limiting the amount of time that an individual may be placed in restrictive housing; requiring all restrictive housing units to create the least restrictive environment necessary for certain purposes; prohibiting the placement of a certain member of a vulnerable population in restrictive housing for any period of time; requiring a certain individual in restrictive housing to be offered a certain amount of time outside the individual's cell each day; etc.
Title: Correctional Services - Restrictive Housing
Status: In the House - Hearing 2/26 at 1:00 p.m.

NarrowSubjects.Name: Elderly Persons (65+) -see also- Elder Abuse and Neglect

bill_summary: This bill limits the use of restrictive housing (solitary confinement) in Maryland correctional facilities by redefining it as confinement for 20 or more hours a day. It restricts placement to a maximum of 15 consecutive days and 20 total days within a 60-day period, while requiring at least 4 hours of out-of-cell time daily. Crucially, the bill prohibits placing members of 'vulnerable populations'—including youth under 22, seniors over 55, pregnant individuals, and those with mental or physical disabilities—in restrictive housing for any duration. The Correctional Ombudsman is tasked with monitoring implementation and reporting results in 2028 and 2030.
responsible_party: Maryland Department of Public Safety and Correctional Services and the Office of the Correctional Ombudsman
stakeholders: Incarcerated individuals (particularly youth, seniors, and those with disabilities), correctional facility staff, and the Correctional Ombudsman.
fiscal_impact_summary: Specific dollar estimates are unavailable as a formal Fiscal Note was not included in the provided text. Financial implications include potential increases in state and local expenditures for staffing to facilitate the mandated 4 hours of daily out-of-cell time, facility modifications to provide less restrictive environments, and administrative costs for the Correctional Ombudsman to conduct reviews and surveys.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Department of Public Safety and Correctional Services
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: As the primary department responsible for managing state correctional facilities and pretrial detention centers, this bill directly impacts their core operations, housing protocols, and staffing requirements regarding restrictive housing.

The bill regulates the use of restrictive housing for minors and individuals under the age of 22, directly impacting the department's management and rehabilitation of youth within the juvenile justice system.

The OAG provides legal counsel to correctional agencies and administratively houses the Office of the Correctional Ombudsman, which is specifically tasked by the bill to monitor and report on implementation.

The bill establishes vulnerable population categories based on mental illness, developmental disabilities, and serious medical conditions, requiring health assessments and clinical treatment plans that involve coordination with health officials.

The mandate to provide at least 4 hours of out-of-cell time and the prohibition of restrictive housing for various populations will likely require significant changes in staffing levels and operational budgets.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Governor's Office of Crime Prevention and Policy
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: As the Governor's coordinating body for public safety and criminal justice strategy, this office would be involved in the policy development and interagency collaboration required to implement these restrictive housing reforms.
The bill mandates increased programming and education time for incarcerated individuals, particularly those under 22, which may impact educational services provided within facilities by MSDE.

The bill specifically designates individuals with various types of disabilities (mental, developmental, physical, and sensory) as vulnerable populations, aligning with the department's mission to ensure inclusive and integrated services.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Governor's Office of the Deaf and Hard of Hearing
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: Individuals with significant auditory impairments are explicitly listed as a 'vulnerable population' protected from restrictive housing under this legislation.
The bill includes protections for individuals perceived as LGBTQI+ within the definition of vulnerable populations, intersecting with the Commission's role in enforcing anti-discrimination laws.
The Governor's Office oversees the executive branch departments involved in corrections and would be responsible for the broad policy direction and administrative support for these reforms.

Qualifying assets include water towers, flow meters, and other water and sewer assets. The contracts may encompass planning, design, construction, operation, maintenance, modification, revitalization, and decommissioning.
responsible_party: Calvert County Board of County Commissioners
stakeholders: Calvert County government, infrastructure and asset management contractors, and county residents served by water and sewer infrastructure.
fiscal_impact_summary: There is no state fiscal impact. Locally, the bill does not materially affect Calvert County government finances, although the Department of Legislative Services notes it may result in operational efficiencies for the county by allowing longer-term procurement cycles for specific infrastructure assets.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Governor's Office is responsible for signing the bill into law and oversees the administration's relationship with local jurisdictions regarding infrastructure and procurement authorities.

The Office of the Attorney General provides legal review of all legislation for constitutionality and legal sufficiency and serves as legal counsel to the state agencies (MDE and MES) involved in infrastructure oversight and service delivery.

The bill specifically authorizes long-term contracts for water and sewer assets, such as water towers and flow meters, which are infrastructure types regulated and sometimes funded by the Department of the Environment.

The Maryland Environmental Service is a state agency that provides technical and operational management of water, wastewater, and solid waste infrastructure for local governments on a fee-for-service basis. The bill's expansion of 20-year contract authority for these specific assets directly relates to the types of long-term service agreements MES facilitates.

bill_summary: This bill increases the death and burial benefits provided to volunteer fire, rescue, and emergency medical services members in Calvert County under the Length of Service Award Program (LOSAP). Specifically, it raises the benefit for volunteers with 25 years of service from $10,000 to $14,000 and increases the per-year-of-service burial benefit for certain other eligible volunteers from $336 to $560.
stakeholders: Calvert County volunteer fire, rescue, and emergency medical services members and their beneficiaries
fiscal_impact_summary: The bill has no impact on state finances. Calvert County expenditures are projected to increase by approximately $16,000 annually beginning in fiscal year 2027. This estimate is based on a 10-year average of four deaths per year among qualified volunteers and primarily accounts for the $4,000 increase in benefits for members with 25 years of service.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: As an enrolled bill, this legislation must be presented to the Governor for approval and signing into law. The Governor's Office oversees the executive process for local laws passed by the General Assembly.
The Office of the Attorney General provides legal counsel to the Governor and General Assembly and reviews legislation for legal sufficiency, including changes to Public Local Laws.
The Secretary of State is the custodian of the state's official records and is responsible for managing the laws after they are signed by the Governor.

However, the bill authorizes the Maryland Insurance Commissioner to establish regulatory fees or assessments on carriers to recover the costs of implementing the Act and maintaining the required data dashboards. These funds are to be deposited into the Insurance Regulation Fund.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: As the primary regulatory body for insurance in Maryland, the Maryland Insurance Administration (under the Insurance Commissioner) is tasked with developing the reporting template, collecting carrier data, creating the public dashboard, and enforcing compliance.

The commission's mandate to plan for health system needs and provide transparent data on health service costs and availability directly aligns with the bill's requirements for public reporting on carrier reimbursement and network adequacy.

The bill requires data comparisons between insurance plans and carriers, which directly supports the Exchange's mission of providing a centralized marketplace where residents can compare and shop for health insurance.
The bill explicitly authorizes the Insurance Commissioner to refer carriers that fail to comply with reporting requirements to the Attorney General for investigation or civil action.

The bill focuses extensively on mental health, substance use, and behavioral health services, all of which are primary areas of public health oversight and policy coordination for the Maryland Department of Health.

As the agency responsible for managing state employee health benefits, DBM has a fiscal and administrative interest in the reporting and regulation of the insurance carriers that provide these benefits.
The bill mandates that carrier data be disaggregated by youth and adult enrollees, providing critical data for the office's mission to improve access to health services for Maryland's children.

bill_summary: This bill requires the Maryland Department of Health to include specific recommendations in its annual report on the Abortion Care Clinical Training Program to ensure Maryland has a sufficient number of health professionals to provide abortion care. Additionally, it mandates that the Maryland Insurance Commissioner annually collect and report on data from health insurance carriers regarding segregated accounts established under the federal Affordable Care Act for abortion coverage.

stakeholders: Health insurance carriers (including insurers, nonprofit health service plans, and HMOs), health care professionals, and patients seeking abortion care in Maryland.

However, the bill creates new administrative requirements for the Maryland Department of Health and the Maryland Insurance Commissioner to collect financial data and prepare annual reports, which may result in minor increases in state expenditures.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill directly amends the Health - General Article, requiring the Maryland Department of Health to include specific recommendations in its annual report regarding the Abortion Care Clinical Training Program and the sufficiency of the healthcare workforce for abortion care.

The bill adds a new section to the Insurance Article, mandating that the Maryland Insurance Commissioner collect financial data from insurers, nonprofit health service plans, and HMOs regarding segregated accounts for abortion services and report this data to legislative committees.

The bill concerns segregated accounts established under Section 1303 of the Affordable Care Act (ACA), which are used by plans on the state's health insurance marketplace to separate abortion coverage funds from federal subsidies, a key compliance area for the Exchange.

The bill requires the Department of Health to submit its annual report and recommendations directly to the Governor, who oversees the executive agencies responsible for implementing these reporting mandates.

The Office of the Attorney General provides legal counsel to the Department of Health and the Insurance Administration, particularly regarding compliance with federal ACA regulations and the implementation of state reporting requirements.

The Commission is responsible for planning for the state's health system needs and improving access to care; the bill's focus on identifying workforce sufficiency for abortion care overlaps with the Commission's planning and evaluation mission.

Synopsis: Altering the statutory reference to the name Calvert Memorial Hospital to be CalvertHealth Medical Center, Inc., and its successors.
Title: Calvert County - CalvertHealth Medical Center
Status: Approved by the Governor - Chapter 338
bill_summary: This bill updates the Public Local Laws of Calvert County by altering the name of 'Calvert Memorial Hospital' to 'CalvertHealth Medical Center, Inc., and its successors' to reflect the facility's current legal name.
stakeholders: CalvertHealth Medical Center, its successors, and the Calvert County government.
fiscal_impact_summary: The bill is procedural in nature and has no impact on state or local finances.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Governor's Office is responsible for signing all passed legislation into law and oversees the executive branch departments affected by health facility regulations.
The Secretary of State is the principal custodian of Maryland's official records, including the laws and executive orders enacted by the state.
The Archives is the central depository for all government records of permanent value, including the Public Local Laws of Maryland being amended by this bill.
The Maryland Department of Health regulates health care facilities and maintains oversight of health-related entities throughout the state.
The HSCRC regulates hospital rates and revenues; the bill updates the statutory name of a hospital that is authorized to receive county appropriations.

Synopsis: Requiring a State agency to provide certain climate and sustainability information on submission of a certain contract award recommendation or proposed public-private partnership agreement to the Board of Public Works; requiring liaisons to the Board to ensure compliance;  requiring the climate and sustainability information to be placed on the Board agenda; and requiring the Department of General Services to issue certain guidance.
Title: Board of Public Works - Contract Review - Climate and Sustainability Information (BPW Climate Transparency Act)
Status: In the House - Unfavorable Report by Government, Labor, and Elections; Withdrawn

BroadSubjects.Name: State Government - Agencies, Offices, and Officials

NarrowSubjects.Name: Environmental Matters -see also- Conserv; Nat Resrce; Pollut

bill_summary: The BPW Climate Transparency Act requires Maryland State agencies to provide detailed climate and sustainability information when submitting certain contracts—such as construction, energy performance, and architectural services—and public-private partnership agreements to the Board of Public Works for approval. Agencies must disclose how these agreements align with the state's greenhouse gas reduction goals, climate resilience standards, and green building requirements. The Department of General Services is mandated to issue guidance to help agencies comply with these new reporting standards.
responsible_party: The Board of Public Works and the Department of General Services
stakeholders: Maryland State agencies, the Board of Public Works, the offices of the Governor, Comptroller, and State Treasurer, and private contractors or vendors bidding on State projects.
fiscal_impact_summary: A formal Fiscal Note with specific dollar estimates was not provided in the text. However, the bill creates new administrative requirements for state agencies to track and report climate metrics and for the Department of General Services to issue guidance, which likely involves minor indeterminate expenditure increases for personnel time across affected agencies.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill explicitly requires the liaison from the Governor's Office to the Board of Public Works to ensure that mandated climate and sustainability information is included on the Board's agenda.

The bill explicitly requires the liaison from the Comptroller's Office to the Board of Public Works to ensure that mandated climate and sustainability information is included on the Board's agenda. Additionally, the Comptroller is a member of the Board.

The bill explicitly requires the liaison from the State Treasurer's Office to the Board of Public Works to ensure that mandated climate and sustainability information is included on the Board's agenda. Additionally, the Treasurer is a member of the Board.

As the agency responsible for budget execution and long-term fiscal planning, DBM is impacted by the new reporting requirements for various state contracts and may be involved in the fiscal review of climate-related reporting.

The bill specifically mandates DGS to issue guidance to state agencies on complying with the new climate reporting requirements. DGS is also the primary procurement authority for the state and handles many of the contract types (construction, leasing, A&E) covered by the bill.
DNR manages extensive state property and public lands, involving maintenance, construction, and leasing contracts that will be subject to the new climate and sustainability reporting requirements.

As a major modal agency with significant construction, A&E, and public-private partnership (P3) agreements, MDOT will be heavily impacted by the requirement to provide climate and sustainability disclosures for its project submissions to the Board of Public Works.
The bill requires contracts to be consistent with greenhouse gas emissions goals and Building Energy Performance Standards (BEPS), both of which are primarily administered and regulated by MDE.
The Board of Public Works is the primary entity addressed by the bill, which establishes new requirements for the information agencies must provide when submitting contracts for the Board's approval.

The IAC oversees public school construction and capital improvement projects; these construction and A&E contracts submitted for state funding/approval will now require the climate and sustainability disclosures specified in the bill.
The bill specifically covers energy performance contracts, which are a core area of policy and coordination for the MEA in its mission to promote energy efficiency and renewable energy.

The MSA plans and builds major sports, entertainment, and educational facilities. Its construction and A&E contracts submitted to the Board of Public Works will be subject to these new sustainability transparency requirements.

As an independent state agency that manages its own capital projects and submits construction and leasing contracts to the Board of Public Works, Morgan State will be required to comply with the new climate reporting mandates.

As an independent state agency that submits its own construction and maintenance contracts to the Board of Public Works, the college will be required to provide the specified climate and sustainability information.

The USM and its constituent institutions frequently submit major construction, leasing, and maintenance contracts to the Board of Public Works, all of which will now require detailed climate and sustainability disclosures.

Synopsis: Requiring the Special Secretary of Overdose Response to provide funding to counties for medication-assisted treatment programs; requiring certain counties to submit a certain report; authorizing the Governor to include in the annual budget bill an appropriation for the purpose of providing funds under certain circumstances; expanding the authorized uses for the Opioid Restitution Fund; etc.
Title: Correctional Services – Medication–Assisted Treatment Funding
Status: In the House - Hearing 3/10 at 1:00 p.m. (Health)

NarrowSubjects.Name: Counties -see also- Chartered Counties; Code Counties; etc.
Crime Prevention and Policy, Governor's Office of
Drugs -see also- Cannabis; ControlDangSubst; Pharm; etc.
Opioids -see also- Controlled Dangerous Substances; Drugs

bill_summary: This bill requires the Special Secretary of Overdose Response to provide annual funding to Maryland counties to cover the full costs of implementing and operating medication-assisted treatment (MAT) programs for incarcerated individuals in local detention centers. It expands the authorized uses of the Opioid Restitution Fund to include these reimbursements, establishes mandatory reporting requirements for counties to document their expenses, and provides for a reduction in funding if counties fail to submit required data.
stakeholders: Incarcerated individuals with opioid use disorder, county governments, and local detention center administrators.
fiscal_impact_summary: The bill creates a State mandate to reimburse counties for the costs incurred in providing medication-assisted treatment within local detention centers. This will result in a significant increase in State expenditures, with funding sourced from the Opioid Restitution Fund, the state budget, or eligible grants. Conversely, local governments will see an increase in revenue as their MAT program costs are reimbursed by the State. Specific dollar estimates are unavailable because the formal Fiscal Note was not provided in the text.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill authorizes the Governor to include appropriations in the budget for medication-assisted treatment (MAT) and requires the Governor to set performance indicators for the Opioid Restitution Fund. Furthermore, the Special Secretary of Overdose Response, an executive position, is tasked with managing the funding distributions to counties.
The Comptroller is specifically tasked with accounting for the Opioid Restitution Fund, which the bill expands to include funding for county correctional MAT programs.
The State Treasurer is responsible for holding the Opioid Restitution Fund separately and investing its money, both of which are central to the funding mechanisms established by the bill.

The Attorney General manages the Opioids Enforcement Unit funded by the Opioid Restitution Fund and is responsible for designating the controlling versions of settlement agreements that provide the funds used in this bill.

As the agency responsible for developing the state budget and supervising budget execution, DBM is involved in the process of allocating funds for county reimbursements and overseeing the special fund mentioned in the bill.

The Maryland Department of Health (MDH) is responsible for adopting the clinical guidelines and regulations for substance use disorder treatment in jails, evaluating program implementation, and administering the grant programs related to the Opioid Restitution Fund.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Department of Public Safety and Correctional Services
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: DPSCS is specifically required to report to the General Assembly regarding the implementation of medication-assisted treatment at the Baltimore Pre-trial Complex, which it oversees.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Governor's Office of Crime Prevention and Policy
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: GOCPP is a primary implementing agency tasked with evaluating MAT implementation schedules, collecting annual data from individual local correctional facilities, and reporting this information to the General Assembly.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Executive Commissions, Committees, Task Forces, and Advisory Boards
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Opioid Restitution Fund Advisory Council, which falls under this category, must be consulted by the Governor at least twice annually regarding recommended appropriations from the fund.

Synopsis: Authorizing the General Assembly to lower the age at which an individual may vote in an election for members of the Howard County Board of Education; and altering the minimum age at which an individual in Howard County may vote in an election for members of the Howard County Board of Education from 18 years old to 16 years old.
Title: Howard County - Voting Age - Board of Education Elections Ho. Co. 5-26
Status: In the House - Hearing 3/11 at 1:35 p.m.

NarrowSubjects.Name: Age -see also- Age of Maj; Children; Elderly; Inf&Tod.; etc
General Assembly -see also- AELR Cmte; LegislativePolCmte
Public Officials -see also- Atty Gen; Compt; Coun Admin; etc
Voting -see also- Absentee and Mail-In Voting

bill_summary: This bill proposes a constitutional amendment to authorize the General Assembly to lower the voting age to 16 for Howard County Board of Education elections. If approved by voters in the 2026 general election, the bill would allow individuals at least 16 years old to vote specifically for members of the Howard County Board of Education.
responsible_party: Maryland State Board of Elections and Howard County Board of Elections
stakeholders: 16 and 17-year-old residents of Howard County, the Howard County Board of Education, and Howard County voters
fiscal_impact_summary: If the constitutional amendment is approved, State general fund expenditures and Howard County expenditures are each estimated to increase by $149,000 in FY 2027 for one-time programming and pollbook software modifications. In subsequent years, costs for additional ballots are expected to increase by less than $3,000 per election for both the State and Howard County, with the county also facing unquantified costs for personnel and equipment testing.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: As the agency responsible for supervising and administering elections, the State Board of Elections is the primary entity affected by the bill. The fiscal note indicates the agency will incur significant costs for programming changes to the Agency Election Management System, the voter registration system, and pollbook software to accommodate voters under age 18 in Howard County Board of Education elections.

The bill proposes a constitutional amendment. Under the Maryland Constitution and Section 4 and 6 of the act, the Governor is responsible for receiving the election returns and issuing a proclamation declaring the amendment adopted if ratified by the voters.

The bill has a notable fiscal impact on the state's general fund, requiring an estimated $149,000 in FY 2027 for IT and software modifications. DBM is responsible for supervising budget execution and fiscal planning for the state.

The bill requires modifications to the Agency Election Management System (AEMS) and other statewide voter registration databases. DoIT oversees the state's information technology strategy and infrastructure, which includes these centralized systems.

The bill concerns the election of members to the Howard County Board of Education. MSDE oversees local school systems and maintains a general interest in the governance and selection of local boards of education.

The Secretary of State is the custodian of official records, including laws and executive orders. The agency is involved in the processing and recording of constitutional amendments and election certifications.

The OAG provides legal counsel to the Governor, the General Assembly, and state agencies like the Board of Elections. It would likely review the legality of the constitutional amendment and the implementation of the new voting eligibility rules.

Synopsis: Authorizing the Public Service Commission to require a water company, sewage disposal company, or water and sewage disposal company to adopt a certain limited-income mechanism subject to the approval of the Commission; and requiring the Commission to study the feasibility of requiring certain companies to adopt a limited-income mechanism to benefit limited-income customers and to report its findings to the Governor and the General Assembly by December 1, 2026.
Title: Water Companies, Sewage Disposal Companies, and Water and Sewage Disposal Companies - Limited-Income Mechanisms
Status: Approved by the Governor - Chapter 526

NarrowSubjects.Name: Utilities -see also- Recycl; Refuse; Sewage; Teleph; Water
Water -see also- Coastal Bays; Riv,Str,Lks; Wastewater; etc.

bill_summary: This bill requires the Maryland Public Service Commission (PSC) to study the feasibility of requiring water and sewage disposal companies to implement limited-income mechanisms to assist low-income customers. Effective July 1, 2027, the PSC is authorized to require these companies to adopt such mechanisms—including programs, credits, or special rates—to benefit customers with incomes at or below 175% of the federal poverty level, or 200% for customers aged 67 and older.
stakeholders: Privately owned water and sewage disposal companies, eligible limited-income residential customers, and other utility ratepayers including local governments and small businesses.
fiscal_impact_summary: The bill can be implemented using the Public Service Commission's existing budgeted resources. There is no material effect on State expenditures or revenues. However, utility rates for non-limited-income customers (including residential, local government, and small business users) may increase as early as fiscal 2028 to fund the mechanisms if they are adopted by the companies.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill directly mandates the Public Service Commission (PSC) to study the feasibility of limited-income mechanisms for water and sewage companies, authorizes them to require these mechanisms, and expands their evaluation criteria for utility rates.

The Office of the People's Counsel is the statutory advocate for residential utility consumers, including those of private water and sewage services. This bill directly impacts utility rate structures and assistance mechanisms for the consumers they represent.

The bill explicitly requires the Office of Home Energy Programs (OHEP), which is administered by the Department of Human Services, to certify eligible limited-income customers for participation in these utility mechanisms if required.
The bill specifies that eligible customers may also participate in assistance programs offered by the Department of Housing and Community Development (DHCD) and requires coordination of benefits.
The Public Service Commission is required to report its study findings on the feasibility of these limited-income mechanisms to the Governor by December 1, 2026.

Synopsis: Requiring certain apprenticeship programs utilized in certain State procurements to have at least a 25% completion rate, as determined by the Maryland Department of Labor.
Title: State Procurement - Apprenticeship Program Accountability and Completion
Status: Approved by the Governor - Chapter 533

NarrowSubjects.Name: Work, Labor, and Employment -see also- JobTrn; Leave; etc.

bill_summary: This bill requires apprenticeship programs used for State procurement contracts to maintain a completion rate of at least 25% once they have graduated at least one cohort. The requirement applies to 'covered procurements' valued at $1,000,000 or more, prevailing wage public works worth $250,000 or more, and other public works valued at $500,000 or more. The Maryland Department of Labor is responsible for verifying these completion rates, and contractors who do not utilize a qualifying program must pay into the State Apprenticeship Training Fund.
stakeholders: Contractors and subcontractors on State and local public work projects, registered apprenticeship program sponsors, and State procurement units.
fiscal_impact_summary: According to the fiscal note, State special fund revenues will increase beginning in FY 2027 as more contractors may pay into the State Apprenticeship Training Fund (SATF) as an alternative to using an apprenticeship program that meets the new criteria; however, a specific estimate is not feasible. Additionally, project costs for State and local governments may increase if the bill reduces the number of eligible bidders or offerors for specified contracts. The Maryland Department of Labor and other State agencies can implement the bill with existing resources.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Maryland Department of Labor is the primary agency responsible for calculating and verifying the 25% completion rate for apprenticeship programs, managing the State Apprenticeship Training Fund, and enforcing the bill's requirements.
DGS houses the Chief Procurement Officer, who is tasked with adopting regulations for 'covered procurements' and managing state construction projects impacted by these apprenticeship standards.
The Secretary of Information Technology must be consulted by the Chief Procurement Officer regarding 'covered procurements' related to IT contracts under Title 3.5.
MDOT oversees massive public works and infrastructure projects (highways, transit, etc.) that utilize state funds and are subject to the bill's apprenticeship completion requirements.
The Board approves significant state procurements and contracts, which will now be subject to these new accountability and completion standards for apprenticeship programs.
The Comptroller is explicitly tasked with accounting for the State Apprenticeship Training Fund and serves on the Board of Public Works which oversees affected contracts.
The State Treasurer is explicitly tasked with holding the State Apprenticeship Training Fund and serves on the Board of Public Works.
The Authority plans and manages large-scale construction projects using state capital funds, making their contracts subject to the new apprenticeship completion rate mandates.
The System and its member institutions frequently manage capital construction projects funded by the state budget that are subject to these apprenticeship standards.
The IAC oversees public school construction projects that use state funds and typically involve the use of apprentices in the building trades.
DBM is the principal fiscal agency overseeing state budget execution and procurement policies, which are altered by these apprenticeship requirements.
The OAG provides legal counsel to state agencies on procurement law and would be responsible for representing the state in enforcement or compliance litigation.
The bill's definition of 'public work' specifically includes infrastructure like waterworks and sewage disposal plants, which are regulated or overseen by MDE.
As a state agency with its own board, Morgan State manages capital projects subject to the bill's procurement and apprenticeship requirements.
As a public honors college, St. Mary's manages construction and procurement activities that are subject to these apprenticeship completion standards.
The Governor's Office oversees the executive branch and procurement policy, and the Governor serves on the Board of Public Works which approves affected contracts.
The Commission is mentioned in the definition of 'public work' regarding structure or work performed by public service companies under their order.

Synopsis: Prohibiting a motor vehicle dealer from delivering a motor vehicle for which two registration plates are required to a buyer or lessee unless the motor vehicle has a certain front registration plate display mechanism or the buyer or lessee signs a written statement acknowledging declined installation of the display mechanism; requiring a motor vehicle dealer to submit certain information on declined installation of a certain front registration plate display mechanism to the Motor Vehicle Administration; etc.
Title: Motor Vehicles - Dealers - Front Registration Plate Display
Status: In the Senate - Hearing 4/01 at 1:00 p.m.

NarrowSubjects.Name: Crimes and Punishments -see also- Penalties and Sentnc; etc.
License Plates -see also- Motor Vehicle Registration
Records -see also- Land Records; Vital Records

bill_summary: This bill prohibits motor vehicle dealers from delivering new vehicles that require two registration plates unless the vehicle is equipped with a front registration plate mounting hardware or display mechanism. Alternatively, a buyer or lessee may sign a written disclosure statement acknowledging they declined the installation, understand that Maryland law requires a front plate, and are aware that failure to display the plate is a misdemeanor punishable by a fine of up to $500. Dealers must submit these signed statements to the Motor Vehicle Administration on a monthly basis.
stakeholders: Motor vehicle dealers, buyers and lessees of new motor vehicles, and the Maryland Motor Vehicle Administration
fiscal_impact_summary: The Motor Vehicle Administration can implement the bill's requirements with existing budgeted resources. While specific dollar estimates are unavailable, the bill may result in an indeterminate decrease in traffic fine revenue due to improved compliance and a potential increase in toll collection revenue by improving the Maryland Transportation Authority's ability to identify vehicles via camera. Failure to display a front plate remains a misdemeanor subject to a fine of up to $500.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill explicitly tasks the Motor Vehicle Administration (MVA) with developing the required disclosure statement for dealers, receiving monthly reports or submissions from dealers regarding buyers who decline front plate hardware, and adopting regulations to implement the new statutory requirements.

As the parent department for the MVA, MDOT is responsible for the overall implementation of transportation laws. Additionally, the Maryland Transportation Authority (MDTA), a unit within MDOT, is noted in the fiscal note as having a potential impact on toll collection revenues if the bill leads to increased compliance with front plate requirements.

The MDTA relies on front registration plates for toll enforcement via camera systems. The bill's success in increasing the number of vehicles with front plates could improve toll collection accuracy and revenue.

The bill requires the MVA to adopt regulations regarding the use and disclosure of the signed statements to law enforcement for the enforcement of registration plate display laws. The State Police are the primary agency enforcing these traffic laws.

The OAG would provide legal counsel to the MVA in developing the new regulations and ensuring the disclosure statements meet constitutional and statutory requirements, especially regarding the use of collected data for law enforcement.
The MVA may require support from DoIT to manage the monthly digital or manual submission of written statements from dealers and the subsequent storage and disclosure of that data to law enforcement.

The OAH adjudicates contested cases for various state agencies, including the MVA. If the MVA pursues regulatory enforcement actions against dealers for failing to comply with these reporting requirements, the OAH would likely handle the appeals.

The bill text specifically mentions the Department of Human Services as an entity that is excluded from the definition of a 'dealer' when transferring vehicles under certain programs, clarifying their regulatory standing under the amended law.
The Governor's Office oversees the executive branch agencies responsible for implementing this bill and is responsible for signing the legislation into law.
DBM monitors the fiscal impact of legislation and the execution of the state budget, including potential changes to traffic fine revenues mentioned in the fiscal note.

Synopsis: Requiring the Department of Information Technology to convene a workgroup on the Medicaid Management Information System mainframe system replacement; and requiring the workgroup to periodically report to certain committees of the General Assembly on the progress made toward procuring the mainframe system replacement and the timeline for meeting the implementation deadline for the replacement.
Title: Department of Information Technology - Workgroup on the Medicaid Management Information System Mainframe System Replacement
Status: In the Senate - Rereferred to Education, Energy, and the Environment and Finance

Health Insurance -see also- ACA; HMOs; MCOs
Records -see also- Land Records; Vital Records

bill_summary: This bill requires the Department of Information Technology to convene a workgroup to oversee and assist the Maryland Department of Health in replacing the outdated Medicaid Management Information System (MMIS) mainframe system. The replacement system must be implemented by July 1, 2029, and must improve payment accuracy, security, and performance. The workgroup is required to submit quarterly progress reports and annual activity reports to several legislative committees until the transition is complete.
stakeholders: Maryland Department of Health, Department of Information Technology, Department of Human Services, Maryland Health Benefit Exchange, Office of the Comptroller, and health insurance policy experts.
fiscal_impact_summary: The Department of Information Technology and other participating state agencies can implement the bill's requirements using existing budgeted resources. While the bill facilitates the procurement and transition to a new Medicaid Management Information System, it does not directly allocate specific funds for the system itself; however, decisions made by the workgroup may influence future system costs. A 2008 estimate for the system replacement was approximately $111,000,000, but no current funding for the replacement has been requested beyond project planning funds approved for fiscal year 2027.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill explicitly mandates the Department of Information Technology to convene and lead the workgroup responsible for overseeing the Medicaid Management Information System (MMIS) mainframe replacement.
The MMIS is the primary system for Maryland's Medicaid program, which is managed by MDH. The department is a mandated member of the workgroup and the primary entity responsible for the transition.
The Department of Human Services is a mandated member of the workgroup assisting in the procurement and transition of the new Medicaid Management Information System.
The Maryland Health Benefit Exchange is a mandated member of the workgroup assisting in the procurement and transition of the new Medicaid Management Information System.
The Comptroller of Maryland is a mandated member of the workgroup assisting in the procurement and transition of the new Medicaid Management Information System.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Executive Commissions, Committees, Task Forces, and Advisory Boards
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill establishes a new workgroup composed of state officials and experts to coordinate interagency work on a specific technological modernization project.

As the state's central procurement authority, DGS is identified as an information source for the fiscal note and will be involved in the competitive bidding and acquisition process for the replacement system.
The Board of Public Works will likely be required to approve the final, high-value procurement contract for the replacement of the state's MMIS mainframe.
As the principal fiscal agency, DBM oversees the funding and execution of major state IT capital projects such as the MMIS modernization.

Synopsis: Requiring the State Department of Education to develop a model sexual abuse and sexual misconduct response policy that includes, at minimum, certain components; requiring each local school system to adopt a  response policy based on the model policy developed by the Department on or before September 1, 2027, and to post in a conspicuous place on its website a link to a certain centralized statewide resource platform; etc.
Title: State Department of Education - Sexual Abuse and Sexual Misconduct Model Response Policy - Requirements
Status: In the Senate - First Reading Senate Rules

bill_summary: This bill requires the Maryland State Department of Education (MSDE) to develop a model sexual abuse and misconduct response policy for local school systems. Each local school system must adopt its own response policy based on this model by September 1, 2027. These policies must include communication plans, electronic record retention for at least one year, and a structured after-action review process for serious incidents. Additionally, school systems must notify parents of credible allegations of misconduct and maintain a centralized resource platform link on their websites.
stakeholders: Public school students, parents and guardians, local school system employees, contractors, volunteers, and law enforcement agencies.
fiscal_impact_summary: The Maryland State Department of Education can develop the model policy and resource platform using existing budgeted resources. There is no impact on State revenues. Local school systems will face increased legal and programmatic expenditures starting in fiscal 2027 to implement the required policies and conduct reviews. Specific expenditure estimates provided in the fiscal note include approximately $265,000 annually for Prince George’s County Public Schools and $160,000 annually for St. Mary’s Public Schools for additional staffing and legal risk management, while other sampled counties expect to absorb costs within existing budgets.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Maryland State Department of Education (MSDE) is the primary agency responsible for implementing this bill. It is tasked with developing the model sexual abuse and misconduct response policy and the centralized statewide resource platform.

As an independent unit within MSDE focused on school safety, the Center is directly involved in developing and delivering the resources, training, and technical assistance necessary to implement safety-related policies in schools.
The bill explicitly requires the record retention requirements and guidelines within the model policy to be developed in collaboration with the State Archives.
The bill requires coordination with child protective services units, which are administered by DHS, and addresses the reporting and investigation of child abuse involving school employees.
The bill's model policy must address coordination with law enforcement agencies regarding investigations and allow for law enforcement to request delays in public communication for serious incidents.
The OAG provides legal counsel to state agencies like MSDE and will likely be involved in reviewing the model policy for compliance with state law and constitutional protections.

The bill directly aligns with the office's mission to promote the well-being and safety of Maryland's children by establishing standardized protocols for responding to sexual abuse in educational environments.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Governor's Office of Crime Prevention and Policy
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: As the primary coordinating body for public safety, GOCPP may be involved in the interagency collaboration required to develop the model response policy, particularly regarding criminal justice implications.

Synopsis: Authorizing Howard County to decrease the maximum speed limit to not less than 15 miles per hour on highways after performing an engineering and traffic investigation; and prohibiting Howard County from implementing a new speed monitoring system to enforce speed limits on highways on which the speed limit has been reduced under the Act.
Title: Howard County - Highways - Speed Limits Ho. Co. 8-26
Status: In the Senate - Hearing 3/25 at 1:00 p.m.

BroadSubjects.Name: Vehicle Laws - Rules of the Road

NarrowSubjects.Name: Investigations and Inquiries -see also- Crim Bckgrnd Invest

bill_summary: This bill authorizes Howard County to lower speed limits on its highways to a minimum of 15 miles per hour, provided an engineering and traffic investigation is conducted first. It also prohibits the county from installing new speed monitoring systems (speed cameras) on any section of a highway where the speed limit has been reduced under this specific authority.
stakeholders: Howard County residents and motorists
fiscal_impact_summary: State general fund revenues may increase minimally from speeding citations. Howard County expenditures will increase to the extent that engineering and traffic investigations are performed. Local revenues may increase if speed limits are reduced on highways where speed cameras are already in operation; however, the bill prohibits the installation of new speed monitoring systems on these road segments. Specific dollar estimates for these impacts are unavailable.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: As the parent agency for the State Highway Administration (SHA), MDOT oversees the state's multimodal transportation network. The bill directly impacts highway speed limit regulations which fall under MDOT's broad policy and operational scope.

SHA is the primary agency responsible for approving speed limit alterations made by local authorities on State highways. The fiscal note explicitly mentions that any alteration of a maximum speed limit by Howard County on a part of a State highway is not effective until approved by SHA.
The bill may lead to an increase in speeding citations if speed limits are lowered. These citations are adjudicated in the District Court, which is managed by the Administrative Office of the Courts.

The Maryland State Police enforce motor vehicle laws and traffic safety on state highways. Lowering speed limits in Howard County would affect their enforcement operations and potentially increase the volume of manual citations issued.

The Comptroller is responsible for receiving excess revenues from local speed monitoring systems if the balance exceeds 10% of a county's total annual revenue. While the bill prohibits new systems, it allows existing ones to continue, which could impact revenue flows handled by the Comptroller.

The OAG provides legal counsel to state agencies, including the Department of Transportation and the State Highway Administration, and would be responsible for advising on the implementation and legal compliance of speed limit changes and enforcement prohibitions.

Synopsis: Expanding the authorization to place and use speed monitoring systems on highways in Howard County to include U.S. Route 1 (Washington Boulevard).
Title: Howard County - Speed Monitoring Systems - Expansion of Authorization Ho. Co. 9-26
Status: In the House - Hearing 2/26 at 1:00 p.m.

BroadSubjects.Name: Vehicle Laws - Rules of the Road

bill_summary: This bill expands the authorization for speed monitoring systems in Howard County by specifically allowing the placement and use of speed cameras on U.S. Route 1 (Washington Boulevard).
stakeholders: Motorists traveling on U.S. Route 1 in Howard County, Howard County law enforcement, and the Maryland District Court.
fiscal_impact_summary: State general fund revenues from contested cases in District Court may increase minimally starting in fiscal 2027. Howard County revenues and expenditures will increase to the extent that speed cameras are installed and citations are issued. Revenues from citations must first be used to recover the costs of program implementation and administration, with any remaining balance dedicated to public safety purposes. While the Judiciary estimates a $1,400,000 cost for a general system upgrade to handle automated enforcement processing, this cost is not exclusively attributed to this bill.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The fiscal note identifies that the bill will increase the workload of the District Court due to contested speed monitoring citations. The Judiciary (AOC) also notes the need for an IT upgrade to handle the increasing volume of automated enforcement citations statewide.

MDOT is the parent agency for the State Highway Administration and Motor Vehicle Administration. It oversees the state highway network, which includes U.S. Route 1 (Washington Boulevard), the specific location targeted for expanded speed monitoring authorization.

bill_summary: The 'Building Affordably in My Back Yard Act' establishes various requirements and authorizations intended to facilitate residential housing development and affordability in Maryland. Key provisions include the establishment of housing production targets by the Governor starting in 2031, requirements for business entities owning residential property to file contact information with the state, and authorizations for local governments to create administrative review processes for housing projects. The bill also allows local jurisdictions to implement tax and fee incentives for affordable housing, creates special tax subclasses for vacant or underutilized land and non-principal residences, and restricts the sale of certain single-family homes to individuals or nonprofits during the first 30 days of listing.
responsible_party: Maryland Department of Planning, Department of Housing and Community Development, and the Governor's Office
stakeholders: Residential housing developers, homebuyers, local governments, business entities owning residential real estate, and nonprofit community development organizations.
fiscal_impact_summary: State general fund expenditures are estimated to increase by $536,900 in FY 2027 and $521,900 in FY 2028, primarily to fund consultant costs and new staff positions at the Maryland Department of Planning, the Department of Housing and Community Development, and the Comptroller's Office for required studies and target-setting. Local government revenues and expenditures will be affected based on individual jurisdictions' use of authorized tax subclasses, transfer taxes on transitioned owner-occupied properties, and fee exemptions for qualified affordable housing projects.

The bill requires this commission to coordinate with the Department of Planning for the school facility capacity portion of the comprehensive housing infrastructure report.
The bill has significant fiscal and personnel impacts, including the creation of new positions and consultant expenditures, which are overseen by this agency.

bill_summary: The Application Store Accountability Act establishes age verification and parental consent requirements for application store providers and developers. It requires app stores to verify user ages and obtain verifiable parental consent before a minor (under 18) can download or purchase an app or make in-app purchases. It also mandates that app stores protect age-related data, notify parents of significant app changes, and prohibits misrepresenting parental consent disclosures. Violations are categorized as unfair, abusive, or deceptive trade practices subject to enforcement under the Maryland Consumer Protection Act.
responsible_party: The Consumer Protection Division of the Office of the Attorney General
stakeholders: Application store providers, mobile application developers, minors under the age of 18, and parents or legal guardians in Maryland.
fiscal_impact_summary: According to the Fiscal Note, the bill's implementation does not have a material impact on State or local finances. The Consumer Protection Division of the Office of the Attorney General is expected to manage the requirements using existing resources. The bill authorizes civil penalties of up to $7,500 per violation and incorporates existing Maryland Consumer Protection Act penalties (up to $10,000 for a first violation and $25,000 for repeats). Small business app developers may experience meaningful compliance impacts.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill explicitly tasks the Consumer Protection Division within the Office of the Attorney General with adopting regulations for age verification, enforcing the act as an unfair, abusive, or deceptive trade practice, and bringing civil actions to recover penalties.

The bill creates a private right of action for minors harmed by violations, allowing them to seek actual and punitive damages in court. It also introduces new civil penalties that will be adjudicated through the judicial system.

As the agency responsible for adjudicating contested cases involving state regulatory enforcement, the OAH may hear appeals from application store providers or developers regarding enforcement actions taken by the Office of the Attorney General under this Act.

bill_summary: This bill requires public and nonpublic schools to establish policies and procedures for handling student wandering and elopement. It authorizes schools to coordinate the voluntary use of wearable locative devices for students who have a documented history of elopement in their Individualized Education Program (IEP) or behavior intervention plan, provided that parents give informed written consent and privacy protections are maintained. The Maryland State Department of Education is also required to issue advisory guidance regarding the use of these devices and related data protection.
stakeholders: Students with disabilities or a history of wandering or elopement, parents and guardians, public and nonpublic school administrators and staff, and emergency response providers.
fiscal_impact_summary: According to the fiscal note, the bill has no state fiscal impact because the Maryland State Department of Education can issue the required advisory guidance using existing budgeted resources. There is no direct local fiscal impact as the bill is authorizing; schools that choose to implement locative device monitoring may incur discretionary costs for equipment and data plans, but they are not required to purchase or provide the devices.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Department of Education is the primary agency responsible for the oversight of public and nonpublic schools. The bill explicitly mandates the Department to issue advisory guidance to schools regarding the voluntary use of locative devices and associated privacy and data protection considerations.

The Maryland School for the Deaf is explicitly included in the bill's definition of a 'School' that must develop policies and procedures regarding student wandering or elopement and is authorized to coordinate the voluntary use of locative devices.

The Maryland Center for School Safety, an independent unit within the Department of Education, is responsible for providing technical assistance and resources to schools to foster safe environments. This bill addresses student safety issues (wandering and elopement), which falls within the Center's scope of safety training and assistance.

The bill focuses on students with Individualized Education Programs (IEPs) or behavior intervention plans, which are primary mechanisms for delivering services to students with disabilities. The Department of Disabilities coordinates policies for inclusive settings and support for youth transitioning into adulthood.

The Office of the Attorney General provides legal counsel to the Department of Education and all state agencies. It would likely be involved in reviewing the advisory guidance and ensuring that the privacy and data protection safeguards established by the bill comply with state and federal laws.

The Governor's Office oversees the executive branch, including the Department of Education, and coordinates policy initiatives. The Governor is responsible for enforcing state laws, including those related to student safety and educational requirements.

bill_summary: This bill establishes a manufacturer’s limited beer, wine, and liquor permit in Baltimore County. It allows holders of a Class 5 brewery license with an on-site consumption permit to host private events where a third-party licensed caterer provides beer, wine, and liquor products that were not manufactured by the brewery.
responsible_party: Board of License Commissioners for Baltimore County
stakeholders: Class 5 brewery license holders in Baltimore County, licensed caterers, and individuals or groups hosting private events at brewery premises
fiscal_impact_summary: The bill is not expected to materially affect State finances. Baltimore County revenues are projected to increase minimally beginning in fiscal 2027 from the issuance of the new permits. The exact revenue increase depends on the annual permit fee, which is to be set by the Board of License Commissioners. Currently, there are five license holders in the county that may be eligible for the permit. Local enforcement can be handled with existing resources.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Comptroller of Maryland is the primary state regulator of the alcohol industry and is explicitly responsible for the issuance of the Class 5 brewery licenses referenced in this bill. The bill amends statutes governing manufacturer's licenses which fall under the Comptroller's regulatory and tax collection oversight.

The OAG serves as the chief legal officer for the state and provides legal counsel to state agencies, including the Comptroller, regarding the interpretation and enforcement of alcoholic beverage laws and the adoption of new regulations.

The Governor's Office oversees the executive branch and is responsible for signing or vetoing legislation related to state and local industry regulations, including changes to alcoholic beverages laws.

bill_summary: This bill prohibits 501(c)(3) and 501(c)(4) nonprofit organizations registered in Maryland from knowingly providing 'unauthorized support of Israeli settlement activity' in occupied territories including the West Bank and East Jerusalem. It defines such support as aiding and abetting activities banned under the Geneva Conventions, such as the unlawful transfer of civilians, acts of violence, property crimes, or destruction of infrastructure. The bill authorizes the Attorney General or harmed individuals to sue for injunctive relief and damages, and it requires the Secretary of State to remove violating organizations from the Registry of Charitable Solicitation.
responsible_party: Maryland Office of the Attorney General and the Maryland Secretary of State
stakeholders: 501(c)(3) and 501(c)(4) nonprofit organizations registered to solicit donations in Maryland, the Maryland Attorney General, and individuals harmed by unauthorized Israeli settlement activities.
fiscal_impact_summary: State general fund revenues may increase from damages awarded in cases brought by the Attorney General, who is authorized to seek at least 1,000,000 dollars per violation. State general fund expenditures may increase for the Office of the Attorney General due to litigation costs and expert witness fees. The Secretary of State's expenditures are not expected to be materially affected. Local government finances are not anticipated to be significantly impacted.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill grants the Attorney General the primary authority to bring civil actions for injunctive relief and damages (of at least $1 million) against nonprofit organizations and their agents for supporting prohibited activities.

The bill mandates that the Secretary of State remove any nonprofit organization found to be in violation of the Act from the Registry of Charitable Solicitation, an official registry managed by this agency.

The bill establishes a new civil cause of action within the Courts and Judicial Proceedings Article, requiring the state's judicial system to handle new litigation and adjudicate claims involving international law violations by nonprofits.

As the primary diplomatic liaison for Maryland, this division within the Secretary of State's office is relevant due to the bill's focus on activity banned under international Geneva Conventions and its focus on Israeli settlement activity.

The Governor's Office oversees the executive branch agencies responsible for implementing the bill (OAG and SOS) and coordinates policy initiatives regarding the state's relationship with international entities and nonprofit regulation.

DBM is responsible for the state's fiscal planning; the fiscal note indicates that the bill could lead to increased general fund expenditures for legal experts and potential revenue from civil damages.
As the state's tax collector, the Comptroller monitors the tax-exempt status of 501(c)(3) and (4) organizations, which are the specific types of entities targeted by this legislation.

It mandates that the OAH conduct hearings and issue final decisions on these suspension appeals, mirroring the existing process for WSSC employee removals.

stakeholders: Employees of the Washington Suburban Sanitary Commission
fiscal_impact_summary: The Office of Administrative Hearings and the Washington Suburban Sanitary Commission both report that the bill can be implemented using existing resources. No state or local revenue impact is anticipated.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill directly mandates the Office of Administrative Hearings (OAH) to hear and issue final decisions on appeals regarding disciplinary suspensions of Washington Suburban Sanitary Commission (WSSC) employees. The fiscal note indicates OAH will implement this new caseload within existing resources.

The Office of the Attorney General provides legal counsel to state agencies, including the Office of Administrative Hearings and the Washington Suburban Sanitary Commission (a bi-county state agency). It will be responsible for advising these entities on the implementation of the new disciplinary appeal procedures and representing them in related legal matters.

As the state's principal personnel agency, DBM oversees the State Personnel and Pensions Article, which this bill amends. Furthermore, the fiscal note mentions that OAH operates under authority delegated by DBM to conduct State Personnel Management System hearings, which is the framework used for these new WSSC appeals.

bill_summary: This bill updates the insurance and liability framework for peer-to-peer car sharing programs in Maryland. It modifies primary insurance requirements, allowing shared vehicle drivers to provide coverage, and clarifies that the Maryland Automobile Insurance Fund is not required to cover shared vehicles except in specific replacement cases. Additionally, the bill allows peer-to-peer car sharing programs to transfer liability for tolls and traffic citations to the shared vehicle driver and excludes these programs from being considered 'owners' for red light camera violations.
stakeholders: Peer-to-peer car sharing programs, shared vehicle owners, shared vehicle drivers, motor vehicle insurance companies, and the Maryland Automobile Insurance Fund.
fiscal_impact_summary: The bill is expected to result in a minimal increase in special fund revenues for the Maryland Insurance Administration in fiscal year 2027 due to rate and form filing fees. Enforcement and administrative tasks can be managed with existing resources. There is no projected local fiscal impact, and the Maryland Automobile Insurance Fund's finances and operations are not expected to be materially affected. Specific dollar estimates for the revenue increase are not provided in the fiscal note.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: As the primary regulator of the state's insurance market, the MIA is responsible for overseeing the bill's significant changes to motor vehicle liability requirements for peer-to-peer car sharing programs, including the review and approval of new rate and form filings.

The bill explicitly modifies the statutory obligations of MAIF by providing that it is not required to provide coverage to a shared vehicle driver for the use of a shared vehicle that is not a replacement vehicle.

The bill amends several sections of the Transportation Article and affects multiple modal administrations (MVA, MDTA, MAA, SHA) regarding vehicle owner definitions, toll liability, and airport concession fees.

An agency within MDOT, the MVA is responsible for driver and vehicle services; the bill alters the definition of 'owner' for traffic control citations and regulates the operation of peer-to-peer car sharing programs.

The MDTA operates the state's toll facilities; the bill specifically authorizes peer-to-peer car sharing programs to transfer monetary liability for tolls, fees, and fines to the shared vehicle driver.
The bill addresses the recovery of concession fees paid to government-operated airports, which directly impacts the MAA's management of facilities like BWI Thurgood Marshall Airport.

The bill clarifies liability and the definition of 'owner' for citations issued via traffic control signal monitoring systems, which are adjudicated through the state's judicial system supported by the AOC.
The MSP is responsible for traffic safety and law enforcement; the bill's provisions regarding citations for traffic control signal monitoring systems relate to their enforcement context.
The SHA manages traffic signals on state-numbered highways; the bill's changes to the definition of 'owner' for red-light camera citations impact the administrative framework for these systems.

bill_summary: This bill prohibits the Public Service Commission from approving rate increases for private water or sewage disposal companies if a county or municipality has initiated or expressed intent to initiate eminent domain proceedings. Additionally, it requires fact finders in such condemnation cases to consider the cost of necessary system upgrades and the potential for reduced customer rates under public ownership when determining the company's value.
stakeholders: Privately owned water companies, sewage disposal companies, county and municipal governments, and utility customers.
fiscal_impact_summary: A formal Fiscal Note is absent from the provided text, so specific dollar estimates are unavailable. The bill potentially creates an indeterminate revenue decrease for private utility companies by freezing rate increases during condemnation. It also affects the financial valuation of utilities during eminent domain proceedings by requiring consideration of system upgrades and potential ratepayer savings, which may impact acquisition costs for local governments.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill mandates that a fact finder in a condemnation (eminent domain) proceeding, which occurs within the Maryland court system, must consider specific factors such as system upgrades and potential bill reductions when a water or sewage company is being acquired.

The Maryland Department of the Environment (MDE) is the primary regulator of water and sewer system safety and reliability. The bill's requirement for fact-finders to consider 'reasonable system upgrades necessary... to provide safe and reliable service' touches upon MDE's technical standards and regulatory oversight.

The Office of Administrative Hearings may be involved in adjudicating contested cases related to utility regulations or administrative aspects of state agency decisions involving these companies, although the PSC often uses its own hearing examiners.

The Office of the Attorney General serves as the legal counsel for the Public Service Commission and other state agencies. It would be responsible for defending the state's position or interpreting the new legal requirements regarding rate increase prohibitions and eminent domain factors.

The Office of the People's Counsel represents residential utility consumers in proceedings before the Public Service Commission. The bill directly impacts rate increase cases and the valuation of utilities during public acquisition, both of which are central to the agency's advocacy mission.

The Public Service Commission is the primary agency affected by this bill, as it is explicitly prohibited from approving rate increases for water or sewage disposal companies if a local government has initiated or signaled an intent for eminent domain proceedings.

bill_summary: The 'End Hedge Fund Control of Maryland Homes Act of 2026' imposes an excise tax on the acquisition and excess ownership of single-family residences by certain institutional entities such as corporations, LLCs, and hedge funds. It establishes a 50% excise tax on the fair market value of new acquisitions and an annual $10,000 tax per property for residences held in excess of phased-down ownership limits. Revenue from these taxes is directed to the newly established Down Payment and Settlement Expense Loan Program Fund to assist eligible homebuyers.
responsible_party: The Comptroller of Maryland and the Maryland Department of Housing and Community Development
stakeholders: Institutional investors (hedge funds, REITs, corporations, and LLCs), the Comptroller of Maryland, the Department of Housing and Community Development, and eligible Maryland homebuyers.
fiscal_impact_summary: The bill establishes two new revenue sources: a 50% excise tax on the acquisition of single-family residences by institutional investors and an annual $10,000 excise tax for each residence owned beyond specified limits (eventually capped at 25 for general entities and 0 for hedge funds). Revenues are first allocated to cover the Comptroller's administrative costs, with the remainder deposited into the Down Payment and Settlement Expense Loan Program Fund. Because the formal Fiscal Note is not provided in the text, specific aggregate dollar estimates for total revenue or expenditures are unavailable.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill explicitly designates the Comptroller to administer the new Excess Ownership of Single-Family Residences Excise Tax, collect the revenue, distribute administrative costs, account for the new Down Payment and Settlement Expense Loan Program Fund, and adopt regulations for implementation.

The bill mandates that the Department (DHCD) administer the newly created Down Payment and Settlement Expense Loan Program Fund, which is funded by the new excise tax to support the existing Down Payment and Settlement Expense Loan Program.
The State Treasurer is explicitly required to hold the new Down Payment and Settlement Expense Loan Program Fund separately and invest its money in the same manner as other State money.

As the chief legal officer for state agencies, the OAG will provide legal counsel to the Comptroller and DHCD regarding the new tax and fund administration. The bill also establishes criminal penalties (misdemeanors and perjury) for tax violations, which may involve OAG enforcement or prosecution.

The bill amends the Tax - General Article regarding assessments and appeals for the new excise tax; the Maryland Tax Court is the administrative body responsible for hearing appeals from the final decisions of the Comptroller on such tax disputes.

The bill represents a significant executive policy initiative ('End Hedge Fund Control of Maryland Homes Act') that affects state revenue and housing policy, requiring coordination from the Governor's Office.

DBM is the principal fiscal agency; the bill creates a new special, nonlapsing fund and stipulates that expenditures must be made in accordance with the State Budget, affecting fiscal planning and execution.
The bill establishes new criminal offenses (misdemeanors for failure to file tax returns) which will be adjudicated within the state's judicial system, supported by the AOC.
