bill_summary: This bill establishes new expedited processing tiers and associated fees for documents filed with the State Department of Assessments and Taxation (SDAT). It specifically creates a 1-hour processing window for a $1,000 fee and a 30-minute processing window for a $1,500 fee, provided the documents have first been accepted for preclearance. It also updates the existing 2-hour expedited processing fee to $425.
responsible_party: State Department of Assessments and Taxation
stakeholders: Business entities, large law firms, and other parties filing corporate documents that require time-sensitive processing.
fiscal_impact_summary: The State Department of Assessments and Taxation (SDAT) can implement the bill with existing resources. State special fund revenues are expected to increase starting in fiscal 2028 from the new expedited filing fees ($1,000 for 1-hour and $1,500 for 30-minute processing). While the total revenue increase is indeterminate and depends on the volume of filings, the Fiscal Note provides an illustrative estimate that every 100 filings at the 1-hour tier would generate approximately 85000 in additional revenue. Local government finances are not affected.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill mandates that $50 of the $150 processing fee collected for certain nonstock corporations be credited to the Maryland Nonprofit Development Center Program Fund. This fund is established under the Economic Development Article and supports programs typically overseen by the Department of Commerce.

The bill explicitly references the employer-offered savings arrangement definition in the Labor and Employment Article to maintain a filing fee waiver for entities that participate in the MarylandSaves program or provide equivalent retirement savings options.

As the state's principal fiscal agency, DBM is responsible for revenue estimation and fiscal planning. The bill establishes new tiered expedited processing fees that the fiscal note projects will increase special fund revenues.

The Treasurer's Office is the chief financial agency responsible for the management and protection of state funds. It will be responsible for receiving and depositing the increased special fund revenues generated by the new fee tiers.

The OAG serves as the primary legal representative for all state agencies. It would be responsible for providing legal counsel to the State Department of Assessments and Taxation regarding the implementation of the new fee structure and the adoption of required regulations.

Synopsis: Establishing the Task Force to Study Postrelease Services and Requirements; and requiring the Task Force to report its findings and recommendations to the Governor and the General Assembly on or before July 1, 2027.
Title: Task Force to Study Postrelease Services and Requirements (Bri's Law)
Status: In the House - Hearing 3/05 at 1:00 p.m.

NarrowSubjects.Name: Public Safety and Correctional Services, Department of

bill_summary: This bill establishes the Task Force to Study Postrelease Services and Requirements, also known as Bri’s Law. The task force is responsible for studying different types of release from incarceration in Maryland and evaluating postrelease programs and requirements intended to prevent recidivism. The group must submit a report of its findings and recommendations to the Governor and the General Assembly by July 1, 2027.
responsible_party: Department of Public Safety and Correctional Services
stakeholders: Individuals released from incarceration, the Department of Public Safety and Correctional Services, and the Maryland State’s Attorneys’ Association
fiscal_impact_summary: The bill requires the Department of Public Safety and Correctional Services to provide staff for the task force and requires the state budget to cover travel expense reimbursements for task force members. Because a formal Fiscal Note was not provided in the text, specific dollar estimates are unavailable.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Department of Public Safety and Correctional Services
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Department of Public Safety and Correctional Services is the primary agency impacted by this bill. Its Secretary is designated as the Chair of the Task Force, and the department is responsible for providing all staffing and administrative support. Furthermore, the study focus (postrelease services and recidivism) aligns with its core mission of managing correctional facilities and community supervision.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Executive Commissions, Committees, Task Forces, and Advisory Boards
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: This bill directly establishes a new temporary task force within the executive branch to conduct a specialized study on postrelease services and provide recommendations to the Governor.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Governor's Office of Crime Prevention and Policy
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: As the state's primary coordinating body for public safety and recidivism strategies, this agency is highly relevant to a task force focused on improving postrelease programming to prevent individuals from recidivating.

The Governor's Office is responsible for overseeing executive branch agencies and policy initiatives. The Task Force is required to submit its final report of findings and recommendations to the Governor.

Postrelease services often include workforce development and adult learning programs, which are administered by the Department of Labor and are critical to the Task Force's mandate to study programs designed to prevent recidivism.

The OAG provides legal counsel to state boards, commissions, and task forces. They would likely be involved in advising the Task Force on the legal frameworks of various release types and postrelease requirements.
The bill provides for member reimbursement under Standard State Travel Regulations and mentions funding via the State budget, both of which are overseen by DBM.

The bill requires the Task Force to study 'each type of release from incarceration in the State.' While often focused on adults, this scope could include juvenile commitments and post-release aftercare services managed by DJS.

The Judiciary is responsible for setting the legal conditions of many forms of release; findings regarding postrelease requirements and recidivism will directly impact judicial policy and court-ordered programs.
A significant portion of postrelease programming involves behavioral health, substance abuse treatment, and developmental disability support, which are primary functions of the Department of Health.

DHS provides essential social services and economic aid (like SNAP or energy assistance) to vulnerable populations, including those transitioning out of incarceration, which are key postrelease services.
Stable housing is a fundamental component of postrelease programs aimed at reducing recidivism; the Task Force's recommendations may involve programs managed by this agency.

bill_summary: This bill allows mandatory reporters (such as health practitioners, police officers, educators, and human service workers) to notify a regional navigator about suspected child sex or labor trafficking if they believe it is necessary to prevent serious harm. This notification can occur without the child's consent and even over their objection. Additionally, the bill grants the State’s Attorney and the Office of the Attorney General the authority to investigate and prosecute human trafficking offenses.
responsible_party: The Office of the Attorney General and State's Attorney offices
stakeholders: Mandatory reporters (health practitioners, police officers, educators, human service workers), victims of child sex and labor trafficking, regional navigators, and legal authorities (State's Attorneys and the Attorney General).
fiscal_impact_summary: General fund expenditures may increase for the Office of the Attorney General (OAG) depending on the volume of investigations and prosecutions undertaken; the OAG estimates a potential need for approximately $382,384 in fiscal 2027, rising to $522,542 by fiscal 2031, though the exact impact is indeterminate until experience is gained under the bill. Local government finances and State's Attorney' workloads are not expected to be materially affected.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill explicitly authorizes the Attorney General to investigate and prosecute human trafficking violations, granting the office all the powers and duties of a State's Attorney for these cases. The fiscal note indicates a potential need for additional attorneys and investigators to handle the increased workload.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Governor's Office of Crime Prevention and Policy
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: GOCPP manages the grant funding for the Safe Harbor Regional Navigator Grant Program. The bill creates a new reporting pathway for mandatory reporters to notify these regional navigators directly of suspected trafficking.

DHS oversees local departments of social services which are central to child abuse and neglect reporting. Human service workers under DHS are mandatory reporters who gain the authority to report to regional navigators under this bill.

Educators and school staff are mandatory reporters of child abuse, including trafficking. The bill provides these professionals with the discretion to notify regional navigators to prevent harm to children.
Health practitioners are designated as mandatory reporters under the Family Law Article. This bill impacts their reporting protocols regarding suspected child sex and labor trafficking.

As mandatory reporters and the primary state law enforcement agency, the Maryland State Police are impacted by changes to reporting procedures and the authorization of the Attorney General to conduct concurrent investigations into human trafficking.

The bill specifically mentions staff of juvenile detention centers as mandatory reporters. DJS operates these facilities and manages the personnel who will be authorized to report to regional navigators.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Department of Public Safety and Correctional Services
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: Parole and probation officers are considered 'human service workers' under the mandatory reporting laws. This bill expands their reporting options when they suspect child trafficking.
The bill authorizes new prosecutorial power for the Attorney General, which could lead to an increase in human trafficking cases filed and adjudicated within the Maryland court system.

bill_summary: This bill requires the Maryland Public Service Commission to develop an implementation plan to convert formerly operational fossil fuel generating stations into natural gas generating stations. The plan must involve a public stakeholder process and include assessments of feasibility, costs, ownership structures, regulatory barriers, and a conversion timeline to be submitted to the Governor and General Assembly by January 1, 2027.
stakeholders: Maryland Public Service Commission, Office of People's Counsel, Maryland Energy Administration, Department of Natural Resources, Department of the Environment, electric and gas companies, generating station owners, and local governments.
fiscal_impact_summary: Specific dollar estimates are unavailable because the formal Fiscal Note was not provided in the text. The bill mandates that the Public Service Commission conduct a stakeholder process and create a detailed implementation plan, which will require administrative resources and potentially the hiring of external consultants. The resulting plan must include an assessment of costs associated with the plant conversions.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Public Service Commission is the primary agency responsible for developing the implementation plan, conducting the stakeholder process, and providing recommendations to the Governor and General Assembly.
The bill explicitly names the Office of People's Counsel as a mandatory stakeholder to provide input on the implementation plan, particularly regarding ratepayer costs.
The bill explicitly names the Maryland Energy Administration as a mandatory stakeholder to provide input on the state's energy policy and the transition to natural gas.
The bill explicitly names the Department of Natural Resources as a mandatory stakeholder to provide expertise on power plant research, environmental impact, and site evaluation.
The bill explicitly names the Department of the Environment as a mandatory stakeholder to address emissions, environmental regulation, and compliance for converted stations.
The Governor's Office oversees the executive branch and is the recipient of the final implementation plan and legislative recommendations mandated by the bill.
The agency serves as legal counsel to the PSC and the departments named as stakeholders and would likely assist in assessing legal/regulatory barriers and drafting necessary legislation.
The conversion of major industrial infrastructure impacts Maryland's economic competitiveness and energy reliability for businesses, which are primary concerns of the Department of Commerce.
The repurposing of formerly operational fossil fuel stations involves significant land use planning and resource management coordination, falling within the scope of the Department of Planning.

MEDCO is relevant to the bill's requirement to study the feasibility of non-utility entities taking ownership of generating stations and may be involved in the financial or real estate development aspect.
The bill requires a study on the feasibility of state entities taking ownership of generating stations, which would involve the expertise and potential future facility management role of DGS.
DBM oversees the personnel and fiscal resources of the multiple state agencies required to participate in the development of the implementation plan.

Synopsis: Altering certain provisions of law relating to the reporting of child abuse and neglect and the reporting of certain information regarding certain children at risk of harm to require reporting to the Department of Human Services instead of to the local department of social services or the appropriate law enforcement agency; requiring the Department to establish a centralized intake system for reports, assess reports for validity, and assign reports to the appropriate local department to investigate; etc.

bill_summary: This bill requires the Maryland Department of Human Services (DHS) to establish and maintain a centralized intake system for reports of child abuse and neglect. It shifts the responsibility for receiving initial reports of suspected abuse or neglect from local departments of social services and local law enforcement agencies to DHS. Under the new system, DHS must record each report, assess it for validity, and assign it to the appropriate local department for investigation.
stakeholders: Children at risk of abuse or neglect, parents and guardians, mandated reporters (including health practitioners, police officers, educators, and human service workers), and local departments of social services.
fiscal_impact_summary: State general fund expenditures for the Department of Human Services are estimated to increase by approximately 3,900,000 annually for personnel and operating costs. For fiscal year 2027, costs are estimated at 2,600,000 for hiring 33 staff members, plus 230,000 for a hotline platform, 34,908 for software licenses, and a one-time programming update of 177,048. The bill also poses a risk of decreased federal fund revenues if the centralized intake system is found to be out of compliance with federal standards under the Child Abuse Prevention and Treatment Act. Local government operations for law enforcement and State's Attorneys' offices will be impacted, though no material fiscal impact on local finances is anticipated.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: As the primary implementing agency, DHS is tasked with establishing and maintaining the centralized intake system for all child abuse and neglect reports, assessing reports for validity, and assigning them to local departments for investigation.

The bill has a significant fiscal impact, requiring an estimated $3.9 million annually for 33 new personnel and specialized software systems, which falls under DBM's oversight of the state budget and personnel management.

Educators are mandatory reporters under state law; the bill fundamentally changes their reporting process by requiring them to submit reports directly to the DHS centralized system rather than to local departments.

Health practitioners are mandatory reporters. Additionally, the bill specifically outlines reporting and investigation protocols for substance-exposed newborns, which are handled in MDH-regulated healthcare settings.

The fiscal note specifies requirements for a new hotline platform, software licenses, and programming updates for the state's Child Juvenile and Adult Management System to support the centralized intake mandate.

Police officers are mandatory reporters of child abuse. The bill shifts their reporting obligations to the new centralized DHS system and alters how law enforcement agencies coordinate initial reports.
The bill impacts the investigation process and reporting timelines that directly precede Child in Need of Assistance (CINA) petitions and other judicial proceedings in the state court system.

The bill explicitly names juvenile detention center staff as mandatory reporters who must utilize the new centralized reporting system, and DJS is involved in the welfare of youth within the justice system.

The OAG will provide legal counsel to DHS regarding the implementation of the centralized system, regulatory updates, and ensuring compliance with federal Child Abuse Prevention and Treatment Act (CAPTA) standards.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Governor's Office of Crime Prevention and Policy
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: GOCPP coordinates public safety strategies and manages funds related to victim services and juvenile delinquency, both of which are impacted by changes to child abuse reporting and investigation structures.
As an independent unit within MSDE, the center develops training and resources for school safety, which includes protocols for the mandatory reporting of child abuse and neglect.
The office is dedicated to the well-being of Maryland's children and families; the centralized intake system is a major policy shift in the state's framework for protecting vulnerable children.
The implementation of the bill requires significant state expenditures for new IT platforms and staffing, which may require the Board's approval of procurement contracts.

bill_summary: This bill regulates contractors providing disaster mitigation services (such as boarding up windows, water remediation, and tree removal) by requiring them to be licensed by the Maryland Home Improvement Commission. It establishes consumer protection measures, including the right for homeowners to rescind contracts within 5 to 7 days, and authorizes local governments to limit in-person solicitation following a disaster. Additionally, the bill prohibits contractors from offering to pay an insured party's deductible or providing other incentives in connection with insurance claims, classifying such acts as insurance fraud.
responsible_party: Maryland Home Improvement Commission (within the Maryland Department of Labor)
stakeholders: Home improvement contractors, disaster mitigation service providers, homeowners, tree experts, insurance companies, and claimants.
fiscal_impact_summary: The bill has no state fiscal impact in fiscal 2027 or 2028 due to a licensing exemption for contractors until November 2028. Beginning in fiscal 2029, special fund revenues and expenditures may increase minimally due to licensing fee collections and administrative costs. Nonbudgeted revenues and expenditures for the Home Improvement Guaranty Fund may also increase minimally starting in fiscal 2029. Local government finances are not materially affected.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Department of Labor houses the Maryland Home Improvement Commission (MHIC), which is the primary entity responsible for licensing and regulating the home improvement contractors and disaster mitigation services addressed in the bill.

The bill amends the Insurance Article and establishes new definitions and prohibitions regarding fraudulent insurance acts by contractors, which the Maryland Insurance Administration is responsible for regulating and enforcing.

The Office of the Attorney General enforces consumer protection laws, including the contract rescission rights established by the bill, and provides legal counsel to the Maryland Home Improvement Commission and the Maryland Insurance Administration.

The bill expands the definition of home improvement to include work done on trees, creating a regulatory overlap or intersection with the Department of Natural Resources' existing authority to license tree experts.

The Office of Administrative Hearings will be responsible for adjudicating contested cases and appeals resulting from enforcement actions or licensing decisions made by the Department of Labor or the Maryland Insurance Administration under this bill.
The bill modifies and establishes criminal penalties, including felonies and misdemeanors for insurance fraud, which impacts the judicial branch's caseload and administrative responsibilities.

As the state's principal fiscal agency, DBM will oversee the budget execution and potential increase in special fund revenues and expenditures for the Department of Labor and the Maryland Insurance Administration.

The Governor's Office oversees the executive branch agencies implementing the bill and is responsible for proposing the state budget, which will be impacted by the new licensing revenues and administrative costs.
The Office of Appointments assists the Governor in appointing members to the Maryland Home Improvement Commission, which will exercise the new regulatory powers granted by the bill.

bill_summary: This bill requires contractors on State public work contracts valued at $5 million or more in Baltimore City and Anne Arundel, Baltimore, Howard, Montgomery, and Prince George's counties to ensure that at least 35% of apprenticeship hours are performed by Maryland residents. The Maryland Department of Labor is tasked with enforcement, and contractors may alternatively contribute to the State Apprenticeship Training Fund or face penalties for noncompliance.
stakeholders: Construction contractors, Maryland residents enrolled in apprenticeship programs, and the Maryland Department of Labor.
fiscal_impact_summary: State special fund revenues increase from penalties and direct contributions to the State Apprenticeship Training Fund, though a reliable estimate is not feasible. The Maryland Department of Labor and other state agencies can implement the requirements with existing budgeted resources. There is no material impact on local government finances.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill designates the Maryland Department of Labor as the primary agency responsible for enforcing worker residency requirements, adopting necessary regulations, and managing the collection of penalties for the State Apprenticeship Training Fund.

As the state's primary procurement and construction management agency, DGS is responsible for awarding 'covered large projects' (public works over $5 million) and must ensure contractors comply with the residency attestation and reporting requirements.

MDOT oversees massive public works projects involving highways, bridges, and transit systems that frequently exceed $5 million. The agency must implement these residency requirements within its procurement processes for projects in the specified counties.

USM manages significant capital construction and public work projects on its various campuses. The bill's requirements for large projects in specified counties will impact its procurement operations and project oversight.

The Board of Public Works must approve significant state procurement contracts and expenditures. This bill adds a new compliance condition (worker residency) for the large-scale public works contracts under the Board's purview.

The Maryland Stadium Authority plans and builds large-scale sports, entertainment, and educational facilities that qualify as 'covered large projects.' It will be responsible for ensuring its contractors meet the 35% Maryland residency threshold for apprenticeship hours.

As an independent state agency that handles its own large-scale capital projects in Baltimore City (a specified jurisdiction), Morgan State will need to incorporate these worker residency requirements into its public work contracts.

The bill explicitly requires the Comptroller to account for the State Apprenticeship Training Fund, which will receive increased revenues from penalties and alternative contributions related to residency requirements.
The bill explicitly requires the State Treasurer to hold the State Apprenticeship Training Fund separately, as it is the custodian of the state funds receiving the bill's penalties.
The OAG will provide legal counsel to the Department of Labor for drafting the required regulations and may be involved in enforcing penalties against non-compliant contractors.

As the governor's chief policy-making body for the state's workforce system, the board is relevant to the bill's aim of using apprenticeship hours to benefit state residents and support the talent pipeline.
DBM is responsible for fiscal planning and oversight. The bill impacts special fund revenues and potentially administrative costs that fall under DBM's budgetary supervision.

bill_summary: This bill prohibits the Maryland Department of Health from collecting fees for vital records (such as death or marriage certificates) issued to homeless individuals and waives certain driver's license and vehicle emissions inspection fees for the homeless population. Additionally, it reduces the waiting period from nine months to three months for homeless youth under age 19 to take driver's license examinations.
responsible_party: Maryland Department of Health and the Motor Vehicle Administration
stakeholders: Homeless individuals (including children and youth) and homeless service providers in Maryland.
fiscal_impact_summary: State Transportation Trust Fund revenues are expected to decrease minimally beginning in FY 2027 due to the exemption of driver's license and vehicle emissions inspection fees. General fund revenues from vital records fees are anticipated to decrease negligibly. Local health department revenues may also be negligibly impacted, but specific dollar estimates are unavailable as the number of qualifying individuals is unknown.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill directly prohibits the Maryland Department of Health from collecting fees for vital records (birth, death, marriage, and divorce certificates) issued to homeless individuals and requires the department to adopt implementing regulations.

Through the Motor Vehicle Administration (MVA), the department is responsible for implementing the bill's exemptions for driver's license fees and vehicle emissions inspections (VEIP), altering examination wait times for homeless youth, and reporting data to the General Assembly.

MDE co-manages the Vehicle Emissions Inspection Program (VEIP) with the MVA. The bill creates a new mandatory inspection exemption for vehicles owned by homeless individuals, which falls under MDE's regulatory scope for air quality and emissions.

bill_summary: The Maryland Stablecoin Act establishes a regulatory and legal framework for businesses providing payment stablecoin services in Maryland. It requires nondepository trust companies and credit union service organizations to obtain a certificate from the Office of Financial Regulation to operate as payment stablecoin service institutions or state issuers. The bill also aligns Maryland law with the federal GENIUS Act of 2025 and reduces the examination fee for new commercial bank charters from $15,000 to $7,000.
responsible_party: Office of Financial Regulation (OFR) within the Maryland Department of Labor
stakeholders: Financial institutions including nondepository trust companies, credit union service organizations, commercial banks, and credit unions, as well as consumers using digital payment stablecoin services.
fiscal_impact_summary: The Office of Financial Regulation can implement the bill's provisions using existing budgeted resources. State special fund revenues are not expected to be materially affected; while the examination fee for new commercial bank charters is reduced by $8,000 per instance, these applications are infrequent and any lost revenue is expected to be recovered through annual assessments on the regulated institutions. There is no significant impact on local government finances.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Department of Labor's Office of Financial Regulation (OFR) is the primary implementing agency for the Maryland Stablecoin Act. The Commissioner of Financial Regulation is designated as the State Payment Stablecoin Regulator, responsible for certifying issuers, conducting examinations, and enforcing the regulatory framework established under the new Title 14.

The Office of the Attorney General provides primary legal counsel to the Commissioner of Financial Regulation and would represent the state in enforcement actions or legal challenges related to the oversight of stablecoin institutions.

The bill explicitly references the right to a hearing under the Administrative Procedure Act for entities contesting the denial or revocation of a certificate, a function performed by Administrative Law Judges at the OAH.

The Governor's Office oversees the executive branch departments involved in this new regulatory framework and is responsible for the overall coordination of financial and economic policy initiatives within the state.

Stablecoins are digital assets reliant on blockchain technology and complex IT infrastructure; DoIT oversees the state's overarching information technology and cybersecurity strategy which intersects with the regulation of digital assets.

TEDCO supports early-stage technology-based businesses; the regulation of payment stablecoins directly affects the regulatory environment for Maryland fintech startups that TEDCO may support or invest in.

The Comptroller, as the state's chief financial officer, maintains a general interest in laws affecting financial institutions and the potential tax and revenue implications of newly regulated asset classes.

bill_summary: The Maryland Employee Civic Activity and Lawful Expression Protection Act protects employees and job applicants from adverse employment actions based on their engagement in off-duty civic activities, political activities, or lawful expressions. The bill limits when employers can require disclosure of such activities, prohibits retaliation for refusing to participate in employer-favored political events, and allows individuals to seek injunctive relief and significant damages, including triple lost wages, through civil court actions or complaints to the Attorney General.
responsible_party: Maryland Department of Labor and the Maryland Attorney General
stakeholders: Maryland employees (including apprentices, interns, and part-time workers), job applicants, and all Maryland employers including state and local government agencies.
fiscal_impact_summary: Specific dollar estimates from a formal Fiscal Note are unavailable. The bill creates potential fiscal impacts for the state and local governments as employers, who may face increased litigation and significant damage awards (including a minimum of three times lost wages plus one year of wages) for violations. Additionally, the Maryland Department of Labor is responsible for developing employee notices, and the Attorney General is authorized to investigate complaints, which may increase administrative and enforcement expenditures.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill adds a new subtitle to the Labor and Employment Article, which falls under the jurisdiction of the Department of Labor. Additionally, Section 3-1908 specifically requires the Department to develop the mandatory notices that employers with 50 or more employees must post and distribute.

The bill explicitly designates the Attorney General to receive and investigate complaints from individuals regarding violations of the Act, and authorizes the use of all legal remedies available for enforcement.

As the central personnel agency for the State of Maryland, DBM is responsible for managing state employee policies. Since the bill defines 'employer' to include units of State government, DBM must ensure executive branch compliance with these new protections for state workers.

The bill impacts the management and expression rights of all executive branch employees and interns. As the Governor's Office oversees the executive branch and coordinates state policy, it is relevant to the implementation of these protections across the government.

bill_summary: Known as the Dimeka Thornton Act, this bill requires all Maryland law enforcement agencies to submit their police pursuit policies to the Maryland Police Training and Standards Commission annually. The Commission is required to report pursuit data—including reasons for pursuit, outcomes, and any injuries or fatalities—to the Governor and General Assembly. Additionally, the Commission must develop a model pursuit policy by 2028, which all state law enforcement agencies must subsequently adopt or exceed.
responsible_party: Maryland Police Training and Standards Commission
stakeholders: Law enforcement agencies, law enforcement officers, fleeing suspects, and the general public (bystanders).
fiscal_impact_summary: State and local law enforcement agencies will incur administrative costs related to annual policy submission and pursuit data reporting. The Maryland Police Training and Standards Commission will face increased expenditures to analyze data, produce annual reports, and develop a model policy. Specific dollar estimates are unavailable because the formal Fiscal Note was not included in the provided text.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Governor's Office receives the annual report from the Commission regarding pursuit statistics, reasons, outcomes, and recommendations for best practices.
The Commission is required to consult with the Attorney General when developing the annual report on police pursuit data and recommendations.
The agency oversees the public education system, where local school systems may operate law enforcement units that are subject to the bill's pursuit policy requirements.

bill_summary: This bill establishes that a conspiracy to commit a crime involving a controlled dangerous substance (such as distribution or possession with intent to distribute) carries the same penalty as the underlying crime. It also specifies the venue for prosecuting drug-related crimes and crimes committed in furtherance of a criminal organization, allowing prosecution in counties where an act occurred, where the organization's operations were centered, where proceeds or records were kept, or where the defendant resides. Additionally, it permits the joining of causes of action across multiple counties with the consent of the respective State's Attorneys.
responsible_party: Maryland State's Attorneys, the Office of the Attorney General, and the Maryland Judiciary
stakeholders: Individuals charged with drug-related conspiracy or criminal organization offenses, State's Attorneys, the Attorney General, and the Maryland court system.
fiscal_impact_summary: Specific dollar estimates are unavailable as a formal Fiscal Note was not included in the provided text. However, aligning conspiracy penalties with those of underlying drug offenses may increase incarceration costs for the State, and the modified venue and joinder rules may impact administrative expenditures for the judiciary and local State's Attorneys' offices.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill explicitly authorizes the Attorney General to join causes of action in single complaints when controlled dangerous substance violations occur in multiple counties, provided there is consent from the respective State's Attorneys.

The notice informs patients that while breast arterial calcification is a common finding, it may be an indicator of an increased risk of cardiovascular disease and advises them to discuss the results with their physician to assess cardiovascular risks.
stakeholders: Patients receiving mammograms, healthcare providers, and mammography centers including hospitals and clinics
fiscal_impact_summary: The bill is not anticipated to materially affect State or local finances or operations. Small business impact is estimated to be minimal. The Maryland Department of Health may adopt regulations to update the notice content if medical evidence changes.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Maryland Department of Health (MDH) is the primary agency responsible for overseeing the bill's implementation. Under the bill, 'The Department' is specifically authorized to adopt regulations to change the content of the arterial calcification notice if current medical evidence changes.

As an independent regulatory agency within MDH, the MHCC is responsible for health system planning and promoting informed decision-making for patients. The bill's requirement for mammography centers to provide specific diagnostic information directly impacts the commission's mission regarding health quality and patient access to information.

The OAG serves as the chief legal officer for the State of Maryland and provides legal counsel to MDH. It would be involved in reviewing and drafting any regulations the Department adopts to modify the mandatory patient notices.

The University System of Maryland operates extensive clinical facilities and academic medical centers. These centers perform mammography testing and would be required to update their administrative procedures and screening results letters to include the mandated notice.

bill_summary: This bill requires health insurance carriers to provide coverage for the evaluation and management of menopause and associated symptoms. It mandates that health occupations boards grant double continuing education credits (two hours for every one hour of training) for menopause-related education. Additionally, the bill requires the Maryland Department of Health and the Maryland Commission for Women to evaluate and report on state policy initiatives, clinical education opportunities, and methods to increase access to menopause-related healthcare services.
responsible_party: Maryland Department of Health and the Maryland Commission for Women
stakeholders: Individuals experiencing perimenopause, menopause, and postmenopause; healthcare providers; and health insurance carriers.
fiscal_impact_summary: State general fund expenditures increase by $100,300 in FY 2027 and $30,200 in FY 2028 for the Maryland Department of Health to hire a part-time contractual health policy analyst and a vendor to complete required evaluations and reports. Special fund revenues for the Maryland Insurance Administration increase minimally in FY 2027 due to $125 rate and form filing fees. Local governments may experience increased health care expenditures if they purchase fully insured health plans. The State Employee and Retiree Health and Welfare Benefits Program is expected to see no material impact as it already covers these services.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: MDH is the primary agency responsible for the bill's implementation. It must identify training programs, consult with health occupations boards on continuing education, evaluate access to menopause health care with community health workers, and evaluate methods for clinical education in higher education institutions.

MIA is responsible for regulating the insurance market and ensuring that insurers, nonprofit health service plans, and HMOs comply with the new mandate to provide coverage for the evaluation and management of menopause.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Executive Commissions, Committees, Task Forces, and Advisory Boards
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill directly alters the membership and statutory duties of the State Advisory Council on Health and Wellness. It also tasks the Maryland Commission for Women with conducting a major study on policy initiatives to improve health and economic security.
The Maryland Commission for Women is administratively housed within DHS. The bill tasks the Commission with evaluating state policy initiatives and reporting findings to the General Assembly.
DBM oversees the State Employee and Retiree Health and Welfare Benefits Program. The fiscal note indicates the department evaluated the impact of the new insurance mandate on the state plan.
The Secretary of Aging is a permanent member of the State Advisory Council on Health and Wellness, whose membership and structure are modified by this bill.
The Secretary of Disabilities is a permanent member of the State Advisory Council on Health and Wellness, which is being reorganized under the bill.
The State Superintendent of Schools is a permanent member of the State Advisory Council on Health and Wellness, which is being reorganized under the bill.
The bill requires MDH to consult with institutions of higher education to evaluate methods for increasing clinical education on menopause; the Commission coordinates these institutions.
The USM and its member institutions are potential entities for consultation by MDH regarding clinical and postgraduate education methods for menopause treatment.
As a public research university, Morgan State may be consulted by MDH regarding clinical education and treatment methods for menopause as required by Section 5 of the bill.
The Governor's Office oversees the executive branch departments (MDH, DHS) and coordinates the policy initiatives related to public health and women's health addressed in the bill.
The OAG provides legal counsel to MDH and the health occupations boards as they develop new regulations for continuing education and implement new statutory requirements.

Synopsis: Requiring all relief granted under a final protective order to remain effective against a respondent on probation during the period of the respondent's probation.
Title: Family Law - Final Protective Orders - Duration
Status: In the House - Hearing 3/12 at 1:30 p.m.
bill_summary: This bill mandates that all relief granted under a final protective order remains in effect for the duration of a respondent's probation if the respondent is on probation when the order is issued or is placed on probation during the order's effective period. It prevents the termination of such protective relief before the expiration or court-ordered termination of the probation.
stakeholders: Individuals eligible for protective orders (petitioners), respondents of protective orders who are on probation, and the Maryland court system.
fiscal_impact_summary: State general fund expenditures increase by $223,100 in fiscal 2027 for one-time programming costs within the Judiciary to automate the review of respondent probation status before protective orders expire. There is no anticipated material impact on local government finances or state revenues.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Judiciary (Administrative Office of the Courts) is the primary implementing agency. The bill requires the courts to track probation status for respondents and adjust the duration of final protective orders accordingly. The fiscal note identifies a one-time programming cost of $223,100 for the Judiciary to update its systems.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Department of Public Safety and Correctional Services
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: This agency manages the Division of Parole and Probation. Since the bill ties the duration of a final protective order to the respondent's probation period, DPSCS will be responsible for providing the court with accurate data regarding when a respondent's probation begins, expires, or is terminated.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Maryland Office of the Public Defender
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Office of the Public Defender represents indigent individuals who may be respondents in protective order proceedings. This bill increases the duration of legal restrictions and potential penalties for their clients, impacting their defense and legal strategy.

The Maryland State Police are responsible for enforcing protective orders, maintaining the state's registry of active orders, and overseeing the mandatory surrender of firearms for the duration of an order. Extending the duration of these orders extends the agency's enforcement and administrative duties.

As the state's principal fiscal agency, DBM is responsible for managing the state budget and would oversee the allocation of the $223,100 required for the Judiciary to implement the system changes necessitated by this bill.

DHS manages domestic violence support services and works with victims who seek protective orders. Changes to the duration of these orders directly impact the safety planning and resource management for the vulnerable populations the agency serves.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Governor's Office of Crime Prevention and Policy
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: This office serves as the state's coordinating body for public safety and advises on criminal justice strategies. The bill affects victim safety and the legal framework for domestic violence prevention, which falls under their policy purview.

The OAG provides legal counsel to the state agencies and the Judiciary. They would be responsible for interpreting the legal requirements of the bill and representing the state in related litigation or policy development.

Synopsis: Establishing a Commission on Re-Imagining Health Care to envision and make recommendations regarding establishing a comprehensive, patient-centered  health care system in the State; and requiring the Commission to submit a preliminary report by December 1, 2027, and a final report of the Commission's findings and recommendations to the Governor and the General Assembly by December 1, 2029.

bill_summary: This bill establishes the Commission on Re-Imagining Health Care in Maryland to envision and make recommendations for a comprehensive, patient-centered health care system that integrates somatic, behavioral, dental, vision, and hearing services. The commission is tasked with studying global delivery models, reimbursement rates, and insurance barriers to suggest improvements to the State's health care infrastructure.
stakeholders: Maryland residents, health care practitioners, health insurance carriers, hospitals, managed care organizations, and state and local health agencies.
fiscal_impact_summary: The bill's implementation is contingent upon the Maryland Health Care Commission securing private funding. If sufficient private funding is secured and notice is provided to the Department of Legislative Services by June 1, 2027, special fund revenues and expenditures will increase by an indeterminate amount between fiscal 2027 and 2030. These funds would support commission operations, including potential contractual staff and reporting requirements. No local fiscal impact is anticipated.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Maryland Health Care Commission (MHCC) is the primary implementing agency. The bill mandates that MHCC provide staff for the Commission, determine the required funding levels, and secure private funding to enable the Commission to function. The Executive Director of MHCC is also a named member.

The Secretary of Health and the Deputy Secretary of Health Care Financing (Medicaid) are named members of the Commission. The Commission's goal to re-imagine the entire state health care system, including somatic and behavioral health, directly aligns with the Department's core mission and regulatory scope.

The Governor's Office is responsible for appointing 11 members of the Commission, jointly designating the chair, and receiving the Commission's preliminary and final reports. The Commission's findings will likely shape future health policy initiatives proposed by the Executive Department.

The Secretary of Budget and Management is a named member of the Commission. The agency's involvement is critical because the Commission is tasked with envisioning a system that is 'financially sustainable.'

The Maryland Insurance Commissioner is a named member of the Commission. The Commission's study includes analyzing how health insurance deductibles and networks affect care, which falls under the MIA's regulatory oversight.

The Executive Director of the Maryland Health Benefit Exchange is a named member of the Commission. The Commission's focus on universal access and eliminating barriers to care is central to the Exchange's mission of providing accessible and affordable health coverage.

The Executive Director of the HSCRC is a named member of the Commission. The Commission's study of hospital roles and the cost-balance of the health care system is directly relevant to the HSCRC's authority over hospital rate-setting and hospital-payer systems.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Executive Commissions, Committees, Task Forces, and Advisory Boards
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: This bill establishes a new Commission on Re-Imagining Health Care in Maryland, which fits the definition of this collective entity as a temporary body created by the General Assembly to address specific government policy issues.
The bill specifically requires the Commission to study 'the role of the worker's compensation program in an integrated system,' making it directly relevant to this agency's mandate.
The Office of Appointments will assist the Governor in recruiting and vetting the 11 specific representatives and public members appointed to the Commission.

The Commission is tasked with studying 'new models of health care practitioner education and development,' which falls under the regulatory and policy-making purview of the Maryland Higher Education Commission regarding academic programs and financial aid for students in these fields.

As the provider of much of the state's medical and health practitioner education, USM is directly impacted by the Commission's mandate to study new models of education and development for health care practitioners.

The OAG will likely provide legal counsel to the Commission and the various state agencies (MDH, MHCC, MIA, etc.) involved in drafting the recommendations and interpreting the requirements of the bill.

Synopsis: Requiring the parents of a child with a disability who has an individualized education program to receive a written notice when a certain special education or related service aid specified in the individualized education program is missed, incomplete, or interrupted as specified; requiring the notice to explain the missed, incomplete or interrupted service aid and the reason the service aid, or support was missed; requiring the notice to provide parents with information on requesting a certain meeting to discuss certain matters; etc.
Title: Special Education - Individualized Education Program - Notification of Missed Services (Shifra's Act)
Status: In the House - Hearing 3/11 at 1:45 p.m.

bill_summary: Known as Shifra's Act, this bill requires local school systems to notify parents in writing when special education services, related services, or supplementary aids and supports specified in an Individualized Education Program (IEP) are not initiated on time or are missed, incomplete, or interrupted according to specific frequency thresholds. The notification must be provided within three school days and include the reason for the service failure, corrective steps the school system will take, and information for parents to request an IEP meeting for compensatory services or dispute resolution.
stakeholders: Children with disabilities who have an IEP, their parents or guardians, and Maryland local school systems.
fiscal_impact_summary: The bill does not materially affect State operations or finances. However, local school system expenditures are expected to increase substantially beginning in fiscal 2027, potentially by millions of dollars statewide. These costs relate to developing or enhancing service tracking systems, providing compensatory services, conducting additional IEP meetings, and administrative efforts to generate and deliver timely notifications.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: As the primary agency overseeing Maryland's public education system and special education programs, the Department of Education is responsible for the policies and leadership surrounding Individualized Education Programs (IEPs) and ensuring that local school systems comply with the bill's notification requirements.

The Department of Juvenile Services operates the Juvenile Services Education Program, which is specifically identified in the bill's fiscal note as a 'public agency' responsible for providing education to students with disabilities and would thus be required to implement these notification procedures for its students.

As a state agency providing public education and comprehensive services through IEPs to deaf and hard-of-hearing students, the Maryland School for the Deaf is a 'public agency' that must comply with the bill's mandate to track and notify parents of missed or interrupted services.

The Office of Administrative Hearings adjudicates special education due process complaints; the bill's requirement for notifications regarding missed services and compensatory services could lead to an increase in administrative hearings and disputes related to IEP implementation.

The bill directly impacts the delivery and transparency of services for students with disabilities, which is central to this department's mission of coordinating and improving services and policies for Maryland residents with disabilities.

The Office of the Attorney General provides legal counsel to the Department of Education and other state-run educational programs, and would be responsible for advising these agencies on the legal requirements and implementation of 'Shifra's Act'.

The unit provides technical assistance, guidance, and coordination to strengthen internal controls and requires an annual report on the progress of corrective actions to the Joint Audit and Evaluation Committee.

These costs include nine additional regular positions and $650,000 in annual contractor costs. Future years reflect ongoing personnel and operating costs, estimated between $2,140,000 and $2,350,000 through FY 2031. There is no impact on local government finances or state revenues.

DBM is the primary agency responsible for monitoring audit findings across the executive branch and has received significant contingent appropriations to staff the new unit.

The bill deals specifically with unredacted cybersecurity findings, and the fiscal note indicates DoIT is piloting a management tool to track audit findings. DoIT is also specifically identified as an agency with repeat audit findings requiring monitoring.

The bill re-enacts and modifies statutory language requiring the Chief Justice of the Supreme Court of Maryland to implement monitoring systems for the Judiciary's audit findings, which is supported by the Administrative Office of the Courts.

The Comptroller's office is specifically identified in the fiscal note as an executive unit with repeat audit findings in 2024, making it a primary subject of the new monitoring and technical assistance unit.

The Department of General Services is explicitly mentioned in the fiscal note as having repeat audit findings in 2025, which subjects it to oversight and direct assistance from the newly created AFCU.
The Maryland Department of Health is explicitly named as having repeat audit findings in both 2024 and 2025 reports, making it a key focus for the AFCU's direct assistance and monitoring efforts.
This agency was specifically identified in the fiscal note as having repeat audit findings in 2024, requiring monitoring and corrective action under the new AFCU framework.

bill_summary: This bill authorizes the Town of Rising Sun to implement a three-year pilot program for stop sign monitoring systems on highways within school zones. It requires local authorization by the Board of Commissioners and public notice before the automated systems can capture recorded images of violations. Drivers who fail to come to a complete stop at a stop sign are subject to a civil penalty of up to $40, which is adjudicated through the District Court and does not result in points on a driving record or insurance impacts.
responsible_party: Town of Rising Sun Board of Commissioners
stakeholders: Motorists in the Town of Rising Sun and the Town of Rising Sun local government
fiscal_impact_summary: State general fund revenues increase minimally beginning in FY 2027 due to contested citations in District Court. Local revenues and expenditures for the Town of Rising Sun will increase as the town installs monitoring systems and collects civil penalties of up to $40 per violation. The Judiciary notes a general $1,400,000 cost for upgrading case management systems for automated enforcement, though this cost is not exclusively attributable to this bill.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The District Court, supported by the AOC, must develop uniform citation forms, adjudicate contested cases, and adopt procedures for trial and civil penalty collection associated with the pilot program.
SHA is required to authorize the placement of monitoring systems on State highways in school zones and is specifically mandated to install signs providing notice of the systems.
As the parent agency for SHA and MVA, MDOT oversees the state's transportation network and coordinates the implementation of automated enforcement systems across its modal administrations.
The MVA is responsible for enforcing sanctions against vehicle owners who fail to pay citations, including the authority to refuse or suspend vehicle registrations.
The OAG provides legal counsel to the Judiciary and MDOT regarding the establishment of new enforcement protocols and compliance with the Maryland Vehicle Law.
As the primary state law enforcement agency, MSP is involved in state highway safety and may act as the law enforcement agency responsible for reviewing recorded images.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Governor's Office of Crime Prevention and Policy
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: GOCPP advises on statewide public safety strategies and coordinates policies related to law enforcement and the use of technology to reduce traffic violations.
DBM monitors the fiscal impact on the state budget, as fine revenues from contested citations are deposited into the state's general fund.
The Governor's Office oversees the executive branch departments, including MDOT and MSP, which are responsible for the pilot program's implementation and signage requirements.

bill_summary: This bill establishes the Maryland–Africa and the Caribbean Investment and Development Program and the Maryland African Diaspora Investment and Development Fund within the Department of Commerce. The program is designed to foster trade and economic ties between Maryland's African Diaspora and the Africa/Caribbean regions by providing financial and technical assistance to eligible businesses.
stakeholders: Members of the African Diaspora in Maryland, businesses owned by or partnered with the African Diaspora, and residents of Northeast Baltimore and other designated communities.
fiscal_impact_summary: The bill mandates an annual General Fund appropriation of 10000000 dollars from fiscal 2028 through 2032 to the Maryland African Diaspora Investment and Development Fund. The Department of Commerce will incur administrative expenses to manage the program and advisory board. Local fiscal impact includes potential economic development and job creation in Northeast Baltimore and other designated areas, as businesses receiving funds must hire at least 50 percent of new hires from the local community.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill designates the Department of Commerce as the primary agency responsible for administering the Maryland–Africa and the Caribbean Investment and Development Program and the Maryland African Diaspora Investment and Development Fund.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill establishes a new Advisory Board for the Program to conduct studies and make recommendations regarding bilateral trade and investment.
The Governor is responsible for appointing the majority of the members of the newly created Advisory Board and overseeing the executive policy initiatives established by this bill.
This office, within the Executive Department, will be responsible for recruiting and vetting the various candidates for the Advisory Board positions appointed by the Governor.
The bill mandates a significant annual appropriation of $10,000,000 from fiscal year 2028 through 2032, which DBM must oversee and include in the state budget.

The Secretary of State manages international affairs and sister state programs, which aligns with the bill's goal of promoting bilateral trade and economic development between Maryland and the Africa/Caribbean region.

The Division of International Affairs within the Secretary of State's office serves as the primary diplomatic liaison for the state and would be relevant to the program's international trade and development objectives.
The bill requires the State Treasurer to hold the Maryland African Diaspora Investment and Development Fund separately and invest its money.
The Comptroller is tasked with accounting for the newly established Maryland African Diaspora Investment and Development Fund.

The Advisory Board must include a representative from a historically black college or university (HBCU); additionally, the bill's focus on Northeast Baltimore and urban investment aligns with Morgan State's mission and location.
The bill requires academic representatives on the Advisory Board, which may include faculty from USM's HBCU institutions such as Bowie State, Coppin State, or UMES.
The Advisory Board includes a representative of organized labor, and the bill mandates that businesses receiving funds must comply with prevailing wage requirements for construction.

It also requires the Maryland Health Care Commission, in collaboration with the Office of Health Care Quality, to publish facility inspection dates and quality metrics on the Maryland Quality Reporting website. Furthermore, it mandates that health occupations boards certify annually that their information technology systems meet state cybersecurity standards.
responsible_party: Maryland Health Centralization Commission, Maryland Health Care Commission, and the Department of Information Technology
stakeholders: Maryland Department of Health, health occupations boards, health care professionals, health care facilities, and the general public
fiscal_impact_summary: According to the Fiscal Note, the bill's requirements can be handled with existing budgeted resources, and revenues are not affected. Commission members are entitled to reimbursement for travel expenses under standard regulations, but these costs are expected to be absorbed. The analysis does not account for potential future costs associated with implementing the commission's eventual recommendations.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: MDH is the primary agency affected by the bill. Its Office of Health Care Quality must collaborate on publishing inspection data, the Secretary and Deputy Secretary serve on the newly created commission, and the bill focuses on the relationship between MDH and its health occupations boards.

MHCC is a primary implementing agency, required to collaborate with MDH to publish health facility inspection information and quality metrics on its public reporting website, and its future usage is a topic for the commission's recommendations.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill explicitly establishes the Maryland Health Centralization Commission as a new body to study health board oversight and provide recommendations to the General Assembly.

The Secretary of Information Technology is given a new statutory oversight role to ensure health occupations boards comply with minimum cybersecurity standards and must receive annual certifications from those boards.
The bill was introduced based on OLA's fiscal compliance audit findings, and the new commission is specifically mandated to recommend how health boards can remedy OLA audit findings and violations.
The Governor receives annual reports from the new commission and oversees the executive branch departments (MDH, DoIT) tasked with implementing the bill's requirements.
The bill specifies that commission members are reimbursed via standard state travel regulations provided in the state budget, which DBM manages as the state's principal fiscal and personnel agency.

The commission's scope includes recommending policies for criminal history records checks and the receipt of information from the Central Repository, which involves records managed by the state's primary law enforcement and identification systems.
