bill_summary: This bill modifies the regulatory framework for retail electricity and gas suppliers in Maryland by repealing the classification and licensing of 'energy salespersons' and instead regulating 'energy vendors.' It requires the Public Service Commission (PSC) to establish an Energy Choice Multimedia Program for consumer education, updates license renewal procedures for energy suppliers, and mandates new consumer protection notices for automatic renewals and price increases exceeding 10%. Additionally, it grants the PSC authority over energy vendor lists and provides due process protections for licensees.
stakeholders: Residential and small commercial electricity and gas customers, electricity suppliers, gas suppliers, energy vendors, and electric and gas utility companies.
fiscal_impact_summary: The bill has several financial implications: it allows for civil penalties of up to $25,000 per violation to be deposited into the Education and Protection Fund and maintains licensing and renewal fees. It also requires the Public Service Commission to fund and administer a new Energy Choice Multimedia Program, involving annual mailings and bill inserts. Because the formal Fiscal Note was not provided in the text, specific total dollar estimates for expenditures or revenues are unavailable.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Public Service Commission is the primary agency tasked with implementing and enforcing the bill's provisions, including licensing electricity and gas suppliers, establishing the Energy Choice Multimedia Program, and overseeing the Education and Protection Fund.

The bill explicitly references the People's Counsel as having authority in licensing, complaint, and dispute resolution proceedings and allows them to file complaints against suppliers for just cause.

The bill requires the Public Service Commission to consult with the Consumer Protection Division of the Office of the Attorney General before adopting certain regulations and acknowledges the OAG's role in enforcing consumer protection laws.
The bill requires the State Treasurer to hold the Education and Protection Fund separately and invest its money in the same manner as other State money.
The bill mandates that the Comptroller account for the Education and Protection Fund used for customer education and protection initiatives.

The Department of General Services is explicitly mentioned as an entity that sells energy under the Public Utilities Article and is carved out from certain regulatory definitions and licensing requirements amended by the bill.

The bill's education programs are specifically required to inform customers on energy choices that help meet the State’s climate commitments under statutes administered by the Department of the Environment.

As the state's energy policy agency, the MEA is impacted by shifts in the regulatory landscape for retail electricity and gas supply and the state's strategies for consumer education and climate goals.

The bill requires due process before the suspension or revocation of licenses, which often involves the impartial hearing process provided by the Office of Administrative Hearings for contested executive agency cases.
The bill specifies that expenditures from the Education and Protection Fund may only be made in accordance with the State budget, which is overseen by the Department of Budget and Management.
The Governor's Office oversees the Public Service Commission and the executive branch agencies responsible for the bill's fiscal and policy outcomes.

Synopsis: Authorizing the Washington County Health Department to exempt the owner of a certain residential property from compliance with all or part of a certain on-site sewage disposal system regulation if compliance with the regulation would be unduly burdensome; and establishing requirements for the consideration and issuance of exemptions under the Act.
Title: Washington County - On-Site Sewage Disposal System Regulations - Exemptions
Status: In the House - Hearing 3/11 at 1:00 p.m.
bill_summary: This bill authorizes the Washington County Health Department to exempt residential property owners in Washington County Agricultural (Rural) or Rural Village zoning districts from compliance with specific on-site sewage disposal system regulations. To qualify, an owner must prove that compliance is unduly burdensome due to physical or financial impracticality, supported by a report from a licensed on-site wastewater professional. Exemptions are valid for up to three years or until the property changes ownership and may be renewed.
stakeholders: Residential property owners in rural Washington County zones, the Washington County Health Department, and licensed on-site wastewater professionals.
fiscal_impact_summary: A formal Fiscal Note is not provided in the text. The bill creates an application and review process for septic system exemptions which involves administrative duties for the Washington County Health Department and costs for property owners to obtain professional reports. However, property owners could see financial savings by being exempted from expensive septic regulations. Specific dollar estimates are unavailable.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill directly empowers the Washington County Health Department to grant exemptions for on-site sewage disposal systems. The Department of Health oversees local health departments and sets public health policy regarding sanitation.

The regulations from which owners may be exempted (COMAR 26.04.02) are promulgated by the Department of the Environment, which is responsible for implementing and enforcing state environmental laws regarding water quality and pollution control.

The Office of the Attorney General provides legal counsel to the Department of Health and the Department of the Environment regarding the interpretation and enforcement of regulatory exemptions and the definition of 'unduly burdensome' compliance.

As the independent agency that adjudicates contested cases for state and local agencies, the Office of Administrative Hearings would likely handle appeals regarding the denial of exemption permits under this Act.

The bill requires a report from an individual licensed by the State Board of On-Site Wastewater Professionals; the Department of Labor is responsible for the licensing and regulation of various professions and industries in the state.

The bill specifically addresses septic system challenges for residential property owners in rural and agricultural zoning districts, aligning with the Council's mission to support the unique needs of rural Maryland counties.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Governor's Council on the Chesapeake Bay
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: Septic regulations are a key component of watershed management and bay restoration; changes to these standards in rural areas are relevant to the Council's role in advising the Governor on cleaning up the Chesapeake Bay.

This multi-agency initiative promotes sustainable development and environmental protection, including the management of the state's carbon footprint and the protection of the Chesapeake Bay through resource management.

Synopsis: Repealing the 90-day time limit within which an individual receiving services from the Developmental Disabilities Administration must appeal a loss of eligibility for services; establishing requirements related to eligibility determinations and redeterminations under the Maryland Medical Assistance Program; prohibiting the Department from procedurally disenrolling individuals from the Program or home- and community-based services solely on a certain basis except under certain circumstances; etc.
Title: Maryland Medical Assistance Program and Developmental Disabilities Administration - Home- and Community-Based Services Eligibility Determinations (Maryland Protecting People With Disabilities Act)
Status: In the Senate - Second Reading Passed

Home Care Services -see also- Respite Care
Long-Term Care -see also- Continuing Care; Nursing Homes

bill_summary: The Maryland Protecting People With Disabilities Act establishes specific standards and protections regarding eligibility determinations and redeterminations for the Maryland Medical Assistance Program (Medicaid) and services provided by the Developmental Disabilities Administration. The bill prohibits the Maryland Department of Health from procedurally disenrolling individuals from home- and community-based services due to missing documentation unless specific verification and notification steps are exhausted, and it requires retroactive reinstatement for those disenrolled due to department delays. Additionally, the department must provide accessible information regarding program eligibility and rights, reserve waiver slots for reinstated individuals, and submit quarterly reports on eligibility statistics through 2029.
stakeholders: Medicaid recipients receiving home- and community-based services, individuals with developmental disabilities, and applicants for disability-related medical assistance programs.
fiscal_impact_summary: According to the fiscal note, the bill generally codifies existing federal mandates and aligns with current practices for waivers administered by the Developmental Disabilities Administration. The Maryland Department of Health (MDH) advises that the administrative requirements, including reporting and application processing, can be handled with existing budgeted resources. The bill is not expected to affect state revenues or local government finances.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Maryland Department of Health (MDH) is the primary implementing agency for this bill. It oversees the Maryland Medical Assistance Program (Medicaid) and the Developmental Disabilities Administration (DDA), both of which are central to the bill's requirements regarding eligibility redeterminations, procedural disenrollments, and waiver slot management.

The bill's preamble explicitly references the Department of Disabilities' role in compiling data for the State's Olmstead Plan and its collaborative work with the DDA to address barriers to community placement for individuals with disabilities.

The bill alters appeal procedures for individuals receiving services from the Developmental Disabilities Administration who lose eligibility. The Office of Administrative Hearings (OAH) is the independent agency responsible for conducting these impartial hearings.

The bill requires the Department of Health to ensure that service providers can automatically exchange electronic data through an application program interface (API) with the state's Long Term Services and Supports (LTSS) software system, which involves state-level information technology infrastructure.

As the chief legal officer for the state, the Office of the Attorney General provides legal counsel to the Department of Health and represents the state in matters related to Medicaid eligibility laws and the Americans with Disabilities Act.

The Department of Human Services is involved in the administration of Medicaid eligibility through its local departments, and the bill's changes to eligibility redetermination processes directly intersect with their operations.

bill_summary: This bill authorizes school vehicle driver trainers employed by a county school board to administer the commercial driver’s instructional permit knowledge test to applicants seeking a commercial driver’s license with a school bus endorsement.
responsible_party: County school boards and school vehicle driver trainers
stakeholders: Applicants for a commercial driver's license school bus endorsement, county school boards, and school vehicle driver trainers.

The bill identifies a shift in the administration of knowledge tests which may result in a decrease in administrative workload for the Motor Vehicle Administration and a corresponding increase in responsibility for local county school boards.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The MVA is the primary state agency responsible for driver licensing and testing, including commercial driver's instructional permits. This bill directly impacts MVA operations by authorizing external school vehicle driver trainers to perform knowledge tests previously conducted by MVA staff.

As the parent agency of the Motor Vehicle Administration (MVA), MDOT is responsible for the overall management of state transportation laws and the regulatory framework for driver licensing and endorsements.

The Department of Education oversees Maryland's 24 local school systems. The bill involves employees of county school boards (school vehicle driver trainers) and affects the training and certification process for personnel within the public education system's transportation network.

The Maryland Center for School Safety is tasked with providing a comprehensive approach to safety in schools, which includes the safe transportation of students. Changes to the testing and certification process for school bus drivers fall under their broad mandate for student safety.

bill_summary: This bill requires the Maryland Motor Vehicle Administration (MVA) to implement a system to collect address information from vehicle insurance contracts to identify Maryland residents who have improperly registered their vehicles in other states. The MVA is authorized to conduct investigations, hire private contractors for assistance, and assess penalties of $150 for noncompliance and an additional $500 if the vehicle remains unregistered 60 days after notice. All penalties are to be deposited into the Transportation Trust Fund.
stakeholders: Maryland residents owning vehicles registered out-of-state, the Motor Vehicle Administration, and private investigative contractors.
fiscal_impact_summary: The bill creates a new revenue stream for the Transportation Trust Fund through penalties of $150 and $500 assessed against residents with improperly registered vehicles. The MVA will incur costs to establish the data collection system and conduct investigations, which may be performed by private agents under contract. Specific aggregate dollar estimates from a formal Fiscal Note are not available in the provided text.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Motor Vehicle Administration (MVA) is the primary agency tasked with implementing the new system to collect insurance address information, conducting investigations into improper vehicle registration, assessing penalties for noncompliance, and potentially contracting with private parties for these services.

As the parent agency of the MVA, the Department of Transportation oversees motor vehicle registration and manages the Transportation Trust Fund, which is the designated recipient of the penalties collected under this bill.
The Office of Administrative Hearings typically adjudicates contested administrative decisions and penalties assessed by the MVA, such as those authorized by this bill for improper registration.

The Board of Public Works oversees significant state procurement contracts; its approval would likely be required if the MVA enters into substantial contracts with private parties to procure the services of independent agents.

The Department of Budget and Management oversees state agency expenditures and personnel; it would be responsible for managing the fiscal impact on the MVA's budget and the resulting revenue for the Transportation Trust Fund.
The State Treasurer acts as the custodian of state funds, including the receipt and distribution of penalties directed to the Transportation Trust Fund.

The Office of the Attorney General provides legal counsel to the MVA and would likely be involved in drafting or reviewing the new regulations, investigation protocols, and private contracts authorized by this bill.

bill_summary: This bill requires Maryland municipalities to submit candidate qualifications, election dates, candidate lists, and voting procedure information to the State Board of Elections (SBE) for publication on the board's website. Municipalities using ranked-choice voting are also required to submit their tabulation regulations. The SBE must publish this information immediately upon receipt to ensure public access to municipal election details.
stakeholders: Maryland municipalities, candidates for municipal office, and voters in municipal elections.
fiscal_impact_summary: The Maryland State Board of Elections can implement the bill's requirements using existing resources, resulting in no State fiscal impact. Similarly, the bill is not expected to materially affect local government finances.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill directly mandates the State Board of Elections to receive candidate qualifications, candidate lists, and voting procedures from municipalities and requires the Board to publish this information on its website immediately upon receipt.

As the chief legal officer for state agencies, the Office of the Attorney General would provide legal counsel to the State Board of Elections regarding the implementation of these new reporting requirements and the publication of municipal regulations for ranked-choice voting.

bill_summary: This bill establishes the Maryland Office of the Inspector General (OIG) and an Advisory Board to provide oversight and appoint an Inspector General. The OIG is authorized to investigate waste, mismanagement, misconduct, fraud, and corruption within the executive branch of the State government, conduct audits, and issue subpoenas. It also extends whistleblower protections to State employees who report information to the OIG and allows for the transfer of existing staff and funding to the new office.
responsible_party: Maryland Office of the Inspector General and the Maryland Office of the Inspector General Advisory Board
stakeholders: Maryland State employees, Executive Branch agencies and units, and Maryland residents
fiscal_impact_summary: The bill establishes a new state office, resulting in increased state expenditures for salaries, equipment, and operations as provided in the state budget. The Governor is authorized to transfer existing funds and positions from executive agencies to the OIG. While specific dollar estimates from a formal Fiscal Note are absent in the provided text, the bill establishes a potential revenue source through misdemeanor fines of up to $2,000 for unauthorized disclosure of confidential investigation records.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Governor or a designee serves as a member of the Maryland Office of the Inspector General Advisory Board. Additionally, the Governor appoints one professional member to the board, receives annual and final investigative reports, and is authorized to transfer positions and funds from other executive units to the new Office of the Inspector General.

The Comptroller or a designee serves as a member of the Maryland Office of the Inspector General Advisory Board, which is responsible for appointing and overseeing the Inspector General. The board requires the Comptroller's participation for a quorum and a majority vote for leadership decisions.

DBM is the state's principal fiscal and personnel agency. It will be responsible for managing the transfer of funds and positions to the new office and overseeing the implementation of the expanded whistleblower protections in the State Personnel and Pensions Article.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Executive Commissions, Committees, Task Forces, and Advisory Boards
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill establishes a new permanent advisory board, the Maryland Office of the Inspector General Advisory Board, to appoint, oversee, and potentially remove the Inspector General.

The bill establishes legal frameworks for investigations and criminal referrals. It also explicitly includes the Inspector General alongside the Attorney General as a protected recipient of disclosures in the state's whistleblower statute.
The bill requires the Inspector General to obtain approval from a circuit court judge to issue subpoenas. This creates a new administrative interaction between the executive branch and the judiciary.

The bill mandates that the state maintain and equip office space for the Maryland Office of the Inspector General, a core responsibility of DGS. Additionally, the Inspector General's oversight of 'waste and mismanagement' often involves procurement and facility management audits.

The bill requires the Inspector General to take steps to avoid duplicative investigations or audits. As OLA is the primary agency responsible for auditing executive units, the two offices must coordinate closely to ensure oversight efficiency.

The Inspector General is required to establish a toll-free hotline and a public website to receive complaints and post reports, which typically requires coordination with and technical support from DoIT.

The Inspector General is mandated to notify the appropriate law enforcement agency if an investigation discovers evidence of criminal activity. As the primary state-level law enforcement agency, the Maryland State Police would likely receive such referrals.
The bill contains specific protections ensuring that employees transferred to the new Maryland Office of the Inspector General do so without diminution of their retirement status or benefits.

bill_summary: This bill requires health insurance carriers to take responsibility for identifying primary and secondary payors, determining payable amounts, and coordinating benefits when a claim involves multiple payors. It also shortens the window for a carrier to retroactively deny reimbursement to a healthcare provider from 18 months to 9 months for claims subject to coordination of benefits with another carrier, while maintaining the 18-month window for Medicare and Medicaid claims.
stakeholders: Health insurance carriers, healthcare providers, and the Maryland Insurance Commissioner.
fiscal_impact_summary: The Maryland Insurance Administration will see a minimal increase in special fund revenues from a $125 rate and form filing fee starting in fiscal year 2027. There is a potential indeterminate increase in administrative costs for the State Employee and Retiree Health and Welfare Benefits Program. Small business healthcare providers may experience a positive impact due to reduced administrative burdens and shorter retroactive denial windows.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill directly amends the Insurance Article and imposes new regulatory requirements on health insurance carriers. The Maryland Insurance Administration is the primary regulator for these entities and is specifically tasked with receiving the newly required annual reports from carriers regarding their coordination of benefits activities.

The fiscal note indicates that the Department of Budget and Management (DBM) anticipates a potential increase in administrative costs for the State Employee and Retiree Health and Welfare Benefits Program due to the bill's requirements on coordination of benefits and retroactive denials.

The bill specifically defines 'Payor' to include the Maryland Medical Assistance Program (Medicaid) and includes Managed Care Organizations (MCOs) under the definition of 'Carrier'. These programs and entities are overseen by the Department of Health, and the bill regulates their reimbursement and coordination of benefits processes.

As the agency responsible for administering the state's health insurance marketplace, the Exchange has a significant interest in regulations affecting the carriers that provide health plans on the platform, particularly regarding claims processing and coordination of benefits.

The Office of the Attorney General provides legal counsel to the Maryland Insurance Administration and the Department of Health, both of which will be responsible for implementing or complying with the changes in insurance law established by this bill.

The Commission is responsible for planning for the state's health system needs and improving access to health care. Regulations concerning reimbursement and coordination of benefits impact the financial stability and operational efficiency of health care providers and the overall health system.

bill_summary: This bill requires the Maryland Department of Health to establish a standardized system for the annual collection and compilation of cost data related to various women's health services, including prenatal care, birth, postpartum care, pregnancy care, abortion services, and menopausal care. The Department must analyze this data to identify trends and evaluate spending efficiency, and then submit an annual report to the General Assembly while strictly maintaining patient privacy and de-identifying data.
stakeholders: Licensed hospitals, health care providers, and women receiving maternal, reproductive, or menopausal health care services in Maryland.
fiscal_impact_summary: According to the Fiscal Note, State general fund expenditures increase by $298,000 in FY 2027 for the Maryland Department of Health to hire three staff members (a database specialist, an epidemiologist, and a part-time contractual health policy analyst) to develop the reporting system and perform the required data analysis. Ongoing annual expenditures for the permanent positions are estimated to range from approximately $223,800 in FY 2028 to $255,400 by FY 2031. The bill has no effect on State revenues or local government finances.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: As an independent unit within the Department of Health responsible for planning the state's health system needs and providing information on the cost and quality of health services, the Commission is the primary entity likely to implement and manage the new women's health care cost and utilization reporting system.

The bill explicitly mandates that the Maryland Department of Health develop the standardized reporting system, collect cost data from providers, track Medicaid (Maryland Medical Assistance Program) expenditures for specific services, and submit annual reports to the General Assembly.

Since the bill requires data collection on hospital-based delivery costs, neonatal care, and complications, HSCRC is impacted due to its role in regulating hospital rates and monitoring the financial stability and costs of hospital services in Maryland.

The fiscal note indicates a significant impact on state general fund expenditures ($298,011 in FY 2027) to support new personnel and database infrastructure required by the bill, which falls under DBM's oversight of the state budget and personnel.

The OAG will be required to provide legal counsel to the Department of Health regarding the development of reporting systems that must comply with complex state and federal privacy laws, including HIPAA and Maryland's health care shield laws.

The bill requires the collection of cost data for services often paid by private funds; as the state's insurance regulator, MIA has a high interest in data regarding the financial impact, effectiveness, and utilization trends of private health expenditures.

University institutions that operate hospitals or provide clinical health services (such as the University of Maryland Medical Center) will be required to comply with the bill's mandatory standardized reporting of costs and utilization for women's health services.

The bill's findings on the financial impact of reproductive health services will inform the Governor's policy decisions and the annual budget proposals regarding public health and maternal health outcomes.
The bill's data on the cost and utilization of women's health care services is relevant to the Exchange's mission of making health coverage accessible and affordable for Maryland residents.
GOPI's focus on efficiency and data-driven accountability makes this bill relevant, as it creates new metrics and transparency requirements for significant state and private health care expenditures.

As a state-operated public university that may provide clinical health services or training, it would be subject to the bill's reporting requirements if it functions as a healthcare provider for the specified services.

bill_summary: This bill establishes the Suitland Development Authority in Prince George’s County to revitalize and develop neighborhoods along the Suitland Road and Silver Hill Road corridor. The Authority is authorized to coordinate with residents to create a comprehensive revitalization plan, acquire and manage property, provide loans and grants, and oversee economic, housing, and transportation projects to promote community growth and safety.
responsible_party: Prince George's County Suitland Development Authority
stakeholders: Residents and commercial property owners in the Suitland Road and Silver Hill Road corridor of Prince George's County.
fiscal_impact_summary: The Fiscal Note assumes State general fund expenditures will increase by at least $10,000,000 annually from FY 2027 through 2035 to ensure the Authority is viable, with a mandated annual appropriation of $500,000 starting in FY 2028. The Authority is required to be self-sustaining starting in FY 2036. Prince George's County finances may be impacted by potential local funding contributions and changes in real property tax revenues resulting from development and tax exemptions provided by the bill.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill creates the Suitland Development Authority as a state instrumentality and mandates that the Governor include a $500,000 annual appropriation in the state budget for the Authority. The Governor is also responsible for the overall execution of laws relating to this new executive-branch entity.

The Comptroller is explicitly required by the bill to account for the Suitland Development Authority Fund and is responsible for managing the state's tax laws, which include the specific sales and use tax and recordation tax exemptions granted to the Authority.
The bill requires the State Treasurer to hold the Suitland Development Authority Fund separately and to invest the money of the Fund in the same manner as other State money.

As the chief legal officer for the State, the OAG will be responsible for providing legal counsel to the newly established Suitland Development Authority and representing it in its capacity as an instrumentality of the State.

DBM is the principal agency for developing the state budget and managing personnel. Although the Authority is exempt from certain DBM oversight, the department must manage the mandated $500,000 appropriation and potential multi-million dollar fiscal impacts noted in the fiscal note.

The Secretary of Commerce (or a designee) is a mandated member of the Authority's Board of Directors. The agency's mission of economic development and job attraction is a core purpose of the new Authority.

The Secretary of Housing and Community Development (or a designee) is a mandated member of the Authority's Board of Directors. The Authority's focus on neighborhood revitalization, housing development, and community improvement directly aligns with DHCD's core mission.

The Secretary of Transportation (or a designee) is a mandated member of the Authority's Board of Directors. The Authority's mission specifically includes transportation planning for motor vehicles and pedestrians within the revitalization area.

The Authority is subject to State Finance and Procurement Article Title 12, Subtitle 4, which requires exempt units to submit their written procurement policies and procedures to the Board of Public Works for review.

The Executive Director of the Maryland Economic Development Corporation (MEDCO) is a mandated member of the Authority's Board of Directors, providing a direct link between the state's primary economic development instrumentality and this new local authority.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Governor's Office of Small, Minority & Women Business Affairs
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill explicitly subjects the Authority to Title 14, Subtitle 3 of the State Finance and Procurement Article regarding Minority Business Enterprise (MBE) participation, which this office monitors and implements across state agencies.
The bill explicitly subjects the Authority's board members, officers, and employees to the Maryland Public Ethics Law, which is administered and enforced by this commission.

As a new state instrumentality with mandated funding and a dedicated special fund, the Authority will be subject to periodic fiscal compliance and performance audits by the OLA to ensure accountability and efficiency.

bill_summary: This bill regulates the extension of credit to players by video lottery operation licensees, requiring the State Lottery and Gaming Control Commission to maintain a central registry of players with approved credit and adopt regulations for player protections. It increases the maximum administrative penalty for gaming and sports wagering violations from $5,000 to $50,000 per violation. The bill also reallocates 1% of fantasy competition and online sports wagering proceeds to the Problem Gambling Fund, prohibits the use of credit cards for online sports wagering, and caps wagers on a single sporting event at $100,000.
responsible_party: State Lottery and Gaming Control Commission
stakeholders: Video lottery operation licensees, fantasy competition operators, sports wagering licensees, and individuals participating in gaming activities.
fiscal_impact_summary: The bill increases state revenue by redirecting 1% of total fantasy competition proceeds (previously retained by operators) to the Problem Gambling Fund. For online sports wagering, the bill redirects 1% of proceeds from the General Fund to the Problem Gambling Fund, resulting in a revenue-neutral shift between state funds. Potential revenue from administrative penalties increases significantly as the maximum fine per violation is raised from $5,000 to $50,000. Specific total dollar estimates are unavailable as the formal Fiscal Note was not provided.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Maryland State Lottery & Gaming Control Agency
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: This agency is the primary regulator and implementer of the bill's provisions. It is tasked with adopting regulations for credit extensions, creating a central player credit list, enforcing significantly higher penalties for violations, and managing the distribution of gambling and fantasy competition proceeds.

The bill redirects 1% of fantasy competition and online sports wagering proceeds to the Problem Gambling Fund, which is administered by the Maryland Department of Health to support responsible gambling and treatment services.
The bill alters the distribution of proceeds away from the Blueprint for Maryland's Future Fund, which supports the state's public education system, to the Problem Gambling Fund.

As the principal fiscal agency, DBM is affected by the changes in revenue distribution between the General Fund, the Blueprint for Maryland's Future Fund, and the Problem Gambling Fund, which impacts state budget planning.

The Comptroller is the state's chief financial officer and tax collector responsible for managing state revenues and the distribution of funds; the bill changes the allocation of specific gaming-related revenues.
The OAG provides legal counsel to the State Lottery and Gaming Control Commission and would be responsible for advising on the new regulatory framework and enforcement of increased civil penalties.
The Governor's Office oversees the executive branch and proposes the annual state budget; the bill impacts state revenue policy and the regulatory duties of agencies within the executive branch.

bill_summary: This bill allows campaign finance entities to use campaign funds for security-related expenditures, such as electronic security systems and personal security services, for candidates, elected officials, their immediate families, and staff. Such expenditures are authorized when a threat arises from the protectee's status or activities associated with the candidate or official. The bill sets a $10,000 lifetime limit on these expenditures per candidate or official, prohibits certain items like firearms, and requires documentation of threats and the eventual return or reimbursement for tangible security items.
stakeholders: Candidates for office, elected officials, immediate family members of candidates or elected officials, campaign staff, and campaign finance entities.
fiscal_impact_summary: The bill authorizes campaign finance entities to make security expenditures from their own funds, subject to a lifetime cap of $10,000 per candidate or elected official. It also allows campaign entities to reimburse the State for security goods or services. Because a formal Fiscal Note is not provided with this text, specific aggregate State and local revenue or expenditure estimates are unavailable; however, the bill mandates record-keeping and reporting requirements for the State Board of Elections.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The agency is the primary regulator of campaign finance. The bill requires the Board to develop forms for reporting security expenditures and documentation for the verification of threats.

As a primary law enforcement agency, it would be responsible for verifying threats that necessitate expenditures. It also provides executive security services for which the state may be reimbursed under this bill.

The OAG serves as legal counsel to the State Board of Elections and law enforcement agencies. It would provide legal guidance on the interpretation and enforcement of these new provisions in the Election Law Article.

This office investigates and prosecutes criminal offenses related to state election laws and would be responsible for investigating potential fraud or misconduct regarding security expenditure reports.

The Governor and executive staff are defined as protectees. The bill allows campaign funds to be used for their security, impacting the administrative and campaign operations for the state's chief executive.
The Lieutenant Governor is an elected official and a protectee. This bill directly authorizes their campaign finance entity to pay for security services under specific threat conditions.
The agency provides security through the Maryland Capitol Police, who may be involved in verifying threats or providing security services that are reimbursable to the state under this act.

The Treasurer is an elected official and protectee. The office also manages the receipt and management of state funds, which would include reimbursements from campaign entities for state-provided security.
Judges are elected officials in Maryland. The AOC supports the judicial branch, and judicial candidates or officials would qualify as protectees who can use campaign funds for security.
As an elected official and protectee, the Comptroller is impacted. The agency also functions as the state's principal revenue collector and would handle reimbursements from campaign entities.
As the state's fiscal agency, DBM oversees budget execution and would be involved in managing the accounting process for campaign reimbursements to state agencies.

bill_summary: This bill requires the Board of Trustees of the Maryland State Retirement and Pension System to identify and divest from investments associated with the government of Israel, including sovereign debt, securities, and assets held in the government. It prohibits new investments in these categories and mandates semi-annual reporting on divestment activities, provided these actions are consistent with the Board's fiduciary duties and can be executed at fair market value.
responsible_party: Board of Trustees for the State Retirement and Pension System
stakeholders: State employees and retirees who are members of the Maryland State Retirement and Pension System, the Board of Trustees of the system, and the government of Israel.
fiscal_impact_summary: A formal Fiscal Note is not provided in the text. The bill creates administrative requirements for the Board of Trustees to review investment holdings and submit reports twice a year, which will likely result in indeterminate administrative costs. The impact on investment returns is mitigated by provisions that excuse divestment if it violates fiduciary duties or if assets cannot be sold for fair market value.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill directly mandates the Board of Trustees for the State Retirement and Pension System, which this agency administers, to review investment holdings, take divestment actions regarding Israeli investments, and report to the General Assembly.

The State Treasurer serves as a key member of the Board of Trustees for the State Retirement and Pension System and acts as the state's chief financial officer responsible for the management and protection of state funds.
The Comptroller is a principal financial officer of the state and serves as a member of the Board of Trustees for the State Retirement and Pension System.

The OAG provides legal counsel to the Board of Trustees and state agencies; they would be responsible for advising on the legal implications of divestment, fiduciary responsibilities, and the liability immunities established in the bill.
The Governor oversees the executive branch, including the Retirement Agency, and is responsible for appointing members to the boards and commissions that manage state investments.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: As the primary implementing agency, DHCD is responsible for administering the Appraisal Gap From Historic Redlining Financial Assistance Program and is specifically tasked by the bill with establishing criteria to identify neighborhoods that have been historically redlined or undergone urban renewal.

The bill references 'sustainable communities,' a designation that involves the state's planning visions and coordination between agencies including the Department of Planning to promote community revitalization and sustainable growth.

The bill directly addresses enhancing economic mobility and supporting underinvested communities by mitigating historical redlining, which aligns with the Innovation Team's mandate to pilot novel initiatives for these specific goals.
The program's goal of improving economic opportunities and addressing historical disinvestment in neighborhoods supports the office's mission to enhance the well-being of families and reduce poverty.
The OAG provides legal counsel to DHCD and would be involved in the development of regulations and the legal interpretation of the newly established criteria for 'qualified properties.'
This multi-agency initiative coordinates community revitalization and sustainable development efforts, which are central to the definitions and objectives of the Appraisal Gap program.

As the state's principal fiscal agency, DBM oversees the budget for DHCD and the execution of funding for the financial assistance program, even if the bill's fiscal impact is determined to be minimal.
The Governor oversees the executive branch, including DHCD, and coordinates the broader policy initiatives related to housing equity and urban renewal that this bill addresses.

The bill addresses the effects of historical redlining, a form of housing discrimination; while the bill is programmatic rather than enforcement-based, it aligns with the Commission's interest in fair housing and addressing historical inequities.

Synopsis: Providing that a specified conviction from another state or a federal, military, or Native American tribal court may serve as a predicate crime for a specified enhanced penalty for certain repeat sex offenders.

bill_summary: This bill expands the application of an enhanced penalty for fourth-degree sexual offenses to individuals who have prior convictions for specified sexual crimes in other states or in federal, military, or Native American tribal courts. Under the bill, such out-of-state convictions serve as predicate offenses for a prison sentence of up to three years if the crime would have constituted a violation of specific Maryland sexual offense laws if committed within the state.
responsible_party: Maryland Judiciary; Department of Public Safety and Correctional Services
stakeholders: Individuals with prior out-of-state sexual offense convictions; Maryland state and local courts; Maryland Department of Public Safety and Correctional Services; Office of the Public Defender
fiscal_impact_summary: The bill is not expected to materially affect State or local finances or operations. Although the Office of the Public Defender suggested a potential need for additional staff, the Department of Legislative Services determined that initial caseloads are likely insufficient to justify immediate additional staffing. Any necessary resources can be requested through the annual budget process if case volumes increase significantly.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Maryland Office of the Public Defender
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The fiscal note specifically identifies the Office of the Public Defender as being potentially impacted, noting that enhanced penalties for repeat offenders and the inclusion of out-of-state convictions could increase attorney caseloads and the complexity of defense for indigent clients.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Department of Public Safety and Correctional Services
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill increases the maximum sentence for repeat fourth-degree sexual offenders from 1 year to 3 years. Sentences over 1 year are typically served in State correctional facilities rather than local jails, directly impacting DPSCS intake and population management.

The agency provides operational and technological support for the Judiciary. The bill introduces new procedural requirements for sentencing, specifically regarding the verification and processing of out-of-state and federal predicate convictions for subsequent offender penalties.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Governor's Office of Crime Prevention and Policy
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: As the primary coordinating body for public safety and criminal justice strategies, this agency is responsible for policy development related to reducing crime and managing victim services, which aligns with the bill's focus on repeat sexual offenders.

The bill defines and prohibits sexual offenses by 'persons in a position of authority' within schools and youth programs. The Center is responsible for comprehensive school safety approaches and training personnel, making the conduct standards in this bill highly relevant to their mission.

The OAG represents the state in criminal appeals and provides legal counsel to state agencies. The expansion of predicate offenses for enhanced sentencing may lead to an increase in appellate litigation concerning the interpretation of out-of-state statutes.

The bill targets 'persons in a position of authority' specifically including teachers, coaches, and school counselors. MSDE oversight of local school systems and educator certification standards is relevant to the bill's focus on school-based authority figures.

DHS is the primary provider of protective services for children facing abuse. Since the bill involves sexual offenses against minors by persons in authority, it intersects with the agency's mission to protect vulnerable children from neglect and abuse.
As the state's primary law enforcement agency, the Maryland State Police are responsible for investigating criminal violations, including sexual offenses, and maintaining safety across the state.

The Governor's Office oversees the executive branch and proposes the state budget. It would coordinate the policy implementation across relevant departments like DPSCS and GOCPP and manage any fiscal adjustments required by the bill.

bill_summary: This bill prohibits hospitals from discharging or transferring a patient in active labor unless a written 'safe discharge labor plan' is completed, except in emergency cases. The plan must include clinical justification, a travel safety assessment, and a signed acknowledgment of risks and symptoms from the patient. Hospitals are required to maintain these records for 21 years, provide annual staff training on maternal health and racial disparities, and publicly post patient rights. The Maryland Department of Health is responsible for enforcement, imposing civil penalties for violations, and submitting annual reports to the General Assembly.
stakeholders: Pregnant individuals, hospitals, obstetric and emergency care medical staff, and the Maryland Department of Health.
fiscal_impact_summary: State general fund revenues increase by an indeterminate amount starting in FY 2027 from civil penalties ($25,000 for discharge violations; $5,000 for training or record-keeping violations). State general fund expenditures may increase by approximately $72,896 in FY 2027 if an additional nurse surveyor is required for enforcement, though the Maryland Department of Health may be able to implement the bill with existing resources. There is no local fiscal impact.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: As the primary regulator of hospitals and health care professionals in Maryland, MDH is the lead agency responsible for enforcing the bill's safe discharge labor plan requirements, imposing civil monetary penalties, managing plans of correction, and compiling the required annual reports for the General Assembly.

OAH is responsible for adjudicating contested cases and providing an impartial hearing process for hospitals that choose to appeal the substantial civil monetary penalties ($25,000 per violation) imposed by the Department of Health under this bill.

The OAG serves as the chief legal representative for the state and will provide legal counsel to the Department of Health and the relevant health occupations boards regarding regulatory enforcement and practitioner disciplinary referrals mandated by the bill.

As the state's principal revenue collector, the Comptroller's office is responsible for collecting the civil monetary penalties imposed for violations of the safe discharge labor plan requirements, which are credited to the General Fund.

DBM oversees the personnel and fiscal impact of the bill, including the review and approval of potential new state positions, such as nurse surveyors within the Department of Health, required to monitor hospital compliance and training standards.

MHCC is a regulatory agency within the Department of Health tasked with increasing hospital accountability and tracking health care quality; the bill's focus on maternal health standards and adverse event reporting aligns directly with their clinical oversight mission.

bill_summary: This bill requires the Maryland Insurance Administration to establish a workgroup to study the definition of "specialty drug" used in health insurance. The workgroup is tasked with evaluating how the current definition affects stakeholders and patients, comparing it with federal, state, and international definitions, and recommending a new definition by January 1, 2027.
stakeholders: Pharmacy benefit managers, independent pharmacists, insurance carriers, managed care organizations, hospitals, health care providers, and patients.
fiscal_impact_summary: Specific dollar estimates for revenue or expenditures are unavailable in the provided bill text. The fiscal impact consists of administrative costs for the Maryland Insurance Administration to convene the study workgroup and submit the required report to the Governor and General Assembly.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Maryland Insurance Administration is the primary agency tasked with convening the workgroup, staffing it, conducting the study of 'specialty drug' definitions, and reporting the final recommendations to the Governor and General Assembly.

The Department of Health is highly relevant as it oversees the state's Medicaid program and the managed care organizations (MCOs) that are required to have a representative in the workgroup. Changing the definition of specialty drugs will significantly impact health policy and pharmacy benefit management under the department's purview.

The Maryland Health Care Commission is responsible for health system planning and promoting informed decision-making regarding the cost and quality of health services, making the definition of specialty drugs a core area of interest for their regulatory and planning functions.
The definition of specialty drugs directly affects the design, cost, and coverage of health plans offered on the Maryland Health Connection, which the Exchange is responsible for administering.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Executive Commissions, Committees, Task Forces, and Advisory Boards
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: This bill creates a new, temporary workgroup composed of various stakeholders to address a specific government issue, fitting the description of this collective entity.

The Maryland Insurance Administration reports the workgroup's findings directly to the Governor, who also oversees the administrative support for executive policy initiatives and the management of state agencies like the MIA.
The OAG provides legal counsel to the Maryland Insurance Administration and would likely be involved in reviewing the new proposed definition for compliance with state and federal laws.

The workgroup is required to include a representative from a hospital. The HSCRC regulates hospital rates and revenues, which are directly impacted by how specialty drugs are defined and billed within hospital settings.

The definition of specialty drugs significantly impacts access to and the cost of life-sustaining medications for many individuals with disabilities, making the department's role in advancing inclusive community living relevant to the outcomes of this workgroup.

bill_summary: This bill requires the Maryland Department of Health to conduct an in-State cost-of-dispensing survey for the Maryland Medical Assistance Program at least once every three years, beginning in 2026. The department is also required to report the results of each survey to the General Assembly by December 1 of the year it is conducted.

fiscal_impact_summary: State Medicaid expenditures increase by $81,000 in FY 2027, FY 2030, and every three years thereafter to conduct the cost-of-dispensing survey. The Maryland Department of Health can report the survey results using existing budgeted resources.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Maryland Department of Health is the primary agency responsible for the Maryland Medical Assistance Program (Medicaid) and is specifically mandated by the bill to conduct the in-State cost-of-dispensing survey every three years and report the results to the General Assembly.

The Department of Budget and Management is responsible for state budget development and supervising budget execution. As the bill creates a recurring fiscal impact on general and federal funds for Medicaid expenditures ($81,000 every three years), the department will oversee the fiscal planning for these costs.

As the head of the executive branch, the Governor's Office oversees the Department of Health and is responsible for proposing the state budget, which must now account for the recurring costs of the mandated cost-of-dispensing surveys.

The Office of the Attorney General serves as the primary legal representative for all state agencies, including the Department of Health, and would provide legal counsel regarding the implementation of the survey and compliance with federal and state Medicaid regulations.

Synopsis: Authorizing a consumer to send certain notice relating to alleged identity theft debt to a creditor; requiring a creditor to conduct a certain investigation following receipt of notice and to provide certain notice or take certain actions under certain circumstances; authorizing a consumer to file a civil action under certain circumstances and authorizing a consumer to demand a jury trial; prohibiting collection of certain debt under certain circumstances; etc.

bill_summary: This bill establishes procedures for consumers to challenge and resolve debt resulting from identity theft. It requires creditors to cease collection and investigate claims within 30 days of receiving written notice from a consumer. If the debt is confirmed as identity theft debt, the creditor must permanently stop collection activities and notify credit reporting agencies. Consumers are also authorized to file civil actions in circuit court to seek declaratory judgments, injunctions, damages, and attorney's fees.
responsible_party: Maryland Judiciary and the Office of the Attorney General
stakeholders: Individual consumers (debtors) and creditors (including debt collectors)
fiscal_impact_summary: According to the Fiscal Note, State general fund expenditures increase by $12,952 in FY 2027 only for one-time computer programming by the Judiciary. The bill is not anticipated to materially affect local government finances or operations, and the impact on small businesses is expected to be minimal.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill establishes a new civil cause of action in the Circuit Court for consumers to challenge identity theft debt and allows for jury trials. The fiscal note also specifies a one-time general fund expenditure of approximately $13,000 for the Judiciary to perform computer programming related to the bill's implementation.

The bill explicitly mentions the Office of the Attorney General as a recipient of reports that constitute evidence for identity theft debt and identifies the 'Identity Theft Passport' issued by the OAG as a key evidentiary document. Additionally, the OAG's Consumer Protection Division is a primary source of fiscal and policy information for this legislation.

The Maryland Department of Labor regulates financial institutions and debt collection agencies. As the bill imposes new investigatory, reporting, and collection-cessation mandates on 'creditors' and 'collectors,' it directly impacts the regulatory framework overseen by this department.

The bill carries a specific fiscal impact on the general fund for the required IT modifications. DBM is responsible for the overall execution of the state budget and fiscal planning which would include the appropriation for these costs.

The bill specifies that police reports and reports made to law enforcement agencies are essential forms of evidence a consumer can use to support an allegation of identity theft debt. As the primary state law enforcement agency, MSP records are central to the consumer's ability to fulfill the bill's notice requirements.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Governor's Office of Crime Prevention and Policy
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: GOCPP is the state's primary coordinating body for public safety and criminal justice policy. Since the bill integrates criminal outcomes (convictions or guilty pleas for identity fraud) into civil debt relief and presumption of theft, it aligns with GOCPP's mission to address the fallout of criminal activity.

The team is tasked with addressing child poverty and enhancing economic mobility. Protecting residents from the financial burdens of debt incurred through fraud and identity theft is directly relevant to their mission of improving outcomes for Maryland families.

bill_summary: This bill exempts health benefit plans provided by professional employer organizations (PEOs) that engage in employee leasing from Maryland's small group health insurance laws and the requirements of the Maryland Health Benefit Exchange. This allows small businesses to obtain large group health insurance coverage through PEO co-employment arrangements. Additionally, the bill requires PEOs to provide written disclosures to small businesses regarding insurance benefits, costs, and termination rights.
stakeholders: Small employers, employees of small businesses, professional employer organizations (PEOs), and health insurance carriers.
fiscal_impact_summary: According to the Fiscal Note, the bill has no fiscal or operational impact on the Maryland Insurance Administration, and State revenues are not affected. There is no local fiscal impact. The bill's impact on small businesses is considered meaningful; small employers who join PEOs may obtain lower premium rates, while those who remain in the small group market could potentially face premium increases.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Maryland Insurance Administration is the primary regulator for the Insurance Article, which this bill extensively amends. The agency is responsible for reviewing insurance policy forms, ensuring compliance with small group laws, and overseeing the health benefit plans provided by professional employer organizations (PEOs).

The bill directly amends Title 31 of the Insurance Article, which governs the Maryland Health Benefit Exchange. It specifically modifies requirements for carriers regarding the Small Business Health Options Program (SHOP) and changes definitions of small employers within the Exchange's jurisdiction.

Professional employer organizations (PEOs) are business entities that manage employer responsibilities and co-employment relationships. This falls under the Department of Labor's mission to protect workers and foster economic growth for businesses through the regulation of workforce and professional industries.

The 'Better Small Business Employee Benefit Act of 2026' aims to enhance the competitiveness and retention of small businesses in Maryland by providing more affordable health insurance options, aligning with the Department of Commerce's mission to stimulate economic growth.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Governor's Office of Small, Minority & Women Business Affairs
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: This office is responsible for connecting the small business community to economic opportunities and monitoring socioeconomic programs. The bill's focus on small business employee benefits is directly relevant to their advocacy and support mission for the small business sector.

The Governor's Office coordinates policy initiatives and oversees the executive branch. This bill represents a significant policy shift regarding health insurance regulation and small business support, which falls under the Governor's executive leadership and policy coordination roles.

The OAG provides legal counsel to the primary implementing agencies (MIA and MHBE) and enforces consumer protection laws. The bill introduces new mandatory written disclosure requirements for PEOs, which the OAG may be involved in overseeing or enforcing.

bill_summary: This bill establishes the Maryland’s Future Board within the Department of Commerce to develop, evaluate, and revise a long-term visionary plan for the state's economic future, focusing on emerging trends such as artificial intelligence, robotics, and advanced manufacturing. It also creates the Maryland’s Future Fund, a special nonlapsing fund to finance projects recommended by the Board, and requires the Comptroller to study and report on Maryland's economic growth trends and competitive industries.
stakeholders: Maryland residents, entrepreneurs, academic institutions, labor organizations, business leaders, and nonprofit organizations.
fiscal_impact_summary: According to the fiscal note, State general fund expenditures will increase by $1,700,000 in FY 2027, which includes $200,000 for the Comptroller’s economic study and $1,500,000 for the Maryland’s Future Fund and Board administration. Ongoing general fund expenditures will be required through FY 2031 for board operations and to capitalize the Maryland’s Future Fund for project execution, which could potentially require at least several million dollars annually starting in FY 2029. Local governments are not directly affected but may benefit from future visionary projects.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill establishes the Maryland’s Future Board within the Department of Commerce and designates the Department as the administrator of the newly created Maryland’s Future Fund.

The Comptroller (or a designee) is a mandated member of the Board and is explicitly required by the bill to conduct a study on economic growth trends and identify growth needs in competitive industries.
The Governor appoints three members to the Board and is the primary recipient of the visionary plan and project recommendations designed to advance the state’s socioeconomic wellbeing.
The State Treasurer is responsible for holding the Maryland’s Future Fund separately and investing its money, with interest earnings being credited back to the fund.

As the agency responsible for the state's budget development, DBM is impacted by the Board's recommendations for projects which specifically include allocations in the state's operating and capital budgets.

The Board's mission to identify and test novel initiatives related to economic mobility and industry disruptive technologies aligns closely with the Innovation Team's role as a solution incubator for the Governor's top priorities.

The bill focuses on future industry trends like robotics and AI, which directly intersects with the GWDB's responsibility for developing innovative workforce solutions and setting the statewide vision for workforce development.
The Board is required to include leaders from labor organizations, and the visionary plan covers areas such as advanced technology workforce training and job replacement due to AI.
The Board's membership includes leaders from higher education and academia to help develop strategies for a future economic landscape that attracts residents who want to learn in Maryland.

GOPI oversees the implementation of the State Comprehensive Plan and aligns agency activities with Governor priorities; the board's visionary plan for future economic strength will require interagency alignment.

bill_summary: This bill repeals prohibitions on the transfer of alcoholic beverages licenses to different premises or their conversion to different classes in Baltimore County. It specifically requires certain Class B licenses (including those in the Towson Commercial Revitalization District, Hunt Valley, and Metro Center at Owings Mills) to be converted into standard Class B hotel and restaurant licenses by July 1, 2026, and removes restrictions on moving licenses between election districts or reissuing revoked licenses.
responsible_party: Baltimore County Board of License Commissioners
stakeholders: Alcoholic beverage license holders in Baltimore County, particularly those in specific commercial districts like Towson and Hunt Valley, and the Baltimore County Board of License Commissioners.
fiscal_impact_summary: The bill has no impact on State finances. According to the Fiscal Note, the bill is not expected to materially affect Baltimore County finances or operations, and the impact on small businesses is estimated to be minimal.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Comptroller of Maryland is the principal state agency responsible for regulating the alcohol industry and enforcing related tax laws. This bill directly amends the Alcoholic Beverages and Cannabis Article to repeal prohibitions on license transfers and require the conversion of specific license classes in Baltimore County, which impacts the regulatory and oversight framework managed by the Comptroller's office.

bill_summary: This bill requires merchants to provide a clear and conspicuous disclosure statement when using personalized algorithmic pricing based on a consumer's personal data. It also prohibits residential rental property owners and managers from using algorithmic software or data analytics services to coordinate and set rental prices or lease terms across different ownership entities. Violations of these provisions are classified as unfair, abusive, or deceptive trade practices, making them subject to enforcement and civil penalties by the Office of the Attorney General under the Maryland Consumer Protection Act.
responsible_party: Maryland Office of the Attorney General
stakeholders: Maryland consumers, retail merchants, residential rental property owners, property management companies, and developers of algorithmic pricing and data analytics software.
fiscal_impact_summary: The bill's fiscal impact is indeterminate as no specific dollar estimates were provided in the text and the formal Fiscal Note is absent. However, classifying violations as unfair or deceptive trade practices under the Maryland Consumer Protection Act is expected to result in an indeterminate increase in State general fund revenue from civil penalties and an indeterminate increase in State expenditures for the Office of the Attorney General to manage enforcement and investigations.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: As the state's chief legal officer and primary enforcement authority for the Maryland Consumer Protection Act, the OAG is responsible for investigating and prosecuting the unfair, abusive, or deceptive trade practices defined in this bill regarding algorithmic pricing and rent-setting coordination.

This department oversees rental housing programs and community development. The bill's restrictions on algorithmic rent-setting directly affect the residential rental market and the affordability of housing in the state, which are central to the agency's mission to ensure safe and secure housing.

The bill creates new causes of action and enforcement mechanisms under the Commercial Law and Real Property Articles, which will involve the state's judicial branch in resolving civil disputes and enforcement actions brought by individuals or the state.

The OAH may be required to adjudicate administrative enforcement actions brought by state agencies, such as the Office of the Attorney General, against merchants or property owners accused of violating the new price-setting and disclosure regulations.

The bill contains an explicit exemption for conduct regulated under the Insurance Article, which delineates the limits of the new dynamic pricing regulations and defines the agency's distinct regulatory jurisdiction over insurance industry pricing.

bill_summary: This emergency bill requires the Maryland Public Service Commission (PSC) to develop and implement a successor program to the current net energy metering (NEM) program. It sets a 3,000-megawatt capacity limit for the existing program and a combined 6,000-megawatt cap for both the current and successor programs. The PSC is mandated to conduct a formal proceeding with stakeholder input and submit a report by December 15, 2026, recommending a program structure that balances distributed generation incentives with grid maintenance, ratepayer costs, and energy equity.
stakeholders: Eligible customer-generators (owners/operators of solar, wind, biomass, and other distributed generation), electric utility companies, retail electricity ratepayers, renewable energy industry experts, and consumer advocates.
fiscal_impact_summary: State expenditures will increase for the Public Service Commission to conduct the required proceeding and develop the mandated report by December 2026. Specific dollar estimates are unavailable because the formal Fiscal Note was not included in the provided text. Long-term fiscal impacts may include changes in state and local electricity expenditures and utility grid maintenance costs depending on the design of the successor program.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Public Service Commission is the primary agency responsible for the bill's implementation. It is mandated to develop and implement the successor net energy metering program, conduct a formal proceeding with stakeholders, and report its recommendations to the Governor and General Assembly.

The OPC represents residential utility consumers in proceedings before the Public Service Commission. Since the bill requires the PSC to evaluate ratepayer costs and energy equity in the new program, the OPC's advocacy for affordable and reliable utility services is directly involved.

The MEA coordinates state energy policy and promotes renewable energy. The development of a successor net energy metering program directly impacts the state's renewable energy goals and the distributed generation initiatives that the MEA manages and advises upon.

As the state's green bank, the MCEC facilitates the adoption of clean energy technologies. Changes to the financial structure of net energy metering will affect the economic viability of the distributed energy projects that MCEC helps finance.

Many agricultural operations in Maryland function as 'eligible customer-generators' using solar or biomass systems. The successor program will impact the economic viability of these on-farm renewable energy investments.

DGS manages state-owned facilities and leads sustainability and energy conservation initiatives for the government. As a manager of property that utilizes net energy metering, DGS is an affected customer-generator under the program's changes.

The MDE is responsible for the state's environmental protection and carbon reduction goals. Net energy metering is a key policy tool for promoting renewable energy, which directly supports the agency's mission to reduce greenhouse gas emissions and improve air quality.

The OAG provides legal counsel to the Public Service Commission and the Governor. The agency will likely provide legal guidance during the PSC's formal proceeding and the development of the required legislative report.

The bill requires the Public Service Commission to submit a formal report on the successor program to the Governor. The office also oversees the executive branch agencies (PSC, MEA) responsible for the program's policy direction.

USM institutions are significant 'eligible customer-generators' through various campus-based distributed generation projects. Changes to the net energy metering program will impact their energy costs and sustainability targets.

MDOT operates numerous facilities, including airports and transit stations, that may utilize net energy metering. As a customer-generator, MDOT would be impacted by the successor program's tariffs and contracts.
As an independent state university and customer-generator, the university would be impacted by changes to the net energy metering program affecting its facility operations and energy budget.
As an independent public college, St. Mary's may participate in net energy metering for its campus facilities, making the successor program relevant to its operational and utility costs.

bill_summary: This bill establishes the Ibogaine Clinical Research Grant Program within the Maryland Department of Health to provide grants to eligible Maryland research institutions for conducting FDA-overseen clinical trials on the use of ibogaine to treat opioid use disorder and other neurological conditions. The program is primarily funded by mandated appropriations from the Opioid Restitution Fund and requires grant recipients to provide matching funds.
stakeholders: Maryland research institutions, veterans, and individuals with opioid use disorder or other neurological conditions
fiscal_impact_summary: The bill mandates an annual appropriation of $500,000 from the Opioid Restitution Fund for fiscal 2028 through 2030. Additionally, Maryland Department of Health general fund expenditures are estimated to increase by $43,041 in fiscal 2028 and approximately $38,000 to $39,000 annually in fiscal 2029 and 2030 for contractual staff to administer the grant program. No local fiscal impact is expected.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Maryland Department of Health is the primary agency responsible for establishing and administering the Ibogaine Clinical Research Grant Program, adopting regulations, and reporting outcomes to the General Assembly.

The bill explicitly requires the Maryland Department of Health to consult with the Department of Veterans and Military Families in the administration of the program, which is titled the 'Veterans Mental Health Innovations Act.'
The bill mandates that the Governor include an appropriation of $500,000 in the annual budget for the program and involves a significant policy initiative overseen by the executive branch.
As the state's principal fiscal agency, DBM is responsible for implementing the mandated $500,000 annual appropriation and managing the budget execution for the grant program.
The Treasurer is the custodian of the Opioid Restitution Fund, which is the funding source for the clinical research grants mandated by this bill.
The Comptroller is responsible for accounting for the Opioid Restitution Fund and managing the payment of state funds for the grants.
The OAG provides legal counsel to the implementing agencies and oversees the Opioids Enforcement Unit, which is directly linked to the management and utilization of the Opioid Restitution Fund.

Public research universities within the System, such as the University of Maryland, Baltimore, are likely 'eligible research institutions' that would apply for and receive grants to conduct the clinical trials.

The Lieutenant Governor's office often coordinates opioid policy initiatives, and the fiscal note indicates that staff within the office are funded through the Opioid Restitution Fund, which this bill utilizes.
As the regulatory body for the state's higher education institutions, MHEC is relevant to the oversight of the academic and research programs conducted at the institutions receiving grants.
As a public urban research university, Morgan State could qualify as an eligible research institution to apply for grants under the Ibogaine Clinical Research Grant Program.
The Board of Public Works may be required to approve significant state expenditures or contracts related to the administration of the clinical research grants.

Synopsis: Requiring a contractor to pay a subcontractor or supplier at least 95% of an undisputed amount to which the subcontractor or supplier is entitled within 10 days of receiving payment from the State.
