bill_summary: This bill allows physicians licensed out-of-state to certify medical exemptions for motor vehicle window tinting and repeals the requirement that such certifications be renewed every two years, effectively making them valid indefinitely once issued.
responsible_party: Automotive Safety Enforcement Division of the Department of State Police
stakeholders: Maryland motor vehicle owners with medical conditions requiring sun protection, out-of-state physicians, and the Department of State Police.
fiscal_impact_summary: Specific dollar estimates are unavailable as a formal Fiscal Note was not included in the text. Potential financial implications include a negligible decrease in fine revenue from window tint violations and minor administrative costs for the Department of State Police to update certification guidelines.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill explicitly requires the Automotive Safety Enforcement Division of the Department of State Police to determine the manner and format of the medical certifications and directly affects the agency's traffic enforcement procedures.
As the agency responsible for vehicle registration and equipment regulations, the MVA is directly impacted by changes to window tinting standards and the Administrator's regulatory authority.
MDOT is the parent department for the MVA and oversees the state's multi-modal transportation network and safety policies addressed in the bill.
The MDTA maintains an independent police force that enforces vehicle equipment and safety laws on the state's toll facilities.
The judicial branch is responsible for the adjudication of traffic citations and safety equipment repair orders issued for tinted window violations.
The OAG provides legal counsel to the MVA and State Police regarding the implementation of the new medical exemption criteria and out-of-state physician verification.

The bill pertains to medical exemptions for individuals requiring sun protection, which is relevant to the department's mission of advocating for policies that accommodate residents with various medical conditions and disabilities.

Synopsis: Requiring an applicant for a certain work permit on a State highway to provide certain notice, including certain information, within 10 days after the applicant submits the application to each member of the General Assembly who represents the legislative district in which the proposed work is to be performed.
Title: State Highways - Highway Work Permits - Notice
Status: In the Senate - Hearing 4/03 at 1:00 p.m.
bill_summary: The bill requires applicants for Type 2 or Type 3 State highway work permits to provide written notice of their application to the members of the Maryland General Assembly who represent the legislative district where the work is to be performed. This notice must be sent within 10 days of application and include the applicant's name, the location and description of the work, and the expected start date.
stakeholders: Applicants for Type 2 and Type 3 highway work permits (including private developers and local governments), members of the Maryland General Assembly, and the State Highway Administration.
fiscal_impact_summary: The State Highway Administration and local governments that apply for permits can implement the bill's requirements using existing budgeted resources. There is no impact on State or local revenues, and the impact on small businesses is expected to be minimal.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: As the primary agency responsible for the oversight, maintenance, and permitting of State highways, SHA (referred to as the Administration in the bill) is directly responsible for defining the 'Type 2' and 'Type 3' project categories that trigger the bill's notification requirements. The bill's requirements are integrated into the permit application process managed by SHA.

The Department of Transportation (MDOT) is the parent agency of the State Highway Administration. It oversees the state's transportation network and the regulatory framework for highway work permits established under the Transportation Article, which this bill amends.

The Office of the Attorney General serves as legal counsel to MDOT and SHA. It would be responsible for reviewing the revised permit application procedures and ensuring that the shift of notification responsibility to the applicant complies with state law and procedural requirements.

Synopsis: Requiring a mortgage servicer that receives certain insurance proceeds to deposit the proceeds into a certain interest bearing account; requiring a borrower to elect the use of the interest earnings on the insurance proceeds; requiring certain interest earnings to begin accruing by a certain date; authorizing a mortgage servicer to charge a fee for disbursement of interest earnings subject to certain limitations; and requiring certain methods and procedures for disbursement of insurance proceeds and interest earnings.
Title: Financial Institutions - Mortgage Servicers - Insurance Proceeds
Status: In the House - Hearing canceled

NarrowSubjects.Name: Fees -see also- Attys' Fees; Devt Fees & Taxes
Financial Institutions -see also- Banks; Credit Unions; etc.
Insurance -see also- Health Ins; MAIF; Motor Vehicle Ins

bill_summary: This bill requires mortgage servicers that receive insurance proceeds for repairs or rebuilding of a dwelling to deposit those funds into an interest-bearing 'loss draft account' with a simple interest rate of at least 2%. It mandates that borrowers be notified of their rights regarding these funds and allowed to choose how interest earnings are distributed, while also regulating the fees and methods used for disbursement.
stakeholders: Homeowners with mortgaged properties (borrowers) and mortgage servicers
fiscal_impact_summary: The Office of Financial Regulation can handle enforcement with existing budgeted resources, and state revenues are not affected. There is no local fiscal impact. Small business mortgage servicers may experience a meaningful financial impact due to lost interest earnings and additional administrative costs associated with managing the loss draft accounts and payment mechanisms.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Department of Labor's Office of Financial Regulation (OFR) is responsible for the licensing and regulation of mortgage lenders and servicers. This bill introduces new requirements for these entities to maintain interest-bearing accounts for insurance proceeds, which the department would be responsible for enforcing.

The OAG serves as the chief legal officer for state agencies, including the Department of Labor, and enforces consumer protection laws. This bill creates new consumer rights regarding mortgage insurance proceeds and interest earnings, which may require legal interpretation or enforcement by the OAG.

While the bill primarily regulates mortgage servicers, the subject matter involves insurance proceeds and claim payments issued for property damage. The MIA regulates the insurance market and consumer protections related to insurance, making this bill relevant to their broader policy area.

The bill references license suspension or revocation for violations of mortgage lending laws. The OAH conducts impartial hearings for contested cases involving regulatory enforcement by state agencies like the Department of Labor.

As the principal fiscal and personnel agency for the state, DBM oversees the budget and resource allocation for the Department of Labor (OFR) to ensure it can handle any increased enforcement or oversight workload resulting from this legislation.

The Governor's Office oversees the executive branch and coordinates policy initiatives. The bill impacts the regulation of the financial services sector and protects residential property owners, aligning with the Governor's role in overseeing state law enforcement and economic policy.

Synopsis: Altering and establishing certain requirements related to the prevention, detection, and enforcement of unemployment insurance fraud in the State, including requirements related to the use of multifactor authentication under certain circumstances, reviews of claims for benefits, and the submission of proof of identification by claimants; authorizing the Maryland Department of Labor to recover overpaid benefits through State income tax withholding; etc.
Title: Unemployment Insurance - Fraud Prevention, Detection, and Enforcement
Status: In the House - Hearing 3/11 at 1:00 p.m.

NarrowSubjects.Name: Crimes and Punishments -see also- Penalties and Sentnc; etc.
Debt Collection -see also- Attachments and Garnishments
Insurance -see also- Health Ins; MAIF; Motor Vehicle Ins
Penalties and Sentences -see also- Death Penalty
Work, Labor, and Employment -see also- JobTrn; Leave; etc.

bill_summary: This bill establishes comprehensive requirements for the prevention, detection, and enforcement of unemployment insurance (UI) fraud. It mandates the use of multifactor authentication for the Department of Labor's online UI portals, requires claimants to provide specific forms of identification, and necessitates mandatory reviews of claims involving duplicate bank accounts, addresses, or out-of-state IP addresses. Additionally, the bill increases the monetary penalty for fraud from 15% to 20%, extends UI disqualification for fraudulent claimants to 10 years, allows for the recovery of overpayments through State income tax withholding, and requires the referral of fraud cases to law enforcement. It also mandates the termination of government employees or contractors found to have committed UI fraud.
stakeholders: Unemployment insurance claimants, employers, the Maryland Department of Labor, law enforcement agencies, and government employees or contractors.
fiscal_impact_summary: The bill is expected to result in an indeterminate increase in State revenue due to the increased fraud penalty (from 15% to 20%) and the authorization to recover overpaid benefits through State income tax refund withholding. State expenditures will increase to implement technological requirements like multifactor authentication, conduct mandated claim reviews, and fulfill new annual reporting obligations. Local fiscal impact may include increased costs for county law enforcement agencies tasked with investigating and prosecuting referred fraud cases. Specific dollar estimates from a formal Fiscal Note were not available in the provided text.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Maryland Department of Labor is the primary agency responsible for administering the state's unemployment insurance program. This bill directly mandates new operational requirements for the department, including multifactor authentication, specific claim review procedures, annual reporting on fraud, and enhanced enforcement and recovery mechanisms.

The bill authorizes the recovery of overpaid unemployment benefits through State income tax withholding and references procedures for withholding tax refunds under the Tax – General Article, which the Comptroller oversees as the state's principal tax collector.

DBM oversees the Central Collection Unit (CCU), which the bill explicitly authorizes to collect unemployment insurance overpayments caused by fraud. Additionally, DBM is the central personnel agency for the state; the bill's mandate to terminate government employees who commit unemployment fraud directly impacts its personnel management and policy duties.

The bill specifies that a final determination of unemployment fraud is grounds for immediate termination of a state employee, notwithstanding any terms of a collective bargaining agreement. As the agency responsible for administering collective bargaining and labor laws for state employees, PERB would be impacted by this statutory override of labor contracts.

The bill requires the use of multifactor authentication for the Department of Labor's publicly accessible websites and online portals. As the agency responsible for the state's information technology strategy and cybersecurity standards, DoIT would likely be involved in the technical implementation and security oversight of these requirements.

The bill discusses 'final determinations' after the exhaustion of administrative appeals. The OAH conducts hearings for contested cases involving state agencies, including the Department of Labor. New fraud review protocols and disqualification criteria would likely result in an increased volume or change in the nature of administrative hearings handled by this agency.

The bill requires the Secretary of Labor to refer final determinations of unemployment fraud to appropriate law enforcement agencies for prosecution. As the primary state law enforcement agency responsible for criminal investigations, MSP is a likely recipient of these referrals.

The OAG provides legal counsel to the Department of Labor and the Comptroller. The bill specifically mentions the Attorney General's role in advising on the validity of debts before they are certified for tax refund withholding.

The Governor's Office oversees the executive branch and the Secretary of Labor. The bill requires the Department of Labor to submit an annual report on fraud prevention and enforcement efforts to the Governor.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Governor's Office of Crime Prevention and Policy
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: GOCPP coordinates the state's criminal justice strategies and manages funds for law enforcement. The bill's emphasis on referring fraud for prosecution aligns with GOCPP's mission to reduce crime and recidivism through interagency collaboration.

Synopsis: Renaming and transferring the State Clearinghouse for Missing Children to be the State Clearinghouse for Missing Persons; requiring the Department of State Police to study the Department's capacity to report about persons who have disappeared from, or are thought to be located in, Maryland to the National Missing and Unidentified Persons System; and requiring the Department to submit its findings to the Governor and the General Assembly by December 1, 2026.
Title: Public Safety - State Clearinghouse for Missing Persons
Status: In the House - Hearing 3/10 at 1:00 p.m.

NarrowSubjects.Name: Law Enforcement -see also- SRO; Sheriffs; State Police

bill_summary: This bill renames the State Clearinghouse for Missing Children to the State Clearinghouse for Missing Persons and expands its scope to include the collection, receipt, and distribution of information regarding all missing persons. It also requires the Department of State Police to study and report on its capacity to share information with the National Missing and Unidentified Persons System.
stakeholders: Missing persons and their families, law enforcement agencies, and volunteer search organizations.
fiscal_impact_summary: The Department of State Police can implement the bill's requirements using existing budgeted resources. There is no impact on State or local revenues, and local law enforcement agencies can handle the bill's changes within existing resources.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Maryland State Police is the primary implementing agency. It operates the State Clearinghouse, is responsible for the expanded scope of collecting data on all missing persons, and is mandated to study and report on its capacity to integrate with the National Missing and Unidentified Persons System.

The Governor's Office is the recipient of the mandated report from the Department of State Police regarding its findings on the National Missing and Unidentified Persons System. Additionally, the office oversees the executive branch departments involved in the clearinghouse's operation.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Governor's Office of Crime Prevention and Policy
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: This office serves as the primary coordinating body for public safety and criminal justice strategies. The expansion of the missing persons clearinghouse and its interagency coordination requirements fall within its policy development and public safety advisory mandate.

The Department of Natural Resources operates the Natural Resources Police, which coordinates with the State Police on law enforcement matters. The bill explicitly requires the clearinghouse to coordinate with law enforcement agencies regarding information on missing persons.

The Maryland Department of Transportation oversees agencies such as the Motor Vehicle Administration and the Maryland Transportation Authority Police, which frequently coordinate with state clearinghouses on missing persons investigations and vehicle-related data.

Synopsis: Requiring, if a merchant rounds up the price of a cash transaction for a good or service in a certain manner, the merchant to remit to the Comptroller the difference between the total price the customer is required to pay after the rounding occurs and the price before the rounding occurs; and requiring the Comptroller to distribute certain revenue to the General Fund of the State.
Title: Business Regulation - Rounding Cash Transactions - Remittance to Comptroller
Status: In the House - Hearing 3/11 at 1:00 p.m.

NarrowSubjects.Name: Commerce and Business -see also- ElectrComm; ForeignTr; etc.
Goods and Services -see also- Retail Sales; TermnSvc; TrfGds

bill_summary: This bill requires merchants who round up the total price of a cash transaction to the nearest 5 cents to remit the difference between the rounded price and the original price to the State Comptroller, provided the customer did not consent to the rounding for a donation. The Comptroller is required to distribute this revenue to the State General Fund.
stakeholders: Merchants, cash-paying customers, and the State of Maryland
fiscal_impact_summary: The bill will result in an indeterminate increase in State General Fund revenue from remitted cash transaction rounding differences. Specific dollar estimates are unavailable because no formal Fiscal Note was provided with the bill text.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: As the state's chief financial officer and principal tax collector, the Comptroller is explicitly tasked by the bill with prescribing the manner of remittance for the rounded amounts and distributing the collected revenue to the General Fund.

The OAG provides legal counsel to state agencies, including the Comptroller, and would likely be involved in interpreting the requirements of the bill or representing the state in legal challenges regarding merchant remittance.
DBM is the principal fiscal agency responsible for estimating revenues and overseeing budget execution; this bill introduces a new revenue stream for the General Fund.
The Treasurer's Office is responsible for receiving and distributing state funds; it would manage the funds collected under this bill once remitted to the General Fund.

The bill impacts every 'merchant' engaged in the sale of goods or services in Maryland. The Department of Commerce, as the primary business development agency, may need to coordinate with the Comptroller to inform businesses of the new regulation.

As the administrative body that hears appeals regarding final decisions of taxing authorities, the Maryland Tax Court would have jurisdiction over disputes between merchants and the Comptroller regarding the remittance of rounded cash transaction differences.

Synopsis: Authorizing and empowering the County Commissioners of Calvert County, from time to time, to borrow not more than $80,957,080 to finance the construction, improvement, or development of certain public buildings, roads, and facilities in Calvert County, and to effect such borrowing by the issuance and sale at public or private sale of its general obligation bonds in like par amount; etc.
Title: Calvert County - Public Facilities Bonds
Status: Approved by the Governor - Chapter 339

NarrowSubjects.Name: Bonds -see also- County & Baltimore City Bonds; State Bonds
Public Buildings and Facilities -see also- Stadiums; St Hse
Public Officials -see also- Atty Gen; Compt; Coun Admin; etc

bill_summary: This bill authorizes the Calvert County Commissioners to borrow up to $80,957,080 through the issuance of general obligation bonds to finance the construction, improvement, or development of various public facilities, including public buildings, roads, and storm drainage systems.
stakeholders: Residents and taxpayers of Calvert County, Calvert County Government, and users of local public facilities such as schools and senior centers.
fiscal_impact_summary: Calvert County will receive up to $80,957,080 in bond proceeds for capital projects. The fiscal note estimates that annual debt service expenditures will increase by approximately $6,300,000 (roughly $4.6 million for 15-year bonds and $1.7 million for 25-year bonds). The bill has no impact on Maryland State finances.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Governor is responsible for signing the bill into law, which provides the necessary legislative authorization for Calvert County to borrow funds and issue general obligation bonds for public facilities.

The bill explicitly exempts the authorized bonds and the interest derived from them from all Maryland state and local taxation, which is relevant to the Comptroller's role as the state's principal tax collector and revenue administrator.

The bond proceeds are specifically intended to fund renovations at the Calvert Pines Senior Center, which aligns with the department's mission to oversee programs and facilities that improve the quality of life for older adults.

The bill authorizes funding for several public school projects, including Northern Middle School and Southern Middle School, which are part of the state's public education system overseen by the department.

The bond authority includes $1.5 million for local health department facilities, which are regulated and overseen by the Maryland Department of Health as part of the state's public health infrastructure.

A significant portion of the bond request (over $26 million) is allocated for wastewater treatment plant (WWTP) upgrades, sewer collection, and landfill projects, all of which fall under the environmental and water quality regulatory authority of the Department of the Environment.

The bill authorizes funding for county road paving and construction projects, including the Prince Frederick Loop Road and Boyd's Turn Road, which connect to the broader state transportation network managed by MDOT.

The bill facilitates the funding and execution of public school capital improvement projects, such as Northern and Southern Middle Schools, which are specifically overseen by the Commission to ensure facility sufficiency.

Synopsis: Altering the salaries of the County Commissioners of Calvert County, the president and members of the Calvert County Board of Education, and the County Treasurer of Calvert County; repealing a provision that the salary of State's Attorneys shall take effect at the beginning of the elected term of office and may not increase during the term of office; altering certain retirement benefits for the County Treasurer of Calvert County; providing that the Act does not apply to the salary or compensation of certain incumbent officials; etc.
Title: Calvert County - County Officials and Board of Education - Salaries and Benefits
Status: Approved by the Governor - Chapter 574

NarrowSubjects.Name: Health Insurance -see also- ACA; HMOs; MCOs
Public Officials -see also- Atty Gen; Compt; Coun Admin; etc
Salaries and Compensation -see also- Overtime; Reimb. Rates

bill_summary: This bill increases the annual salaries for several Calvert County officials, including the President and members of the Board of County Commissioners, the President and members of the County Board of Education, and the County Treasurer. It also adjusts retirement health benefits for County Commissioners and aligns the County Treasurer's pension benefits with those of other county employees. Additionally, it repeals a restriction that prevented the State's Attorney's salary from increasing during a term, allowing it to fluctuate with the salary of a circuit court judge.
responsible_party: Calvert County Board of County Commissioners
stakeholders: Calvert County Board of County Commissioners, Calvert County Board of Education, Calvert County Treasurer, Calvert County State's Attorney, and Calvert County taxpayers.
fiscal_impact_summary: According to the Fiscal Note, Calvert County expenditures are expected to increase by approximately $52,300 in fiscal 2027 and by a minimum of $100,900 annually thereafter. Specifically, the costs are estimated at $106,800 in fiscal 2029 and $112,700 in fiscal 2030. These estimates account for salary increases but do not reflect potential additional costs from increased fringe benefits or specific pension benefit changes.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Governor's Office is responsible for signing or vetoing legislation passed by the Maryland General Assembly, including this bill which impacts the salaries and benefits of local Calvert County officials.

The bill amends Section 3–303 of the Education Article to alter the annual compensation for the president and members of the Calvert County Board of Education. The Department of Education oversees the state's 24 local school systems, including their leadership structure and compensation standards.

The bill links the salary of the Calvert County State’s Attorney to the salary of a circuit court judge. The Administrative Office of the Courts provides financial and operational support to the judicial branch, including the management of judicial salaries used as the benchmark in this legislation.

The bill modifies the pension benefits for the Calvert County Treasurer to align with those of other county employees. Because many Maryland counties participate in the State Retirement and Pension System (SRPS) as participating governmental units, the SRA may be responsible for the administration and oversight of these modified benefits.

The Office of the Attorney General provides legal counsel to the Governor and the General Assembly, reviewing legislation for constitutionality and legal sufficiency, particularly regarding local government authority and public official compensation.

Synopsis: Applying certain provisions of law establishing that certain noncompete and conflict of interest provisions in certain employment contracts are null and void as being against the public policy of the State to employees of certain employers that relocate majority of its employees or principal place of business outside the State.
Title: Labor and Employment - Noncompete and Conflict of Interest Clauses - Employer Relocation
Status: In the House - Unfavorable Report by Government, Labor, and Elections; Withdrawn

NarrowSubjects.Name: Commerce and Business -see also- ElectrComm; ForeignTr; etc.
Work, Labor, and Employment -see also- JobTrn; Leave; etc.

bill_summary: This bill expands existing laws regarding noncompete and conflict of interest clauses to include employees of certain large employers that relocate outside of Maryland. Specifically, it renders noncompete and conflict of interest provisions null and void for employees whose employer previously had more than 30 employees in Maryland and, after the employee's departure, relocates the majority of its workforce or its principal place of business to a location outside the state.
stakeholders: Maryland employees, Maryland employers with more than 30 employees that may relocate out of state, and legal practitioners specializing in employment law.
fiscal_impact_summary: A formal Fiscal Note is absent from the provided text, and specific dollar estimates for revenue or expenditure changes are unavailable. The bill's financial impact is primarily private, affecting the enforceability of employment contracts for relocating businesses. It does not explicitly mandate new State spending or change existing tax revenues.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Department of Labor is the primary agency responsible for enforcing Maryland's labor and employment laws. This bill directly amends the Labor and Employment Article regarding the validity of noncompete and conflict of interest clauses in employment contracts.

The Office of the Attorney General provides legal counsel to the General Assembly and state agencies on the interpretation and enforcement of state laws. It would likely represent the state's interest in defending the public policy regarding voided noncompete clauses.

The Department of Commerce is Maryland's primary economic development agency. The bill's provisions regarding employer relocation outside the state directly impact the business climate and the agency's mission to retain and expand companies within Maryland.

The Maryland Judicial Branch will be responsible for adjudicating civil disputes where employment contracts containing noncompete or conflict of interest clauses are challenged as null and void under this new provision.

The Governor's Office oversees executive branch policy and legislative initiatives. This bill introduces a significant shift in labor policy by linking the validity of private employment contracts to an employer's relocation status.

The bill amends Section 3-716 of the Labor and Employment Article, which specifically includes noncompete regulations for health care professionals licensed under the Health Occupations Article, a sector regulated by the Department of Health.
The bill modifies the section of the Labor and Employment code that explicitly governs noncompete clauses for veterinary practitioners and technicians licensed under the Agriculture Article.

MEDCO supports the state's economy by providing services for business retention and expansion. The bill's focus on employer relocation and its legal consequences for employment agreements is relevant to their economic mission.

The board coordinates partnerships and strategies to ensure residents have access to employment. Policies that nullify noncompete clauses promote labor mobility, which is a key interest of the state's workforce strategy.

Synopsis: Transferring the administration of the electric universal service program from the Public Service Commission to the Office of Home Energy Programs in the Department of Human Services; and altering the authorized uses of the Strategic Energy Investment Fund to include fuel assistance programs.
Title: Human Services - Energy Assistance Programs - Administration and Funding
Status: In the House - Hearing 3/10 at 1:00 p.m. (Environment and Transportation)

NarrowSubjects.Name: Energy Matters -see also- Fuel; NuclearMatt; PwrPlnts; etc.
Public Benefits -see also- Housing; MedAsst;  SupplNutrAsstP
Utilities -see also- Recycl; Refuse; Sewage; Teleph; Water
Work, Labor, and Employment -see also- JobTrn; Leave; etc.

bill_summary: This bill transfers the administration of the Electric Universal Service Program from the Public Service Commission to the Office of Home Energy Programs within the Department of Human Services. It also expands the authorized uses of the Strategic Energy Investment Fund to include fuel assistance programs and allows for income eligibility waivers to align with other energy assistance programs.
responsible_party: Office of Home Energy Programs in the Department of Human Services
stakeholders: Low-income electric customers (at or below 200% of the federal poverty level), the Department of Human Services, and the Public Service Commission.
fiscal_impact_summary: The bill codifies the existing practice of the Department of Human Services (DHS) administering the Electric Universal Service Program (EUSP). The bill maintains a mandated annual funding level of $37,000,000 for the EUSP, collected from industrial, commercial, and residential ratepayer classes. Additionally, the bill alters the authorized uses of the Strategic Energy Investment Fund (SEIF) to allow funds to be used for fuel assistance programs, providing OHEP with greater flexibility to utilize SEIF funds when federal LIHEAP funding is unavailable.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill transfers the primary administration of the Electric Universal Service Program (EUSP) to the Office of Home Energy Programs, which is a unit within the Department of Human Services. DHS will now be responsible for implementing the bill assistance and arrearage retirement components of the program.

The bill transfers the statutory authority to establish and administer the Electric Universal Service Program from the PSC to DHS. However, the PSC retains oversight responsibility for certain program components and continues to determine funding allocations among customer classes.

The Maryland Energy Administration manages the Strategic Energy Investment Fund (SEIF). The bill alters the authorized uses of SEIF proceeds, specifically allowing them to be used for fuel assistance programs within DHS, which provides more flexibility during federal funding gaps.

The Department of Housing and Community Development remains responsible for the low-income residential weatherization component of the Electric Universal Service Program, and the bill updates statutory references to reflect the transfer of the broader program's administration.

The bill explicitly tasks the Comptroller with collecting revenue for the Electric Universal Service Program fund from electric companies and disbursing specific weatherization funds to DHCD as provided in the state budget.
The bill contains a specific provision requiring the Electric Universal Service Program to be subject to audit by the Office of Legislative Audits to ensure financial accountability and compliance.

As the state's central personnel and budget agency, DBM is relevant due to the bill's provisions regarding the transfer of employees between agencies without loss of rights or benefits, as well as the fiscal restructuring of program funding.

Synopsis: Establishing that a "qualified project" is a certain residential project that has been subject to retaliatory downzoning; requiring a local jurisdiction to allow the density of a certain qualified project to exceed the density otherwise authorized; and permitting a certain qualified project to consist of certain types of developments with certain density limits under certain circumstances.
Title: Land Use - Qualified Project - Retaliatory Downzoning
Status: In the House - Hearing 3/12 at 1:00 p.m.

NarrowSubjects.Name: Counties -see also- Chartered Counties; Code Counties; etc.
Housing -see also- Apartments; Condos; Mobile & Manuf  Homes
Public Officials -see also- Atty Gen; Compt; Coun Admin; etc

bill_summary: This bill defines 'qualified projects' as residential developments targeted by 'retaliatory downzoning'—a situation where local officials publicly oppose a project and subsequently reduce its permitted density in a manner inconsistent with professional recommendations. Local jurisdictions are required to allow these projects to exceed standard density limits, permitting middle housing in single-family zones and significantly increased density in multifamily, mixed-use, and nonresidential zones, provided that 15% to 20% of the units are deed-restricted as affordable for at least 40 years.
responsible_party: Local jurisdictions (Maryland counties and municipal corporations)
stakeholders: Residential developers, local government officials, local planning and transportation departments, and residents in need of affordable housing.
fiscal_impact_summary: Specific dollar estimates are unavailable as a formal Fiscal Note was not provided with the text. Potential financial impacts include increased local administrative costs for processing development applications and changes to local property tax revenue resulting from increased density and mandatory affordable housing requirements.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill directly amends the Land Use Article, which the Department of Planning oversees. The agency is responsible for promoting sustainable growth through comprehensive land use planning and providing technical assistance and policy guidance to local governments, all of which are impacted by new mandates on density and retaliatory downzoning.

The bill mandates density bonuses for residential projects and includes specific requirements for affordable housing units and deed restrictions, directly aligning with this agency's mission to ensure access to safe and affordable housing.

As the chief legal officer for the state, the OAG would be involved in providing legal counsel on the interpretation of 'retaliatory downzoning' and defending the state's authority to override local zoning ordinances in these specific cases.

This multi-agency initiative coordinates efforts across Planning and the Environment to manage land use and sustainable development. The bill's density mandates for 'qualified projects' directly interact with the initiative's goals regarding land use and community revitalization.

The Governor's Office oversees policy initiatives and intergovernmental relations. This bill represents a significant state-level policy intervention into local government zoning authority, a matter of executive branch policy coordination.

DBM is responsible for the state's fiscal planning and would need to evaluate any fiscal note or resource requirements for state agencies tasked with monitoring compliance with these new land use provisions.

The creation of a legal definition for 'retaliatory downzoning' and new density rights is likely to lead to increased litigation between developers and local jurisdictions, impacting the workload of the state's judicial branch.

Synopsis: Altering the triennial assessment cycle for real property for property tax purposes to a 5-year cycle.
Title: Property Tax Assessments - 5-Year Assessment Cycle
Status: In the House - Hearing 3/03 at 1:00 p.m.
bill_summary: This bill alters the assessment cycle for real property in Maryland from a three-year (triennial) cycle to a five-year (quinquennial) cycle. It adjusts the phase-in of property value increases to occur in one-fifth increments over five years, rather than the current one-third increments over three years, and updates related administrative procedures for revaluations and appeals.
responsible_party: Maryland State Department of Assessments and Taxation (SDAT)
stakeholders: Real property owners in Maryland, local governments including Baltimore City and Maryland's 23 counties, and the State Department of Assessments and Taxation.
fiscal_impact_summary: The bill extends the real property assessment and phase-in cycle from three to five years. This change will likely result in a delay of property tax revenue growth for both the State and local governments, as value increases will be spread over a longer duration (five years instead of three). Specific dollar estimates for expenditures or revenue changes were not provided in the bill text, and a formal Fiscal Note was not included in the source material.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: This agency is directly responsible for hearing appeals regarding real property valuations. Changing the assessment cycle from 3 to 5 years fundamentally alters their adjudication process, workload timing, and the statutory standards for the cases they review.

As the highest level of administrative review for tax disputes, the Tax Court will be responsible for interpreting and applying the new 5-year assessment cycle rules, phased-in value calculations, and appeal rights established by this bill.

The bill specifically amends Section 8-209 regarding farm and agricultural use land, changing the income averaging period used to determine tax classification from a 3-year to a 5-year period. This directly impacts the department's mission to support the economic viability of farming.

DBM is responsible for state revenue estimation and long-term fiscal planning. Moving from a 3-year to a 5-year assessment cycle will significantly change the timing and volume of property tax revenue projections, which are critical for state budget development.

The Treasurer manages state funds and oversees the issuance of State bonds. State property tax revenues are typically used to pay debt service on General Obligation bonds; changing the assessment cycle affects the predictability and timing of these funds.

The Board oversees significant state expenditures and bond issuances. Changes to the property tax assessment cycle affect the fiscal projections and revenue streams that support the state's capital projects and fiscal integrity, which the Board monitors.

As the state's chief financial officer and a member of the Board of Public Works, the Comptroller oversees state revenues and fiscal policy, both of which are impacted by changes to property tax assessment cycles and phase-in schedules.

The Governor is responsible for proposing the annual state budget and overseeing the executive branch agencies (like SDAT) that implement property tax laws. Changes to the assessment cycle impact the fiscal resources available for executive priorities.

The OAG provides legal counsel to state agencies involved in tax administration and represents the state in civil appeals. This bill introduces new statutory requirements for assessments and appeals that may require legal interpretation or defense.

OLA conducts fiscal compliance audits and performance evaluations of state agencies. They would be responsible for auditing the transition and adherence to the new 5-year assessment cycle by the relevant tax agencies.

Changes to property tax assessment cycles affect the cost of homeownership and the administration of property tax credits, which are relevant to the department's mission of ensuring access to affordable housing.
While most tax disputes are handled administratively, changes to property tax law can result in litigation that eventually reaches the state's court system, requiring judicial branch support.

bill_summary: This bill modifies Maryland's cannabis laws by altering the definition of business 'control', reducing the mandatory holding period for license transfers from five years to three years, and establishing a process for the Maryland Cannabis Administration (MCA) to approve management services agreements. It also relaxes advertising restrictions to allow outdoor signage and billboards, provided they are at least 500 feet from schools and other specified locations, and increases the maximum criminal fine for unlicensed cannabis sales to $10,000.
stakeholders: Cannabis licensees, management service providers, business investors, and the Maryland public, particularly minors regarding adjusted advertising protections.
fiscal_impact_summary: State special fund expenditures for the Maryland Cannabis Administration increase by $322,213 in FY 2027 for four new administrative positions to oversee management agreements and advertising reviews. Since administrative costs are paid from adult-use cannabis tax revenue, this expenditure results in a $161,107 reduction in General Fund revenues and a $16,111 reduction in county revenues for FY 2027. The bill also increases the maximum fine for the unlicensed sale of cannabis to $10,000 per violation.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: As the primary regulatory body for the cannabis industry, MCA is responsible for implementing the bill's major provisions, including reviewing management services agreements, providing advertising advisory opinions, and updating data publishing schedules.

The Comptroller distributes cannabis tax revenues. The bill increases MCA's administrative costs, which are deducted from tax collections before the Comptroller distributes remaining funds to the General Fund and other accounts.
Commerce administers the Cannabis Business Assistance Fund, which will see a decrease in revenue as a direct result of the bill's impact on the distribution formula for cannabis sales and use tax.

MDH administers the Cannabis Public Health Fund, which will receive reduced revenue under the bill. Additionally, its Office of Controlled Substances Administration regulates the state's controlled dangerous substance list relevant to THC products.
The OAG provides legal counsel to MCA and will be involved in the development and review of the new regulations and advisory opinion procedures required by the bill.
DBM is responsible for the personnel actions associated with the 4 new staff positions required by MCA to implement the bill, as well as overseeing the resulting shifts in state fund allocations.
OAH would likely adjudicate administrative appeals if MCA denies or conditionally approves management services agreements or takes enforcement action against advertising violations.
MSP is responsible for enforcing criminal laws, including the unlicensed sale or distribution of THC products, which the bill addresses by increasing misdemeanor fines.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Executive Commissions, Committees, Task Forces, and Advisory Boards
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: This includes the Advisory Board on Medical and Adult-Use Cannabis, which is tasked with studying and making recommendations on the industry regulations being altered by this legislation.
The judicial branch will process and adjudicate the misdemeanor citations and increased fines for the unlicensed sale of cannabis products established by the bill.

bill_summary: This bill increases the value of personal property that is exempt from execution on a judgment, such as household furnishings and appliances, and establishes new exemptions for firearms and motor vehicles used for work or education. It provides significantly higher exemption limits for debtors who are elderly (at least 60 years old) or who have a disability. Additionally, it exempts federal child tax credit and earned income tax credit payments from being seized to satisfy a judgment.
responsible_party: The Maryland Judiciary and local Sheriffs
stakeholders: Judgment debtors, judgment creditors, small businesses, elderly individuals, and individuals with disabilities
fiscal_impact_summary: According to the fiscal note, the bill is not anticipated to materially affect State or local government finances. There is a potential meaningful negative impact on small businesses that provide goods and services on credit, as higher exemption values and additional exempt categories may reduce their ability to collect on money judgments.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill directly modifies the Courts and Judicial Proceedings Article regarding exemptions from execution on a judgment, which is centrally managed and implemented by the judicial branch and its administrative support systems.

As the state's chief tax collector and financial officer, the Comptroller's debt collection and revenue recovery efforts are impacted by changes to property and cash exemptions, particularly the new protections for the Earned Income Tax Credit and Child Tax Credit.

The OAG represents the state and its agencies in civil litigation and debt collection. Changes to statutory exemptions affect the legal strategies and capabilities for recovering funds owed to the state.
The bill creates specific value-based exemptions for motor vehicles necessary for work or education, which relates to the vehicle records and titling managed by the MVA.
The bill establishes specific, higher exemption thresholds (up to $10,000 for household goods and $25,000 for a vehicle) for individuals who are 'elderly' (60 years or older).
The bill establishes specific, higher exemption thresholds for individuals with a disability, as defined in the bill, to protect their essential assets from judgment.
The bill addresses the exemption status of child support payments and the ability to execute judgments against personal injury or workers' compensation recoveries for child support arrearages.
The bill references subrogation rights of the Maryland Department of Health and specifically excludes MDH claims from certain retirement asset protections.
The bill specifies how judgments for child support arrearages may be executed against workers' compensation indemnity benefits.
As the administrator for state employee workers' compensation claims, this agency is impacted by the rules governing the execution on indemnity benefits.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Maryland Office of the Public Defender
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The OPD represents indigent clients who are frequently impacted by civil judgments and debt collection; changes to asset exemptions are highly relevant to their clients' economic stability.
As the parent department of the Motor Vehicle Administration, MDOT is relevant to the administration of new policies concerning motor vehicle exemptions.
DBM is responsible for state fiscal planning and was identified as an information source for the bill's fiscal impact analysis.
The bill creates motor vehicle exemptions specifically for students enrolled in elementary or secondary schools.
The bill creates motor vehicle exemptions specifically for students enrolled in institutions of higher education.

bill_summary: House Bill 1521 establishes a State income tax credit to incentivize financial contributions, volunteerism, and the employment of at-risk youth (ages 12 to 25) in designated high-crime or high-poverty zip codes, including all of Baltimore City and Baltimore County. The bill allows for a 50% credit for donations to certified organizations, a $25 daily credit for professional volunteering in schools, and a $1,000 credit per at-risk youth employed for a minimum duration.
stakeholders: At-risk youth, nonprofit organizations, local education agencies, business entities, and individual taxpayers in high-crime or high-poverty areas.
fiscal_impact_summary: State general fund revenues will decrease by an estimated maximum of $10,000,000 annually between fiscal years 2027 and 2033, as the bill caps the total amount of certified tax credits at this amount per taxable year. Although a formal Fiscal Note was not provided in the text, the bill explicitly limits the Department of Commerce to certifying no more than $10,000,000 in credits each year.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Department of Commerce is the primary agency responsible for certifying eligible organizations, establishing the tax credit application process, certifying the credit amounts for taxpayers, and reporting annually to the General Assembly on the program's impact.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Governor's Office of Crime Prevention and Policy
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The office is explicitly required to consult with the Department of Commerce to certify eligible organizations and adopt regulations, and it serves as the lead agency for the public safety and juvenile crime prevention aspects of the bill.
As the state's chief tax collector, the Comptroller's office is responsible for administering the new income tax credits, processing claims, and managing the fiscal impact on state revenue.

The bill designates local education agencies and public schools as eligible organizations for contributions and volunteerism; it also targets youth who are chronically absent or have dropped out of school, which are metrics tracked by MSDE.

The bill's definition of at-risk youth includes individuals involved in prevention or diversion programs under the Human Services Article, as well as those aging out of foster care or experiencing homelessness, both of which fall under DHS jurisdiction.
The bill specifically targets youth involved in the juvenile justice system for support services, development programs, and employment initiatives to reduce juvenile crime.
The bill provides a tax credit for employers who hire at-risk youth, which directly relates to the Department of Labor's mission of supervising workforce development and enforcing labor laws.
The bill's focus on reducing child poverty, youth homelessness, and improving outcomes for underinvested communities aligns directly with the central mission and the ENOUGH Initiative of this office.
DBM oversees the state's revenue estimations and fiscal planning, which will be impacted by the $10 million annual cap on the tax credits established by this bill.

The bill requires that individuals claiming the volunteer credit must be accompanied by school safety personnel while on school grounds, which falls under the safety standards and personnel oversight of this agency.

The bill targets at-risk youth experiencing homelessness and promotes community revitalization in high-poverty ZIP codes, areas managed through DHCD's community investment and homeless solution programs.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Department of Service and Civic Innovation
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: This agency promotes service and volunteerism to create workforce pathways, aligning with the bill's provisions for professional volunteerism and youth employment credits.

The bill's primary objectives of reducing child poverty and enhancing economic mobility for at-risk youth are the core priorities this team was established to address through novel policy initiatives.
The bill includes faith-based organizations as eligible recipients for supporting at-risk youth, a sector primarily engaged by GOCI through its community and faith-based commissions.

As the administrative support for the Governor, this office oversees the executive branch agencies (Commerce and GOCPP) tasked with implementing the bill and coordinates the broader policy initiative.

Synopsis: Repealing the exemptions for a motor vehicle that is owned by a motor vehicle rental or leasing company or that displays certain registration plates from liability for citations produced as a result of images recorded by a traffic control signal monitoring system or a speed monitoring system.

bill_summary: This bill repeals the exemptions from liability for traffic control signal (red light) and speed monitoring system citations for motor vehicle rental companies, motor vehicle leasing companies, short-term lessees (under 6 months), and holders of special registration plates (such as motor vehicle dealers and transporters), making these owners or lessees liable for the civil penalties.
responsible_party: Maryland Department of Transportation (State Highway Administration), Maryland Transportation Authority, and local jurisdictions
stakeholders: Motor vehicle rental and leasing companies, short-term lessees, and holders of special registration plates including dealers and transporters.
fiscal_impact_summary: State and local revenues are expected to increase annually starting in fiscal 2027 due to the repeal of several exemptions from automated traffic enforcement fines. General fund, Transportation Trust Fund (special fund), and Maryland Transportation Authority (nonbudgeted) revenues will increase depending on the volume of citations issued and paid. Local government revenues and expenditures for public safety are also expected to increase accordingly. Specific dollar estimates are unavailable because the impact depends on the number of additional citations issued.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Department of Transportation oversees the state's transportation network, including the State Highway Administration and Motor Vehicle Administration, which are directly involved in operating speed monitoring systems and managing vehicle registrations affected by this bill.

The bill specifically references the Maryland Transportation Authority's use of speed monitoring systems on Route 200. The fiscal note indicates that nonbudgeted revenues for MDTA will likely increase as a result of repealing exemptions for rental vehicles and special plates.

The State Highway Administration is explicitly mentioned in the bill as an authorized user of speed monitoring systems. The agency will see a direct impact on its revenues and expenditures, particularly regarding safety initiatives on Maryland Route 210.

The MVA manages vehicle titling, registration, and the 'special registration plates' (such as those for dealers and transporters) that are specifically mentioned in the bill's repeal of exemptions. It is also responsible for maintaining the owner records used to issue citations.

The District Court of Maryland, supported by the AOC, adjudicates contested automated enforcement citations. The fiscal note indicates an increase in general fund revenue from these cases and notes the court's role in processing the additional caseload.

As the principal fiscal agency, DBM is responsible for estimating state revenues. The bill is expected to increase general and special fund revenues through citation collections, which affects the state's fiscal planning.

The Comptroller receives excess local speed camera revenues that exceed 10% of a county's total revenue. An increase in local fine collections could result in more funds being remitted to the Comptroller's office.

The Maryland State Police is the primary law enforcement agency for the state and is involved in ensuring traffic safety. While automated systems are often handled by specific administrations or local jurisdictions, the MSP provides specialized services and support for highway patrol and criminal investigations related to motor vehicle laws.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Governor's Office of Crime Prevention and Policy
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: This office coordinates public safety strategies and advises the Governor on criminal justice policies. Automated enforcement is a public safety tool used to reduce traffic violations and improve road safety.

The Governor's Office oversees the executive branch agencies (MDOT, SHA, MSP) responsible for implementing these programs and proposes the state budget, which will be affected by the changes in revenue.
Since many speed monitoring systems are authorized for use in school zones, this agency has an interest in changes that affect the enforcement and liability of traffic laws in those areas.
The Treasurer acts as the chief financial agency responsible for receiving and distributing state funds, including the increased general and special fund revenues resulting from this legislation.
The OAG provides legal counsel to the state agencies implementing the automated enforcement programs and may represent the state in appeals related to citation liability.

The Maryland Insurance Administration was consulted for the fiscal note, as changes to vehicle owner liability for rental and leasing companies may have secondary impacts on the insurance industry and liability coverage practices.

bill_summary: This bill authorizes the Alcohol, Tobacco, and Cannabis Commission (ATCC) to regulate, seize, and destroy 'unauthorized consumable products,' which include tianeptine, non-compliant kratom, and phenibut. It prohibits retailers from selling or advertising these substances, especially to minors, and mandates that the Maryland Department of Health notify the ATCC of changes in the regulatory status of such products. Violations are classified as misdemeanors subject to fines and potential license revocation.
stakeholders: Retailers (including manufacturers, wholesalers, and stores), consumers of herbal or synthetic supplements, and the Maryland Department of Health.
fiscal_impact_summary: State and local fiscal impacts are expected to be minimal. The Alcohol, Tobacco, and Cannabis Commission and the Maryland Department of Health can implement the bill's provisions using existing budgeted resources. While the bill establishes criminal fines up to $5,000 and civil liability for retailers, these are not anticipated to have a material financial impact on State or local government operations.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Maryland Department of Health is explicitly required to monitor the regulatory status of products like kratom, tianeptine, and phenibut and notify the Alcohol, Tobacco, and Cannabis Commission of changes. The Secretary of Health also has the authority to designate certain consumable products for enforcement.

The bill authorizes the District Court to order the Comptroller to suspend or revoke specific licenses (such as tobacco or general business licenses) for retailers found in violation of the unauthorized consumable product prohibitions.

The bill grants new authority to the District Court to impose sanctions, order the seizure and destruction of products, and adjudicate misdemeanor criminal cases and civil liability claims arising from the bill's provisions.

The OAG serves as the primary legal counsel for the state agencies (MDH and ATCC) tasked with implementing these enforcement, seizure, and notification requirements, and would likely be involved in legal challenges or complex forfeiture proceedings.

The Governor's Office oversees the executive agencies involved (including MDH and the commissions within the executive branch) and the Governor must approve the designation of enforcement authorities and sign the bill into law.

DBM is responsible for the state budget and personnel management; the bill specifically references the Field Enforcement Division's ability to employ officers and employees as provided in the state budget.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Department of Public Safety and Correctional Services
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill establishes misdemeanor penalties that include potential imprisonment for up to 90 days, which would fall under the broader jurisdiction of state correctional and supervision systems if individuals are incarcerated.

bill_summary: This bill requires employers with 15 or more employees and all governmental units to provide employees who are parents with at least 20 hours of paid leave per year to attend school functions at their child's elementary or secondary school. Employees may use no more than 2 hours of this leave per month and must provide proof of the school function within 48 hours of the event.
responsible_party: Commissioner of Labor and Industry (Maryland Department of Labor)
stakeholders: Maryland employers with 15 or more employees, state and local government agencies, and employees who are parents, stepparents, or legal guardians of children in elementary or secondary schools.
fiscal_impact_summary: State and local expenditures may increase starting in fiscal year 2027 due to overtime costs for coverage of employees using the leave, particularly in 24/7 facilities such as prisons and hospitals. While specific dollar estimates are unavailable, the impact is described as potentially significant for some agencies. Small businesses with at least 15 employees may also experience operational disruptions and increased costs.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill designates the Commissioner (of Labor and Industry, within this department) as the enforcement authority responsible for investigating violations and issuing compliance orders. The department must also provide public guidance on the program.

As the state's central personnel agency, DBM is responsible for implementing the new leave category within the State Personnel Management System, training HR staff, and managing fiscal impacts on state agencies.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Department of Public Safety and Correctional Services
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: As an agency with 24/7 facilities (prisons), DPSCS is specifically noted in the fiscal note as potentially incurring significant overtime costs to provide coverage for employees using this paid leave.
MDH operates 24/7 facilities (hospitals) and, according to the fiscal note, may face significant overtime costs to maintain coverage when employees utilize the new paid school function leave.

The leave is specifically for attending functions at elementary and secondary schools overseen by MSDE. Schools will likely be responsible for providing the 'proof of school function' required by the bill for employees to qualify for the leave.
USM is a major state employer with an independent personnel system; the fiscal note identifies it as an agency that will be impacted by the leave requirements and related administrative burdens.
MDOT is a large state employer with varied operational shifts; it was consulted for the fiscal note regarding the impact on state personnel expenditures and operational coverage.
The AOC manages the personnel system for the Judicial Branch and was identified in the fiscal note as an entity impacted by the new leave requirements for its employees.
The OAG would provide legal counsel to the Department of Labor regarding the enforcement of the new labor law and to DBM regarding its implementation for state employees.
The bill explicitly states that the leave use must comply with collective bargaining agreements; PERB oversees these agreements and labor disputes for the public sector.
As an independent state agency and large employer, Morgan State University will be required to provide this paid leave to its eligible employees and manage the fiscal and administrative impacts.

bill_summary: This bill requires the Governor to withdraw Maryland from the Regional Greenhouse Gas Initiative (RGGI) by January 1, 2027, and defines specific conditions for rejoining. It also repeals the surcharge on customer bills used by utilities to recover costs for EmPOWER Maryland energy efficiency and conservation programs and limits the rate at which electric companies must purchase or provide bill credits for electricity from community solar energy generating systems.
responsible_party: The Governor and the Maryland Public Service Commission
stakeholders: Electric and gas companies, electricity and gas ratepayers, low-income residents receiving energy assistance, and community solar developers and subscribers.
fiscal_impact_summary: State special fund revenues and expenditures are estimated to decrease by $138,300,000 in fiscal 2027 and by $276,600,000 annually thereafter due to the withdrawal from RGGI. General fund expenditures may increase significantly to maintain programs previously supported by RGGI funds. The repeal of the EmPOWER surcharge eliminates a primary funding source for energy efficiency programs, likely requiring the Public Service Commission to establish alternative funding mechanisms such as increased base rates.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill explicitly requires the Governor to withdraw the State from the Regional Greenhouse Gas Initiative (RGGI) by January 1, 2027, and provides conditions under which the Governor may rejoin.

The Public Service Commission (PSC) is responsible for implementing the repeal of the EmPOWER surcharge on utility bills and regulating the tariff structure for community solar energy generating systems as mandated by the bill.

The Department of Housing and Community Development (DHCD) administers the LIEEP and MEEHA energy efficiency programs, which are currently funded by the EmPOWER surcharge and RGGI proceeds, both of which are significantly altered or eliminated by the bill.

The Department of Human Services (DHS) is a primary recipient of RGGI funding (at least 50% of proceeds) used for the Electric Universal Service Program (EUSP) and other low-income energy assistance programs, which will face a significant funding loss.

The bill amends the Environment Article regarding the state's participation in RGGI. MDE is the primary agency for environmental protection and currently receives a portion of RGGI funding for various climate initiatives.

OPC represents residential utility consumers. The fiscal note indicates their workload and costs may increase as they advocate for consumers in base rate proceedings that could replace the EmPOWER surcharge.

DBM is the principal fiscal agency responsible for state budget development. The bill results in a significant decrease in special fund revenues (over $276 million annually) and potential increases in general fund expenditures to replace lost funding for essential programs.
The Maryland Clean Energy Center is identified in the fiscal note as a recipient of RGGI funding for renewable energy and climate change programs, which will be reduced due to the state's withdrawal.
DGS receives RGGI funding to implement energy efficiency and conservation initiatives in state-owned facilities, which are impacted by the withdrawal from the initiative.
DNR receives RGGI proceeds to support the Power Plant Research Program, which investigates the environmental impact of power generation and supports conservation efforts.
MDOT is a recipient of RGGI proceeds for climate resiliency and energy programs related to transportation, which will experience a reduction in funding.
The OAG provides legal counsel to state agencies like the PSC and MDE, who will require legal guidance on the statutory changes and regulatory shifts required by the bill.
The University System of Maryland, including the Maryland Energy Innovation Institute, receives RGGI funds for energy efficiency research and campus projects.
As a state university, Morgan State may receive funding from the Strategic Energy Investment Fund (SEIF) for energy efficiency projects which will be impacted by the loss of RGGI revenues.
St. Mary's College is a public institution eligible for energy efficiency funding through the SEIF, which is primarily funded by RGGI proceeds.

The Comptroller serves as the chief financial officer overseeing state revenues. The significant reduction in RGGI auction proceeds affects the state's revenue stream and the Strategic Energy Investment Fund.
The Treasurer manages and protects state funds, including the Strategic Energy Investment Fund (SEIF), which will lose hundreds of millions of dollars in annual RGGI auction proceeds.

bill_summary: This bill establishes a Class 1 distillery on-premises consumption permit in Carroll County, which allows the local Board of License Commissioners to grant permit holders the authority to sell, prepare, and serve food, nonalcoholic beverages, and specific distillery-produced alcoholic beverages for on-site consumption. responsible_party: Carroll County Board of License Commissioners
stakeholders: Class 1 distillery license holders in Carroll County, the Carroll County Health Department, and the Carroll County Board of License Commissioners.
fiscal_impact_summary: According to the Fiscal Note, Carroll County revenues may increase minimally beginning in fiscal 2027, depending on the permit fees established by the Board of License Commissioners. The bill is not expected to materially affect State finances or operations.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Comptroller of Maryland is the primary state official responsible for regulating the alcohol industry and issuing manufacturer's licenses. This bill directly references the Class 1 distillery license and its issuance by the Comptroller, and establishes a specific on-premises consumption permit for Carroll County relating to those licenses.

The bill explicitly requires that the authorization to sell, prepare, and serve food and non-alcoholic beverages at these distilleries be approved by the Carroll County Health Department, which operates under the oversight and policy guidance of the Maryland Department of Health.

The Governor is responsible for signing the bill into law and oversees the executive branch departments, such as the Comptroller and the Department of Health, that are involved in alcohol and food safety regulation.

The Office of the Attorney General serves as the primary legal representative for the state and its agencies, including providing counsel on the implementation of new licensing and permitting laws within the Alcoholic Beverages and Cannabis Article.

bill_summary: This bill establishes the Complementary and Alternative Health Care Practice Act, which authorizes individuals to provide various alternative health services—such as acupressure, aromatherapy, and herbology—without obtaining a license or certification from a state health occupations board. Practitioners are required to provide clients with written disclosures regarding their credentials and services and are strictly prohibited from performing specific medical procedures, including surgery, prescribing controlled substances, and manipulating joints.
stakeholders: Complementary and alternative health care practitioners, health care consumers, and Maryland state health occupation boards.
fiscal_impact_summary: The Maryland Department of Health special fund expenditures increase by at least $244,300 in FY 2027 to hire investigative and legal staff for the Board of Physicians and the Board of Pharmacy to handle complaints. These expenditures are projected to grow annually to approximately $319,800 by FY 2031. The bill has no impact on state revenues or local government finances.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Maryland Department of Health (MDH) is the primary agency responsible for the oversight of health care professionals. The bill directly impacts the regulatory framework managed by MDH by allowing individuals to practice various forms of health care without standard licensure. The fiscal note identifies significant special fund expenditure increases for MDH to manage investigative staff for boards such as the Board of Physicians and the Board of Pharmacy.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Executive Commissions, Committees, Task Forces, and Advisory Boards
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill amends the specific statutory authority of 19 different health occupation boards, including the State Board of Physicians, State Board of Nursing, and State Board of Pharmacy. These boards, which function as permanent regulatory bodies within the executive branch, will have their licensing jurisdiction bypassed for practitioners of complementary and alternative health care.

The Office of the Attorney General provides legal counsel to all state agencies and boards. The fiscal note specifically anticipates the need for additional part-time legal counsel to support the Boards of Physicians and Pharmacy in handling complaints and legal issues arising from the authorization of unlicensed practitioners.

The Office of Administrative Hearings adjudicates contested cases for state agencies, including MDH and its various health occupation boards. If the boards take enforcement action against alternative practitioners for exceeding the scope of the bill (e.g., performing surgery or prescribing drugs), the OAH would likely handle the appeals.

As a division of MDH that enforces the state's Controlled Dangerous Substance Act, this office is relevant because the bill explicitly prohibits unlicensed alternative health care practitioners from prescribing or dispensing controlled substances. Enforcement of this provision would fall under this agency's purview.

As the state's central personnel agency, DBM is involved in the creation and management of the new investigator and legal counsel positions identified in the fiscal note as necessary to implement the bill's oversight requirements.

The MHCC is responsible for health system planning and improving access and accountability. The authorization of a new class of health care providers and the modification of licensing standards are relevant to the commission's broad mandate for health policy planning.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Health Care Alternative Dispute Resolution Office
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: This office administers the mandatory arbitration system for medical malpractice claims. Because the bill authorizes practitioners to provide various health services, disputes regarding liability and damages for these services may fall under this office's jurisdiction.

Synopsis: Authorizing a public school to allow a student participating in a certain home instruction program to participate in extracurricular activities sponsored by the school under certain circumstances; and requiring a public school to give placement priority to a student enrolled in a certain school over a student who is not enrolled in the school if certain limitations exist.

bill_summary: This bill authorizes Maryland public schools to allow students in home instruction programs to participate in school-sponsored extracurricular activities, including athletics and interscholastic sports, provided the local school system approves. It requires schools to prioritize students enrolled at the school over non-enrolled students if space in an activity is limited.
responsible_party: Maryland local school systems and individual public schools
stakeholders: Homeschool students, public school students, and local school administrators
fiscal_impact_summary: A formal Fiscal Note with specific estimates is not included in the provided text. Potential financial implications involve minor administrative costs for local school systems to coordinate and oversee the participation of homeschool students in school-sponsored activities.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: As the primary agency responsible for overseeing Maryland's public education system and setting statewide educational policies and standards, MSDE is highly relevant. This bill directly concerns the eligibility of students in home instruction programs to participate in public school extracurricular activities and references COMAR guidelines, which fall under MSDE's regulatory authority.

The OAG serves as the legal representative for the Maryland State Department of Education and all state agencies. They would likely be required to provide legal guidance and interpretation regarding the implementation of this new statutory section, particularly concerning liability, equal access, and the rights of non-enrolled students.
