responsible_party: The Mayor and City Council of Baltimore City and the governing bodies of Maryland counties
stakeholders: Owners and operators of qualified data centers, Baltimore City, and Maryland county governments
fiscal_impact_summary: The bill's fiscal impact on local revenue is indeterminate, as it depends on whether local jurisdictions choose to exercise the authority to establish a special personal property tax subclass and what rate they set. No specific state or local revenue or expenditure estimates are provided in the bill text, and a formal Fiscal Note was not included in the provided text.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill utilizes the definition of a qualified data center from the Tax-General Article, which is administered by the Comptroller's office through the sales and use tax exemption application and certification process.

As Maryland's primary economic development agency, the Department of Commerce uses industry-specific tax incentives to attract major investments and high-tech jobs, such as those associated with qualified data centers.

The board provides administrative review for property tax disputes and would be responsible for hearing appeals regarding the valuation or classification of property within the new data center subclass.

The Tax Court adjudicates appeals from final decisions of local taxing authorities, including those related to the assessment and special tax rates authorized by this bill for data center personal property.
The department oversees the state's fiscal planning and monitors the budgetary impact of changes to tax law and local taxing authority.
The expansion of data centers is a key component of the state's digital infrastructure strategy, which is coordinated and overseen by this department.
The office provides legal counsel to the state and local governments on the implementation and constitutionality of changes to the Tax-Property and Tax-General articles.
The Governor's Office coordinates policy initiatives and economic development strategies, including the use of local tax incentives to attract specialized industries.
This quasi-governmental corporation assists in the attraction and retention of businesses by providing development and financing services for commercial and industrial projects like data centers.

bill_summary: This bill establishes the Maryland Growth Initiative and the Maryland Growth Initiative Fund within the Maryland Technology Development Corporation (TEDCO) to support start-up companies transitioning from early development to scaling. The initiative provides postseed and Series A funding, technical expertise, and infrastructure support, with priority given to minority business enterprises and previous TEDCO funding recipients.
stakeholders: Maryland start-up companies in the phase between early development and scaling, minority business enterprises, and recipients of funding from TEDCO or the Maryland Innovation Initiative.
fiscal_impact_summary: The bill mandates an annual general fund appropriation of 5000000 dollars starting in FY 2028, with corresponding increases in special fund revenues and expenditures. There is no fiscal impact in FY 2027. TEDCO expects to allocate 1000000 dollars for administrative costs and 4000000 dollars for investment awards annually.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: TEDCO is the primary implementing agency for the bill. It is tasked with establishing the Maryland Growth Initiative, administering the Maryland Growth Initiative Fund, creating a curated list of start-up companies, and providing investment awards and technical expertise.
As the state's principal fiscal agency, DBM is responsible for managing the $5 million annual mandated appropriation from the General Fund to the Maryland Growth Initiative Fund starting in FY 2028.
The bill explicitly requires the Governor to include a $5 million appropriation for the Initiative in the annual budget bill starting in FY 2028.
The bill explicitly requires the Comptroller to account for the Maryland Growth Initiative Fund and exempts the Fund's interest earnings from accruing to the General Fund.
The bill explicitly requires the State Treasurer to hold the Maryland Growth Initiative Fund separately and invest the money of the Fund, ensuring interest earnings are credited back to it.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Governor's Office of Small, Minority & Women Business Affairs
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill requires that priority for the Initiative's curated list of companies be given to Minority Business Enterprises (MBEs), a program monitored and implemented by this office.

As the state's primary economic development agency, the Department of Commerce has a secondary interest in the Initiative's goals of attracting and retaining businesses and fostering job growth, though TEDCO is the lead agency.

The OAG serves as legal counsel for TEDCO and the state agencies involved, which will likely involve reviewing regulations, contracts for infrastructure support, and investment award agreements authorized by the bill.

Synopsis: Establishing an unregulated space in hospital operating suites pilot project; requiring the Health Services Cost Review Commission to administer the pilot project; requiring the Commission to develop certain criteria and standards for the pilot project; requiring the Commission by December 1 annually to submit a certain report to certain committees of the General Assembly; and requiring certain ambulatory surgical centers and freestanding surgical centers to provide the Commission with certain information.

bill_summary: This bill establishes a three-year pilot project, administered by the Health Services Cost Review Commission (HSCRC), allowing up to five hospitals to maintain unregulated operating room space within their facilities. Participating hospitals may be subject to alternate rate determination methods, provided they meet specific criteria including offering charity care, ensuring costs to Medicaid and Medicare are lower than regulated services, and increasing consumer awareness about physician charges.
stakeholders: Hospitals, ambulatory surgical centers, freestanding surgical centers, patients, and healthcare payers including Medicare and Medicaid.
fiscal_impact_summary: State special fund expenditures for the Health Services Cost Review Commission increase by $400,000 in FY 2027 and $50,000 annually through FY 2029 to cover contractual costs for administering the pilot project. Although the bill mandates that costs for the Medical Assistance Program and Medicare be lower than similar regulated hospital services, potential Medicaid savings are indeterminate and depend on utilization and the HSCRC's rate-setting methodology. There is no local fiscal impact.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: As the primary agency responsible for regulating hospital rates and revenues, the HSCRC is tasked with administering the pilot project, developing its criteria and standards, and reporting results to the General Assembly.

As the parent department for HSCRC and the administrator of the Medical Assistance Program (Medicaid), MDH is directly impacted by the bill's requirement that costs to Medicaid must be lower than similar regulated hospital services.
The MHCC oversees health system planning and the regulation of freestanding surgical centers, which are required by the bill to provide data to HSCRC for the pilot project report.

The OAG provides legal counsel to state agencies like the HSCRC and MDH and would likely be involved in drafting or reviewing the legal standards and alternate rate determination methods for the pilot project.
DBM oversees the state budget and personnel; it will be involved in managing the HSCRC's special fund expenditure increases ($400,000 in FY 2027) identified in the fiscal note.
The Governor's Office oversees executive branch policy initiatives and budget proposals; the pilot project represents a significant shift in hospital rate policy that requires executive coordination.
OLA is responsible for auditing executive agencies and would likely review the fiscal compliance and performance outcomes of this new pilot project.
The pilot project affects hospital billing and 'all-payer' rates, which could have downstream effects on the private health plans offered through the state's insurance marketplace.

Synopsis: Authorizing, rather than requiring, a certain racing licensee to receive a grant for a capital construction plan from the Racetrack Facility Renewal Account without providing and expending a matching fund; requiring the racing licensee that receives the grant without providing and expending a matching fund to conduct live racing in the State for at least 10 years after the construction plan is complete; and requiring the State Racing Commission to recapture certain grant funds under certain circumstances and in a certain manner.

bill_summary: This bill allows standardbred horse racing licensees to obtain capital construction grants from the Racetrack Facility Renewal Account without providing matching funds, provided they commit to continuing live racing for at least 10 years after the project is completed. It also mandates the recapture of grant money if racing or construction requirements are not met and adjusts the redistribution of unencumbered funds between tracks in the event of a facility closure.
stakeholders: Standardbred racing licensees (Rosecroft Raceway and Ocean Downs Racetrack), horse owners, and trainers.
fiscal_impact_summary: The bill is estimated to have no state or local fiscal impact, as it alters the eligibility criteria for receiving existing grants from the Racetrack Facility Renewal Account without changing the total amount of funding distributed to the account. The standardbred tracks currently receive an estimated $2,400,000 annually from video lottery terminal proceeds, and the account balance is approximately $17,100,000.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Maryland Racing Commission (MRC), which is a unit within the Department of Labor, has primary authority over the Racetrack Facility Renewal Account (RFRA). This bill directly alters the MRC's requirements for issuing grants, monitoring construction plans, and recapturing funds. Additionally, the Secretary of Labor is specifically named as the authority to whom licensees apply for certain reimbursements.

The bill explicitly requires the Maryland Racing Commission to consult with the Department of General Services (DGS) to monitor the implementation of capital construction plans and mandates that DGS participate in the certification process for completed construction projects.

The Office of the Attorney General provides legal counsel to the Maryland Racing Commission and will be responsible for drafting the legal mechanisms for the new grant recapture provisions and any new regulations required by the bill.

The Board of Public Works oversees and approves significant state expenditures and contracts. Because RFRA grants represent significant capital investments and often involve grant agreements with the state, they are subject to the Board's fiscal oversight.

As the state's principal fiscal agency, DBM oversees the execution of the state budget and estimates revenues. This bill affects the management and potential recapture of funds within the Racetrack Facility Renewal Account, which is funded by video lottery terminal proceeds.

The Governor's Office oversees the executive branch and appoints the members of the State Racing Commission. The bill also changes policies related to a state-regulated industry and account under the Governor's executive authority.

The Comptroller acts as the state's chief financial officer and is responsible for the collection and distribution of state revenues, including the VLT proceeds that fund the Racetrack Facility Renewal Account.

bill_summary: This bill establishes the Chesapeake Bay Enhancement Program to support oyster propagation and replenishment projects intended to offset the environmental impacts of transportation projects at the Helen Delich Bentley Port of Baltimore. It also creates the Maryland Seafood Industry Financial Assistance Fund to provide loans and financial aid to commercial watermen and small seafood businesses. Additionally, the bill prevents the Department of Natural Resources from approving the transfer of tidal fish licenses for individuals who are delinquent on loans from the Maryland Agricultural and Resource-Based Industry Development Corporation (MARBIDCO).
responsible_party: Maryland Department of Natural Resources and the Maryland Agricultural and Resource-Based Industry Development Corporation
stakeholders: Commercial watermen, small businesses in the seafood industry, and the Maryland oyster population.
fiscal_impact_summary: State general fund expenditures increase by $2,000,000 in FY 2027 to capitalize the Maryland Seafood Industry Financial Assistance Fund. Beginning in FY 2028, the bill mandates an annual $2,000,000 appropriation from the Transportation Trust Fund for the Chesapeake Bay Enhancement Program, although the Fiscal Note indicates this may codify existing agency agreements. MARBIDCO is authorized to transfer up to $675,000 from other loan programs to the new fund, with a repayment deadline of June 30, 2028. There is no local fiscal impact.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill establishes the Chesapeake Bay Enhancement Program within DNR and requires the department to manage oyster propagation, replenishment projects, and enforce tidal fish license transfer prohibitions for delinquent borrowers.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Maryland Agricultural & Resource-Based Industry Development Corp.
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: MARBIDCO is the primary administrator of the newly established Maryland Seafood Industry Financial Assistance Fund and is responsible for determining loan criteria, managing transfers from existing microloan programs, and notifying DNR of borrower delinquencies.

MDOT is the source of the $2 million annual appropriation from the Transportation Trust Fund and oversees the Port of Baltimore and other transportation projects whose environmental impacts necessitate the mitigation activities funded by this bill.
The bill specifically links the mitigation funding to transportation projects that maintain or expand the Helen Delich Bentley Port of Baltimore, which is managed and operated by the MPA.

DBM is responsible for the state budget, which must include the mandated $2 million annual appropriation for the oyster program and oversaw the $2 million general fund capitalization for the seafood fund in the fiscal note.
The Governor is required to include specific appropriations in the annual budget bill and provides overall executive oversight for the new inter-agency program and fund.
The bill identifies bridge and transportation projects as triggers for oyster mitigation funding; the MDTA is responsible for the state's toll bridges and facilities involved in such projects.
The SHA's construction and maintenance of non-toll bridges and shipping infrastructure are among the transportation projects that trigger the requirement for oyster population mitigation.

The BPW oversees significant state expenditures and procurement contracts, including those related to capital projects at the Port of Baltimore and potentially the administration of new financial assistance programs.
The OAG provides legal counsel to DNR, MDOT, and MARBIDCO regarding the implementation of new regulations, loan agreements, and license transfer restrictions.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Governor's Council on the Chesapeake Bay
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Council advises the Governor on the restoration of the Chesapeake Bay, and the bill's focus on oyster propagation for mitigation aligns with its primary mission.
The RMC supports the economic viability of resource-based industries, such as seafood and agriculture, and partners with MARBIDCO on rural financial assistance programs.
As the state's primary economic development agency, Commerce has a secondary interest in the financial assistance provided to small businesses in the Maryland seafood industry.
This multi-agency initiative coordinates Bay restoration efforts across departments, including the replenishment activities established by this program.
MDE is responsible for environmental protection and water quality in the Bay; it is involved in monitoring the impacts of the projects and the success of the oyster replenishment efforts.
As a modal administration within MDOT, the MTA is part of the transportation network whose projects may contribute to the environmental effects addressed by the mitigation program.

Synopsis: Requiring that books and records kept by or on behalf of certain homeowners associations be posted online; clarifying that a governing body of a homeowners association may secure a line of credit or loan to fund reserves; requiring that certain homeowners associations provide notice of a meeting by electronic transmission 14 days prior to the meeting; etc.

bill_summary: This bill requires Maryland homeowners associations (HOAs) with at least 100 lots to maintain a website, online portal, or mobile application for the purpose of providing lot owners access to governing documents and meeting records. It mandates that meeting notices be delivered via electronic transmission when authorized by owners and allows HOA governing bodies to secure loans or lines of credit for reserve funding with approval from a majority of owners. The bill also establishes a process for lot owners to petition for electronic voting capabilities and requires HOAs to maintain recordings of meetings conducted via telephone or video conference as official records.
responsible_party: Maryland Office of the Attorney General
stakeholders: Homeowners associations with 100 or more lots, HOA governing bodies, and lot owners in Maryland.
fiscal_impact_summary: Specific dollar estimates are unavailable because a formal Fiscal Note was not included in the provided text. The bill creates private administrative and compliance costs for homeowners associations with 100 or more lots, as they are required to establish and maintain digital platforms for record-keeping. There are no identified impacts on State or local government revenues or expenditures stated in the bill text.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Office of the Attorney General's Consumer Protection Division is the principal state body that enforces the Maryland Homeowners Association Act and provides legal guidance to lot owners and boards. This bill introduces substantial new regulatory requirements for digital records access, meeting notices, and reserve funding that fall directly under the agency's enforcement and mediation responsibilities.

The Administrative Office of the Courts supports the judicial branch where HOA governance disputes are litigated. Furthermore, the bill involves the amendment of governing documents and the creation of official records, which are managed or recorded by the Clerks of the Circuit Court overseen by the agency.

The Department of Housing and Community Development focuses on community stability and residential policy. This bill's focus on HOA transparency, fiscal reserve requirements, and governance procedures directly relates to the department's mission of maintaining secure and well-managed residential communities across the state.

The Secretary of State manages the registration and oversight of similar common ownership communities, such as condominiums and time-shares. Although homeowners associations are governed by a separate title of the Real Property Article, the agency's role in overseeing related residential governance frameworks makes the bill relevant to their policy coordination efforts.

Synopsis: Requiring a deed presented for recording effecting a change in ownership of residential property to contain the name of the title insurer and the policy number if the purchaser or other party has obtained title insurance.

bill_summary: This bill requires any deed presented for recording that involves a change in ownership of residential property to include the name of the title insurer and the policy number, provided that the purchaser or another party has obtained title insurance for the transaction.
responsible_party: Maryland Judiciary (Clerks of the Circuit Court)
stakeholders: Residential property purchasers, title insurance companies, and settlement agents.
fiscal_impact_summary: The bill text does not include a formal Fiscal Note or specific revenue and expenditure estimates. Financial implications are likely limited to minor administrative adjustments for parties preparing deeds and for the Clerks of the Circuit Court who process them. Specific dollar estimates are unavailable.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Administrative Office of the Courts provides support to the Maryland Judicial Branch, specifically the Clerks of the Circuit Court. Since the bill creates a new requirement for the recordation of residential property deeds, the Clerks' offices will be responsible for ensuring that deeds presented for recording contain the required title insurer name and policy number.

The Maryland Insurance Administration regulates the state's insurance market, including title insurers. As the bill requires deeds to include the name of the title insurer and a policy number, it directly involves an insurance product and industry regulated by this agency.

The Comptroller's office oversees the collection of state revenues, including recordation and transfer taxes that are paid when deeds are recorded. Any change to the deed recordation process can impact the workflow and timing of revenue collection at the local courthouses.

The Maryland State Archives is the central depository for permanent judicial records, including land records. A change in the statutory content requirements for deeds affects the nature of the records being preserved and maintained by the Archives.

The Office of the Attorney General provides legal counsel to state agencies, including the Judicial Branch. They would likely be involved in providing legal interpretations or guidance regarding the enforcement of these new deed recordation requirements.

Synopsis: Requiring counties in which a volunteer fire company is located to offer no-cost preventive cancer screenings in accordance with certain guidelines to volunteer firefighters volunteering and retired volunteer firefighters who volunteered with the volunteer fire company; authorizing a county to satisfy the requirement by providing a certain annual examination or applying for a certain grant; requiring the volunteer fire companies to maintain a list of volunteer firefighters and retired volunteer firefighters; etc.

bill_summary: This bill requires Maryland counties with volunteer fire companies to provide no-cost preventive cancer screenings to active volunteer firefighters involved in fire suppression and eligible retired volunteer firefighters who completed at least three years of service. Screenings must adhere to the latest guidelines from the International Association of Fire Fighters (IAFF). Counties may meet this requirement by providing annual examinations or by applying for grants through the State's Professional and Volunteer Firefighter Innovative Cancer Screening Technologies Program. Volunteer fire companies are mandated to maintain and share annual lists of eligible personnel with their respective counties.
responsible_party: Maryland counties and the Maryland Department of Health
stakeholders: Active volunteer firefighters, retired volunteer firefighters with at least three years of service and specific point accruals, volunteer fire companies, and Maryland county governments.
fiscal_impact_summary: State general fund expenditures may increase as counties seek grants from the Professional and Volunteer Firefighter Innovative Cancer Screening Technologies Program to cover screening costs; the program's FY 2027 budget is 900000. Local expenditures for counties will increase, potentially significantly depending on the number of eligible volunteers. For instance, Montgomery County estimates its annual costs could range from 717395 to several million dollars.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Maryland Department of Health administers the Professional and Volunteer Firefighter Innovative Cancer Screening Technologies Program, which counties may utilize to satisfy the bill's requirements. The fiscal note indicates that MDH expenditures will likely increase due to a higher volume of grant applications for this program.

The Department of Budget and Management is responsible for state budget oversight and the allocation of funds; the bill's fiscal note explicitly mentions a potential increase in general fund expenditures to support the fire service cancer screening grant program managed by MDH.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Department of Service and Civic Innovation
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: As the agency responsible for promoting service and volunteerism, the bill is relevant to their mission of strengthening communities by supporting the health and retention of the volunteer firefighter workforce.

The Council addresses challenges in rural counties, where volunteer fire companies are the primary emergency service providers. This bill directly impacts the health resources available to these critical rural volunteers and their local governments.

The Department of Emergency Management coordinates with local jurisdictions and relies on the readiness of the fire service; the bill supports the long-term welfare of the volunteer personnel who comprise a significant portion of the state's emergency response infrastructure.

Synopsis: Establishing requirements for certain vision benefits, vision benefit plans, and vision benefit discount plans; requiring an insurer or a vision benefit manager to disclose certain information on its website and in certain communications and maintain certain methods of communication for use by participating eye care providers; establishing certain requirements and prohibitions for contracts between insurers or vision benefit managers and participating eye care providers; etc.

bill_summary: House Bill 1603 establishes a regulatory framework for vision benefit plans and vision benefit managers in Maryland. It mandates transparency through website disclosures, regulates contract terms between insurers and eye care providers, and standardizes reimbursement and credentialing processes. Key provisions include prohibiting insurers from setting fees for non-covered services, requiring standardized coding for claims, and granting providers the right to appeal credentialing denials and seek civil damages for violations.
stakeholders: Eye care providers (optometrists and physicians), vision benefit managers, health insurers, and enrollees of vision benefit plans.
fiscal_impact_summary: A formal Fiscal Note is absent from the provided text, so specific dollar estimates are unavailable. Financial implications identified in the bill include the Insurance Commissioner's authority to impose administrative penalties and a provision allowing eye care providers to recover monetary damages up to $10,000 per violation. The Maryland Insurance Administration will incur administrative costs to adopt regulations and manage the complaint and appeal processes.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: As the primary regulator of the state insurance market, the MIA is responsible for enforcing the bill's new requirements for vision benefit managers and insurers, including rulemaking, licensing, and complaint resolution.

The department oversees the licensing boards for optometrists and physicians defined in the bill and manages the state's Medicaid program, which provides vision benefits through managed care organizations subject to health benefit plan regulations.

The department manages the health and vision benefit plans for state employees and retirees; changes to vision plan regulations and provider reimbursement mandates will directly impact the administration and cost of these state-procured benefits.

The Exchange administers the state's health insurance marketplace where regulated vision benefit plans are offered, and it will be responsible for ensuring that participating plans comply with the new transparency and disclosure requirements.

The Office serves as the chief legal representative for the Maryland Insurance Administration and will provide legal counsel regarding the enforcement of these new statutory requirements and defense of regulatory actions.

The commission is responsible for health system planning and promoting transparency; the bill's requirements for disclosure of fee schedules and cost-sharing amounts fall within its oversight of healthcare accountability and information access.
The bill creates a new private right of action for eye care providers to seek injunctive relief and monetary damages for violations, which will fall under the jurisdiction of the state court system.

The office provides an impartial hearing process for contested cases, which may include administrative appeals of regulatory or disciplinary decisions made by the Maryland Insurance Commissioner under this new subtitle.

bill_summary: This bill prohibits specific provisions from being included in Maryland public school system contracts, such as clauses requiring indemnification without appropriation, binding arbitration, or selecting a legal venue outside of the state. If these provisions are included, they are considered void ab initio, and the contract is enforceable as if they were absent. The bill applies prospectively to contracts executed or renewed on or after July 1, 2026, and excludes collective bargaining agreements.
stakeholders: Local school boards, third-party contractors, and small businesses entering into agreements with public schools.
fiscal_impact_summary: There is no impact on State finances. Local school system expenditures may increase starting in FY 2027 if contractors choose not to bid due to the new restrictions, though costs could potentially decrease through reduced risk and fewer unanticipated expenses. Prince George's County anticipates a specific need for additional legal staff for contract review.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: As the primary state agency responsible for the oversight and leadership of the 24 local school systems, MSDE is highly relevant as the bill creates new statutory requirements for the contracts entered into by those local systems.

The IAC oversees the planning and funding of public school construction projects. These projects involve major capital contracts that will be directly subject to the bill's prohibited provisions regarding indemnification, liability, and dispute resolution.

The MSA is responsible for the design and construction of public schools under the 21st Century School Buildings Program and the Built to Learn Act. The agency manages a significant portfolio of public school construction contracts that must comply with the bill's restrictions.

OLA conducts periodic fiscal compliance audits of local school systems. The agency will be responsible for ensuring that school systems are adhering to the new legal requirements and avoiding prohibited contract provisions during their oversight audits.

By prohibiting binding arbitration and other extrajudicial dispute resolution processes in school contracts, the bill may shift a higher volume of contract disputes into the Maryland judicial system, impacting court caseloads and resources.

As the chief legal officer for the state, the OAG provides legal counsel to MSDE and the IAC. The agency will likely provide legal guidance and interpretation to ensure state oversight of local school system contracts aligns with the bill's requirements.

DGS is the state's central procurement authority and is listed as an information source in the fiscal note. The bill mirrors contract prohibitions established for state agencies in 2024, making DGS a key technical stakeholder in procurement policy.

bill_summary: This bill repeals the requirement that Maryland county governments pay 50% of the compensation awarded to individuals erroneously convicted, sentenced, and confined for crimes they did not commit, thereby shifting full financial responsibility for these payments back to the State.
stakeholders: Individuals erroneously convicted of crimes and Maryland county governments.
fiscal_impact_summary: State general fund revenues are projected to decrease by at least $1,000,000 annually starting in fiscal 2027 due to the loss of 50% cost-sharing reimbursements from local jurisdictions. Local government expenditures are expected to decrease by at least $1,000,000 annually as they are no longer required to contribute to the compensation awards.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill directly amends the responsibilities of the Board of Public Works, which is the primary agency responsible for compensating erroneously convicted individuals and was previously tasked with notifying the Comptroller and counties regarding cost-sharing amounts.

The bill repeals the Comptroller's responsibility to receive remitted payments from counties for their share of the compensation and removes the Comptroller's authority to withhold local income tax distributions from non-compliant counties.

The compensation process described in the bill is triggered by an order from an Administrative Law Judge (ALJ). The Office of Administrative Hearings provides the ALJs who adjudicate these petitions for eligibility.

As the principal fiscal agency, DBM is concerned with the bill's impact on state general fund revenues, which are projected to decrease by at least $1.0 million annually due to the repeal of the local cost-sharing requirement.

The Governor serves as a member of the Board of Public Works, which oversees these compensation payments, and the office oversees the executive branch agencies involved in implementing this policy change.
The State Treasurer is a member of the Board of Public Works, which is responsible for the distribution of these funds and the notification processes altered by the bill.

Synopsis: Prohibiting a person from charging an annual interest rate above 6% per year on a certain obligation held by an active service member or jointly by an active service member and the active service member's spouse; requiring that the active service member or the active service member's spouse provide the creditor with certain notice and documentation not later than 180 days after termination or discharge from active duty; and authorizing a court to grant a creditor relief from application of the Act after a certain finding.

bill_summary: This bill limits the annual interest rate to 6% on loans and other financing obligations held by active-duty service members or jointly with their spouses. It requires creditors to forgive interest charges exceeding this rate and recalculate periodic payments for the duration of the member's active duty service upon receiving written notice and documentation.
stakeholders: Active-duty service members, spouses of active-duty service members, and creditors or lenders operating in Maryland.
fiscal_impact_summary: Specific dollar estimates are unavailable as a formal Fiscal Note was not included in the provided text. The bill creates a mandate for creditors to reduce interest rates to 6% and forgive the excess interest for qualifying service members, which will result in an indeterminate reduction in interest revenue for private lenders and potentially public entities acting as creditors.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Department of Labor, through the Commissioner of Financial Regulation, is the primary regulator of financial institutions and consumer credit in Maryland. The department would be responsible for overseeing creditor compliance with the new interest rate caps and handling related consumer complaints.

The Office of the Attorney General, particularly its Consumer Protection Division, enforces state laws regarding fair credit and consumer rights. This agency would be responsible for investigating and prosecuting creditors who fail to provide the mandated interest rate reductions to service members.

As the lead state agency for active-duty service members and their families, this department would be critical in coordinating policy, providing outreach, and assisting service members in securing the financial benefits and protections established by this bill.

The Adjutant General is the senior military advisor to the Governor and oversees the Maryland National Guard. Since the bill applies to members called to active duty via gubernatorial orders, the agency is directly involved in the administrative processes and documentation required for members to claim these protections.

The members of the Maryland National Guard are the primary beneficiaries of this legislation. The bill provides specific financial relief for these service members while they are on active-duty assignment, directly impacting the financial readiness of the Guard's personnel.

The bill explicitly authorizes courts to grant creditors relief from the interest rate limitation if it is determined that a service member's ability to pay is not materially affected by active duty, requiring the judicial branch to adjudicate these specific disputes.

bill_summary: This bill repeals the prohibition on locating a community solar energy generating system on a parcel of land adjacent to an existing or proposed system when their combined capacity would exceed 5 megawatts. It maintains the existing 5-megawatt capacity limit for multiple systems located on the same parcel of land.
stakeholders: Solar energy developers, low- and moderate-income (LMI) subscribers, electric distribution companies, and small businesses in the solar construction and consulting sectors.
fiscal_impact_summary: The Public Service Commission, the Office of People’s Counsel, and the Department of Natural Resources can implement the bill using existing budgeted resources. There is no direct impact on State revenues or local government finances, although small businesses in the solar development sector may see increased demand for their services.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: As the primary regulator of the Community Solar Energy Generating Systems Program, the PSC is the lead authority on the rules regarding project capacity and location modified by this bill.

The OPC is a statutory advocate representing residential utility consumers; changes to community solar siting regulations directly impact their caseload and consumer advocacy mission, as noted in the fiscal note.

The DNR, through its Power Plant Research Program, is responsible for evaluating the environmental and socio-economic impacts of solar facilities during the state's Certificate of Public Convenience and Necessity (CPCN) process.
The MEA manages state energy policy and solar incentives, including the Strategic Energy Investment Fund, which are directly supported by the expansion of community solar siting capability.
The bill explicitly addresses agrivoltaics and the placement of solar systems on land parcels, which directly impacts agricultural land use and the state's farming community.
MDE is involved in the environmental review and permitting process for solar generation facilities, particularly regarding land quality and pollution control on brownfields and clean fill sites.
The department oversees state land use guidelines and planning visions that are relevant to the siting and co-location of community solar arrays on adjacent parcels.

Commerce is concerned with the economic development and job creation potential within Maryland's solar industry, which is impacted by expanded siting options for small businesses in construction and consulting.
As the state's green bank, the MCEC is tasked with advancing the adoption of clean energy technologies, including the financing of community solar systems impacted by this legislation.

MES provides technical services for government entities regarding the management of land and infrastructure, including potential solar development on brownfields or clean fill sites mentioned in the bill.

The OAG serves as the chief legal officer for the state agencies regulating and reviewing the development of community solar energy projects, providing counsel on the interpretation of Public Utilities law.
The Governor's Office oversees executive branch policy coordination and the implementation of state priorities regarding renewable energy expansion and climate change.
This multi-agency initiative promotes sustainable development, aligning with the bill's focus on expanding renewable energy capacity through modified parcel location restrictions.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Governor's Office of Small, Minority & Women Business Affairs
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The office monitors socioeconomic procurement and business growth; the bill's expansion of solar projects could impact small businesses in the renewable energy sector.

bill_summary: This bill expands Maryland's firearm storage laws by requiring that firearms not under the direct control of an authorized user be stored in a locked secure storage depository. It also prohibits leaving a firearm in a location where the owner knows or should know a minor is likely to gain unsupervised access. The bill establishes misdemeanor penalties for violations, including fines and the potential loss of firearm possession and permit rights for repeat offenders or in cases where unauthorized access results in serious bodily injury or death.
stakeholders: Firearm owners, minors, and Maryland state and local law enforcement agencies
fiscal_impact_summary: Specific dollar estimates from a formal Fiscal Note are unavailable as the note was not provided. The bill text establishes misdemeanor penalties with fines ranging from $500 to $1,000, which will result in an indeterminate increase in state revenue. There may also be minor administrative and enforcement costs for the Department of State Police regarding the monitoring of firearm possession disqualifications and permit denials.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill directly impacts the Maryland State Police (MSP) as it mandates the Secretary (of State Police) to deny handgun permits and Qualification Licenses to individuals convicted of the new firearm storage violations. As the primary agency for firearm licensing and statewide law enforcement, MSP is responsible for enforcing these storage requirements and managing the resulting permit disqualifications.

The OAG serves as the chief legal officer for the state and will be responsible for providing legal counsel to the Maryland State Police and the General Assembly regarding the implementation and enforcement of these new criminal statutes and firearm possession prohibitions.

The Maryland Judiciary will be responsible for adjudicating the new misdemeanor charges created by the bill (violations of firearm storage requirements). The AOC must also ensure that conviction records are properly tracked and shared to enforce the firearm possession and permit disqualifications outlined in the bill.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Maryland Office of the Public Defender
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill creates new criminal misdemeanor offenses related to the storage of firearms. The OPD will be responsible for providing legal representation to indigent defendants charged with these offenses, particularly in cases involving serious bodily injury or death which carry higher penalties and permanent loss of firearm rights.

The OAH often hears appeals related to the denial or revocation of handgun permits and licenses by the Maryland State Police. Since the bill establishes new grounds for the mandatory denial of these permits, the OAH may see an increase in contested cases regarding these administrative decisions.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Governor's Office of Crime Prevention and Policy
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: GOCPP is the primary coordinating body for public safety and criminal justice strategies in Maryland. This bill aligns with their mission to develop policies that reduce crime and enhance public safety through regulated firearm access and storage.

As the head of the executive branch, the Governor oversees the agencies responsible for enforcing this bill (MSP, GOCPP). The Governor's Office coordinates high-level public safety policy and initiatives, including those related to gun violence prevention and firearm regulation.

The bill explicitly references Section 10-301.1 of the Natural Resources Article regarding hunter safety certificates as an exemption for minors. The DNR's Natural Resources Police also encounter firearms in their enforcement duties and may be involved in education regarding these safety requirements for hunters.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Department of Public Safety and Correctional Services
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: DPSCS oversees the Division of Parole and Probation. Individuals convicted of these new misdemeanors may be placed under supervision, and the department will need to monitor compliance with court-ordered firearm possession bans.

The Maryland Department of Health is concerned with public health and safety, including the prevention of injuries and deaths. Firearm storage is a key component of public health efforts to reduce accidental shootings and suicides among minors.

fiscal_impact_summary: According to the Fiscal Note, there is no state or local fiscal impact. The bill does not affect Frederick County's finances, and local impact grants from gaming revenues are not materially affected.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Maryland State Lottery & Gaming Control Agency
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: As the primary regulatory body for all commercial and state gaming operations in Maryland, this agency is directly relevant to any legislation that modifies gaming laws, payment methods, or compliance requirements for gaming events, even those conducted by local volunteer organizations.

The OAG is responsible for providing legal counsel to state agencies and interpreting state law. This bill amends the Criminal Law Article regarding gaming violations, which requires legal oversight and potential enforcement guidance.

The Comptroller's Office was consulted for the fiscal note and serves as the state's chief financial officer. While the bill primarily affects local non-profit gaming, the Comptroller oversees general revenue collection and regulatory compliance for various industries.

The Maryland State Police are responsible for enforcing the state's criminal laws. Since the bill modifies what constitutes a misdemeanor under the Criminal Law Article regarding gaming events, it impacts their law enforcement scope.
The bill impacts the judicial branch because it creates or modifies exceptions to criminal misdemeanors related to gaming, which are adjudicated within the state court system.

Synopsis: Repealing the requirement that a school bus be constructed with materials that enable it to meet all criteria of the school bus seat upholstery fire block test established by the National School Transportation specifications and procedures adopted by the most recent National Congress on School Transportation.
Title: Education - School Bus - Fire Safety Standards
Status: In the House - First Reading House Rules and Executive Nominations
bill_summary: This bill repeals the statutory requirement that school buses be constructed using materials that meet specific upholstery fire block test criteria established by the National School Transportation specifications. Instead, it mandates that the Motor Vehicle Administration, with advice from the Maryland State Department of Education, adopt regulations to promote school bus fire safety standards.
responsible_party: Maryland Motor Vehicle Administration and the Maryland State Department of Education
stakeholders: Local school systems, school bus manufacturers, and Maryland students
fiscal_impact_summary: Specific dollar estimates are unavailable as a formal Fiscal Note was not included in the provided text. The bill shifts the authority for school bus fire safety standards from statutory requirements to administrative regulations, which may have future implications for school bus procurement costs depending on the standards adopted.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill explicitly mandates the Motor Vehicle Administration to adopt regulations to promote fire safety standards for school buses, replacing a specific statutory material requirement with agency-led regulation.

The bill amends the Education Article and specifies that the Department of Education must provide advice to the Motor Vehicle Administration during the development and adoption of school bus fire safety regulations.

As the parent department of the Motor Vehicle Administration, MDOT oversees the state's transportation network and the implementation of vehicle safety standards for state-regulated transport like school buses.

The Maryland Center for School Safety coordinates school safety policies and standards; changes to fire safety equipment standards for school buses fall within their mission to foster safe learning environments.

The Office of the Attorney General would likely provide legal counsel to the Motor Vehicle Administration and the Department of Education regarding the repeal of statutory requirements and the subsequent drafting of new administrative regulations.

The Maryland State Police enforce motor vehicle laws and ensure traffic safety; they may be impacted by changes to equipment standards and fire safety compliance for school buses operating on state highways.

As a state agency that operates its own educational facilities and student transportation, the Maryland School for the Deaf is directly impacted by changes to the fire safety standards required for school bus construction and procurement.

bill_summary: This bill modifies the eligibility requirements for a local option property tax credit available to certain disabled veterans and their surviving spouses. stakeholders: Honorably discharged veterans with service-connected disabilities of at least 50%, surviving spouses of such veterans, and local taxing authorities in Maryland.
fiscal_impact_summary: The bill has no impact on State finances. Local property tax revenues may decrease starting in fiscal 2027 to the extent that local jurisdictions grant the property tax credit and the increased income limits allow additional individuals to qualify. agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: As the principal state agency for assisting veterans in securing benefits, this department is directly involved in advocating for and providing information regarding benefits like property tax credits for disabled veterans. This agency provides administrative review for disputes concerning property tax assessments and property tax credits, which would include the specific local option credits modified by this bill.

The Tax Court adjudicates appeals from taxing authorities regarding property tax assessments and credits, serving as the highest level of administrative review for the tax matters affected by this bill.
As the state's principal tax collector, the Comptroller oversees tax law enforcement and is consulted on changes to tax eligibility criteria involving federal adjusted gross income.
The OAG provides legal counsel to state agencies and the General Assembly regarding the interpretation and implementation of new tax laws and eligibility criteria.

This department coordinates policies for residents with disabilities; while not the primary administrator, it has a secondary interest in legislation defining disability ratings for state or local benefits.
The Governor's Office oversees the executive branch and is responsible for signing the legislation into law and overseeing the general administration of state policy regarding veterans.
As the principal fiscal agency, DBM monitors legislation for fiscal impacts, although the bill primarily affects local rather than state revenues.

fiscal_impact_summary: The bill is not expected to materially affect State or local finances. The State Lottery and Gaming Control Agency can conduct the required study on independent evaluators for sports wagering content using existing budgeted resources.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Maryland State Lottery & Gaming Control Agency
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill explicitly mandates the agency to conduct a study and report to the Governor and General Assembly regarding independent evaluators for sports wagering content. The agency also regulates the video lottery facilities and sports wagering licensees mentioned in the bill.

The bill repeals a significant prohibition within the Election Law Article regarding campaign contributions from gaming entities. The State Board of Elections is the primary agency responsible for administering election laws and enforcing campaign finance regulations.

The Office of the State Prosecutor is responsible for investigating and prosecuting criminal offenses related to the electoral process and public ethics laws. Repealing a contribution prohibition directly impacts the legal framework they enforce.

The Governor's Office receives the required study and report from the State Lottery and Gaming Control Agency. As the head of the executive branch, the Governor oversees the agencies involved and sets policy priorities regarding gaming and election law.

The OAG provides legal counsel to the State Board of Elections and the State Lottery and Gaming Control Agency. They would likely advise on the implementation of the new law and the legal parameters of the required study.

The commission is responsible for maintaining public confidence in the integrity of state government. Changes to campaign finance laws regarding specific industries (like gaming) intersect with the broader mandate of ethics and influence in state government.
OAH may be involved in adjudicating administrative disputes or contested cases arising from changes to gaming or election law regulations.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Executive Commissions, Committees, Task Forces, and Advisory Boards
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Board of License Commissioners for Caroline County is a permanent regulatory body established by state law to oversee alcoholic beverages. The Comptroller of Maryland is the primary state agency responsible for regulating the alcohol industry and enforcing state alcohol laws. stakeholders: Motorists and vehicle owners using Maryland Transportation Authority highways (including bridges and tunnels), the Maryland Transportation Authority, and the District Court of Maryland.
fiscal_impact_summary: The bill results in a one-time State general fund expenditure of $22,900 in FY 2027 for Judiciary programming costs. agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill explicitly authorizes the Maryland Transportation Authority (MDTA) to implement and operate lane use control signal monitoring systems on highways under its jurisdiction, adopt relevant regulations, and receive remitted civil penalties.

The Maryland Transportation Authority (MDTA) and the Motor Vehicle Administration (MVA) are both administrations within the Department of Transportation, and the bill modifies the Transportation Article of the Maryland Code.

The District Court, supported by the Administrative Office of the Courts, is responsible for processing citations, adjudicating contested cases, and remitting penalty revenues to the MDTA. The fiscal note indicates a $22,900 one-time programming cost for the Judiciary.

The bill amends the Insurance Article to prohibit insurers from considering civil penalties from lane use monitoring systems for the purpose of reclassifying an insured in a manner that increases premiums.
The bill requires the Chief Judge of the District Court and the Comptroller to agree upon a system for remitting costs, fines, and penalties to the State.

The OAG enforces state laws regarding consumer protection and provides legal counsel on the interpretation of the Real Property and Corporations and Associations Articles, which this bill amends.

responsible_party: Maryland Economic Development Corporation (MEDCO), Prince George’s County Council, and local zoning authorities
stakeholders: Residents of communities with high health disparities, low-income households, minority populations, immigrant populations, grocery store owners, pharmacy operators, and primary and specialty healthcare providers.
fiscal_impact_summary: State general fund expenditures increase by at least 250,000 in fiscal 2028 for MEDCO administrative costs, with indeterminate but significant expenditure increases beginning in fiscal 2029 to provide business incentives in Prince George’s County. Prince George’s County expenditures will increase as early as fiscal 2027 to provide local incentives for its mandated zones. Other counties that choose to designate zones will also see increased expenditures, and local revenues may decrease depending on the specific tax incentives implemented.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: MEDCO is the primary state entity tasked with implementing the bill's fiscal incentives, managing the distribution of funding to businesses in health innovation zones, and seeking additional funding sources.

The bill adds a new subtitle to the Health – General Article and establishes health innovation zones based on clinical health outcomes and disparities, which are core areas of public health policy overseen by this department.

The bill explicitly exempts grocery stores, pharmacies, and healthcare providers within these zones from local zoning and land use laws, directly impacting the department's role in promoting sustainable growth and land use guidance.
The bill authorizes the Governor to include a significant annual appropriation in the state budget for MEDCO starting in fiscal year 2028, which DBM would manage and supervise.
The Governor has the authority to include appropriations for the zones in the annual budget bill and coordinates the inter-agency policy goals related to health and economic mobility.

The commission's mission includes planning for the state's health system needs and improving access to health care, which aligns with the bill's goal of establishing healthcare providers in underserved areas.
The bill targets 'food deserts' by incentivizing the establishment of grocery stores, which aligns with the department's work in food quality assurance and marketing local agricultural products.
The bill specifically mandates that health innovation zones address disability-related health disparities, particularly in rural communities.
OAG would likely provide legal counsel regarding the bill's preemption of local zoning authority and oversee legal agreements between the state and MEDCO.
The bill's focus on maternal and newborn health complications in disadvantaged communities aligns with the office's mission to improve well-being for Maryland's children and families.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Governor's Office of Small, Minority & Women Business Affairs
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill targets 'communities of color' and 'economically disadvantaged communities' for business development, which relates to the office's oversight of socioeconomic procurement and development.
The team is charged with piloting novel initiatives to reduce child poverty and enhance economic mobility, which are the intended outcomes of designating these zones in underinvested communities.
The bill addresses health disparities in rural communities, and the council is tasked with advocating for rural interests and addressing geographic challenges in Maryland's 18 rural counties.

Synopsis: Requiring the Department of the Environment, in coordination with the Department of Commerce, to adopt procedures on or before October 1, 2027, to streamline the permitting process for certain entities and certain environmental permits; requiring the Department to issue a determination on a certain application within 60 days after receipt of the application; etc.
Title: Department of the Environment - Procedures for Permitting Efficiency - Requirements
Status: In the House - First Reading House Rules and Executive Nominations

NarrowSubjects.Name: Environmental Matters -see also- Conserv; Nat Resrce; Pollut

bill_summary: This bill requires the Maryland Department of the Environment, in coordination with the Department of Commerce, to streamline the environmental permitting process for manufacturing businesses in NAICS sectors 31, 32, and 33. The Department must establish a single digital application portal, provide a dedicated navigator to assist applicants personally, and issue permit determinations within 60 days of application receipt.
stakeholders: Manufacturing businesses (NAICS sectors 31, 32, and 33) and the Maryland Department of the Environment.
fiscal_impact_summary: Specific dollar estimates are unavailable because a formal Fiscal Note was not provided; however, the bill creates significant new administrative requirements for the Department of the Environment, including the development and maintenance of a single digital portal and the provision of dedicated navigators for permit applicants, which will likely increase state expenditures.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: As the primary agency for environmental protection and permitting, MDE is tasked with implementing the bill's requirements, including adopting streamlined procedures, meeting a 60-day determination deadline, providing dedicated navigators, and establishing a single digital portal for specific manufacturing sectors.

The bill explicitly requires the Department of the Environment to coordinate with the Department of Commerce to adopt the streamlined permitting procedures, aligning with Commerce's mission to support businesses and economic development in the manufacturing sector.

The mandate to establish a single digital portal for permit applications directly involves DoIT, which is responsible for the state's IT strategy, infrastructure, and ensuring efficient digital services for government operations.

Implementing the 'dedicated navigator' role and building a new digital portal will likely have fiscal and personnel impacts, requiring DBM's involvement in budgeting for new positions and IT expenditures.

The OAG provides legal counsel to state agencies like MDE and Commerce. They would be responsible for reviewing the newly adopted permitting procedures and digital portal requirements for compliance with state and federal environmental laws.

The Governor's Office oversees the executive branch and coordinates policy initiatives between departments. This bill affects two cabinet-level departments (MDE and Commerce) and relates to economic and environmental policy priorities.

Synopsis: Altering certain requirements related to the development of a certain project at State Center; establishing a State Center Advisory Group to provide community input on the development of State Center, leverage benefits from the development for neighborhoods and residents in the surrounding area, and facilitate transparency and information-sharing; requiring the Advisory Group to adopt a conflict of interest policy; etc.
Title: State Center – Development – Contract, Plan Requirements, and Advisory Group
Status: In the House - Rereferred to Economic Matters and Appropriations

bill_summary: This bill modifies the requirements for the development of the 28-acre State Center property in Baltimore City. It establishes the State Center Advisory Group to provide community input, facilitate transparency, and leverage benefits for surrounding neighborhoods. The bill replaces previous requirements for agreements with the State Center Neighborhood Alliance with requirements for a community benefit agreement with the new Advisory Group. It also updates the preferred tenant profile from State agencies to anchor institutions providing public or community services, removes the requirement for parking facilities, and extends the timeline for a developer to begin construction from 18 to 24 months after contract execution.
responsible_party: The State or its reporting agency (specifically the Department of General Services and Department of Budget and Management per the Fiscal Note)
stakeholders: Residents and neighborhood associations within a one-mile radius of State Center, anchor institutions in Baltimore City, minority- and women-owned businesses, and real estate developers.
fiscal_impact_summary: The fiscal note indicates there is no material financial impact on State or local government operations or finances. The creation of the State Center Advisory Group is expected to be handled within existing governmental resources.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: As the agency responsible for the planning, design, and management of state-owned facilities and real estate leasing, DGS is the primary 'reporting agency' for the State Center redevelopment project. The bill directly impacts DGS operations by altering contract requirements and requiring the department to convene and engage with a new advisory group.

The Board of Public Works must approve significant state procurement contracts and the lease or transfer of state property. Any new or modified development contract for State Center, as described in the bill, would require BPW approval.

DBM is responsible for long-term fiscal planning and the state's budget execution. The department is explicitly mentioned in the fiscal note and is involved in the oversight of state-owned property usage and personnel policies related to the development.

The University of Baltimore, which is a member institution of the University System of Maryland, is explicitly named as a member of the State Center Advisory Group and is identified as an anchor institution for the project area.

The OAG provides legal counsel to state agencies and the Board of Public Works. It would be responsible for reviewing the legality of the new contract requirements and the enforceable community benefits agreements mandated by the bill.

The bill references the Baltimore City Department of Planning's directory for advisory group membership and relates to large-scale urban development and land use planning, which falls under the broad policy and technical assistance scope of MDP.

The Governor oversees the executive branch departments involved in the project (DGS and DBM) and serves as a member of the Board of Public Works, which has final approval over the development contracts.
The Comptroller is a member of the Board of Public Works, which is the body that must approve the modified development contracts and property transfers for State Center.
The State Treasurer is a member of the Board of Public Works, which is the body that must approve the modified development contracts and property transfers for State Center.

Status: In the House - First Reading House Rules and Executive Nominations

bill_summary: This bill requires a custodian of public records to allow an inspector general whose office is created by state or local law to inspect a public record if the inspector general is legally authorized to access it and requires the record to perform their official duties. The bill also provides that any redisclosure of records by an inspector general is subject to the provisions of the Public Information Act.
responsible_party: Custodians of public records and State or local Inspectors General
stakeholders: State and local government inspectors general, custodians of public records, and state and local government agencies subject to oversight.
fiscal_impact_summary: Specific dollar estimates are unavailable as a formal Fiscal Note was not provided in the bill text. The legislation likely has an administrative impact on state and local governments as it codifies access protocols for inspectors general, but it does not specify any direct financial allocations, revenue changes, or spending mandates.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The OAG provides legal counsel to all state agencies regarding the Public Information Act and houses the Ombudsman, who handles disputes and appeals regarding record access and denials.
MSDE houses the Office of the Inspector General for Education, a major state-level oversight body that will directly utilize the expanded record access authority provided by this bill.
MDOT houses its own statutory Office of Inspector General, which requires robust access to multi-modal transportation and administrative records to fulfill its oversight mandates.

MDH houses an Office of Inspector General and serves as the custodian for sensitive public health and Medicaid data that may be subject to inspection by oversight officials notwithstanding other PIA restrictions.
DJS houses an Office of Inspector General whose investigative duties regarding youth and facility management require access to confidential records that this bill clarifies can be inspected.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Department of Public Safety and Correctional Services
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: DPSCS houses an Office of Inspector General that investigates matters within the state's correctional and parole systems, necessitating access to sensitive security and personnel records.
DHS houses an Office of Inspector General that monitors large-scale social service programs and serves as a custodian for sensitive beneficiary and administrative data.
The Department of Labor houses an Office of Inspector General responsible for overseeing unemployment insurance and workforce programs, requiring access to regulatory and employer records.

As the primary law enforcement agency and a custodian of sensitive investigative records, MSP is impacted by changes to the Public Information Act that prioritize Inspector General access over traditional denials.

The Comptroller is the state's chief financial officer and a major custodian of tax and revenue records which are frequently the subject of financial and compliance investigations by Inspectors General.

The Secretary of State is a principal custodian of official state records and is directly affected by amendments to the Public Information Act governing the inspection and redisclosure of such records.

As the central depository for government records of permanent value, the Archives is impacted by any legislative changes affecting access rights for oversight bodies and subsequent redisclosure rules.
DBM is the central personnel agency and custodian of state employee records, which are frequently scrutinized by Inspectors General during investigations into misconduct or fiscal waste.
DoIT manages statewide data governance and information security, impacting the technical and policy frameworks through which Inspectors General access digital public records.
The Governor oversees the executive branch and coordinates policy for the various departments whose internal Inspectors General and record custodians are the primary parties affected by this bill.
DGS is the central procurement authority for the state; its contract and facility records are essential to the oversight work of Inspectors General investigating procurement integrity.

Synopsis: Requiring certain wastewater treatment plants to maintain a publicly accessible website on which certain information relating to certain discharges is required to be published in a certain manner; and requiring certain wastewater treatment plants to begin certain testing within 24 hours after a bypass, overflow, or treatment failure that requires testing for certain chemicals or bacteria.
Title: Wastewater Treatment Plants - Discharges - Requirements
Status: In the Senate - Favorable with Amendments Report by Education, Energy, and the Environment

NarrowSubjects.Name: Environmental Matters -see also- Conserv; Nat Resrce; Pollut
Hazardous and Toxic Substances -see also- Asbestos; Radiatn

bill_summary: This bill requires wastewater treatment plants with an annual average effluent flow of at least 50 million gallons per day to maintain a publicly accessible website. These facilities must publish monthly bacteria results, provide plain-language explanations and volume estimates for any bypass, overflow, or treatment failure within five days, and begin required water quality testing within 24 hours of such incidents, publishing the results within 24 hours of receipt.
stakeholders: Owners and operators of large wastewater treatment plants (specifically Baltimore City's Back River and Patapsco plants) and the general public residing near or using affected waterways.
fiscal_impact_summary: State finances and operations are not materially affected. The local fiscal impact is anticipated to be minimal; while the bill imposes new operational requirements on Baltimore City for its two affected wastewater treatment plants, both the city and the Maryland Association of Municipal Wastewater Agencies expect the costs to be negligible.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Maryland Department of the Environment (MDE) is the primary regulatory agency responsible for issuing discharge permits and enforcing the environmental laws modified by this bill. The bill requires MDE to receive reports, manage a searchable database for industrial pretreatment permits, and oversee the monitoring and testing requirements for wastewater treatment plants.

The bill involves public health determinations related to sewer overflows and treatment plant bypasses. The Maryland Department of Health (MDH) coordinates with MDE and local health departments to develop procedures for public notification and to address health risks associated with wastewater discharges.

The Maryland Environmental Service (MES) provides technical and operational services for wastewater treatment and management to state and local governments. As an agency that operates many wastewater facilities on a fee-for-service basis, it would be directly impacted by the new testing, monitoring, and reporting requirements.

The Office of the Attorney General provides legal counsel to the Department of the Environment and the Department of Health. It would be involved in interpreting the new regulations, providing guidance on compliance, and representing the state in enforcement actions related to wastewater discharge violations.

The bill requires immediate notification to the Department of Natural Resources (DNR) in the event of sewer overflows or treatment plant bypasses that impact State surface waters or state parks, as DNR is responsible for managing these resources and ensuring their conservation.

The bill requires the Department of the Environment to establish a publicly available and searchable database of industrial users with pretreatment permits and their compliance status. DoIT would likely support the strategy, infrastructure, and security required for this state database.

The Office of Administrative Hearings adjudicates contested cases for state agencies, including the Department of the Environment. Disputes regarding discharge permits, industrial pretreatment permits, or penalties issued under the new requirements would be heard by this agency.

The Maryland Department of Emergency Management (MDEM) coordinates responses to emergencies and disasters. Significant wastewater treatment failures or massive overflows that threaten public safety or property would fall under their interagency coordination efforts.

The Governor's Office oversees the executive branch, including MDE and MDH. The bill adds new reporting requirements for wastewater treatment plants to the General Assembly and involves high-level policy initiatives related to environmental protection and public safety.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Governor's Council on the Chesapeake Bay
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: This council coordinates interagency efforts to restore the Chesapeake Bay. Since the bill regulates nutrient discharges (nitrogen and phosphorus) and bacterial levels in major treatment plants affecting the Bay watershed, it aligns with the Council's management and restoration goals.

As the principal fiscal and personnel agency, DBM is responsible for the budget execution of the Department of the Environment. Any administrative or fiscal changes required for MDE to manage the new database and oversight programs would be reviewed by DBM.

The Office of Legislative Audits (OLA) conducts performance and fiscal compliance audits of the Department of the Environment. OLA would be responsible for auditing MDE's implementation and enforcement of the new wastewater discharge and database requirements.

Synopsis: Repealing certain provisions authorizing a county or municipal corporation to impose certain assessments on transportation network services; prohibiting a county or municipal corporation from imposing an assessment, a tax, a fee, or a charge on transportation network services; repealing the Transportation Network Assessment Fund; prohibiting the Maryland Aviation Administration from fixing any charges, rentals, or fees on the privilege of providing transportation network services at an airport or a facility; etc.
Title: Maryland Aviation Administration and Local Governments - Transportation Network Services - Prohibition on Taxes, Fees, and Charges
Status: In the House - First Reading House Rules and Executive Nominations
